_schema_note: Key is Coptic 'month-day' (e.g. '12-25' = Mesore 25). Add an entry each time you check Coptic Reader while planning a service. hasHymn should reflect whether the saint has a dedicated entry with hymns on Coptic Reader's Index page.

12-1.name: St. Apoli, Son of Justus
12-1.summary: Martyred in 304 A.D., St. Apoli was a horseman and courageous commander, and crown prince of the Roman Empire, son of Emperor Numerianus. Returning from war to find Diocletian had abandoned the faith and revived pagan worship, Apoli confessed Christ along with his parents Justus and Theoclia and was martyred with them in Alexandria.

12-1.name: Pope Kyrillos V (Cyril), 112th Patriarch of Alexandria
12-1.summary: Born in the village of Tazmant, near the city of Beni Suef, to devout parents who named him John and brought him up with a Christian upbringing, Kyrillos inclined from his young age to quietness, contemplation, and studying the Holy Bible. He went on to a monastic and patriarchal life of service to the Church, shepherding it as the 112th Patriarch of Alexandria. He departed in 1927 A.D., concluding a life devoted to prayer, Scripture, and the service of his flock.

12-2.name: St. Pa'esa (Athanasia)
12-2.summary: A 4th-century saint born to wealthy Christian parents in Menouf, known for her charity, prayer, and fasting. After her parents' death she gave away her fortune to the poor, but was later led astray by evil people until the desert fathers sent St. John the Short to guide her back to repentance in the wilderness.

12-3.name: St. Simon (Simeon) the Stylite
12-3.summary: Commemorates the relocation of the body of St. Simon the Stylite in 471 A.D. from the city of Antioch to Constantinople during the reign of Emperor Zeno, in a splendid celebration.

12-3.name: Pope Ebrimus (Primus), Fifth Patriarch of Alexandria
12-3.summary: Born in Alexandria and baptized by St. Mark the Evangelist himself, Ebrimus was one of only three men ordained priests by St. Mark. He was unanimously chosen to succeed Pope Kerdonus and was consecrated in 106 A.D., shepherding the church with special attention to guiding clergy and instructing the flock in Christian manners.

12-4.name: King Hezekiah
12-4.summary: Commemorates the righteous King Hezekiah of Judah, who was healed by God after fervent prayer and given fifteen more years of life (2 Kings 20:1-11). Hezekiah abolished idol worship, destroyed pagan altars, and restored true worship in the temple, reigning 29 years before departing in peace.

12-4.name: St. Anthony the Great (Antonius)
12-4.summary: Commemorates the consecration of the church of St. Anthony, father of all monks, at his monastery in Mount Arabah (Mount Araklio) — a church that still stands today, where monks continue to pray daily. St. Anthony is one of the most significant fathers of monasticism in Coptic tradition.
hymnIds: Doxology for St. Anthony and St. Paul the Hermit together
Praxis Response (consistent with every other saint page checked)

12-5.name: St. John the Soldier
12-5.summary: Born in Ashroubah (Beni Mazar, Minya) to pious Christian parents, John joined the army of the apostate Emperor Julian. While outwardly appearing to persecute Christians alongside his fellow soldiers, he secretly protected and provided for them. When the emperor discovered his account, he had John severely tortured and beheaded, earning the crown of martyrdom.

12-6.name: St. Julietta
12-6.summary: Born in Caesarea, Cappadocia, to wealthy Christian parents, Julietta inherited great wealth which an oppressor tried to defraud from her. When she sought to reclaim it, he accused her of being Christian before the governor, who tortured her and cast her into fire; she delivered her spirit to the Lord and her body remained unharmed by the flames.

12-6.name: St. Jacob al-Baradai (Jacobus Baradaeus)
12-6.summary: Son of a priest from Tela near Edessa, Jacob became a monk in his youth and gained vast knowledge in theology and Syriac/Greek literature. Empress Theodora had him consecrated Metropolitan of Edessa to shepherd Orthodox Christians who rejected the Council of Chalcedon; disguised in a poor beggar's garb (giving rise to his name 'al-Baradai'), he traveled tirelessly ordaining an extraordinary number of clergy — reportedly 100,000 clergy and 89 bishops — before dying at 73 while traveling to meet the Coptic Pope in Egypt.

12-6.name: Abba Besa, Disciple of St. Shenouda the Archimandrite
12-6.summary: Born in the city of Absay to a wealthy, charitable father who prayed for a son and was granted one by God. Educated from age five in reading, writing, and the Scriptures, Besa grew in grace and became a devoted disciple of St. Shenouda the Archimandrite, eventually taking up the monastic life himself.

12-7.name: The Annunciation of the Angel to St. Joachim, with the Birth of the Virgin St. Mary
12-7.summary: God sent the angel Gabriel to announce to St. Joachim the birth of the Virgin Theotokos, St. Mary. Joachim and his wife Anna (Hannah), both from the tribe of Judah and house of David, had been barren for thirty-one years and vowed that if given a child they would dedicate them to the Lord as Samuel was. Gabriel announced that their offspring would bring salvation to the world, and Anna conceived and bore the pure Virgin Mary.

12-7.name: Pope Timothy II (Timotheos), 26th Patriarch of Alexandria
12-7.summary: A monk and a staunch defender of the Orthodox faith, Timothy succeeded St. Dioscorus on the See of Alexandria as the 26th Patriarch. He shepherded his flock through a troubled period, remaining steadfast under persecution and exile for the faith. He departed in peace in 477 A.D., after a patriarchate marked by firm defense of Orthodoxy and care for his people.

12-7.name: St. Pisentius (Pisentios), Bishop of Qift
12-7.summary: A monk known for asceticism, humility, and love, Pisentius was chosen bishop of Qift for his virtues. He shepherded his flock with great care, teaching and comforting them, and was known for miracles and for his spiritual counsel. He departed in peace after a godly and virtuous life of service as bishop of Qift.

12-8.name: Sts. Eleazar, Salome, and their Seven Children (The Seven Maccabees)
12-8.summary: Martyred in 161 B.C., Eleazar was a descendant of Aaron the priest and a teacher of the Jewish Law who taught his children to keep the Law of Moses. When the Syrian king Antiochus besieged Jerusalem and tried to force the Jewish people to break their fathers' Law, this righteous family refused to comply. Antiochus tortured them severely — flogging, crucifixion, burning, and combing their bodies with metal combs — while Salome encouraged them until all received the crown of martyrdom.

12-9.name: St. Ari (Ori), the Priest of Shatanof
12-9.summary: Martyred in 304 A.D., St. Ari was a priest from Shatanof known for his purity and mercy, gifted by God with healing of the sick and casting out unclean spirits, even foretelling future events by divine inspiration. When the Governor of Nakyos demanded he worship idols, he refused and was severely tortured; Christ appeared to him in prison to heal and strengthen him before he was sent on to further persecution in Alexandria.

12-10.name: St. Pihebs (Bekhibs)
12-10.summary: A soldier from Ashmoon Tanah under the command of Prince Antiochus, Pihebs was summoned along with Anba Klog the bishop, Anba Nehru, and Anba Phillip when it was learned he was Christian. All confessed their faith and were tortured; Pihebs was bound and sent by ship to el-Baramoon, enduring 27 days without food or drink before being severely tortured and finally hacked with a cleaver, receiving the crown of martyrdom. A Christian man retrieved his body and returned it to his hometown.

12-10.name: St. Matra
12-10.summary: Martyred in 250 A.D., during the papacy of Pope Demetrius, 12th Patriarch of Alexandria, and in the days of Emperor Decius, Matra heard the emperor's edict dictating the worship of idols and cut off the arm of the idol Apollo, which was made of pure gold, cut it into pieces, and gave them to the poor. He then went and confessed before the governor that he was the one who had done this, and they tortured him greatly and cast him into the fire, but the angel of the Lord saved him. They then cut off his hands and legs after crucifying him on a tree, and a blind man who smeared his eyes with the saint's blood regained his sight. Finally they beheaded Matra, and he received the crown of martyrdom.

12-11.name: St. Moisis (Moses), Bishop of Ouseem
12-11.summary: Pure and chaste since his youth, Moisis studied church subjects, was ordained a deacon, then went to the desert of Scetis to become a monk, serving a holy elder for eighteen years with devotion to prayer, fasting, humility, and love. Once his virtues became known, he was consecrated bishop of Ouseem, where he shepherded Christ's flock with great care, remaining ascetic and owning nothing his whole life. He suffered many tribulations alongside Pope Khail I, and God worked many signs and miracles by his hands before he reached old age and departed in peace, having served more than twenty years on his episcopal seat.

12-12.name: Archangel Michael
12-12.summary: The church celebrates the monthly commemoration of the honorable Archangel Michael, through whose intercession God brings the water of the rivers up to its measure and blesses the fruits of the earth and the plants of the field.
hymnIds: Doxology (for Michael alone, and a separate one for Michael and Gabriel)

12-12.name: The Commemoration of the Reign of Emperor Constantine, in Rome
12-12.summary: Commemorates the enthronement of Emperor Constantine the Great in Rome in 306 A.D. After his father Constantius Chlorus died, Constantine became emperor and abolished injustice throughout his realm. When the nobles of Rome asked for deliverance from the tyrant Maxentius, Constantine saw a cross in the sky with the words 'With this sign you will conquer,' defeated Maxentius at the Milvian Bridge in 312 A.D., and was received into Rome with great celebration.

12-13.name: Feast of the Transfiguration of Our Lord on Mount Tabor
12-13.summary: One of the minor feasts of our Lord. Jesus took Peter, James, and John up Mount Tabor to pray; His face and robe became radiant, and Moses and Elijah appeared speaking with Him of His departure to be accomplished in Jerusalem. Peter offered to build three tabernacles, but a bright cloud overshadowed them and a voice declared, 'This is My beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased. Hear Him,' after which the disciples fell on their faces in fear (Matthew 17:1-8).

12-14.name: The Commemoration of the Great Sign which the Lord performed for the holy Cross
12-14.summary: Commemorated during the papacy of Pope Theophilus, 23rd Patriarch of Alexandria, this sign concerns a wealthy Jewish man in Alexandria named Philoxinus, who had two poor Christian friends, one of whom remained unconvinced of the Christian faith. That friend went to Philoxinus and adopted his faith, and the ruler of the synagogue then had a cross made of wood, before which the apostate repeatedly denied Christ. The cross was then beaten with a reed, given a sponge of vinegar, spat upon, and pierced with a spear, and blood and water flowed from it. The apostate then dropped dead and became dried up like a rock, which struck fear into those present and led many to believe, saying that they believed in the Lord Christ, the true God.

12-15.name: St. Mary Known as Marina, the Ascetic
12-15.summary: An 8th-century saint born Mary to a wealthy Christian father, Euganius, and pious mother, Sarah, in Bithynia, Asia Minor. When her father wished to remarry her off but instead chose monastic life himself, she refused to be left behind, cut her hair, donned men's clothing, and joined him at the monastery disguised as his 'son' Marina. She lived for years undetected among the monks, her gentle voice attributed to her ascetic discipline, persevering in prayer and fasting until her father's death, after which she continued the monastic life as 'the monk Marina.'

12-15.name: The Saintly Archdeacon Habib Girgis
12-15.summary: Coptic Reader lists the departure of the saintly Archdeacon Habib Girgis on this day, but the Synaxarion page as checked gives this heading with no further narrative about him, so no life, place, or circumstances of his departure can be recorded from Coptic Reader for this entry.

12-16.name: The Assumption of the Body of the Virgin St. Mary to Heaven
12-16.summary: Commemorates the revealing of the assumption of the body of St. Mary to heaven. She had departed on the 21st of Tobe, surrounded by the apostles; St. Thomas, absent while preaching in India, arrived after her burial in Gethsemane and was shown her body being taken up by angels. Angelic praises and the aroma of incense surrounded her tomb for three days before her pure body was assumed into heaven.
hymnIds: Adam Psali for the Feast of the Revelation of the Assumption of St. Mary's Body
Watos Psali for the Feast of the Revelation of the Assumption of St. Mary's Body
The Midnight Doxology for the Virgin
plus the standard set shared across St. Mary's occasions: Verses of the Cymbals, Doxology, Gospel Response, Hymn of the Intercessions

12-16.name: Pope Matthew IV (Mattheos), 102nd Patriarch of Alexandria
12-16.summary: Born in the city of Meer to pious Christian parents, Matthew was raised in a true Christian upbringing, taught church subjects, and later became a monk at the monastery of St. Mary known as El-Baramos in the wilderness of Scetis, where he lived a righteous and ascetic monastic life. After Pope Mark VI departed, bishops, priests, and lay leaders unanimously chose him, and he was consecrated in 1660 A.D. in a splendid celebration attended by many from other Christian denominations. He remained meek and largely monastic in his way of life, was merciful to the poor, widows, orphans, and prisoners, cared for the monks and their monasteries, ordained two successive metropolitans for the Ethiopian church, and moved the patriarchal residence from Haret Zowaila to Haret el-Rom in 1660 A.D. After suffering many hardships with patience and prayer, he departed in peace in 1675 A.D., after sitting on the apostolic throne for fourteen years, eight months, and nine days, and was buried in the tomb of the patriarchs in the church of Abu Safain in Old Cairo.

12-17.name: St. James the Soldier
12-17.summary: Martyred in 304 A.D., James was born in the village of Mengoug to God-fearing Christian parents who had three daughters before him and dedicated him to God in answer to prayer. He tended his father's sheep under a devout shepherd he took as a role model. When persecution arose, the shepherd went to confess Christ, and James asked his father to let him accompany the shepherd to martyrdom.

12-18.name: St. Alexander, Patriarch of Constantinople
12-18.summary: Departed in 336 A.D., an honorable scholar who suffered many hardships opposing the Arian heresy. When St. Athanasius the Apostolic renewed the excommunication of Arius, Emperor Constantine pressured St. Alexander to readmit Arius to communion, but Alexander firmly replied that only the universal council which stripped Arius of his rank could restore it. St. James, Bishop of Nisibis, joined him in prayer that the Lord would keep this danger from the Church.

12-18.name: St. Eudaemon, of Armant (El-Armanti)
12-18.summary: Eudaemon, of the city of Armant, was martyred after hosting idol worshipers in his house who spoke of a lady who had arrived in the city of Ashmonain carrying a young Child who looked like the children of kings. After they left, he rode his donkey to Ashmonain, searched for the holy family, found the Child Jesus with His mother Mary, and worshiped Him, and the Child told him that He would stay in Eudaemon's home, which would be a house for Him forever, and that when Eudaemon returned home the heathen would be indignant, hurt him, and shed his blood in his house, but that he should not fear, because he would be received into the heavenly kingdom and would be the first martyr in Upper Egypt. Eudaemon knelt before the Lord Christ, who blessed him, and returned home, where the news of his visit spread and the heathen hurried to him and asked whether what was said about him was true; when he confirmed that he had gone to the Lord Christ, they drew their swords and slew him, so he received the crown of martyrdom that day. After paganism was abolished and Christianity spread, Christians converted his house into a church for the Virgin St. Mary and her Son, called el-Gishouna, meaning 'The church of the living,' in the outskirts of Armant, and there was another church named for the Virgin St. Mary and the martyred Eudaemon in el-Ashmonain in Mallawy.

12-19.name: The Return of the Body of St. Macarius the Great to His Monastery in Scetis
12-19.summary: In 793 A.D., during the papacy of Pope Yoannis IV, the body of St. Macarius the Great was returned to his monastery in Scetis (Wadi El Natrun). It had been away since 480 A.D., when it was moved first to Shabsheer and then to Almay, each city building a great church to house it. Pope Yoannis IV, spending the holy forty days at the saint's monastery, expressed his yearning that the body be returned, and it was accomplished that year.

12-20.name: The Seven Young Men of Ephesus (Seven Sleepers)
12-20.summary: Martyred around 250 A.D.: Maximus, Malchus, Martinianus, Dionysius, John, Serapion, and Constantine — soldiers of Emperor Decius trusted to guard the royal treasury. When accused of Christianity for refusing idol worship, they hid in a cave outside Ephesus; the emperor had the entrance sealed, delivering their spirits to the Lord. About 200 years later, God revealed their bodies to the bishop of Ephesus in a vision during the reign of Emperor Theodosius the Less, so their story could be a testimony to the resurrection of the dead.

12-21.name: The Commemoration of the Virgin St. Mary, the Mother of God
12-21.summary: The monthly commemoration of the Mother of God, the Virgin St. Mary, intercessor of mankind, the chosen queen, the burning bush, the tabernacle, the pot of manna, Aaron's rod, and the Holy of Holies.
hymnIds: The Midnight Doxology for the Virgin (the central Theotokia)
Adam Psali for the Birth of the Virgin
Adam Psali for the Departure of the Virgin
plus the standard set shared across St. Mary's occasions: Verses of the Cymbals, Doxology, Gospel Response, Hymn of the Intercessions

12-21.name: St. Irene (Eirene)
12-21.summary: A first-century saint, daughter of King Lucianus (Licinius) of Macedonia. She was born after her parents lost all previous children, and her father, concerned for her exceptional beauty, built her a fortified mansion with thirteen maiden servants when she was six. Though her idol-worshiping parents left statues for her to worship, her Christian tutor Apellianus (Aplianus) instructed her wisely and justly instead.

12-22.name: Micah the Prophet
12-22.summary: Departed in 696 B.C.: a righteous Old Testament prophet from the tribe of Judah, born in Moresheth Gath and called Micah el-Morashti. A quiet, wise, and compassionate poet, he prophesied for about sixty years during the reigns of Jotham, Ahaz, and Hezekiah, kings of Judah, contemporary with the prophet Isaiah. He foretold the destruction of Samaria and Jerusalem, called the people to repentance, and prophesied the return of God's mercy.

12-22.name: St. Augustine, Bishop of Hippo
12-22.summary: Born in Thagaste in 354 A.D. to a pagan father, Patricius, and a devout Christian mother, St. Monica, who taught him Christian principles in childhood, Augustine studied at home and then in Carthage, lived in sin and immorality, and traveled to Rome and then Milan, where he became a teacher of rhetoric. His mother followed him to Milan and prayed fervently, and Bishop Ambrose comforted her that the son of these tears would not perish; meeting Ambrose, reading the Bible, and reading St. Athanasius's Life of Anba Antonius awakened his conscience, and he confessed to Ambrose, prepared in seclusion outside Milan, and was baptized by Ambrose in 387 A.D. He returned to Thagaste, sold his possessions and gave them to the poor, went to Hippo, lived in asceticism and worship, gathered disciples, established a monastery, and became a father and guide of monasticism. Ordained priest in 389, consecrated auxiliary bishop in 395, and succeeding as bishop in 396 at age forty-one, he served with pastoral care, compassion for the poor and needy, and a call to repentance, consecrated an auxiliary bishop at age seventy-two to assist him, and departed in peace at age seventy-six in 430 A.D., after a long illness, leaving a rich spiritual heritage and profound writings.
hymnIds: Doxology for St. Monica and St. Augustine

12-23.name: The Martyrdom of Thirty Thousand Christians in Alexandria
12-23.summary: Commemorates a massacre following the exile of Pope Dioscorus, 25th Patriarch of Alexandria, by Emperor Marcianus to the island of Gagra. The Chalcedonian Brotarius was appointed patriarch in his place, but the Egyptian bishops refused fellowship with him and convened a council rejecting the Council of Chalcedon and the Tome of Leo. Brotarius, enraged, used government forces to plunder monasteries and churches, growing wealthy, until thieves killed him in the night; the Chalcedonians blamed the followers of Dioscorus, and the furious Emperor sent soldiers who killed about thirty thousand Christians in Alexandria.

12-23.name: St. Demian in Antioch
12-23.summary: Demian went and confessed the Lord Christ before the governor of Antioch when persecution was incited against the Christians. He was tortured severely, but God healed, comforted, and strengthened him under torment. When the governor grew weary of torturing him, he ordered him beheaded, and Demian thus received the crown of martyrdom.

12-24.name: St. Thomas, Bishop of Mar'ash (Syria)
12-24.summary: An ascetic worshiper diligent in fasting and prayer, merciful to the poor and needy, consecrated bishop of Mar'ash in Syria for his devoted shepherding. When Diocletian incited persecution against Christians, the governor summoned Thomas and demanded he worship idols; upon his refusal he was severely tortured, had organs dismembered one at a time, and was cast into an abandoned prison for twenty-two years — his congregation presuming him dead — sustained secretly at night by a faithful woman through a small opening in the prison wall, until Emperor Constantine ordered the release of imprisoned Christians.

12-24.name: St. Takla Haymanot, the Ethiopian
12-24.summary: One of the seventh-century saints, Takla Haymanot was born in Ethiopia to a priestly family that had relocated from a village nearby Jerusalem; his parents were righteous and merciful to the poor and needy, and his mother, who was barren, entreated God often for a son who would please Him, until the Archangel Michael announced that she would conceive and bring forth a son loved by God, the angels, and people. She raised him with a Christian upbringing from childhood; at seven he began memorizing the Holy Books, and at fifteen Anba Kyrillos the bishop ordained him a deacon, then a priest by the name Takla Haymanot, and he was celibate. After his parents' departure he distributed all his possessions to the poor and needy, wandered about Ethiopia preaching the name of the Lord Christ, and many believed at his hands, joining an ascetic life to his evangelical work, spending almost all of the holy forty-day fast in austere asceticism in the wilderness, then returning to ministry. He continued for about fifty years moving from place to place, living among monks in worship and asceticism and at other times among the people in service and evangelism, and God granted him the gift of performing miracles and healing the sick, while he endured many hardships from the heathen. When his departure drew near, the Lord Christ appeared to him, bid him peace, and informed him of the time of his departure; he gathered the brethren, commanded them to adhere closely to the spiritual struggle of the Holy Fathers who followed monasticism until they resembled angels while still on earth, blessed them, departed in peace, and was buried with great veneration.
hymnIds: Adam Psali for the Departure of Saint Takla Haymanot the Ethiopian
Watos Psali for the Departure of Saint Takla Haymanot the Ethiopian

12-28.name: The Patriarchs Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob
12-28.summary: Commemorates the holy fathers Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob. Abraham, born in Ur of the Chaldeans to the idol-worshiper Terah, was called by God to leave his country for the land God would show him, with the promise to make him a great nation and a blessing to all families of the earth. He settled in Canaan, was given Isaac in his old age, and was tested by God's command to offer Isaac as a burnt offering on Mount Moriah.

12-29.name: The Commemoration of the Three Major Feasts of the Lord (Joyful 29th)
12-29.summary: The monthly commemoration of the three major feasts of the Lord: the Annunciation, the Nativity, and the Resurrection. The liturgy is prayed in the joyful tune, with no strict abstinence or prostrations that day.
hymnIds: plus an extensive weekday Theotokia cycle (Psalis) covering the Annunciation, Nativity, and Resurrection in turn

12-29.name: St. Athanasius the Bishop and His Two Servants, Gerasimus and Theodotus
12-29.summary: Martyred in 303 A.D. St. Athanasius the bishop was an honorable, zealous man of the Christian faith. Accused before Arianus the Governor of having baptized the daughter of the chancellor Antonius, he was arrested and endured many torments, remaining steadfast in his confession until he provoked the governor's wrath along with his two faithful servants, Gerasimus and Theodotus, who were martyred with him.

12-29.name: The Arrival of the Relic of St. John, the Short, to the Wilderness of Scetis
12-29.summary: In 804 A.D., during the papacy of Pope Yoannis IV, 48th Patriarch of Alexandria, the body of the great saint Anba John the Short was relocated from el-Qulzum on the Red Sea to the wilderness of Shiheet. An Arab prince appointed in charge of Al-Qulzum was a friend of Anba Michael the bishop; the Patriarch wrote to the bishop expressing his wish to relocate the body of St. John, and the bishop informed the prince of the Patriarch's wish. Monks of the wilderness of Scetis came in Arab attire over their monastic garments, entered el-Qulzum to the place where the body was, carried the body, and walked all night until they came to the monastery of St. Macarius the Great, where the monks met him with songs and hymns. After receiving the blessing from the body, they carried him to his own monastery, where they placed him with great veneration, and when the monastery of St. John the Short was ruined, the monks moved the body back to the monastery of St. Macarius and placed it along with the bodies of the three Macarii until this day.
hymnIds: Doxology for St. John the Short

12-30.name: Malachi the Prophet
12-30.summary: Departed in 430 B.C.: one of the twelve Minor Prophets and the last prophet of the Old Testament, prophesying post-exile during the absence of Nehemiah at Shushan around 432 B.C., after the building of the temple. He exposed the corruption of the priests and people, declared God's hatred of divorce, rebuked the rich for hard-heartedness toward the poor, warned of coming plagues, and prophesied the abolishing of Old Testament sacrifice for the New. He also foretold the divine incarnation: 'the Lord, whom you seek, will suddenly come to His temple... Behold, He is coming, says the LORD of hosts' (Malachi 3:1).

12-25.name: St. Bessarion the Great
12-25.summary: A 4th-century Egyptian ascetic who trained under Anba Anthony and Anba Macarius before withdrawing into the desert, owning nothing but a coarse garment and the Gospels. Known for walking on water, sweetening salt water for a thirsty companion, healing a paralyzed child, and guiding St. Taor to repentance.

12-25.name: Pope Macarius III, 114th Patriarch of Alexandria
12-25.summary: Born in El-Mahalla El-Koubra, became a monk at St. Pishoy Monastery, served as Bishop of Assiut for 47 years, then Pope of Alexandria from 1944 until his death in 1945. His short papacy included reforms on divorce law, family legislation, and monastic education.

12-26.name: St. Moses (Moisees) and his Sister Sarah
12-26.summary: Martyred in 250 A.D., these two siblings were born to wealthy Christian parents in Alexandria. After their parents' death, Moses gave away all their possessions to the poor rather than marry, and took his sister to a convent of virgins while he withdrew to a nearby mountain in seclusion, the two not seeing each other for ten years, before their eventual martyrdom.

12-26.name: St. Agabius, the Soldier, and his Sister Thecla
12-26.summary: Agabius the Soldier and his pious sister Thecla were martyred during the reign of Emperor Julian, who incited persecution against the Christians. They went and confessed the Lord Christ before him, and he tortured them much for their confession. He then cast them to the lions, and thus they received the crowns of martyrdom.

12-27.name: Sts. Benjamin and his sister Eudoxia
12-27.summary: Two siblings born in Shabsheer, Egypt, to pious Christian parents devoted to hospitality and asceticism. Benjamin, longing to shed his blood for Christ, confessed his faith before the governor of Shatanof and was tortured and imprisoned; his sister Eudoxia refused to be separated from him, choosing to die with him rather than leave his side. Both were martyred together after the governor bound them with heavy stones and threw them into the river, from which they were miraculously freed by an angel before ultimately winning their crowns of martyrdom.

12-27.name: St. Mary, the Armenian
12-27.summary: Mary the Armenian was a captive of a Moslem soldier of King Zaher Baibars, the Sultan of Egypt, who asked her to deny her faith in the Lord Christ, but she did not hearken to him and confessed that she was Christian. He tortured her severely, but the Lord strengthened and comforted her, and when he became weary of torturing her, he informed el-Sultan, who brought her and asked her to abandon her faith. She did not listen to him and remained steadfast in confessing her Christian faith, so the Sultan ordered her to be burned alive in a blazing pit by Zoweila's gate in Cairo. While they were throwing her in the pit she was saying that it was good that she delivered up her soul in the hands of her Master, Lord, and Savior Jesus Christ, and thus she received the crown of martyrdom.

_template.name: Saint Name (as shown on Coptic Reader)
_template.summary: 3-4 sentence summary, written the way you'd want to read it before a service.

13-1.name: St. Eutychus
13-1.summary: A disciple of St. John the Evangelist who was present at the coming of the Holy Spirit on Pentecost. He later took John's permission to join St. Paul in preaching. He is the young man of Acts 20 who fell asleep during Paul's long sermon in Troas, fell from the third-story window and was taken up dead, but Paul embraced him and restored his life, after which Paul continued preaching until daybreak. St. Eutychus went on to preach the gospel and bring many Jews and Gentiles to faith in Christ.

13-1.name: St. Pishay (Abshai), the Antiochian
13-1.summary: Pishay, the brother of St. Abba Or, was a native of the city of Antioch and, because of his piety and knowledge, was ordained a priest. His brother Abba Or and his mother went to Alexandria, where they received the crowns of martyrdom, and Pishay gave all his possessions to the poor and the needy and came to Alexandria to see their bodies and receive their blessings. When he saw the two bodies, he wept, then went to the governor and confessed the Lord Christ before him, and the governor tortured him much until he delivered up his pure soul. The governor then ordered his body burned along with the bodies of his brother, his mother, and eighty-eight other martyrs, yet the fire did not harm them, and some believers came, took the bodies of the saints, shrouded them, and buried them with great veneration.

13-2.name: St. Titus, the Apostle
13-2.summary: Born in Crete, nephew of the island's governor, learned in Greek language and literature, meek and merciful. Sent by the governor to Palestine to verify reports of Christ, he witnessed the Lord's signs and teachings and believed; Christ chose him among the Seventy Apostles. After the Ascension he received the Holy Spirit with the other disciples and accompanied St. Paul on his missionary journeys, who eventually consecrated him bishop of Crete, where he preached.

13-3.name: The Archangel Raphael
13-3.summary: Commemorates the consecration of the church of the honorable Archangel Raphael near Alexandria, during the papacy of Pope Theophilus, 23rd Patriarch. A faithful woman from Rome, who had inherited great wealth from her husband, came with her children and a large icon of Archangel Raphael, desiring to build churches; the Pope showed her a place where she built a church he consecrated on this day in Raphael's name. Raphael, a Hebrew word meaning 'God heals,' is mentioned in the Book of Tobit as the angel who accompanied young Tobit on his successful journey.

13-3.name: Sts. Andrianus and his companions
13-3.summary: Andrianus, one of the commanders of the army of the emperor, was martyred after seeing martyrs enduring tortures and asking them why they did so to themselves; they answered that it was for the sake of their hope of eternal life and the everlasting kingdom, until his heart became inflamed with the love of Christ and of eternal life. He went to the emperor and confessed the Lord Christ before him, and the emperor tortured him much and then imprisoned him with many of the martyrs. His wife Anatolia cut off her hair, dressed in the garb of men, came to the prison, and strengthened, comforted, and consoled her husband as she ministered also to the other martyrs. After a series of tortures, Andrianus was martyred along with all who were with him, and they received the crowns of martyrdom, and some believers relocated the pure bodies to Pisidia.

13-3.name: Pope Yoannis XIV, 96th Patriarch of Alexandria
13-3.summary: Born in Manfalut to Christian parents who raised him with a true Christian upbringing, Yoannis longed when he grew to live the ascetic life of the monks, went and became a monk at El-Baramous monastery, and lived an honorable life. After the departure of Pope Gabriel VII, he was chosen for the patriarchate and consecrated in 1571 A.D. by the name Pope Yoannis XIV. During his papacy he suffered many hardships because el-sultan levied on him an excessive tax, which he exerted great effort in collecting from the people, traveling around the land visiting his children and collecting the levied tax; during his days the government also issued a decree for Christians to wear black turbans instead of the blue ones, and the Pope of Rome renewed efforts to join the Coptic Church to the Catholic Church when he saw the hardships of the Copts, but his attempts failed. In one of his pastoral visits he went to Alexandria, and on his way back felt weak and ill at the city of El-Nahrawiah, departed there in peace, and was buried at the Church of St. George in Birma, after sitting on the apostolic throne for fifteen years, four months, and nineteen days; his body was later relocated to the monastery of St. Mary known as Dair el-Saurian in the wilderness of Shiheet.

13-4.name: St. Poimen (Anba Baymon) the Hermit
13-4.summary: Departed in 460 A.D. Born in 350 A.D. to a godly family with six brothers (John, Job, Joseph, Paisios, James, and Abraham), they forsook the world and lived in seclusion in the wilderness of Shiheet (Scetis) around 390 A.D., dedicated to fasting, prayer, and worship. When Berber raids struck the wilderness in 407, 434, and 444 A.D., he and his brothers relocated repeatedly — to Tarnout, Manf (Memphis), and Upper Egypt — before finally returning to Shiheet. He was discipled under St. Macarius the Great, loved quietness and seclusion, fled vainglory, and ate only from the work of his hands.

13-5.name: Amos the Prophet
13-5.summary: One of the twelve Minor Prophets, born in Tekoa, south of Jerusalem, to a poor family. He tended sheep and was a tender of sycamore fruits. He prophesied in the days of Uzziah, king of Judah, and in the days of Jeroboam II, son of Joash, King of Israel, contemporary with the prophet Hosea who succeeded him. God sent him to caution the children of Israel to bear fruits of repentance before the day of vengeance; he prophesied the Lord's Passion, the darkening of the sun at the Crucifixion, and the coming dispersion and sorrow of Israel. He was called 'the prophet of afflictions' for his harsh rebuke of sinners, and prophesied about eight hundred years before the Lord Christ.

13-5.name: St. Yoannis XV (John XV), 99th Pope of Alexandria
13-5.summary: Departed in 1346 A.M. (1629 A.D.), 99th Patriarch of Alexandria. Born in the city of Mallawy to Christian parents who raised him in piety and godliness; became a monk in the monastery of Anba Antonius (St. Anthony), living a righteous monastic life, upright and devoted to reading books and manuscripts. When Pope Marcus V departed, the bishops, priests, and lay leaders (Archons) unanimously chose him for the patriarchate; he was consecrated on the 7th of Thoout, 1336 A.M. (1619 A.D.). Known as 'the just judge' for his strong, impartial character, he was kind to priests, merciful to the needy, and never asked anything of anyone all his life. During his papacy a grave epidemic spread, and he visited his flock in Upper Egypt many times.

13-5.name: Anba Barsoum (Parsouma) the Naked (El-Erian)
13-5.summary: Departed in 1033 of the martyrs (1317 A.D.). Born in Misr (Cairo); his father El-Wageeh was scribe to Queen Shagaret el-Dor. When his parents died his uncle seized his inheritance; Barsoum did not quarrel but forsook the world for the life of a hermit, living outside the city for five years enduring summer heat and winter cold, wearing only hairy sackcloth. He then shut himself in a cave inside the church of St. Mercurius Abu-Safain in Old Cairo for twenty years in ceaseless prayer and fasting, where he tamed a huge serpent through prayer and the sign of the cross. He later lived on the church roof, was later imprisoned and beaten during a persecution, then went to the monastery of El-Shahran (Ma'asaret Helwan), where he continued his asceticism and was visited by rulers seeking his blessing. He departed at age sixty and was buried at El-Shahran, which was later renamed the Monastery of St. Barsoum el-Erian in his honor.
hymnIds: Adam Psali for the Departure of Abba Parsouma the Naked
Watos Psali for the Departure of Abba Parsouma the Naked
Doxology for St. Parsouma the Naked

13-5.name: St. James, Bishop of Misr
13-5.summary: Coptic Reader presents James as a monk who became Bishop of Misr (Cairo), completed his good endeavor, and departed in peace, giving no further birthplace or career details in the entry as checked.

1-1.name: Feast of El-Nayrouz (Coptic New Year)
1-1.summary: The beginning of the new Coptic year, kept in veneration of the Christian martyrs to immortalize their memory. The Coptic Calendar (Calendar of the Martyrs) began with the reign of Emperor Diocletian in 284 A.D. The Church presents the story of early Christianity, when Christians offered themselves as examples of love, sacrifice, faith, endurance, and love of enemies, teaching that the Christian faith spread through the shedding of the blood of the martyrs alongside preaching and teaching.
hymnIds: Doxology for the Coptic New Year

1-1.name: Pope Marcus V (Mark V), 98th Pope of Alexandria
1-1.summary: Departed in 1619 A.D. Native of El-Bayadiah (Mallawy, El-Minia Governorate), inclined to the ascetic life from a young age; became a monk at the monastery of St. Macarius in the wilderness of Scetis (Shiheet). After the departure of Pope Gabriel VIII, he was chosen and ordained Patriarch, enthroned Sunday, 26th of Paone, 1319 A.M. (1603 A.D.) at the church of St. Philopateer Mercurius (Abu-Saifain) in Old Cairo. Well educated in ecclesiastical subjects, canons, and laws, he remained steadfast defending the teachings of Scripture amid hardships over the Personal Status Law. He made pastoral visits to Upper Egypt and Jerusalem; his patriarchal seat was at the church of St. Mary in Haret Zewailah. He was buried with great veneration at the monastery of St. Macarius in Scetis.

1-1.name: The Commemoration of the Healing of the Righteous Job
1-1.summary: Job is presented as the righteous man who endured severe affliction and loss, remained steadfast, and was then healed by God. God restored his fortunes and his children, and he lived one hundred and forty years after his affliction, seeing his children and descendants.

1-1.name: St. Bartholomew the Apostle
1-1.summary: Bartholomew was one of the twelve apostles, who preached in El-Yemen, then went to Armenia, India, and Asia Minor, preaching the Gospel of Christ. Coptic Reader says he was martyred in Armenia in 71 A.D., giving no specific method of martyrdom in the text as checked.

1-1.name: Pope Milius, the Second Patriarch
1-1.summary: Milius was the second patriarch after St. Mark, succeeding St. Anianus, and was enthroned in 83 A.D. He shepherded the flock with care, completed his good endeavor, and departed in peace in 95 A.D.

1-2.name: St. John the Baptist (Martyrdom)
1-2.summary: Martyred in 31 A.D. by order of King Herod Antipas. St. John, the forerunner, son of Zacharias the priest, rebuked Herod for taking Herodias, the wife of his brother Philip, saying it was not lawful. Herodias held it against him and sought to kill him, but Herod feared John, knowing him to be a just and holy man, and protected him, hearing him gladly. At a birthday feast, Herodias' daughter danced and pleased Herod, who swore to give her whatever she asked; prompted by her mother, she asked for the head of John the Baptist on a platter, and the king, though sorry, granted it because of his oath.
hymnIds: Adam Psali for the Appearance of the Relics
Watos Psali for the Appearance of the Relics

1-2.name: St. Dasya the Soldier
1-2.summary: Martyred; one of the soldiers of Arianus, governor of Ansena. A native of the city of Tanda, district of Mallawy, El-Menia Governorate. When he saw the prominence of the Christians and their endurance of tortures before martyrdom, he declared his faith in the Lord Christ. When the governor failed to persuade him to forsake his faith, he ordered him beheaded, and St. Dasya received the crown of martyrdom.

1-3.name: Council of Alexandria on the Immortality of the Spirit (Pope Dionysius)
1-3.summary: In 247 A.D., a holy synod convened in Alexandria in the second year of the papacy of St. Dionysius, the 14th Pope of Alexandria. It was convened because certain people in Arabian countries taught that the spirit dies with the body and would be raised together on the day of resurrection; they sent a treatise on this belief to Christians in Alexandria. Abba Dionysius assembled the synod, debated and refuted them, and excommunicated them when they refused to recant, writing a treatise affirming that the spirit neither dies nor perishes but is immutable and incorruptible, going to paradise or Hades according to its worthiness, to be reunited with the body at the resurrection.

1-3.name: St. Theodora the Penitent (of Alexandria)
1-3.summary: Born in the fifth century to noble parents in Alexandria, Theodora was a beautiful and virtuous young woman married to a pure and wealthy young man, until she fell into adultery and, overcome with guilt and tears, left the world. Disguised in men's clothing with her hair shaved, she entered the men's monastery of Ennaton as the monk Theodore, living in prayer, obedience, humility, and intense asceticism and gaining a gift of miracles. When a woman falsely accused Theodore of defiling her, Theodora endured the mockery without defending herself, was entrusted with the resulting infant, was expelled in disgrace, and spent seven years in a hut near the monastery, feeding the child on shepherds' milk and eating only wild vegetables, before being readmitted to seclusion in a cell with the child. She departed in 510 A.D., and when the monks prepared her body they discovered she was a woman; her husband then became a monk in her cell, and the child later became abbot of the monastery.

1-4.name: Joshua, the son of Nun
1-4.summary: Great Old Testament prophet, departed in the year 2570 of the world. Born in Egypt in 2460 of the world, of the tribe of Ephraim, he left Egypt with Moses in the Exodus and became his disciple. He led Israel's army against Amalek while Moses prayed on the hilltop, defeating them by the sword. One of the twelve spies sent by Moses to Canaan, he and Caleb alone brought a faithful report and were the only two of that generation to enter the Promised Land. After Moses' death, the Lord commanded Joshua to lead Israel into Canaan.

1-4.name: Pope Macarius II, 69th Pope of Alexandria
1-4.summary: Pious and ascetic from his youth, Macarius longed for monastic life and became a monk of the Monastery of St. Macarius, devoting himself to worship, asceticism, and reading the Holy Scriptures, and growing in virtue and knowledge as a skillful painter of icons and decorator of manuscripts. After the departure of Pope Mikhail II, the Holy Synod elected him, and though he was taken bound against his will and wept, begging to be released as unfit, he was consecrated Patriarch in the Church of St. Mark in Alexandria in 1102 A.D. and then enthroned in Cairo in the Church of the Holy Virgin, El-Muallaqah. During his papacy he added to worship and piety, taught and preached daily, and gave alms and works of mercy to the poor and needy, before departing in peace in 1128 A.D. after a papacy of twenty-five years and nine months; he was buried with great honor in the Church of the Holy Virgin, El-Muallaqah.

1-4.name: St. Verena
1-4.summary: Born in the village of Garagous in the Theban region to Christian parents, Verena was baptized by Bishop Chaerimon of Nilus, who oversaw her religious upbringing, and she grew in grace and faith while visiting and ministering to imprisoned Christians. She went with the Theban Legion from Thebes to Gaul in the reign of Emperor Diocletian, and after the legion's martyrdom at Agaunum she withdrew to a cave near Salodurum, living an austere life of prayer and fasting supported by her handiwork, performing many healings through her prayers, and teaching young girls chastity and sound hygienic practices. Arrested by the ruler, she was consoled in prison by an appearance of St. Maurice and released after the Lord healed the governor through her; she then lived at Zurzach in Switzerland, in a house beside the Church of the Virgin St. Mary, where she cared for the poor and sick, before spending eleven years in solitary life in a cave. Near her departure the Holy Virgin appeared to her with virgins in the cave and told her of eternal life and Paradise, and Verena departed amid incense, was buried with great honor, and became the patron saint of Zurzach, where a church was built in her name.

1-5.name: St. Sophia
1-5.summary: Martyred in the second Christian century. Born in Manf, Egypt, to pagan parents, she came to believe in Christ through her Christian neighbors and was baptized by the Bishop of Manf during the papacy of Pope Omanious (Eumenes), 7th Patriarch, and during the reign of Emperor Hadrian, who incited severe persecution against Coptic Christians. Accused of being Christian by her pagan neighbors before Claudianus the Governor, she confessed her faith and was tortured repeatedly — whipped with an oxen tail and burned in her joints — yet remained steadfast, continually crying out 'I am a Christian.'

1-6.name: Isaiah the Prophet
1-6.summary: Martyred about 710 years before the advent of the Lord. One of the Major Prophets, a descendant of the kings of Judah; his name means 'Salvation is of the Lord.' He prophesied in the days of five kings of Judah — Uzziah, Jotham, Ahaz, Hezekiah, and Manasseh — and was contemporary with the prophets Amos, Hosea, Obadiah, Micah, and Nahum. In the year King Ahaz died (740 B.C.), Isaiah saw a heavenly vision in the temple and heard God's call to be a prophet. He named his sons symbolically: Shear-Jashub ('a remnant shall return') and Maher-Shalal-Hash-Baz ('making a swift plunder of spoils'), prophesying the coming Babylonian exile of Judah.

1-6.name: St. Basilissa
1-6.summary: A pious Christian girl only nine years old, Basilissa was martyred in the days of the Emperor Diocletian. She was seized, bound hand and foot, and cast into the fire, but the Lord saved her from the burning and she remained steadfast in her faith in Christ. Through her prayers God caused water to spring up, she drank, and then she committed her soul into the hand of the Lord, receiving the crown of martyrdom.

1-7.name: Pope Dioscorus I, 25th Pope of Alexandria
1-7.summary: Departed in 171 A.M. (454 A.D.). Born in Alexandria and educated in its theological school, his brilliance drew the admiration of St. Cyril I, 24th Patriarch, who appointed him his private secretary; he continued researching the works of the fathers despite the position. Enthroned on the throne of St. Mark on 2 Misra, 160 A.M. (444 A.D.), succeeding Pope Cyril I, the Pillar of Faith, during the reign of Emperor Theodosius II. He presided over the Second Council of Ephesus in August 449 A.D.

1-7.name: Pope Youannes (John) XII, 93rd Pope of Alexandria
1-7.summary: Born in the city of Naqada in the province of Quena, Youannes was raised by his parents in a true Christian upbringing, longed for monastic life when he grew, went to the Monastery of the Virgin known as Dair Al-Muharraq, became a monk, grew in virtue and asceticism, and was ordained a priest. When the papal throne became vacant after the departure of Pope Michael IV, the bishops and people chose him, and he was consecrated patriarch by the name Youannes XII in 1480 A.D. He shepherded the Christian people with the best of care, remaining on the throne for three years and four months teaching and interpreting the Holy Scriptures in uprightness, before departing in peace in 1483 A.D.; he was buried in the Church of the Virgin, Babylon, in Old Cairo.

1-7.name: St. Rebecca and her five children, Agathon, Peter, John, Amun and Amuna
1-7.summary: From Kamola in the district of Kus, Rebecca and her five children were martyred during the reign of Emperor Diocletian, in the years 303 to 305 A.D. When they heard that Diocletian had ordered the persecution of Christians and the closing of churches, they spent the night in prayer, and an angel announced that they would receive the crown of martyrdom, so they rejoiced, gave all their possessions to the poor, and released their servants. They confessed Christ before Dionysius, the governor of Kus, who tortured them severely, beginning with their mother, who bore it patiently and with joy and strengthened her children to endure; they were then sent to Armanius, governor of Alexandria, who tortured them and cast them into a cauldron of boiling oil, yet the Lord raised them whole, and the governor at last ordered them beheaded. Their bodies were placed in a boat to be cast into the sea, but an angel directed a rich man from Nakraha to take them, and he laid them in the church, where God manifested many signs and wonders from their relics; after later relocations they came to rest at Sonbat, where a church known as El-Sitt Refqa and her five children still stands and their bodies remain to the present time.
hymnIds: Adam Psali for the Martyrdom of Saints Rebecca and Her Five Children
Watos Psali for the Martyrdom of Saints Rebecca and Her Five Children
Melody for St. Rebecca and Her Five Children
Second Melody for St. Rebecca and Her Five Children

1-7.name: St. Severian (Severianus), Bishop of Gabala
1-7.summary: A well-educated and righteous father, Severian departed in 405 A.D. as Bishop of Gabala in Greece. After his parents departed and left him great wealth, he built a guest house for strangers, the poor, and the afflicted, and distributed the rest of his money to the poor and needy; when this was reported to Emperor Honorius, the emperor invited him to stay in the palace, but Severian, fearing to lose his labor amid such honor, was commanded by an angel to go to Gabala, where he dwelt in a monastery and became a comfort to many souls, teaching the monks until they became like angels. God performed many wonders at his hands, including casting an evil spirit out of the governor of Gabala's daughter, and the bishop of Gabala learned in a vision that Severian would succeed him, so after that bishop's departure Severian was consecrated bishop and cared for his people so that many Jews, pagans, and sorcerers believed at his hands. He wrote many valuable discourses, homilies, and sermons that still exist in the church books, and when he grew old, reaching one hundred years, an angel informed him of the day of his departure, and he commended his people and departed in peace.

1-8.name: Moses the Prophet
1-8.summary: Departed in 1485 B.C. The great righteous head of the prophets, born in Egypt in 1605 B.C. to Amram and Jochebed of the tribe of Levi, during the reign of King Aminophees, Pharaoh of Egypt, who ordered every male Hebrew child killed. By faith his parents hid him three months, then set him adrift on the Nile in an ark of bulrushes; Pharaoh's daughter found and adopted him, and his sister Miriam arranged for his own mother to nurse him.

1-8.name: St. Zacharias the Priest
1-8.summary: Zacharias was a priest serving in the temple, the husband of Elizabeth and father of John the Baptist. In their old age the angel Gabriel told him that Elizabeth would bear John, and after the child's birth Zacharias confirmed his name. When Herod's soldiers sought the infant, Zacharias refused to reveal where John was hidden, and the soldiers killed him between the altar and the temple.

1-8.name: St. Dimides (Diomede), the Presbyter
1-8.summary: Dimides was a presbyter living in the time of the persecutions against Christians. He was seized for refusing to sacrifice to idols, and he was tortured for his refusal. Remaining steadfast in his faith, he was beheaded and received the crown of martyrdom.

1-9.name: St. Pisora the Bishop
1-9.summary: Martyred during the reign of Emperor Diocletian. Bishop of the city of Masil (today Meslil, a center of Shebin El-Kom, El-Monufia Governorate). When he learned that Diocletian had apostatized, worshipped idols, and declared persecution against Christians, he gathered his flock, commanded them to remain steadfast in the Orthodox faith, and bid them farewell. Three fellow bishops — Pisikhos, Fanalikhos, and Theodore — agreed to go with him; together they confronted the governor and confessed Christ. The governor tortured them cruelly to make an example of them, and when their faith held firm, ordered their heads cut off, and they received the crowns of martyrdom.
hymnIds: Adam Psali for the Martyrdom of Abba Pisoura the Bishop
Watos Psali for the Martyrdom of Abba Pisoura the Bishop

1-9.name: Sts. Pilus and Nylios
1-9.summary: Pilus and Nylios were Christians in Upper Egypt during the persecution of the Church. They were seized and tortured for refusing to deny Christ, and they remained steadfast under torment. They were beheaded together, receiving the crown of martyrdom.

1-10.name: St. Youannes the Egyptian and his Twenty Companions
1-10.summary: Martyred during the reign of Emperor Maximinus Daza (305–313 A.D.). St. Youannes loved the Lord with all his heart and memorized Holy Scripture until it was imprinted deep in his soul; he met Eusebius of Caesarea, the father of church history, who was amazed at his vast knowledge of the Holy Book. He and his twenty companions confessed Christ before the Governor, who sentenced them to hard labor under the scourching sun, then ordered St. Youannes' eyes plucked out and one of his legs burned with red-hot iron, and finally ordered them all beheaded, so they received the crowns of martyrdom.

1-10.name: St. Matruna
1-10.summary: Matruna was raised in a Christian home, but as she grew up life forced her to work as a maid-servant in the home of a Jewish lady. Her mistress tried to entice her to adopt the Jewish religion, but Matruna would not yield, so her mistress humiliated, ill-treated, and over-burdened her with servitude. One day her mistress imprisoned her in a dark room for four days without food or drink, then took her out, beat her painfully, and returned her to imprisonment. There she died, receiving the crown of martyrdom for her steadfastness in the faith.

1-10.name: Sts. Basin and Her Three Children
1-10.summary: Coptic Reader lists the commemoration of Sts. Basin and her three children on this day, but the Synaxarion page as checked gives this heading with no further narrative about them, so no life, place, or manner of death can be recorded from Coptic Reader for this entry.

1-11.name: St. Basilides (Wasilides), the Minister
1-11.summary: Martyred during the reign of Emperor Diocletian. A member of the cabinet and counselor during the reign of Emperor Numerianus, who married Basilides' sister; Basilides had two sons, Eusabius and Macarius. When the Persians waged war against Rome, Numerianus sent his son Yustus to fight them, and was later killed by his in-law Arrius Aper; Diocletian, Numerianus' servant, rose up, killed Arrius, and was proclaimed Emperor in Antioch in 284 A.D. Diocletian later renounced Christ, worshipped idols, and on 23 February 303 A.D. issued his edict of persecution, beginning by eliminating the royal family; he sent Basilides to Masrus, governor of the Five Western Cities (Pentapolis), who tortured him severely.

1-11.name: The Three Farmers in Esna
1-11.summary: Three farmers from Esna in Upper Egypt confessed Christ during the persecution of the Church. They were seized and tortured for refusing to sacrifice to idols, and they would not waver in their faith. They were beheaded together, receiving the crown of martyrdom.

1-12.name: Archangel Michael (Monthly Commemoration)
1-12.summary: Monthly commemoration of the pure Archangel Michael, head of the heavenly hosts.

1-12.name: Assembly of the Third Ecumenical Council at Ephesus
1-12.summary: In 147 A.M. (431 A.D.), the Ecumenical Council convened at Ephesus in Asia Minor, attended by 200 bishops. Emperor Theodosius II convened the council to examine the heresy of Nestorius, Archbishop of Constantinople, who taught that St. Mary did not give birth to the incarnate God but only to a human being, and that the Son of God afterward dwelt in him — a dwelling of will rather than unity — and therefore it was not lawful to call her Theotokos (God-bearer).

1-12.name: The Translocation of the Relics of St. Clemus and his companions to Alexandria
1-12.summary: Coptic Reader lists the translocation of the relics of St. Clemus and his companions to Alexandria on this day, but the Synaxarion page as checked gives this heading with no further narrative about Clemus, his companions, or the translocation itself.

1-13.name: Miracle of St. Basilius (Basil) the Great, Bishop of Caesarea
1-13.summary: Commemorates a miracle performed by St. Basil the Great, Bishop of Caesarea, Cappadocia. A young man of Caesarea loved his master’s daughter; unable to marry her, he resorted to a magician, who had him sign a covenant with the devil at midnight in an unbelievers’ cemetery, denying faith in Christ. Satan then kindled lust for the young man in the girl’s heart, and her father gave her in marriage to him. Through her parents’ prayers, God opened the wife’s eyes to realize he was not a true Christian.

1-13.name: Pope Mettaos II (Matthew II), 90th Patriarch of the See of St. Mark
1-13.summary: Formerly Matta El-Sa'idy, Mettaos was a monk of the Monastery of St. Mary, El-Muharraq, and was chosen after Pope Youannes XI, the 89th Patriarch, being consecrated in 1452 A.D. during the days of Sultan Fakhr-El-Deen Othman. He resided at the ancient church of St. Mary in Haret Zeewailah in Old Cairo, ordained Anba Gabriel as metropolitan for Ethiopia, and made the Holy Myron at the Church of the Holy Virgin in Haret El-Roum, Cairo, with six bishops. He sat on the throne of St. Mark for thirteen years in peace and tranquility, departed in peace in 1465 A.D., and was buried in Dair El-Khandaq, nowadays known as Dair El-Anba-Rewis.

1-14.name: St. Agathon the Stylite
1-14.summary: Departed in the year 444 of the martyrs (728 A.D.). From the city of Tinnis (an ancient Egyptian city, formerly called Sawan, now in El-Sharqia Governorate); his father was Matra and mother Mariam, both righteous and charitable. He grew up loving God and inclined to monastic life, and was ordained a priest at age 35, devoting himself to perpetual prayer day and night and serving God's people with love and sincerity. He asked Christ to help him leave the world for the desert; an angel appeared to him in the form of a monk and led him to the monastery of St. Macarius the Great in Scetis.

1-14.name: Sts. Felix and Regula, his Sister, and St. Exuperantius
1-14.summary: Felix, his sister Regula, and Exuperantius were from Thebes in Upper Egypt; Felix and Exuperantius joined the Theban Legion headed by St. Maurice, and Regula accompanied her brother Felix. After Maurice advised the steadfast legion to leave Agaunum, they went to Zurich spreading the Christian faith, while Emperor Maximian ordered the whole legion slain and its associates pursued. The governor seized the three, who confessed Christ and their association with Maurice, and tortured them severely without making them waver, including Regula's healing after being placed in boiling wax and forced to drink melted lead. They were then ordered beheaded, after which they stood, carried their heads in their hands, walked about twenty-eight yards, knelt, and fell again; they were shrouded and buried, churches were built for them in Zurich, and part of their relics was later transferred in 1610 A.D. to the Church of Sts. Peter and Paul in Andermatt, Switzerland.

1-15.name: St. Stephen the Archdeacon (Translocation of the Body)
1-15.summary: Commemorates the translocation of the body of St. Stephen the Archdeacon and first Christian martyr. After his martyrdom in Jerusalem, pious men buried his body in a village called Gamaliel near Jerusalem; its location was unknown for about 300 years until St. Stephen appeared to a priest named Lucianus in a vision revealing where his body lay. Bishop John of Jerusalem and two other bishops found the body after a mighty earthquake revealed a coffin, and carried it to Jerusalem with great veneration. Alexander of Constantinople later built a church for him there; years later, Alexander's widow, intending to take her husband's body back to Constantinople, unknowingly carried St. Stephen's coffin instead (realizing it from the sounds of singing coming from within), and it was ultimately enshrined in Constantinople by Emperor Constantine the Great.
hymnIds: Adam Psali for the Relocation of Saint Stephen the Archdeacon's Relics
Watos Psali for the Relocation of Saint Stephen the Archdeacon's Relics

1-15.name: Anba Athanasius El-Quosy
1-15.summary: Departed; a bright star and bishop, son of the eminent priest and skillful teacher Fr. Saleeb, native of west Kamola. Became a monk at the monastery of the martyr Mar-Boctor (El-Kolah, west of Kamola in Naqada); consecrated bishop of Quos by Pope Youannes X (John), 85th Patriarch, around 1365 A.D., assisted by Anba Timotheos of Ebreem and Abu-Khras of Nubba. Dedicated to preserving the Coptic language, he published an introductory book on interpretation in Bohairic and Sahidic dialects (Kiladet El-Tahreer Fi Elm El-Tafseer), a book on personal and family law, and one on the consecration of Holy Myron; he participated with Pope Gabriel IV in consecrating Holy Myron at St. Macarius monastery in 1374 A.D. He also authored El-Triadon in 1322 A.D., a 734-verse rhymed poem in Coptic Sahidic on religious instruction featuring biblical and church figures, and laid down many canons on marriage, baptism, Myron consecration, priesthood, and other matters. He departed in peace in the city of Quos.

1-16.name: Consecration of the Church of the Resurrection in Jerusalem
1-16.summary: In the year 51 of the martyrs (335 A.D.), the church of the Resurrection in Jerusalem was consecrated. After Queen Helena discovered the Holy Cross, she ordered the church built; when finished, Emperor Constantine asked Pope Athanasius of Alexandria, the Patriarch of Constantinople, and the Patriarch of Antioch to go to Jerusalem with their bishops, where they were received by St. Macarius, Bishop of Jerusalem. They consecrated the church and its altars, and the next day processed with the Holy Cross around the church and holy places before returning to their countries in peace.

1-17.name: Feast of the Honorable Cross (Commemoration at Church of Resurrection)
1-17.summary: In 51 of the martyrs (335 A.D.), the Patriarchs of the Christian churches celebrated the Honorable Cross: Pope Athanasius the Apostolic of Alexandria, the Patriarch of Constantinople, the Patriarch of Antioch, and St. Macarius, Patriarch of Jerusalem. They carried the Cross in procession inside the church of Resurrection, offered prayers, celebrated the Divine Liturgies, venerated the Cross, and placed it in a silver vault. The feast also coincides with the appearance of the sign of the Cross to Emperor Constantine the Great in 312 A.D., on his way to fight the tyrant Maxentius; he saw the sign in the sky with his officers and soldiers, a light brighter than the sun, with the words 'With this sign you shall conquer' written beneath it.

1-17.name: St. Theognosta
1-17.summary: Departed during the reign of Emperors Honorius and Arcadius. She lived in a convent near Rome and was taken captive by the men of the ruler of El-Raha, who gave her as a maidservant to his wife. She served with joy, was made head of the palace maidservants, and lived a life devoted to prayer and asceticism. She healed the ruler's son through prayer and was freed; later healed the ruler's wife, and guided the lost ruler back to the city by a light in the shape of the cross. This led the people to ask for a priest; Theophanius was sent, preached the faith until all believed, and was ordained bishop for El-Raha. St. Theognosta served the women and taught them the faith until her peaceful departure after a short illness.

1-17.name: St. Castor, the Presbyter
1-17.summary: Martyred during the reign of Emperor Diocletian in the fourth century. Born in the village of Bardanouha, Upper Egypt, to Christian parents; ordained a reader, then married and ordained presbyter for his village church, shepherding his people with great care. He had a son Afraham and a daughter Dermoudah. When Diocletian incited persecution, Fr. Castor went about confirming the faithful, visiting imprisoned Christians in el-Kais to strengthen them. Seized when the governor learned of this, he was tortured but the Lord comforted and healed him; he was then sent to the governor of Old Cairo, Kelkianus, for further torture, during which many miracles were manifested, and finally sent to the Governor of Alexandria who also tortured him.

1-17.name: El-Moallem (Master) Girgis el-Gohari
1-17.summary: Departed in 1557 of the martyrs (1810 A.D.). One of the famous Copts of the late 18th and early 19th centuries, brother of El-Moallem Ibrahim El-Gohari; he was raised and educated alongside his brother in the Kuttab (training school) for head scribes of Egypt. He held the position of head of El-Mobashereen after his brother's departure, serving under four different periods: the Mamalik, the French expedition, the Turks, and the beginning of Muhammad Ali Pasha's reign. Generous in giving, he donated much to the poor, needy, churches, and monasteries, and supported Pope Marcus VIII (Mark VIII) in building the great St. Mark church in el-Azbakiya and the adjacent Patriarchal residence. Pope Mark VIII appointed him administrator for many churches in Cairo and Old Cairo. He fell ill later in life and departed in peace, buried beside his brother near the church of St. George in Darb-El-Taqa, Old Cairo.

1-18.name: The Second day of the Feast of the Cross
1-18.summary: The church celebrates the second day of the feast of the Honorable Cross, with its rites and prayers performed in Hossana and with joyful tunes, and the entry closes with the blessing of the Honorable Cross.
hymnIds: Doxology for the Feast of the Cross
Watos Psali for the Feast of the Cross
Adam Psali for the Feast of the Cross
Syrian Fraction for the Feasts of the Cross and Standard Days
Fraction to the Father on the Slaughter of Isaac

1-18.name: St. Prophorius (Porphyrius)
1-18.summary: Prophorius was a pagan performer in the time of the Emperor Julian who was mocking Christian rites in a play, including baptism. During the mock baptism, the sign of the Cross and divine grace changed his heart, and he immersed himself three times in the name of the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit and confessed himself a Christian. Julian first tried to win him back with friendship and gifts and then threatened him, but Prophorius remained firm, rebuked the emperor, and was martyred by having his neck cut off.

1-18.name: St. Stephen, the Presbyter, and St. Niceta (Niketa), the Martyr
1-18.summary: Coptic Reader lists the martyrdom of St. Stephen the Presbyter and St. Niceta the Martyr on this day, but the Synaxarion page as checked gives this as a one-line commemoration with no further narrative about their lives, places, or manner of death.

1-19.name: The Third day of the Feast of the Cross
1-19.summary: The church celebrates the third day, and the last day, of the feast of the Honorable Cross, with its rites and prayers performed in Hossana and with joyful tunes, and the entry closes with the blessing of the Honorable Cross.

Watos Psali for the Feast of the Cross
Adam Psali for the Feast of the Cross
Syrian Fraction for the Feasts of the Cross and Standard Days
Fraction to the Father on the Slaughter of Isaac

1-19.name: The Commemoration of Lifting up St. Gregory from the Pit
1-19.summary: St. Gregory was of the royal family of Armenia. After refusing to sacrifice to idols and enduring severe tortures, during which he was repeatedly healed, he was thrown into a deep pit to die of thirst and hunger. The Lord preserved him there, and an old widow was shown in a vision that she should bring him bread daily, which she did for fifteen years. When King Tiridates became seriously ill, his sister was told in a vision that he would not be healed unless Gregory was brought out of the pit, so Gregory was lifted out with a rope, like a new Daniel, venerated by the king, and, at his sister's request, forgave the king and prayed for him, after which the Lord answered his prayer and the king was healed.

1-20.name: St. Theopista
1-20.summary: Theopista was a married woman whose husband died while she was still young, leaving her with a son. She vowed to spend the rest of her life in worship and asceticism while raising her son in the fear of God, with fasting, prayers, and kneelings. She later asked Abba Macarius, bishop of Nekios, for the monastic garb, and after a year of trial he shut her in a small room, where her twelve-year-old son cared for her needs. The bishop then forgot her, but in a night vision a shining figure told him that she was passing away that night, and he woke holding the silver cross she had given him in the vision, after he had, in the vision, ordained monks and put the holy Eskeem and his own Kalansowa on her. He went to her house, where her son was weeping beside her room; she called her son at midnight, bade him farewell, said she was departing that night to the Lord Christ, and told him to obey whatever the bishop said, and then departed in peace. The bishop found her departed, wearing the Eskeem and Kalansowa from the vision, and after she was carried to the church, the sick, paralytics, and those possessed by evil spirits who were brought to her body were healed.

1-20.name: Pope Athanasius the Second, the 28th Patriarch of the See of St. Mark
1-20.summary: Athanasius was steward of the churches of Alexandria. After the departure of Pope Peter III, the 27th Patriarch, the bishops, elders, and people agreed to consecrate Athanasius for his Orthodox faith and piety, and he is called Athanasius the Less to distinguish him from Athanasius the Apostolic. His reign was in the time of Emperor Zeno, and he participated with Emperor Anastasius, who came after Zeno, in re-establishing peace between the churches of the East after the disruption caused by the Council of Chalcedon. His time was peaceful and tranquil, he shepherded his flock in purity and righteousness, and he departed in peace in the year 213 of the martyrs (496 A.D.), after sitting on the throne for seven years.

1-20.name: St. Melitina, the Virgin
1-20.summary: Coptic Reader lists the martyrdom of St. Melitina the Virgin on this day, but the Synaxarion page as checked gives this as a one-line commemoration with no further narrative about her life, place, or manner of death.

1-21.name: The Commemoration of the Virgin St. Mary, the Theotokos
1-21.summary: The holy church arranged for the 21st day of every Coptic month to be a commemoration of the pure Lady, the Virgin St. Mary, the Theotokos. The entry recalls that during her earthly life, and on the 21st of Paone, the miracle occurred of the melting and dissolution of iron, by which the Apostle St. Matthias was rescued from prison. Her departure was also on the 21st of Tubah, and some fathers and apostles also consecrated the first church after her name in Philippi on the 21st of Baounah, after her departure.

Watos Psali for the Assumption of the Virgin St. Mary
