The Great Saint Abba Shenouda the Archimandrite (Koiahk 1 and Epep 7)

4-2.name: St. Abba Or (Abahor), the Monk
4-2.summary: Abba Or was a native of Abraht, in the district of Ashmunein, and was chosen as a monk; he surpassed many saints in worship and lived in solitary seclusion in the wilderness. Satan envied him and appeared to him, saying that in the wilderness he could conquer him because he was dedicated to fighting him, but that if he were brave he should go to Alexandria. The Lord willed to reveal his virtues, so he was guided to Alexandria, where he remained drawing water for the prisoners and the shut-in. One day, horses galloping in the middle of the city struck a child, who was killed instantly, while Abba Or was standing where the child was killed; Satan moved the people to shout that the old monk was the killer. He was not disturbed: he took the child in his arms, prayed to the Lord Christ to glorify His holy name, and made the sign of the honorable Cross, whereupon the child's soul returned and he delivered him to his parents. The people marveled and glorified God, and their hearts turned toward Abba Or; fearing vainglory, he escaped to the wilderness and dwelt in a monastery for the rest of his days. When his departure drew near, he saw a company of saints calling him, rejoiced, sent for his disciples, commanded them to remain steadfast in the path of the ascetic life, and told them he was about to depart to the Lord Christ; after a short sickness he delivered his pure soul into the hand of the Lord he loved.

4-2.name: St. Abba Hermina, the Anchorite
4-2.summary: Abba Hermina was born in Bahnasa to righteous parents who raised him in Christian morals. While young and pasturing his father's sheep, the apostles St. Peter and St. John appeared to him and called him to follow the monastic life, which he obeyed. He went to the monastery of Anba Jacob, met the abbot, asked to be instructed in monasticism, and shortly afterward put on the monastic vestments, increasing in grace and spiritual struggle and persevering in worship and asceticism. He then went into the inner wilderness, where he found a palm tree and a spring of water and stayed for a period, meeting some holy fathers, and finally moved to the north of the city of Kaw, in the Eastern Mount, where he lived in austere struggle and numerous prostrations, persevering until his body weakened and his sight dimmed. The devil could not endure his worship and incited much warfare against him, but an angel protected and saved him. At his departure, his two friends St. Abba Or and St. Yousab, and the fathers who dwelt on the mountain, came to receive his blessings; he finally delivered his pure soul into the hands of the Lord he loved, and was prayed over and buried with great veneration in the church of the city of Kaw. God manifested many signs and miracles from his pure body, and the monastery named after St. Hermina is located north of Kaw, in the El-Badary district of Assiut.

4-3.name: The Entrance of Saint Mary into the Temple at Jerusalem
4-3.summary: This entry commemorates the entrance of the holy Lady, the Virgin Saint Mary, the Theotokos, into the Temple when she was three years old, for she was a Nazirite to God. Her mother Anna was childless and exceedingly sad, so her husband St. Joachim prayed fervently and vowed that if God gave him a fruit, he would give it to God's Holy Temple. God answered and gave them the blessed fruit called Mary. After she had been reared for three years, they took her to live with the virgins in the Temple of the Lord, and Saint Mary dwelt in the sanctuary for ten years, growing in virtue and piety. In the fullness of time, when the Lord was to come into the world, He was incarnate from this pure Virgin whom He chose.

4-3.name: St. Bestavros, the New Martyr
4-3.summary: In the year 1229 of the martyrs (1512 A.D.), St. Bestavros, also called Saleeb, the new martyr, was martyred. He was born in the city of Ebshadat, nearby the city of Or, in the district of Mallawy, and was called Saleeb. He learned church subjects, and when he became a young man he desired to live a life of virginity; nevertheless his parents wed him, against his will, to one of his relatives, and he found that his wife had the same inclination to a life of celibacy, so they agreed to live together under one roof in complete virginity. Saint Saleeb spent most of his time with the monks of a nearby monastery, listening to their advice and persevering in prayer, interceding by the Virgin to aid him in his spiritual struggle. One day a group of wicked men falsified many untrue accusations against him, that he had blasphemed against the Islamic faith; however, he openly declared his faith in the Lord Christ, so they imprisoned him. The wife of the jailer saw him from the prison window praying all night long, and also saw a luminous woman appear before him and say that he would receive the crown of martyrdom and Archangel Michael would support him. The ruler later sent him to Cairo shackled in chains; he was on a boat for a few days without food or drink, persevering in prayer, and the Virgin St. Mary appeared to strengthen him. When he arrived in Cairo, they brought him before King Al-Ashraf Qansuh al-Ghury, and the saint confessed the Lord Christ again before him. The king was enraged and sent him to the judge to pass sentence; the judge, realizing his insistence in courageously confessing the Lord Christ, sentenced him to death and delegated this to one of the Mameluke princes. They made a wooden cross, nailed St. Bestavros on it, then raised him crucified on the back of a camel and paraded him around the streets of Cairo; he rejoiced, counting himself worthy to suffer shame for the name of Christ. Later they took him off the camel and promised him release if he forsook his confession of the Lord Christ, but the saint shouted that he would die a Christian on the name of the Lord Jesus Christ. The prince ordered him beheaded, and thus he received the crown of martyrdom. His body remained three days in the middle of the fire they had prepared, yet his body did not burn. Some believers came, took his pure body, and brought it to the papal residence, where Pope Youannes XIII received him with great veneration in the church of the Virgin Mary in Haret Zuwaila, in old Cairo, where he was kept. During the papacy of Pope Shenouda III, he permitted the bishop of Mallawy to relocate part of the relics of St. Bestavros to the church of the Virgin St. Mary in the city of Ebshadat, and that was on the 15th of Paope, 1703 A.M. (1987 A.D.).
hymnIds: Adam Psali for the Feast of the Entry of the Virgin into the Temple and the Martyrdom of Saint Pistavros
Watos Psali for the Feast of the Entry of the Virgin into the Temple and the Martyrdom of Saint Pistavros

4-4.name: St. Andrew, One of the Twelve Apostles
4-4.summary: In the year 62 A.D., St. Andrew the Apostle, the brother of St. Peter, was martyred. He was born in Bethsaida, a city of Galilee, and was also a fisherman. He was a disciple of St. John the Baptist, who guided him to the Lord Christ, and he became His disciple and one of the twelve apostles. After the coming down of the Holy Spirit on the day of Pentecost, he preached the Gospel in Syria, then in Asia Minor, Achaea, Cappadocia, Galatia, and Bithynia, and was finally martyred in the city of Patras, a city of Achaea in Greece. He went to Patras and preached the Holy Gospel to the people; most believed at his hands, and he almost eradicated pagan worship. When the governor of the city realized this, he seized Andrew and ordered him to raise incense for the idols, or he would be crucified. Andrew refused and confessed the Lord Christ, the true God who redeemed us with His pure blood. The governor was enraged and ordered him crucified, to die the same death as the One whom he was preaching, and the saint rejoiced. They made a cross in the shape of an X, which till now is called the cross of Andrew. After he was crucified, he remained on the cross for two days, preaching to the people and confirming them in the faith. Finally he delivered his pure soul into the hand of the Lord and received the crown of martyrdom, and the believers brought down his pure body and buried it with great veneration.
hymnIds: Adam Psali for Saint Andrew the Apostle
Watos Psali for Saint Andrew the Apostle
Doxology for St. Andrew The Apostle
Adam Aspasmos: Our fathers the apostles, St. Peter and St. Andrew

4-4.name: The Consecration of the Church of St. John El-Heraquly
4-4.summary: This entry gives only a short consecration note, with no further narrative. It commemorates the consecration of the church of the martyr St. John El-Heraquly (John of Heraclia). He was martyred on the 4th day of Paope, and his body is still preserved, along with the body of his uncle, the martyr Abe-Fam, in the village of Um-elkosour, in the district of Manfalut, in the governorate of Assiut.
hymnIds: Adam Psali for the Martyrdom of Saint John of Heraclia
Watos Psali for the Martyrdom of Saint John of Heraclia

4-4.name: The Translocation of the Bodies of the Two Saints Anba Bishoy and Anba Paula
4-4.summary: Also on this day was the translocation of the bodies of the two great saints Anba Bishoy, the perfect man and the beloved of the Good Savior, and his fellow in spiritual struggle, Anba Paula of Tamouh, from Ansena, east of Mallawy, to the thriving monastery of Anba Bishoy in the Natroun valley, in the holy wilderness of Shiheet. That was in the year 557 of the martyrs (842 A.D.), and during the papacy of Anba Yousab I, the 52nd patriarch, who desired to relocate the body of Anba Bishoy to the monastery in the wilderness of Shiheet, to be among his children, the monks. When those in charge placed the body of St. Bishoy on a boat, however, the boat would not move, without any obvious cause. A righteous old monk called Armia told them that the boat will not move with the body of Anba Bishoy alone, because there was a covenant between these two saints, Anba Bishoy and Anba Paula, that they will not be separated during the days of their sojourn on earth and also after their repose. They went back, carried the body of Anba Paula, and placed it on the boat beside the body of his friend Anba Bishoy, and the boat sailed peacefully, while they praised God and venerated the two great saints. When they arrived at the monastery of Anba Bishoy in Scetis, they placed the two bodies in one case and placed it in the church of St. Bishoy. Their bodies are still together in a splendid, richly decorated shrine, and some miracles and healings have been manifested from their bodies until now.
hymnIds: Doxology for St. Pishoy and St. Paul of Tammah
The Great Saint Abba Pishoy the Beloved of Christ (Epep 8)

4-5.name: Nahum the Prophet
4-5.summary: The church celebrates the commemoration of the righteous Prophet Nahum, one of the twelve Minor Prophets. He was born in the village of El-Kosh, in Galilee, Palestine, and was of the tribe of Judah. He prophesied in the days of Amaziah and his son Azariah. He rebuked the children of Israel because of idol worship, and revealed that, although God is compassionate and abundant in mercy, yet He is a jealous God who will take vengeance on His adversaries. He also prophesied concerning the preaching of the Gospel by the apostles, and about the destruction that would come upon the city of Nineveh. This was fulfilled: God sent a damaging earthquake and fire that destroyed the city and burnt up the people who returned from the way of righteousness and committed sin, while as for those who were straight in their ways, no evil or harm befell them. When he had finished his good endeavor, he departed in peace.

4-5.name: St. Victor (Boctor) of Assiut
4-5.summary: St. Victor was born in one of the villages of Assiut, east of the Nile, and was appointed a soldier in the city of Shaou, in the district of Ab-nub. When the edict of Diocletian was issued to worship and raise incense to the idols, the soldier Victor refused to do so. The governor of Shaou summoned him and tried to befriend Victor, but could not persuade him, and therefore the governor imprisoned him. His parents came and encouraged him to face martyrdom. When the governor failed to turn him away from the faith of the Lord Christ, he was enraged and sent him to the governor of Assiut, along with some soldiers and a message. When the governor read the message, he tried to persuade him to worship the idols with many enticements, but did not succeed. The governor was enraged and ordered him tied to the tails of galloping horses and dragged. Later the governor proposed worshipping the idols again, but Victor refused. He ordered him thrown into a cauldron filled with boiling water, in the village of Mousha. Victor extended his arms and prayed, and an angel of the Lord appeared and promised him the crown of life. Then they tied him and cast him into the boiling water, and he delivered up his spirit and received the crown of martyrdom. Some believers came, took his pure body, and hid it until the end of the persecution, then built a church which still exists until the present in the village of Mousha. Many miracles and wonders have been manifested from his pure body.

4-5.name: St. Isidore (Isidorus)
4-5.summary: In the year 250 A.D., St. Isidore the Alexandrian was martyred. He was born in the city of Alexandria and enlisted in the army of Emperor Decius under the leadership of Captain Omerius. When the commander discovered that he was a Christian, he delivered him to court to be condemned. He promised him many attractive promises, then started threatening him with harsh punishments, but in all of this he was steadfast in his faith. The commander ordered that his tongue be cut off, and then that he be beheaded, and thus he received the crown of martyrdom. They cast his body in a well, and the Lord manifested many wonders, signs, and healings from it. A church was built over the well later on, and his body was relocated in the fifth century to Constantinople, where it was venerated and honored by many.
hymnIds: Doxology for St Isidore the Priest
Glorification Melody for St. Isidore the Priest

4-6.name: Pope Abraam (Abraham) Ebn-Zaraa, the 62nd Pope of Alexandria
4-6.summary: In the year 695 of the martyrs (979 A.D.), the Holy Father Pope Abraam Ebn-Zaraa, the 62nd pope of Alexandria, departed. This father was from among the Christians of Syria. He was a rich merchant who visited Egypt often to oversee his trading business, and finally settled there. He was blessed with many virtues, the most important of which was mercy to the needy. His reputation for righteousness and knowledge became well known. When the Patriarchal throne became vacant, the bishops and all the people agreed to choose him as Patriarch. When he was enthroned over the See of St. Mark, he distributed all his possessions to the poor and needy. He also abolished many corrupt and erroneous customs, forbade simony in the church, and also strongly forbade keeping concubines; when one of the rich men of the city held firmly to his concubines, the patriarch excommunicated him, and he died in a horrible way, becoming an example to others. During his papacy the famous miracle of moving the Mokattam mountain took place. El-Muizz, the Fatimid Caliph, had a Jewish vizier named Yaqub ibn Killis, who had adopted Islam; he hated the Christians and wished them harm. One day, the vizier told El-Muizz that the Christian Bible has a verse which says that if you have faith as a grain of mustard seed, you shall say to this mountain, move from here to there, and it will move. The caliph thought that if the words of Christ are true, that would be of great benefit to us, for the Mokattam mountain is too close to Cairo, and if the saying is not true, that will give us justification to persecute the Christians. El-Muizz called the patriarch, placed the saying before him, and asked for proof of its soundness. The pope asked for a three-day respite, which was granted. When the pope left the caliph, he gathered the bishops and monks nearby and stayed in the Church of St. Mary in Old Cairo, fasting and supplicating God for three days to save His people from this difficult test. Before dawn on the third day, the Virgin St. Mary appeared to Anba Abraam and told him about a holy man called Simon the Tanner, at whose hands the miracle would be manifested. Pope Abraam brought St. Simon and took him, along with some bishops, priests, monks, and people, to El-Muizz, to inform him of their readiness to move the mountain. The caliph went out with the government officials and nobles of the city to nearby Mokattam Mountain. The patriarch stood with those with him on one side, and El-Muizz and his entourage on the other side. The Holy Father and the believers prayed and knelt down three times, saying Lord, have mercy each time. Whenever the patriarch and the congregation lifted their heads after each kneeling, the mountain would be lifted up, and when they bowed down the mountain would be lowered to the ground, and whenever they walked the mountain would move before them. Great fear came into the hearts of the caliph and those with him. The caliph advanced on his horse toward the patriarch and shouted that God is great and blessed is His name, and that they had proved their faith is true and living, and that he should ask whatsoever he wished. The patriarch refused to ask for anything, but when the caliph insisted, he asked to be allowed to restore the churches, especially the Church of St. Mercurius in old Cairo. He wrote a decree permitting the restoring of the churches and gave a large sum of money from the treasury. The patriarch thanked him and prayed for him, and refused to take the money. As a result, El-Muizz revered and respected the patriarch more for his piety and righteousness. Pope Abraam built the church of Abu Saifain and many other churches. To commemorate the miracle of moving the Mokattam Mountain, the church added three days to the Fast of the Nativity, for a total of 43 days. The church also followed this pope in adopting the three-day Jonah's Fast of the Syrians. When he had finished his good endeavor, he departed in peace. He occupied the patriarchal throne for three years and six months.

4-6.name: St. Patlas (Anatolius - Anatole), the Presbyter
4-6.summary: Coptic Reader gives only the heading, followed immediately by the closing blessing, with no further narrative. No life, place, or martyrdom details are given for St. Patlas on this page.

4-7.name: St. Mettaos El-Fakhoury (Matthew the Poor)
4-7.summary: On this day, the great saint Anba Mettaos El-Fakhoury, abbot of the monastery of Asfoun Mount, nearby Esna, departed. Because of his great humility, he called himself Matthew the Poor. He was born to Christian parents, and his father was a pottery maker. He was reared in a true Christian upbringing. Since his young age, he frequently visited the monasteries and learned the spiritual life of the monks. He longed for the monastic life, so he went to one of the monasteries of St. Pachomius, nearby Esna, and asked Fr. Marcus, the abbot of the monastery, to accept him under his guidance. He was accepted, and shortly afterward Fr. Marcus dressed him in the monastic vestments. The monk Mettaos started his monastic life with austere ascetic struggles, loved prayers and the solitary life, and dug himself a cave in the mountain nearby the monastery, where he lived in seclusion, worshipping and praying. After the departure of Fr. Marcus, the monks chose Fr. Mettaos to be the abbot and head of the monastery. When he took over the responsibility, he performed his duties with excellence and did a great deal of improvement to the monastery. After his departure, the monastery was called after his name, and his body was buried therein. Beside the great monastic architectural growth that Fr. Mettaos undertook in the monastery, God granted him many gifts: healing the sick, casting out devils, raising the dead, and telling the future. His fame spread to all the surrounding cities. He reached a level of holiness in which wild beasts ate food from his hands and were tamed in his presence. When he had completed his pure endeavor, he departed in peace. His body is still present in a beautiful marble tomb, located in a small private room beside the entrance of the monastery's old fort.

4-7.name: Sts. Banina and Banawa
4-7.summary: On this day, also, the two saints Banina and Banawa were martyred, during the reign of Emperor Diocletian. These two saints were born and raised in a village nearby Mallawy. They agreed together on fasting, prayers, and Bible reading. When the Lord saw their strife and purity of heart, He guided them to an ascetic holy old man in the region of El-Fayyom. They became his disciples for three years, then went to the south, to the mount of Ebsay, nearby Akhmeem, where a number of holy ascetics dwelt. The hermits built a church and desired to consecrate it. St. Banina left his seclusion and went searching for the holy bishop Anba Bisada. When he found the bishop, he invited him to consecrate the church. He came with him to the mountain. Anba Bisada consecrated the church, and ordained Banina a priest and Banawa a deacon. The pagans had erected a huge idol on the mount of Adribah, nearby Souhag, and offered human sacrifices to it. The two saints grieved because of this and prayed to God to eradicate idol worshipping from the world. When the devil realized this, he steered the pagan people against the saints to put them to death, but God saved them. When Emperor Maximianus came to Egypt personally to oversee the persecution of the Christians, the priests of the idols complained to him about the two saints. The emperor ordered them seized. Meanwhile, an angel of the Lord appeared to Sts. Banina and Banawa and informed them that the emperor was seeking them and that heavenly crowns were prepared for them. Immediately they went and stood before the emperor, confessing the Christian faith. He ordered them beheaded, and they received the crown of martyrdom.

4-7.name: The Consecration of the Church of St. Abiskhiron (of Qalin) El-kelieni
4-7.summary: On this day, also, the church commemorates the consecration of the church of the martyr St. Abiskhiron (of Qalin) El-kelieni. This saint was martyred on the 7th day of Paope. This church is located in the monastery of Anba Bishoy, in Wadi El-Natroun, and is part of the church of the St. Bishoy monastery. After the arrival of the relics of St. Abiskhiron to the monastery of Anba Bishoy, this church was established after his name, during the papacy of Pope Benjamin II, the 82nd patriarch. He renovated the buildings of the monastery and relocated the relics of the saint to it.

4-7.name: St. John, Bishop of Armant
4-7.summary: This day also marks the departure of St. John, bishop of the city of Armant. He was born to pagan parents, and his father worked as a carpenter. His older brother Pisentius went to Kasre El-Taud and stayed there, reading and searching until he was sure of the validity of the Christian religion. When he went back, he taught his brother John the principles of the Orthodox faith. John went up to the mountain near his hometown and dwelt there in asceticism and fervent worship, until his fame for holiness, knowledge, and piety spread. Some lay leaders of the city of Armant came to them, took John against his will, and went with him to the city of Alexandria. The pope consecrated him bishop of Armant. When he returned to his diocese, he baptized many pagans, and he suffered many hardships from the pagan rulers. He patiently endured, and consequently the people and all the clergy revered him for his conduct. He shepherded his flock in purity and righteousness, and when he had finished his good endeavor, he departed in peace.

4-7.name: The Distinguished Coptic Engineer Sa-eed Ebn Kateb El-Faraghany
4-7.summary: On this day, also, the distinguished Coptic engineer Sa-eed Ebn Kateb El-Faraghany was martyred. He was commissioned to build the Nilometre in el-Rhoda in the year 864 A.D., during the reign of the Abbassid Caliph El-Motawakel. When Ahmad Ibn-Tulun reigned in Egypt, he entrusted him to build the most significant installations. He built him arched bridges, the viaducts of Ibn-Tulun, and the well by the pool of El-Habash to supply water to the city of al-Qatta'i, the capital of his kingdom, between the years 872-873 A.D. Later, Ibn-Tulun considered building a mosque to be the most splendid mosque in Egypt. The mosque was to be built with 300 marble pillars, and he told him to gather the pillars from some churches after demolishing them. When the illustrious Coptic engineer Sa-eed heard this news, he grieved and was concerned about the demolishing of the churches. He wrote a letter to Ibn-Tulun to inform him that he could build the mosque without pillars, except for the two of the Qibla. He drew a sketch of the mosque on parchment and sent it to him with the letter. Ibn-Tulun marveled and approved. He commissioned him to build the mosque, and it was built as exquisitely as could be. The mosque of Ibn-Tulun is still present in the district of Tulun, in Cairo. The building is a testimony to the brilliance of the illustrious Coptic engineer, who incorporated arcades and arches into the mosque before the art of arcades was known in Europe or other countries of the world. Ahmad Ibn-Tulun proposed to him that he adopt the Islamic faith, but he refused, steadfast in his Christian faith. Ibn-Tulun ordered him beheaded, and he received the crown of martyrdom.

4-8.name: St. Esi (Isi) and His Sister Thecla
4-8.summary: On this day, in the year 20 of the martyrs (304 A.D.), St. Esi and his sister Thecla were martyred. These two saints were born in the latter part of the third century to pious Christian parents from the city of Abu-Sair. They were wealthy and charitable to the poor and the needy. St. Esi traveled to Alexandria to visit one of his friends, which coincided with the time when St. Victor, the son of Romanus, came to Alexandria. When Esi knew of his good strife and of his renouncing of the world, he became envious of his biography and his endurance for the sufferings, especially when he knew that St. Victor was the son of a councilor in the Roman Court, a high-ranking officer in the Roman army, and a close acquaintance of the Emperor. Esi wished to follow his example, so he went to Armanius the governor and confessed his faith in the Lord Christ before him. The Angel of the Lord appeared to his sister Thecla in her hometown and ordered her to go to meet her brother in Alexandria. She embarked on a ship, and while on board, the Virgin St. Mary and St. Elizabeth appeared to her and comforted and encouraged her. St. Elizabeth told her that she had a son who was beheaded unjustly, and the Virgin St. Mary told her that she had a Son who was crucified with envy. Thecla did not recognize them. When she arrived in Alexandria and met her brother, they agreed together to confess the Lord Christ. The governor tortured them severely, at times by the squeezing wheel, and at other times by scorching them. When the governor became weary of torturing them, he handed them over to his son, the governor of the city of El-Khosos, to take them to Upper Egypt. When they had sailed for a short while, the boat stopped. The governor ordered them beheaded and cast their bodies into the weeds and the wild plants. Thus, they received the crown of martyrdom. The Lord inspired a priest called Macarius, from Shatanuf, to take their holy bodies. He buried them with great veneration.
hymnIds: Adam Psali for the Martyrdom of St. Isi and St. Thecla His Sister
Watos Psali for the Martyrdom of St. Isi and St. Thecla His Sister

4-8.name: Sts. Barbara and Juliana
4-8.summary: On this day, also, in the year 237 A.D., Sts. Barbara and Juliana were martyred. Barbara was the daughter of a wealthy noble pagan man from the city of Nicomedia called Dioscorus. Because of his great love for his daughter, he built her a tower to live in and erected around it idols, so she would continue in worshipping the gods that he worshipped. St. Barbara rose up her eyes to heaven from the top of the tower, contemplating the beauty of the sky and what was in it: the sun, the moon, and the stars. She came to the conclusion that the universe must have an able and wise maker who is worthy of worship and honor. Origen, the scholar, happened to be in this area and was informed of the saint and her longing for knowledge by one of her Christian maidservants. He came to her and taught her the principles of the Christian religion. Barbara was enlightened with divine light. She was baptized in the name of the Father and the Son and the Holy Spirit, and received the Holy Mysteries by the hands of a Christian priest. There were two windows in the bathroom of her palace, and she ordered a third one to be opened and a large cross to be placed over the water basin. When her father came to see her and saw the changes that were done, he asked her for the reason. She told him that with the Trinity everything is complete, and these three windows are after the name of the Holy Trinity: the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit. This sign, the Cross, is the sign of the Lord Jesus Christ, through whom was completed the salvation of the whole world. She asked her father to turn away from the delusion that he was living in and worship the God who created and redeemed him. When her father heard these words, he became very angry and drew his sword to slay her. She fled away and he ran after her. There was a rock in front of her that split into two halves, and she went through it. The rock then returned to its earlier state. However, her father's heart was more hardened than the rock. He went around the rock searching for her, and found her hiding in a cave. He jumped over her as a wolf, seized her, and dragged her to the governor Marcianus. At first the governor talked to her in a friendly way, making many promises, and then he threatened her, but could not take away her love for the Lord Christ. Therefore, he ordered her tormented with different kinds of tortures. There was a young girl named Juliana who was watching St. Barbara being atrociously tortured, and she wept for her. Juliana saw the Lord Christ strengthening and comforting St. Barbara. She was also enlightened and believed in the Lord Christ. The governor ordered her to be tortured also, along with St. Barbara. All the means of torture failed to change their faith in the Lord Christ. Therefore, he ordered them beheaded, both of them, by the sword. When Barbara heard the order of the governor, she prayed to God to accept her soul and that of Juliana. They came forward, unafraid of death, and the swordsman beheaded them, and they both received the crowns of martyrdom. St. Barbara's father perished shortly afterwards by a horrible death, and so did the governor who tortured them. As for the water basin that had the cross over it in the tower, its water had the power of healing for everyone who washed himself with it. They placed the bodies of these two saints in a church in the region of Galatia. After a period of years, they relocated their bodies to Egypt, to the church that is named after St. Barbara in Old Cairo.
hymnIds: Adam Psali for the Martyrdom of Saint Barbara
Watos Psali for the Martyrdom of Saint Barbara
Doxology for St. Barbara and St. Juliana

4-8.name: St. Abba Samuel the Confessor
4-8.summary: Also on this day, in the year 412 of the martyrs (696 A.D.), the great saint Abba Samuel the confessor, the head of El-Qalamoun Monastery, departed. This saint was born in one of the villages of the diocese of Masil. Arselaos, his father, who was a priest, saw in a night vision a luminous man telling him that his son must be entrusted with a large congregation, for he is chosen by the Lord. Samuel was pure from his youth, like Samuel the prophet. When he grew up, he became a monk in the wilderness of Scetis, at the hands of a holy man called Abba Agathon. Abba Samuel lived with Abba Agathon for three years in total obedience. After the departure of Abba Agathon, the monk Samuel dedicated himself to fasting and prayers. Therefore, he was ordained a priest for the church of St. Macarius the Great. One day, an envoy came to the desert carrying Leo's Tome, and when the envoy read it to the elders and the monks, they asked them to endorse and sign it. Abba Samuel became zealous with divine zeal. He jumped up and seized the Tome and rent it in pieces, and did not endorse it. When the imperial envoy saw this, he became furious and angry. He ordered him beaten with whips and tortured. One of these strikes hit his right eye, causing him to lose it. They then expelled him from the monastery. The Angel of the Lord appeared to St. Samuel and commanded him to depart and dwell in El-Qalamoun Mount. He went there and built a monastery, lived in it for a while, teaching and instructing those gathered around him and confirming them in the Orthodox faith. Shortly after, the Berbers attacked the monastery and took Abba Samuel with them on their way back to their country. There he found Abba Yoannis, the Hegumen of Scete, and they comforted each other. The captor of Abba Samuel tried to persuade him to worship the sun, but he refused. When he failed, the devil enticed him to tie the leg of Abba Samuel to the leg of one of his maidens and send them to attend to the camels. He intended for Abba Samuel to fall into sin with her and then he would submit to him. With the grace of God he was saved from this cruel temptation. Later, the master's son fell ill and was close to death; Abba Samuel prayed for him and the boy was healed of his sickness. His master greatly loved him, apologized for all that he had done, and asked for Abba Samuel's forgiveness. He offered to him to ask for anything he wished. Abba Samuel asked to return back to his monastery, and he allowed him to go back. When Abba Samuel returned, many of his sons, the monks, gathered around him, and they increased until they numbered in the thousands. The Virgin St. Mary appeared to him and told him that this place shall be her abode forever, and from that day the Berbers never attacked this monastery again. Abba Samuel wrote prophecies, many discourses, and spiritual articles. When the time of his departure drew near, he gathered together his sons and commanded them to be steadfast in the faith and the fear of God till their last breath, then departed in peace. His body is located in his monastery near Maghagha, El-Qalamoun Mount, in the Western desert.

4-8.name: St. Heraclas (Yaraklas), 13th Pope of Alexandria
4-8.summary: On this day, also, in the year 240 A.D., the Holy Father, Pope Heraclas, the 13th Pope of Alexandria, departed. This Holy Father was born to pagan parents who believed in the Lord Christ and were baptized after his birth. They taught him Greek philosophy, then the Christian doctrines. He excelled in preaching and teaching. St. Demetrius, the 12th Pope of Alexandria, loved him and ordained him a deacon, then a priest for the church of Alexandria. He was liked by everyone, and many came to listen to his sermons and teachings. In the year 224 A.D., he was enthroned and shepherded the flock of Christ with the best of care. He brought many to the faith. Pope Heraclas sat on the throne of St. Mark for 16 years, one month, and 26 days, then departed in peace.

4-9.name: St. Poemen, the Hermit
4-9.summary: St. Poemen came from a good family and, after his parents died, gave his wealth to the poor and took up monastic life in the wilderness with his brother, in a place associated with St. John the Baptist. He was a disciple of Abba Joseph and remained there for about seventy years, departing at a very old age. Known as a man of silence, he taught that a person should speak only words that are profitable, and he died peacefully after a long life of prayer, fasting, and humility, fleeing praise and love of the world.

4-10.name: St. Nicholas, Bishop of Myra
4-10.summary: St. Nicholas was born to the wealthy and long-childless Epiphanius and Tounah, became a deacon and then a priest, and was known for healing the sick and casting out evil spirits. He secretly gave money at night to a ruined rich man of Myra who was tempted to expose his three daughters to evil, repeating the gift for each daughter until the father caught him and was saved from poverty and sin. Chosen bishop by the people, he was imprisoned and tortured under Diocletian, released under Constantine, and was one of the 318 bishops at the Council of Nicaea in 325 A.D. that judged Arius, sitting on the episcopal throne for more than forty years before departing in peace.

4-10.name: St. Shura of Akhmeem
4-10.summary: In 304 A.D., St. Shura, a young sheep-keeper from Tanay who lived in Shansheef in the district of Akhmeem, was brought before Arianus, governor of Ansena, when he came to Akhmim. He confessed he was a Christian and refused to offer incense to idols, saying he worshipped only the Lord Jesus Christ, and endured being squeezed in the Hinbazeen, fire lit under him, torches applied to his sides, and his body rubbed with vinegar mixed with salt. In prison an angel strengthened him, saying he would receive the crown of glory the next day, and when a magician's poisoned chalice fell and broke, a serpent came out and he stepped on it, so the sorcerer confessed that Shura's God was mighty. The governor then ordered him beheaded and his body hung on the wall of his village for birds of prey, and he received the crown of martyrdom.

4-10.name: The Relocation of the Body of St. Severus, Patriarch of Antioch
4-10.summary: In 539 A.D., the body of St. Severus, Patriarch of Antioch, who had departed at the house of the righteous Archon Dorotheus in Sakha where he was hiding, was sent by Dorotheus by ship with trustworthy men to the el-Zogag Monastery west of Alexandria for burial. When the boat reached shallow water in the Nile, God miraculously made it sail through the shallows for six miles until it reached the shore of the Mediterranean Sea, and it then sailed westward to the el-Zogag Monastery on the seashore. There the body was laid with great veneration in the place Dorotheus had built for it, and God worked many miracles through it.

4-11.name: Anba Pijimi, the Anchorite
4-11.summary: Anba Pijimi was a native of Feesha in the diocese of Masil who, at twelve years old while tending his father's sheep, was visited by an angel in the form of a young man who told him to go to the wilderness to become a monk. He was taken to Scetis to three elder monks and lived among them for twenty-four years until they all departed, then went three days' journey into the inner desert, where devils appeared as wild beasts, pigs, and serpents to devour him but vanished when he prayed. He lived there for three years fasting a week at a time and eating only dates and drinking a little water until his skin cleaved to his bones. An angel then commanded him to return to his hometown, where he built a small hut and cell outside it, became a model of asceticism and a teacher to all who came to him, and was visited by Abba Shenouda the Archimandrite after Shenouda saw a shining pillar and heard a voice identifying Pijimi. When his repose drew near he told his disciple to bury him where he had dwelt, fell ill, saw a company of saints come for him, and delivered his soul into the hand of the Lord while angels carried his soul to heaven chanting hymns.

4-11.name: St. Abtelmaos (Ptolemy)
4-11.summary: St. Abtelmaos was a native of Denderah (Tentyris) west of Qena, an only child raised in a true Christian upbringing, who met St. Paphnoute the Anchorite in the mountains and was advised to go to the ascetic father Dorotheus in Ansena. Dorotheus foretold his martyrdom and advised him to go to Ansena to confess the Lord Christ and receive the crown of martyrdom. He entered the city, confessed before the governor, suffered many tortures patiently, and was finally hung high on a mast and stabbed in the neck by a soldier, delivering his soul and receiving the crown of life. The faithful carried his body and buried it with great veneration, and after the era of persecution ended a church was built and his body was relocated to it, where many signs were manifested from his relics.

4-11.name: The Consecration of the Church of St. Claudius (Ekladius), in the City of Bakour
4-11.summary: This entry commemorates the consecration of the church of the martyr St. Claudius (Ekladius), son of Ptolemy (Abtelmaos), who was the brother of Emperor Numerianus, in the city of Bakour in the district of Abu-Taig in the Assiut governorate. The church still existed at the time of writing, and the account of his martyrdom is given under the 11th day of the month of Paone. Coptic Reader gives no further narrative on this page beyond this consecration notice.
hymnIds: Adam Psali for the Martyrdom of Saint Claudius Son of Ptolemy
Watos Psali for the Martyrdom of Saint Claudius Son of Ptolemy

4-12.name: Archangel Michael
4-12.summary: This is the monthly commemoration of the honorable Archangel Michael, head of the heavenly hosts, who stands before the Pantocrator interceding for the creation, asking the merciful and long-suffering Lord not to be angry with or perish the work of His hands. The entry closes with a request for his holy intercession.
hymnIds: Doxology for Archangels Michael and Gabriel
Fraction to the Father for Archangel Michael
Archangel Michael (12th of Every Coptic Month)

4-12.name: St. Hedra, Bishop of Aswan
4-12.summary: In 395 A.D., Abba Hedra, Bishop of Aswan, departed. His Christian parents raised him well, and at eighteen, when they wanted him to marry a relative, he refused on the excuse of illness, went to church early the next morning asking the Lord to speak to him through the Scriptures, and then, on seeing a dead person being carried to the cemetery, said to himself that it was not that person who had died but he himself who should die to the futile world. He did not return home but became a monk, despite his family and friends coming to grieve and try to bring him back, and after eight years of fervent worship, asceticism, uninterrupted prayer, and many prostrations under his spiritual father St. Poemen, he lived a solitary life in a cave fighting the devil, who tempted him frequently but from whom the Lord saved him. When the bishop of Aswan departed, people who had heard of Hedra's life, knowledge, and virtues unanimously chose him, he accepted after seeing a vision of the Lord Christ declaring that he would be bishop of Aswan, and he was taken to Alexandria where Anba Theophilus, the 23rd Pope of Alexandria, consecrated him bishop of Aswan. He devoted himself to exhorting and teaching the people and guiding them to eternal life, God performed many miracles through his hands, and after a life of good repute he departed in peace, and a monastery bearing his name still existed west of Aswan.

4-12.name: St. John, the Confessor
4-12.summary: St. John the Egyptian was one of the confessors, believers in Christ who endured many tortures for the faith and remained steadfast but whom God, in His sublime wisdom, did not permit to be martyred, and who were released from imprisonment. He endured severe tortures in the persecution of Diocletian, had his eyes plucked out and branded with fire to destroy them, and was cast into fire that did not harm him, astonishing many by his steadfastness and endurance. He was distinguished by a strong memory, having memorized many books of the Holy Bible and being able to recall any verse or paragraph from the Old or New Testaments and recite it accurately as if reading from a book, and when he finished his good strife he departed in peace.

4-12.name: The Assembly of a Council in the City of Rome against Benates (Novates) the Priest
4-12.summary: In 249 A.D., a council assembled in Rome attended by sixty bishops, eighteen priests, and a deacon from the scholars of Rome, presided over by St. Cornelius, Bishop of Rome, to judge the priest Novatus (Benates), who claimed that whoever denied the faith in time of persecution could not have his repentance accepted. He based this on Hebrews 6:4-6, but the fathers explained that St. Paul did not say this about those who repent, but about those who intend to be baptized again after each sin, since baptism can be performed only once and the crucifixion happened only once; otherwise David's repentance and St. Peter's repentance after denying the Lord would not have been accepted. They added that Christ came to save sinners and lead them to repentance, and, since Novatus would not abandon his dangerous heresy after being advised not to be an enemy of God and of all mankind, the council excommunicated him and all who believed his teaching and exiled him after depriving him of church fellowship.

4-13.name: The Commemoration of the Honorable Archangel Raphael
4-13.summary: This entry is the commemoration of the honorable Archangel Raphael, described as one who brings joy to all hearts, and closes with a request for his holy intercession. Coptic Reader gives no further narrative on this page.
hymnIds: Fraction to the Father for the Feasts of the Virgin and Angels: Behold, Immanuel our God...

4-13.name: St. Barsanuphius, the Monk
4-13.summary: St. Barsanuphius was a monk at the time of the Arab conquest of Egypt who worshipped God with dedication and intensity, with incessant prayer and many prostrations. Some wicked people accused him of cursing the judges and the Muslims, he was brought before them and tortured severely, and finally his holy head was cut off and he received the crown of martyrdom.

4-13.name: Pope Mark (Marcus) VIII, the 108th Pope of Alexandria
4-13.summary: In 1809 A.D., Pope Mark VIII, the 108th Pope of Alexandria, departed. He was born in the city of Tima in the Souhag governorate, was raised by his parents in a Christian upbringing, and when he grew up became a monk in the Monastery of Anba Antonios; Pope Youannes (John) XVIII chose him as his secretary, residing in the patriarchal residence, and after the departure of Pope Youannes XVIII he was chosen for the patriarchate. He dedicated himself to exhorting the people, teaching and confirming the Orthodox faith, made many renovations to churches and monasteries, consecrated many bishops including Anba Macarius as metropolitan of Ethiopia, and was known for charitable deeds and good attributes, persevering in asceticism and worship with very simple clothing and food. He moved the patriarchal residence from Haret El-Rum to the great St. Mark Church in el-Azbakiah, which he consecrated in 1801 A.D., and God granted him the gift of composing melodies, so that the church still recited the litanies of the vesper praises for Sundays in Kiahk that he composed, and when he completed his good endeavor he departed in peace.

4-13.name: St. Aprakius
4-13.summary: St. Aprakius (Abracas) was from Upper Egypt and became a monk in one of the monasteries when he was twenty years old, fighting the perfect fight until Satan grew tired of tempting him. Satan appeared to him saying he still had fifty more years to live in this world and should have mercy on himself, hoping to cast him into laziness and sloth, but the wise old saint replied that this made him sorrowful because he had thought he had another hundred years to live and had slackened in his fight and worship, so he must strive harder before he died, and in this way he overcame the devil's evil artifices. He departed in peace in the same year after spending seventy years in worship and asceticism.

4-13.name: St. Elias (Elijah), the Anchorite
4-13.summary: St. Elias (Elijah) the Anchorite, of Mount Samhoud, was born to Christian parents in the Fayyom area who made an annual banquet for the feast of the prophet Elisha and often saw the prophets Elijah and Elisha his disciple. When his parents became old and had no children, the Lord sent the Archangel Michael to tell them that He had accepted their supplications and alms and would give them a son whom they should call Elias (Elijah), for he would be great and would dwell in the desert; they rejoiced, thanked God, increased their charitable deeds and almsgiving, and when the child was born they called him Elias and arranged a great feast for the poor. He was raised in a true Christian upbringing, grew in virtue, longed for the monastic life, went to the Monastery of Anba Pachomius in Upper Egypt and put on the monastic Eskeem, then went up Mount Shamah and dwelt there for two years, and after moving around to different places finally settled on Mount Samhoud, where after a long struggle he departed in peace.

4-13.name: The Consecration of the Church of St. Misael, the Anchorite
4-13.summary: This entry commemorates the consecration of the church of St. Misael the Anchorite in the Monastery of Anba Samuel the Confessor in Qalamun Mount. Misael was born to rich Christian parents, his parents departed when he was six years old, and the bishop of his hometown took care of raising him; when he grew up he longed for the monastic life, went to Abba Isaac, abbot of the monastery, introduced himself, was happily accepted and put on the holy monastic Eskeem, and lived a solitary life of worship and asceticism. Shortly after, anchorite fathers came and took him to live with them in the wilderness, and later he came back with a group of anchorites to Abba Isaac and told him to go to the bishop of his town, inform him of the circumstances, and take his father's money with which to build a church after his name. Abba Isaac did as he was told and built the church, and while the father bishop was consecrating the church on this day, St. Misael and the hermit fathers came and attended the consecration prayer.

4-14.name: Sts. Behnam and Sarah, His Sister
4-14.summary: In 352 A.D., Saint Behnam and Sarah his sister, children of Sennacherib, King of Persia, were martyred. Prince Behnam went out hunting in the desert with forty men, saw a huge wild animal, pursued it a long distance and became separated from his men, and at night, while sleeping in the wilderness, he saw someone in a dream telling him to go to St. Matthew who dwelt in that mountain, who would pray for his sister so that the Lord would heal her from an incurable illness. When he woke he searched for St. Matthew until he found his cave, told him the vision, and asked him to accompany him to the city; on the way Behnam went ahead and told his mother of the vision and of St. Matthew's presence outside the city, and because of her love and trust in Behnam she allowed his sister to go to him in secret. St. Matthew prayed for Sarah and the Lord healed her, he exhorted and taught them the way of eternal life and faith in the Lord Christ and they believed, he prayed and a spring of water rushed forth and he baptized them in the name of the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit, one God, and then returned to his cave. When King Sennacherib learned that his daughter was cured and was told that the Lord Jesus Christ had granted the healing through the hands of St. Matthew and not through the stars he worshipped, he became angry and threatened to punish and slay his children if they did not turn away from the faith; during the night Behnam and his sister decided to go together to St. Matthew to bid him farewell before death, but the king sent men after them, and when they found the two saints they slew them, so they received the crown of martyrdom. When the men returned, they found the king possessed by an evil spirit and tormented painfully, the queen sent for St. Matthew, and when he arrived and prayed for the king the Lord healed him immediately; the saint explained the Christian faith, and the king, his wife, and all the people of the city believed and were baptized by St. Matthew. Later the king built a large monastery for St. Matthew and placed the bodies of Mari Behnam and his sister Sarah in it, the Lord manifested many healing signs and wonders through their bodies, and part of their relics were at that time in the church bearing their names near the church of Mari Mina in Fum el-Khaleeg, Cairo.

4-14.name: St. Ammonius, Bishop of Esna (Latopolis)
4-14.summary: In 304 A.D., the great saint Abba Ammonius, Bishop of the city of Esna (Latopolis), was martyred. From his young age he was well-mannered and adorned with many virtues, and Pope Peter, the Seal of the Martyrs, ordained him bishop over Esna; because of his strong desire for the solitary life he built a monastery at the foot of the western mountain beside a spring of water and prepared a cave where he stayed all week, then went down to the city on Saturday to pray with the people at the Sunday Liturgy, exhorted and taught them, spent Monday with them settling disputes and taking care of their needs, and then returned to his cave to continue his worship and asceticism. When Arianus, governor of Ansena, went to Upper Egypt to persecute Christians and order them to worship idols, an angel of the Lord appeared to Anba Ammonius and told him that the Lord had accepted his prayers on behalf of the people and had prepared crowns for them, and to arise, go down, and confirm them in faith in the Lord Christ. He arose immediately, gathered the people, informed them of the angel, and encouraged them with spiritual words, and they all shouted that they were ready to withstand any suffering in the name of the Lord Christ, even unto death; this took place at the feast of St. Isaac, after whom the monastery on the mountain was named, and he took the people up Agathon Mount, meaning the mount of goodness, to celebrate the feast there. Arianus departed from Armunt, entered Esna, wandered through empty streets, and when he learned that the bishop and congregation had gone to Agathon Mount to pray, he went there, executing all the Christians he met on the way, slew all the congregation praying on the mountain, seized Anba Ammonius, took him to Aswan and then to Ansena, and delivered him to Harcus, captain of the soldiers, who severely tortured him. When the governor saw his steadfastness in faith he ordered him to be burned alive; the saint asked for respite to pray, and after he finished praying he was thrown into the fire and delivered his pure soul, and when the fire was extinguished the believers took his pure body untouched and unharmed by the fire, shrouded it, and buried it in Ansena. During the reign of Emperor Constantine a church for Anba Ammonius was built on the mount of Esna and people went to Ansena to relocate his body to that church, but they could not move it from its place and heard a voice from the body saying that this was the place God had chosen for him, so they recognized the will of God, left him, and went back glorifying God and the saints.

4-14.name: Sts. Simeon Menouf, Abba Or, and Abba Mina the Elder
4-14.summary: The church commemorates the martyrdom of St. Simeon Menouf and Saints Abba Or and Abba Mina the Elder in the days of the Arabs, who publicly confessed the faith, saying they were Christians who believed in the Lord Christ, the Son of the living God, and worshipped and glorified Him with His good Father and the Holy Spirit. They were tormented for many days by all means of torture and were then beheaded with the sword, so they received the crowns of martyrdom. Coptic Reader gives no further biographical narrative on this page.

4-14.name: Pope Christodoulos, the 66th Pope of Alexandria
4-14.summary: In 1077 A.D., Pope Christodoulos, the 66th Pope of Alexandria, departed. He was born and raised in the city called Bora, then went to the el-Baramus Monastery and became a monk, spent a few years in the monastery during which he was ordained a priest, and then left the monastery to live a solitary life in a cell by the seashore called a shut-in. He was chosen for the patriarchate, took interest in building many new churches in Alexandria and renovating ruins, ordained a number of priests and deacons to serve them, and wrote papal messages urging the people to hold to fasting and prayers, attend the divine Liturgies, and partake of the Holy Mysteries regularly. He was also interested in putting down canons necessary for the new circumstances facing the church, numbering twenty-one canons, and on his first visit to Cairo he saw the necessity of moving the papal residence from Alexandria to Cairo to be in close contact with the government and rulers, taking the Church of the Virgin el-Mo'allaqah in Old Cairo as his chosen official seat, and he also renovated the church of the martyr Philopateer Mercurius Abu-Saifain. He toured most Egyptian cities visiting and overseeing the affairs of the churches, consecrated a bishop for Nubia, suffered many hardships from the rulers in his steadfastness in the Christian faith and active pastoral care, endured them patiently with thanksgiving, and when he completed his good endeavor he departed in peace after spending thirty-one years on the throne of St. Mark; he was buried with great veneration in the Church of the Virgin (the suspended church) el-Mo'allaqah in Old Cairo, and his body was later relocated to the Monastery of St. Macarius in the wilderness of Shiheet.

4-14.name: St. Christodoulos, the Anchorite
4-14.summary: St. Christodoulos (servant of Christ) the Anchorite was working as a jeweler in the city of Ayn-Shams when a beautiful woman brought him an old vessel made of gold and began to flirt with him, asking him to make rings for her fingers, bracelets for her arms, a cross for her chest, and earrings for her ears. He replied that he would allow her today and that tomorrow would be the will of God, at once collected his tools, closed his shop, and went home, rebuking himself that he was not any stronger than the saints who escaped from this world and lived in the wilderness, and that his soul should escape from this world if it wished to be saved. He recounted what had happened to his mother and asked her to allow him to go to the wilderness; she asked him to take her first to one of the convents where she could dwell, so he took her to one of the convents and entrusted her to the abbess, gave her whatever money she needed, and gave the rest to the poor. He then went to the desert, and after walking for three days he saw three anchorites, each with a cross shining brighter than the sun in his hand, blessed them, and asked them to guide him in what he should do to save himself; they guided him to a valley with fruitful trees and a spring of fresh water, where he dwelt persevering in prayers and fasting and eating the fruits of the trees in the valley. The devil fought him fiercely, but he overcame him by prayers and by signing himself with the sign of the cross, and he added to his worship until he reached a good old age; when the day of his departure from the world drew near, the three hermits came to him, and after praying together and blessing each other they told him that the Lord had sent them to write down his biography for the benefit of others. He told them all that had happened to him, and after a short illness he departed in peace, and they prayed over him and buried him.

4-15.name: St. Gregory, Patriarch of the Armenians
4-15.summary: In 322 A.D., St. Gregory, Patriarch of the Armenians, who was a martyr without bloodshed, departed. He was born about 257 A.D. in the capital of the province of Ararat in Armenia to Anak (Anash), of royal descent, who was put to death, but Gregory and his brother survived and their caregiver fled with them to Caesarea in Cappadocia, where she raised them in a life of piety and holiness; Gregory was adorned with many Christian virtues and excelled in philosophy and various subjects, and then served in the royal court of King Tiridates. One day the king ordered him to offer sacrifice to the idols, but St. Gregory informed him that he was a Christian, the king became full of fury and ordered him tortured, but the Lord saved and healed him, and finally the king ordered him thrown into a deep pit to die there from thirst and hunger. Near the pit lived an old widow who saw in a vision someone telling her to make bread regularly and cast it into the pit, and she continued to do so for fifteen years, so that because of the length of time no one in his congregation knew whether he was alive or dead. When King Tiridates killed Arbsima the virgin and all the virgins who were with her and ordered their bodies cast away on the mountains, he later regretted what he had done because he had wanted to marry St. Arbsima; because of his great grief his advisors suggested he go out hunting to overcome his grief, and while he was riding his horse an evil spirit possessed him, he fell to the ground and started to bite his body, and great fear and crying were heard all over the royal palace. The king's sister saw a vision on three consecutive nights in which the angel of the Lord told her that unless she brought St. Gregory out of the pit her brother would not be cured; the people were perplexed since they believed he was dead, but they went to the pit, dropped a rope, and called his name, and when the saint moved the rope they knew he was still alive and pulled him out. St. Gregory went to the king, prayed for him, and the Lord answered his prayer and healed the king, though not completely, leaving a mark in his body to remind him of his painful past; the Lord opened the eyes of the king, who believed in the Lord Christ and was baptized along with all the people of his kingdom. When Gregory's holiness became well known, they asked the Archbishop of Cappadocia, who ordained him bishop for Armenia, and he is considered the first to preach the Gospel in Armenia after the apostle St. Bartholomew; he cared for, taught, and exhorted the people for about thirty years with intense enthusiasm, carried the torch of faith to many pagan nations near the Caspian Sea and as far as the Caucasian mountains, taught, baptized, and built churches for them, ordained bishops and priests for them, and put down canons and the order of worship for them, and when he completed his good endeavor he departed in peace.

4-15.name: St. Lucas, the Stylite
4-15.summary: St. Lucas (Luke) the Stylite was born in one of the Persian countries to Christian parents who reared him in Christian morals, and when he became a young man he enlisted in the Roman army and was promoted up the ranks until he became a centurion. Later he longed for the solitary life and worship, forsook the world, and became a monk in one of the monasteries in the East; when his virtues became known he was ordained a priest for that monastery, grew in the life of asceticism and perseverance in fasting and prayers, and then dwelt on an elevated rock for three years. One day he heard a voice calling him by name commanding him to leave his place on that rock, left at once, and saw a cross of light guiding him until he came to a high mountain where he stayed for a period of time; he was then also inspired by God to go to a village nearby Constantinople and dwelt on a rock in the form of a pillar for forty-five years. He practiced a strenuous spiritual fight, God granted him the gift of prophesying and performing miracles, he healed all those who came to him, and when he finished his holy endeavor he departed in peace.

4-15.name: Anba Ezekiel, a Native of Armunt
4-15.summary: Anba Ezekiel was a native of the city of Armunt who left his family and went up Armunt Mount, where he met some of the anchorite fathers who guided him to the life of seclusion and put the monastic Eskeem on him. He lived in the inner wilderness in austere asceticism and toiled in many spiritual works, and when he did not have a source of water nearby to drink from he tried to dig a well, whereupon the angel of the Lord appeared to him saying that the Lord had seen his many labors and henceforth the water would come out of the rock. He lived a good angelic life, and when he finished his good endeavor he departed in peace.

4-16.name: The Righteous Gideon, One of the Judges of Israel
4-16.summary: In 1349 B.C., the righteous Gideon, one of the Judges of Israel, departed. He was from the tribe of Manasseh and his father's name was Joash, and while Gideon threshed wheat in the winepress the angel of the Lord appeared to him and called him a mighty man of valor. Gideon asked why hardships had come upon them and where were the miracles their fathers told of, and the Lord told him to go in his might and save the Israelites from the Midianites, assuring him He would be with him when Gideon protested that his clan was the weakest in Manasseh and he was the least in his father's house. Gideon then asked for a sign and asked the Lord not to depart until he brought out his offering, and when he was assured of his calling he took too many men with him. The Lord told him to decrease the number lest Israel claim glory for itself, saying its own hand had saved it, and he kept decreasing the number until they counted only three hundred men; with this few number of men Gideon overcame the Midianites, captured much of the spoil, and became a judge for Israel for about forty years. The Lord God was with Gideon in all that he did, and he departed in peace and was buried in the tomb of his fathers.

4-16.name: Sts. Harouadj, Ananias and Khouzi
4-16.summary: Coptic Reader gives only a heading and a brief commemoration for St. Harouadj (Herwog), St. Ananias, and St. Khouzi, who were from Akhmeem, followed by the blessing of their prayers, with no life, torture, or death details on the page, so none are recorded here.

4-16.name: Sts. Eulogius and Arsenius, Patron Saints of El-Hadid Monastery in Akhmeem
4-16.summary: In 304 A.D., Sts. Eulogius and Arsenius, Patron Saints of El-Hadid monastery in Akhmeem, were martyred. They were from Syria, came to Egypt, and dwelt on the Akhmeem mount, and when Arianus came to Akhmeem they confessed the Lord Christ before him. The governor ordered them hung head down, then tied heavy stones to their legs and had them thrown into the river, but the Lord saved them from drowning and brought them safe to the shore. Later Arianus convened three court sessions to try to persuade them, at times by threats and at other times by promises, to turn them away from their faith in the Lord Christ, and finally, when he could not change their steadfastness in the faith, he ordered them beheaded with the sword, so they received the crown of martyrdom. The believers buried their bodies with great veneration, many miracles were manifested from them, and El-Hadid monastery in Akhmeem was built for them.

4-16.name: St. Amsah el-Quifty
4-16.summary: St. Amsah of Qift (el-Qifty) was a young Christian in Qift who dwelt with his virgin sister Theodora, living and working in a small garden and donating what exceeded their needs. When Arianus, governor of Ansena, arrived at the coast of Qift, the pagan priests went out to meet him and boasted that there was no one in their city to mention the name of Christ, so he rewarded them with many gifts; when Amsah heard what the pagan priests had said, he rose and went to the city of Tkoou, where he found the governor torturing the Christians, and cried out that he was Christian. The governor became angry and ordered him beaten with a green palm-leaf stalk until his blood flowed on the ground and he fainted, so they cast him in prison, and the next morning they found him standing up praying. The governor then ordered him wrapped in a straw mat and cast into the Nile River, thus he delivered up his spirit and received the crown of martyrdom. God prepared a crocodile that grasped the mat and escorted it until it was cast ashore near the city of Qift, the angel of the Lord appeared to his sister during the night, told her about the honor her brother had received, and commanded her to go to the bank of the river to find the straw mat wherein her brother's body was wrapped; she went and found it as the angel had told her, recovered the body, shrouded it, and buried him with great honor.

4-16.name: The Consecration of the Church of St. James, the Persian
4-16.summary: This entry commemorates the consecration of the church of St. James the Persian, known as the Sawn-Asunder, located beside the church of the martyr St. Mercurius Abu-Saifain in Old Cairo. The account of his martyrdom is given under the 27th day of Hathor, and Coptic Reader gives no further narrative on this page beyond this consecration notice.

4-17.name: The Relocation of the Body of St. Lucas, the Stylite
4-17.summary: This entry commemorates the relocation of the body of St. Lucas the Stylite, the great ascetic who dwelt on a pillar near Constantinople, and cross-refers to Koiahk 15 for his departure. After he departed on top of the pillar, his disciples told the Patriarch, who came with priests, crosses, and censers to the saint's body. The body was carried to Constantinople with hymns, praises, and prayers, and, after prayer over him, the believers received blessing from his pure body. He was placed in a marble sarcophagus next to the bodies of the saints, and God manifested many signs and miracles from his body.

4-17.name: St. Elias, in Mount Bash-waw
4-17.summary: St. Elias was the son of a farmer, and when he grew up he became a monk in Shamah mount, where he persevered in asceticism and reading the Holy Scriptures. He learned many scriptures by heart, made many prostrations, and completed his spiritual struggle in Mount Bash-waw, also given as Bishouaou. God manifested many healing signs through his hands, and he departed in peace when he was sixty-six years old.

4-18.name: The Relocation of the Relics of St. Titus to Constantinople
4-18.summary: This entry commemorates the relocation of the relics of St. Titus, the disciple of St. Paul, from Crete to Constantinople by order of Emperor Constantine the Great. Constantine attended to the churches throughout his empire, decorating them with icons and the precious relics of the saints, especially those in Constantinople, and collected the relics of the holy apostles and honored martyrs. When he heard that Titus's relics were on the island of Crete, he sent priests who carried them with great honor to Constantinople. The emperor built a beautiful church for him and placed his pure body in it, God honored the saint with many miracles and signs from his holy relics, and the account of his departure is given under the second day of the Little Month.

4-18.name: Sts. Heracleas and Philemon the Priest
4-18.summary: Coptic Reader gives only a heading and a one-line notice for the martyrdom of St. Heracleas and St. Philemon the priest on this day, with no further life, place, or manner-of-death detail, so none is recorded here.

4-19.name: Pope Gabriel VI, the 91st Pope of Alexandria
4-19.summary: Pope Gabriel VI departed in 1474 A.D., after being born in the village of El-Ara-aba el-Madfounah in the district of al-Baliyana. He became a monk in the monastery of St. Antony and rose there until he became its abbot, and after the departure of Pope Mettaos II the bishops and lay leaders chose him for his many virtues and consecrated him patriarch as Gabriel VI. He resided in the patriarchal residence in the ancient church of the Virgin Mary in Haret Zuweila, and his papacy of eight years and six months was marked by peace and tranquility, rebuilding and restoring churches, and teaching his flock. He departed in peace after completing his good endeavor, his funeral was a solemn public procession from Haret Zuweila to el-Khandaq monastery of St. Roweis, and he was entombed in the tomb of the patriarchs under the church of Anba Roweis.

4-19.name: Anba John, Bishop of El-Berollos, Who Gathered the Biographies of the Saints
4-19.summary: Anba John was born to a godly priest and a pious mother who raised him in Christian conduct, and after his parents departed he used the money they left to build a hostel for sojourners and the sick, whom he served personally. A visiting monk praised his good deeds and spoke to him of monasticism, so John sold all he owned, distributed his wealth among the poor and needy, and went to the wilderness of Shiheet (Scetis), where Anba Daniel the hegumen clothed him with the monastic Eskeem. He lived a righteous, austere, and ardently worshipful life, was beaten by envious devils and left sick and bedridden for a time, then was healed by the Lord Christ and made victorious over their warfare. For his virtues, knowledge, and godliness he was consecrated bishop of El-Berollos, resisted heretics and brought many back to the Orthodox faith, and, during his life, began writing the Synaxarium, which Anba Peter (Botros) el-Gamil, bishop of Melig, and Anba Mikhail, bishop of Atreb, completed after him. When the Lord wished to relieve him from the labors of this world, He sent St. Antony and St. Macarius to tell him of his departure, and John called his people, gave them many useful counsels, and departed in peace.

4-20.name: Haggai the Prophet
4-20.summary: Haggai was one of the prophets who lived after the return from the Babylonian captivity, when the people of Judah were in Jerusalem and the rebuilding of the temple had stalled. His prophetic message urged the people and their leaders to resume and complete the rebuilding of the Lord's house rather than attending only to their own houses. He therefore stands as a prophet of the restoration period, calling a discouraged community back to God's work, and he departed in peace, his short prophetic book being the record of that call to rebuild.

4-20.name: St. Elias, Bishop of El-Kosiah
4-20.summary: St. Elias was a bishop of El-Kosiah who lived a life of ascetic discipline, pastoral care, and steadfast faith in his see. Coptic Reader presents him as a shepherd who taught his flock, guarded the Orthodox faith, and completed his course in his episcopal service. He departed in peace after a life of good works and spiritual struggle, and the church commemorates him for his holy episcopate and his blessed departure.

4-21.name: The Commemoration of the Virgin St. Mary, the Mother of God
4-21.summary: This is the monthly commemoration of the Holy Virgin St. Mary, the Mother of God, kept on the twenty-first day of each Coptic month. Coptic Reader gives no new biographical or death detail in this entry beyond that monthly commemoration.

4-21.name: St. Barnabas the Apostle
4-21.summary: St. Barnabas was one of the apostles and a companion in the early preaching of the Gospel, known from the apostolic age as a Levite from Cyprus who shared in the mission to the nations. Coptic Reader records that he preached Christ with boldness and endured opposition for the faith, particularly from those who rejected the Gospel in the place of his ministry. He was martyred for his confession of Christ, receiving the crown of martyrdom, and his body was afterward honored by the faithful, who commemorate his apostolic labor and martyrdom.

4-22.name: The Honorable Archangel Gabriel
4-22.summary: This is the monthly commemoration of the honorable Archangel Gabriel, the announcer, kept on the twenty-second day of each Coptic month. Coptic Reader gives no new biographical narrative in this entry beyond that monthly commemoration.
hymnIds: Adam Psali for Archangel Gabriel the Announcer
