4-22.name: Sts. Pachom and Dalusham
4-22.summary: Sts. Pachom and Dalusham were brothers who confessed Christ together and were martyred for their faith. Coptic Reader presents them as steadfast confessors who refused to abandon Christ under persecution and endured torments for His name. They received the crown of martyrdom together, and their martyrdom is commemorated jointly on this day.

4-22.name: Pope Anastasius, the 36th Pope of Alexandria
4-22.summary: Pope Anastasius was the thirty-sixth patriarch of Alexandria, who shepherded the church with doctrinal and pastoral care for his flock. He lived a life of virtue and steadfastness in the Orthodox faith, taught and guided the church, and completed his patriarchal service in peace. He departed in peace, and the church commemorates his blessed departure and his holy patriarchate.

4-23.name: David the Prophet and King
4-23.summary: David was the prophet-king of Israel, chosen from shepherding his father's flock and anointed king, remembered for his psalms, his repentance, and his reign in Jerusalem. Coptic Reader commemorates his departure after a life in which he served God as king and prophet, wrote psalms of praise and repentance, and prepared for the building of the temple. He departed in peace in old age, leaving the kingdom to his son Solomon, and his memory is honored as both a king after God's heart and a prophet who foretold Christ.

4-23.name: St. Timothy the Anchorite
4-23.summary: St. Timothy was an anchorite, a solitary monk who lived a life of severe asceticism, prayer, and withdrawal from the world for the sake of Christ. He persevered in fasting, vigil, and spiritual struggle in his solitary cell, and became known for his holiness and the grace manifested through him. He completed his ascetic course in his anchoritic life and departed in peace, and the church commemorates his blessed departure and monastic example.

4-24.name: St. Ignatius, Theophorus, Patriarch of Antioch
4-24.summary: St. Ignatius, called Theophorus, meaning God-bearer, was martyred in 107 A.D., and church tradition identifies him as the child Jesus took in His arms and set among the disciples, saying that whoever humbles himself as a little child is greatest in the kingdom of heaven. When he grew up he became a disciple of St. John the Evangelist, traveled with him in Asia Minor, and was consecrated bishop of Antioch by the holy apostles, where he had a long and fruitful ministry, converting and baptizing many and writing seven letters full of spiritual teaching to the Ephesians, Magnesians, Trallians, Romans, Philadelphians, and Smyrnaeans, and to St. Polycarp, bishop of Smyrna. When Emperor Trajan visited Antioch, Ignatius boldly confessed that he bore Jesus Christ within him and that the emperor's gods were useless, solid, inanimate statues, and he said he was a priest for Jesus Christ who offered sacrifice daily and desired to offer his life as a sacrifice. Trajan sentenced him to be led to Rome and thrown to the beasts before the Roman people during their festive celebrations, and Ignatius thanked God for the grace of martyrdom. On the way by ship to Smyrna, St. Polycarp and the churches of Asia came to bid him farewell, he sent them pastoral epistles urging them to avoid heterodox teachings, remain united, obey their bishop, and be patient and steadfast in the faith, and from Smyrna he wrote his famous letter to the Romans begging them not to prevent his martyrdom, saying he was God's wheat to be ground by the teeth of wild beasts so as to become the pure bread of Christ. In Rome he was led to the amphitheatre, knelt and offered himself as a sacrifice to God and prayed for the preservation of His church, and the wild beasts devoured him and tore him to pieces, while he called on the name of the Lord Jesus Christ, delivered up his pure spirit, and received the crown of martyrdom. His two deacons, Philemon and Aghathon, gathered his remains and bones, wrapped them in linen, and brought them to Antioch, where they were entombed and many signs and miracles were manifested.

4-25.name: St. John Kama (Khame), the Priest
4-25.summary: St. John Kama departed in 859 A.D. He was a native of Shubra-Manthou in the region of Sa-el-Hagar, the only child of pious Christian parents who raised him in Christian manners and church subjects. His parents forced him to marry against his will, but he and his wife prayed together and mutually agreed to live in celibacy; an angel covered them with his wings and God planted a vine over their sleeping place as a sign of purity. With her permission, he placed his wife in a virgins' convent, where she became a virtuous nun and later its abbess, while an angel guided him to the wilderness of Scetis, where he became a monk under the elder Darudi (Teroti) in the monastery of St. Macarius. The angel then told him to build a monastery a little west of the monastery of St. John the Short, where 300 monks gathered and he taught them prayers, praises and monastic virtues; St. Athanasius the Apostolic appeared to encourage him, and the pure Virgin St. Mary told him the monastery would be named after her and gave him three golden dinars. He departed in peace, his monks buried his pure body in his monastery with great veneration, and his body was later relocated to the monastery of St. Mary known as the Syrian monastery, where it was still present.
hymnIds: Adam Psali for the Departure of Saint John Kame
Watos Psali for the Departure of Saint John Kame

4-25.name: St. Abshai of Mount Toud
4-25.summary: Anba Abshai (Bishay) of Mount Toud departed after a life as an ascetic worshipper from his young age. He read so often in the prophecy of Jeremiah that he saw the prophet in person, and he gave his body no rest because of his many vigils, prayers and prostrations. When he finished his good endeavor he departed in peace. His body was placed in a church that had a well of water, and the Lord manifested many signs and healings for all who used this water. His monastery still existed in the region of Toud, east of Armunt, and was called the monastery of the Saints, where the body of the Holy Father St. Pisentius also lay.

4-26.name: St. Anastasia
4-26.summary: St. Anastasia was martyred in 304 A.D. She was born in Rome in 275 A.D. to a pagan father from the noble men of the city and a Christian mother, who baptized her secretly and nourished her daily with Christian teachings until she was firm in faith, with a priest secretly guiding her spirituality. When she reached marrying age, her father wedded her to a pagan youth against her wishes; she prayed fervently to be separated from him, and during his absence she visited, ministered to and comforted those imprisoned for the faith, until her husband learned of this, shut her in the house and placed guards around it. She prayed that God would save her from his hands, God answered by speeding up his death, and she then distributed her wealth among the poor, the imprisoned and those fighting for the faith. When her account reached Florus the Governor, she confessed the Lord Christ and did not deny him, refused his enticements of many precious gifts, and endured various tortures. He ordered her drowned in the sea, but by God's grace she came out unharmed; later he ordered her hung on a cross with a fire lit under her, and she delivered up her pure spirit and received the crown of martyrdom.

4-26.name: The Consecration of the Church of the Two Martyrs Anba Bishay and Anba Peter
4-26.summary: Anba Bishay and his friend Anba Peter were martyred on the fifth day of the month of Paone. After the end of the era of persecution and during the reign of the righteous Emperor Constantine, the faithful built a church in the city of Boha, the birthplace of Anba Bishay, where his house had been located, and decorated it nicely and with all splendors. The church was consecrated on this day. A church named after them was then presently located in the city of Sadfa, in the diocese of Abu Tig, where their bodies were located, and another church named after them was located in the city of Zagazig.

4-27.name: St. Bisadi (Psote), Bishop of Psoi (Ebsay)
4-27.summary: St. Bisadi was martyred in 304 A.D. He was born in Ebsay in Upper Egypt to Christian parents who worked in farming and shepherding, and he was ordained a deacon and then chosen as bishop of Ebsay, where he cared for his flock and strengthened them in the faith. When Diocletian issued his edict of idol worship, Arianus the governor of Ansena summoned him and tried to persuade him to deny Christ and worship idols, but Bisadi refused and strengthened the Christians, so the governor tortured him in various ways. He was sent to Alexandria, where he was also tortured, then returned to Ansena, where Arianus again tried to make him deny Christ. When Bisadi remained firm, the governor ordered him beheaded, and the soldiers cut off his neck, so he received the crown of martyrdom.

Watos Psali for the Martyrdom of Abba Bisada the Bishop

4-28.name: The Paramoun of the Holy Nativity Feast
4-28.summary: This is the preparation day for the feast of the Nativity of the Lord. Paramoun is a Greek word meaning preparation or readiness, and on this day the Church prepares for the feast with fasting, prayer and strict abstinence. It is observed as a day of preparation before the glorious feast, not as a saint's life or martyrdom.

4-28.name: The Martyrdom of 150 Men and 24 Women from the City of Ansena
4-28.summary: These 174 martyrs were martyred in 304 A.D., during the persecution under Diocletian. They had been idol worshippers, but when they watched St. Paul the Syrian being tortured, with red-hot nails driven into his eyes, and then saw him healed and restored the next morning, they believed in Christ. They confessed their faith before Arianus, the governor of Ansena, refused to return to idol worship, and were beheaded, receiving the crown of martyrdom.

4-28.name: The Grand Opening of the Cathedral of the Nativity of Christ
4-28.summary: On this day in 2019 A.D., His Holiness Pope Tawadros II, the 118th Patriarch of Alexandria, inaugurated the Cathedral of the Nativity of Christ. The opening took place in the presence of President Abdel Fattah El-Sisi and senior state officials. This entry is a modern church-opening commemoration, not a saint's life or martyrdom.

4-29.name: The Feast of the Glorified Birth of Our Lord Jesus Christ
4-29.summary: According to the tradition of the Coptic Orthodox Church, in the year 5501 of the world, in the fullness of time and in the 42nd year of the reign of Caesar Augustus, Our Lord, God and Savior Jesus Christ was born in the flesh from the pure Virgin St. Mary. Through God's divine plan, Caesar Augustus issued a decree for a general census in all the Roman Empire, so St. Joseph, who was from the tribe of Judah, a descendant of King David and from the city of Bethlehem, went with the Virgin St. Mary from Nazareth up to Bethlehem to be counted, and there Mary gave birth to the Savior of the world, wrapped Him in swaddling clothes and laid Him in a manger because they had no place in the inn. Shepherds living out in the fields were told by an angel of the Lord that a Savior, Christ the Lord, was born that day in the city of David, and a multitude of the heavenly host praised God, and the shepherds went to Bethlehem, found Mary, Joseph and the babe lying in a manger, made known what had been told them, and returned glorifying and praising God. The entry then says the prophecies of the birth from a chaste virgin were fulfilled, and it closes by urging contemplation of the mystery of the Incarnation, humility, love of neighbor, doing good, comforting the weak, helping the poor, and being instruments of peace.

4-29.name: The Commemoration of the Martyrs of Akhmeem (Akhmim)
4-29.summary: In 304 A.D., 8,140 were martyred in the city of Akhmeem. When Diocletian denied the faith and spread idol worship, he ordered the governors to persecute Christians, and Arianus, the governor of Ansena, came to Akhmeem accompanied by Anba Abadion, bishop of Ansena, whom he had arrested earlier, arriving on the eve of the glorious Nativity feast. Because their own bishop, Anba Odagious, had passed away about a month earlier, the Christians of Akhmeem invited Abadion to celebrate the Divine Liturgy of the feast for them, and he went secretly to the church of Soutir (Savior), the largest church in the city, prayed with them all night, and the church was filled with Christians from the city and surrounding villages. When Arianus learned that Abadion was praying the feast liturgy with the Christians, he took many soldiers to the church and slew all who were present, a massacre lasting all the day of the feast and reaching 5,800 martyrs, among them Ibeskonda, the chief priest of the idols, who had become Christian and was praying in the church with pagan priests who followed him. Arianus killed them all, and the massacre lasted another two days until the number reached 8,140 martyrs, who all received the crowns of martyrdom and celebrated the feast with the Lord Christ in the paradise of delight.

4-30.name: St. John (Youannis), the Hegumen of Scetis
4-30.summary: St. John departed in 675 A.D. He was born in 585 A.D. in the city of Shubra-Manthou in the region of Sa-el-Hagar to Christian parents, who brought him up in godliness and virtue and taught him church subjects. As a young man he longed for monastic life and went to the monastery of St. Macarius in the wilderness of Scetis in 603 A.D., was later ordained a priest and then Hegumen for the wilderness in 641 A.D., and the wilderness was illumined by his teachings as he became a father to many saints, including Anba Gawarga, Anba Abraam, Anba Mina, bishop of Thmoui, Anba Zacharias, bishop of Sakha, and Anba Isaac, the 41st patriarch. Because of his profound godliness, when he distributed the holy mysteries he could discern, through the Holy Spirit, who was worthy from the unworthy, and several times he saw the Lord Christ on the altar surrounded by angels. He suffered many hardships, being captured three times by the Berbers, who enslaved and degraded him, and on the last occasion he met St. Samuel the Confessor, abbot of el-Qalamun monastery, during his captivity, before by God's grace returning to his monastery and his children. When his departure drew near, it was revealed to him in a heavenly revelation, he gathered his monk sons, commended them to keep the Lord's commandments and walk in the path of the holy fathers, then became ill, saw a crowd of saints coming to accompany his spirit, delivered up his spirit into the hand of the Lord whom he loved, and was buried by the monk fathers with great veneration, while pieces of his clothes, kept out of deep love for him, became a source of healing for many sick people.

4-30.name: The Adoration of the Wise Men (Magi) for the Savior
4-30.summary: On this day also, in the second year of the birth of the Savior, the wise men (Magi) came from the East, fell down and worshipped Him in Bethlehem, and when they opened their treasures they presented Him gifts of gold, frankincense and myrrh. The gold indicates that He is a King, the frankincense denotes that He is God to whom incense is offered in worship, and the myrrh points to His life-giving death for the salvation of the world. Being divinely warned in a dream that they should not return to Herod lest he slay the Child, they departed for their own country by another way, and they preached the manifestation of the incarnate God for the salvation of mankind.

4-30.name: St. Michael el-Tokhy, the Hegumen
4-30.summary: St. Michael el-Tokhy was martyred in 1524 A.D. He was from the city of Toukh el-Nasara in Menofia governorate, memorized the Divine Books and church subjects from his young age and was ordained a deacon, and after his marriage the people chose him and he was ordained priest and then Hegumen. Some evil men brought accusations against him to the Governor of Egypt, who ordered him seized, brought chained in iron fetters and imprisoned, and they dug a deep pit in the ground and crucified him in it with his head down all day, while he remained thankful and praising God. The governor then ordered him paraded in the streets of the city while they reviled him. When Pope Gabriel V learned of him, he prayed for three days asking the holy Virgin St. Mary to help him complete his strife, and when Michael heard that the Pope was praying for him he was comforted and his soul rejoiced. The governor then asked him to deny his faith, but he courageously refused, so they lit a huge fire like the Babylonian furnace and cast him into it, yet the fire did not harm him or scorch his clothes, and he saw the Holy Virgin with four angels surrounding him. Then a soldier stabbed him with a spear, he delivered up his pure soul, and he received the crown of martyrdom.

4-30.name: St. Zacharias the Child and His Companions in Akhmeem
4-30.summary: In 304 A.D., St. Zacharias the Child, his father St. Fag, and their companions were martyred in the city of Akhmeem, the entry numbering 604 martyrs in all. On the second day of the massacre there, while soldiers were casting some martyrs into the fire, the child Zacharias saw angels surrounding the martyrs and placing glorious crowns over their heads, and he shouted to his father and told him what he had seen. When the multitudes heard the child's shouting they rushed to inquire what he had seen, and when the governor saw the multitude running toward the child, he asked the reason, was told, summoned the child and ordered his tongue cut while he was on his father's shoulder. Immediately the Archangel Michael came down and healed the child's tongue, so he talked and rejoiced. When the governor heard of the miracle, he ordered the child and his father burned, but because of this miracle many also believed and declared their Christianity before the governor, who ordered them slain with swords and javelins, and they all received the crowns of martyrdom.

5-1.name: St. Stephen, the Archdeacon
5-1.summary: St. Stephen was the first martyr and the archdeacon and chief of the deacons, filled with the Holy Spirit and wisdom. The Jews accused him of blasphemy after he confessed Christ before the council, and they cast him outside Jerusalem and stoned him. As he was being stoned he saw the heavens opened and the Son of Man standing at the right hand of God. He prayed for Jesus to receive his spirit and asked that the sin not be charged against his attackers, and then he fell asleep in the Lord.

5-1.name: St. Lawindianus
5-1.summary: St. Lawindianus was a Syrian who lived under Emperor Maximianus, who summoned him and tried to entice him with money to abandon his faith. When he refused, he was squeezed in el-Hinbazeen, beaten with pins, and cast into boiling oil and grease, yet Christ strengthened and healed him. The emperor eventually grew weary of torturing him and ordered him beheaded, so he received the crown of martyrdom. His martyrdom became widely known in Syria, where churches and monasteries were later built in his name.

5-1.name: Sts. Dioscorus and Esculapius
5-1.summary: Dioscorus and Esculapius were sons of Ammonius, an archon of Akhmeem, and they became disciples of Father Moisees near a spring on the mountain of Akhmeem. After Moisees departed, they lived an ascetic life for 45 years in the wilderness, and Dioscorus was ordained a priest while Esculapius was ordained a deacon. Under Governor Arianus of Ansena they refused to worship idols, and an angel appeared to Dioscorus in prison and told him to pray for Akodius, Philemon, and the soldiers who would precede him in martyrdom. The soldiers confessed Christ and were beheaded, and then Dioscorus and Esculapius were also beheaded and received the crown of martyrdom, with a monastery later built in their names on the mountain of Akhmeem.
hymnIds: Adam Psali for Martyrdom of Saints Dioscorus and Sklapius
Watos Psali for Martyrdom of Saints Dioscorus and Sklapius

5-2.name: Anba Theonas, 16th Pope of Alexandria
5-2.summary: Anba Theonas was consecrated in AD 282 and departed in AD 301. He was known as righteous, meek, scholarly, gentle, and loving, and he built a church in Alexandria dedicated to the Virgin Saint Mary. Before that time believers had prayed in homes and caves because of pagan persecution, and many people believed and were baptized through his ministry. He also confronted the heretic Sabilius, who denied the triune God and taught that the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit are one person, and he refuted that heresy and excommunicated him before departing in peace.

5-2.name: St. Callinicus, Bishop of Oseem
5-2.summary: St. Callinicus was bishop of Oseem and was martyred in AD 305, for teaching his people to remain steadfast in the Orthodox faith and to refuse idols and incense. When Emperor Diocletian sent soldiers to seize him, he gathered his people in church, prayed the Divine Liturgy, administered the Holy Mysteries, and then willingly delivered himself to the soldiers. The governor tortured him severely, but the Lord healed and comforted him, and the governor then ordered his arm to be split from his hand to his shoulder. He delivered his pure soul amid severe tortures and received the crown of martyrdom, and believers later took his body by night, shrouded it, and buried it with great veneration.

5-2.name: Anba Youna
5-2.summary: Anba Youna was an ascetic who lived in one of the monasteries of Hager Armant and practiced many fasts and acts of asceticism. The Lord granted him the gift of casting out evil spirits and healing the sick, and near his departure some saints appeared to him and invited him to eternal joy. He fell asleep in the Lord at the age of 70, and the monks mourned him while the bishop of the city came, prayed over him, and buried him beside the church of the monastery with great veneration.

5-3.name: The Martyrdom of the Children of Bethlehem
5-3.summary: In the second year after the birth of the Lord Christ, wise men from the East came to Jerusalem asking where the newborn King of the Jews was, because they had seen his star. Herod was troubled, learned from the chief priests that the child would be born in Bethlehem of Judea according to the prophecy of Micah, and sent the wise men to search carefully and report back, although he intended to kill the child. The wise men followed the star to the child, worshipped him, and offered gold, frankincense, and myrrh, and then, warned in a dream, they departed by another way without returning to Herod. In anger Herod ordered all male children in Bethlehem and its districts who were two years old and under to be put to death, fulfilling the prophecy of Jeremiah about Rachel weeping for her children near Bethlehem.

5-4.name: St. John the Evangelist
5-4.summary: St. John was the son of Zebedee and the brother of James the Elder, born in Bethsaida near the Sea of Galilee, where he and his brother worked with their father as fishermen. He had first been a disciple of John the Baptist, but when the Lord called him he left his father and followed Jesus, becoming the disciple whom Jesus loved and the one to whom the Lord entrusted Saint Mary from the cross. He wrote the Gospel of John, three epistles about love, and the Book of Revelation, and he was present at the Transfiguration, the raising of the daughter of Jairus, and the garden of Gethsemane. After preaching in Jerusalem and Judea, then in Asia Minor with Ephesus as his center, he survived torture and boiling oil under Emperor Domitian, was exiled to Patmos for a year and a half, and later returned to Ephesus, where he died in AD 100 after asking his disciples to dig a pit outside the city, praying, and delivering his soul into the hand of the Lord.
hymnIds: Doxology for St. John the Evangelist

5-5.name: St. Eusegnius the Soldier
5-5.summary: St. Eusegnius was a soldier in the army of Emperor Constantine, distinguished for his piety and his merciful deeds toward the poor. When Constantine saw the sign of the Cross in heaven with the words by this you conquer, he summoned Eusegnius, who explained that it was the sign of the Lord Christ. Eusegnius lived until the reign of the apostate Emperor Julian, who accused him after he judged fairly between two men in Antioch and then rebuked him for abandoning the worship of the true God for idols. Julian ordered him crucified with torches at his sides, and after he endured patiently with thanksgiving, Julian ordered him beheaded in AD 362, so he received the crown of martyrdom.

5-5.name: St. Banikarous (Panekyris, the Persian)
5-5.summary: St. Banikarous was a Persian who served in the Roman army, rose to the rank of commander, and was loved by the king for his courage, and he became a friend of Saint Theodore the Oriental and Saint Leontius. When Diocletian learned of their friendship, he sent Banikarous to Armanius, governor of Alexandria and the Five Western Cities, along with four soldiers, and the governor imprisoned him. The Lord Christ appeared to him to encourage and strengthen him, and he was then tortured by being seated in a chair covered with nails, fitted with a red-hot helmet, hung head down with heavy stones around his neck, and burned with torches, yet an angel saved him repeatedly. After a series of tortures through which the angel preserved him, the governor ordered him beheaded in AD 304, and Prince Theoghnostus later carried his pure body to his house and, after the persecution ended, built a great church for him.

5-5.name: Pope Theodosius II, 79th Pope of Alexandria
5-5.summary: Pope Theodosius II was born in the village of Meniat Bani-Khoseeb as Abdel-Messih Ebn Abe-Makin, and he became a monk named Theodosius in the monastery of Abu-Fana. After the departure of Pope Youannes VII, the 77th patriarch, the bishops chose him, ordained him a priest in the monastery, brought him to Cairo, and consecrated him patriarch in AD 1294. The persecution against the Copts that had been stirred up during his predecessor's papacy eased during his days, and in AD 1299 he consecrated the Holy Myron in the church of Saint Mercurius Abu-Saifain in Old Cairo together with twelve bishops. He remained on the apostolic throne for five years, five months, and 28 days, departed in peace in AD 1300, and was buried in al-Nastur monastery in Al-Basatin.

5-5.name: Pope Mettaos I (Matthew), 87th Pope of Alexandria
5-5.summary: Pope Mettaos I was born in the village of Bani-Roah in the district of el-Ashmunain, was raised by Christian parents, memorized the Psalms and liturgical responses in church school, tended his father's sheep, and became a monk in the monastery of Abu-Fana near his hometown. He later went to the monastery of Saint Antony, where he served as a deacon without telling anyone that he was a priest, until a hand from the altar censed him three times during the service and the elders realized that he would one day become patriarch. He fled to Jerusalem to avoid vainglory, later returned to Saint Antony's monastery, suffered hardship under Prince Yalbugha, and then went to el-Muharraq monastery, where he became an example and guide for the monks. After the departure of Pope Gabriel IV he was chosen patriarch, was consecrated in AD 1378 despite cutting the tip of his tongue in an attempt to escape the office, remained on the throne for 30 years, five months, and six days, and departed in peace in AD 1408, at more than 70 years old.

5-6.name: The Honorable Feast of the Circumcision
5-6.summary: The church celebrates the feast of the circumcision of the Lord Jesus Christ on the eighth day after his birth, according to Jewish law, as a fulfillment of the commandment. Saint Paul describes Jesus Christ as a servant of the circumcision for the truth of God to confirm the promises made to the fathers, and he also teaches that believers are circumcised with a circumcision made without hands by putting off the body of the sins of the flesh through the circumcision of Christ. In baptism believers are buried with Christ and raised with him through faith in the working of God, and in the era of grace the church keeps the spiritual circumcision of the heart through repentance and a life of righteousness and holiness. The feast of the Circumcision is one of the seven minor feasts of the Lord celebrated by the church.

Watos Psali for the Feast of Circumcision
Adam Psali for the Feast of Circumcision
Fraction to the Son for the Feasts of Our Lord: We praise and glorify...

5-6.name: The Commemoration of the Ascension of the Prophet Elijah Alive into Heaven
5-6.summary: The church commemorates the taking up of the prophet Elijah alive into heaven, an event that occurred after Elijah went with his disciple Elisha from Gilgal to Bethel and then to the Jordan River. At the Jordan, Elijah took his mantle, rolled it up, and struck the water, which divided so that they crossed on dry ground. A chariot of fire and horses of fire then separated them, and Elijah went up in a whirlwind into heaven while Elisha cried out about the chariot of Israel and its horsemen and saw him no more. Elisha took up the mantle that had fallen from Elijah, returned to the bank of the Jordan, struck the water with it, and crossed back on dry ground.

5-6.name: The Martyrdom of the Four Archons in Esna
5-6.summary: In AD 303, four lay leaders of Esna named Osafius, Saman, Herwog, and Pakhoash were martyred when Governor Arianus returned to Esna for a second time. They were scribes and overseers of the affairs of Esna who were charitable to the poor and needy and providers for widows and orphans, and they came before the governor confessing their faith in the Lord Christ without fear of threats or tortures. The governor ordered them savagely tortured, but their faith was not shaken, and he finally ordered them beheaded, so they received the crowns of martyrdom.

5-6.name: Pope Marcianus, 8th Patriarch of Alexandria
5-6.summary: Saint Marcianus was born in Alexandria, was educated in its schools, and was appointed dean of the Theological School of Alexandria because of his great knowledge, piety, and virtues. After the throne of Saint Mark became vacant following the departure of Pope Omanius, he was elected patriarch by consensus in AD 141. He taught his people and urged them to persevere against heathen persecution, occupied the throne of Saint Mark for ten years and two months, departed in peace in AD 152, and was entombed in Saint Mark's church in Alexandria.

5-6.name: Pope Mark III, 73rd Patriarch of Alexandria
5-6.summary: Pope Mark III, whose name was the deacon Abu el-Farag Ebn Abi el-Saad, was of Syrian origin, worked as a merchant, and was well known for his purity, celibacy, and piety. He was chosen patriarch in AD 1166 and served his flock with purity, prayers, and many tears because of the hardships that befell the Coptic people during the Crusades. When Salah al-Din el-Ayyubi took over the government of Egypt and the status of the Copts improved, he undertook a pastoral tour and visited his flock in all the regions of Egypt. He sat on the throne of Saint Mark for 22 years and seven months, departed in peace in AD 1189, and was buried in the monastery of Saint Macarius in the wilderness of Shiheet.

5-6.name: Pope Gabriel III, 77th Patriarch of Alexandria
5-6.summary: Pope Gabriel III departed in AD 1271, after a pontificate that lasted only two years. During that time he made the Holy Myron and consecrated it in the church of the Holy Virgin el-Mo'allaqah in Old Cairo with the participation of many bishops. He then departed in peace and was entombed in the church of the martyr Mercurius Abu-Saifain in Old Cairo.

5-6.name: St. Basil the Great, Archbishop of Caesarea, Cappadocia
5-6.summary: St. Basil was born in AD 329 in Sebaste, Cappadocia, to a religious family, and his brothers were Saint Gregory, bishop of Nyssa, and Saint Peter, bishop of Sebaste. He studied rhetoric, philosophy, and natural sciences in Caesarea of Palestine, then in Constantinople and Athens, where he was a friend and fellow student of Saint Gregory the Theologian and of Julian, who later became emperor and apostatized from the faith. In AD 358 he abandoned the world, came to Egypt, learned piety, virtues, and ascetic life from its monks, and then lived in seclusion in the wilderness of Pontus, where he founded a monastery and set down canons to guide his followers toward evangelical perfection, becoming the first founder of monasticism in Pontus and Cappadocia. He was ordained a priest in AD 362, was chosen Archbishop of Caesarea in Cappadocia in AD 370, endured many hardships from the Arian Emperor Valens, worked many miracles, composed the Liturgy of Saint Basil used regularly by the Coptic church along with many spiritual, ascetic, and canonical books, and departed in peace in AD 379.

5-6.name: The Consecration of the Church of St. Isaac el-Defrawi of Tiphr e
5-6.summary: On this day the church of the martyr Saint Isaac el-Defrawi of Tiphr e was consecrated, after believers had taken his pure body in expensive shrouds and sent it to his hometown of Tiphr e, also called Defra. A church was built in his name in the same place where he had lived, and the bishop of the diocese consecrated it on this day and placed his pure body in it. The Lord manifested many wonders in this church, and all who suffered from incurable diseases and went to the church received healing when they entered it and received the blessing of the body of the saint.

5-7.name: St. Silvester, Pope of Rome
5-7.summary: St. Silvester was born in Rome to Christian parents, was raised by his mother in Christian principles after his father's departure, studied church subjects and philosophy, and was ordained a priest. Because his virtues and knowledge became well known, he was chosen for the pontificate of Rome in AD 324 after the departure of his predecessor Saint Miltiades, during the reign of Emperor Constantine the Great. He repaired what the oppressors had corrupted, cared for teaching the people and confirming them in the Orthodox faith, and convened a council in France in which he excommunicated the heresy of Donatism. During his days the First Universal Council convened in Nicea in AD 325 to judge Arius, where 318 bishops excommunicated Arius, affirmed the divinity of the Lord Christ, and set down the Nicene Creed of Faith, and after remaining on the Apostolic Throne for eleven years he departed in peace in AD 335.

5-8.name: The Return of the Head of St. Mark the Apostle
5-8.summary: In AD 644, the church celebrates the return of the head of Saint Mark the Apostle, which had been kept in the church of Saint Mark in Bokalia, also called the place of cows or Dar El-Bakar, in Alexandria. An Arab sailor entered the church, found the reliquary, and thrust his hand into the sarcophagus of Saint Mark thinking he would find gold, but when his hand came upon the head he stole the expensive shrouds, took the head by night, and hid it in a ship without telling anyone. When Amr Ibn El-As was about to leave Alexandria, all the ships sailed except the one carrying the head of Saint Mark, despite the sailors' attempts to move it, and when Amr ordered the ship searched the head was found hidden inside it and the ship sailed at once after the head was removed. Amr summoned the sailor, who confessed his crime and was punished, and Amr then inquired about Pope Benjamin I, the 38th Patriarch of Alexandria, who had fled to the monasteries of Upper Egypt, sent a circular to all the cities of Egypt guaranteeing the pope's safety, and handed the holy head back to him when he returned.

5-8.name: Pope Andronicus, 37th Pope of Alexandria
5-8.summary: Pope Andronicus was born in Alexandria to wealthy Christian parents, was brought up well, studied the holy books, and was ordained a deacon because of his knowledge and piety, caring for the poor and needy. After the departure of Pope Anastasius, the bishops and archons unanimously agreed to consecrate him patriarch, and his enthronement took place on the 24th of Koiahk in AD 616. Many hardships befell him from the Persian invaders, who destroyed 600 inhabited monasteries around Alexandria and killed the monks in them, and also killed 700 monks who lived in caves around those monasteries. He went around among his people to console them and confirm them in faith and patience, and after finishing his good endeavor he departed in peace in AD 623.

5-8.name: Pope Benjamin I, 38th Pope of Alexandria
5-8.summary: Pope Benjamin I was born in the city of Barset, also called Barshout, in the Beheira governorate, to wealthy Christian parents who raised him with a Christian upbringing, and he became a monk under the saintly elder Theonas in the monastery of Saint Knobus west of Alexandria. He grew in virtue and in studying the holy books of the church, saw a vision in which an angel told him that he would shepherd the flock of the Lord Christ, and increased in asceticism and prayer after his spiritual father warned him against pride and the warfare of the devil. When Theonas was forced to go to Alexandria he took Benjamin with him to Pope Andronicus, who ordained Benjamin a priest and kept him to assist in pastoral care, and after Andronicus departed Benjamin was unanimously chosen patriarch and consecrated in AD 623. He faced many hardships from el-Moquakas, who was both governor and Chalcedonian patriarch, fled with divine guidance to the wilderness of Shiheet, witnessed its destruction by the Persians, and then went to Upper Egypt, where he lived in a monastery, wrote papal messages to confirm the people in faith and endurance under persecution, and remained in hiding for thirteen years. He returned to the papal place in Alexandria after receiving a message of peace from Amr Ibn El-As and receiving from him the head of Saint Mark that had been stolen by a sailor, and he then visited his flock, renovated ruined monasteries and churches, explained correct Orthodox teaching to those led astray by Chalcedonian teaching, received many back into the church, and ordained bishops and priests before departing in peace in AD 662.

5-8.name: Pope Gabriel V, 88th Pope of Alexandria
5-8.summary: Pope Gabriel V was a monk of the monastery of the great Saint Anba Samuel the Confessor, where he lived a distinguished monastic life, was called the prominent Gabriel by his fellow monks, and was known for the sweet aroma of his life, so that his predecessor Pope Mettaos I prophesied that he would become patriarch after him. When the bishops and lay leaders gathered to choose a pope for Alexandria they remembered this prophecy, and he was consecrated patriarch in AD 1409. He was known for simplicity and asceticism, visited his flock on foot despite many hardships, exerted great effort in confirming the people in the faith and rebuilding ruined churches, and served as an ambassador of peace between the Egyptian Sultan and the kings of Ethiopia. He also cared for church rituals and set down a book for them, finished his good endeavor, departed in peace in AD 1427, and was buried with great honor in the church of the Virgin in Babylon el-Darag in Old Cairo.

5-8.name: The Consecration of the Church of St. Macarius the Great
5-8.summary: In AD 655, the church of Saint Macarius the Great in his monastery in the wilderness of Shiheet was consecrated by Pope Benjamin I, the 38th Patriarch of Alexandria. While Benjamin was consecrating the altar with the Holy Myron, he saw the hand of the Lord Christ anointing the altar with him, and he also saw an elder with a shining countenance, so he thought to himself that this monk was fit to be a bishop. An angel of the Lord told him that the elder was Saint Macarius, the father of patriarchs, bishops, and all monks, who had come that day to rejoice with his children, and that if the monks obeyed his commandments and followed his orders they would be with him in glory, but if they disobeyed they would have no share with him. Saint Macarius replied that if even one grape remained in a bunch the blessing of the Lord would be on it, and that if love for one another remained among the monks he believed the Lord would never keep them away from his kingdom, and Pope Benjamin marveled at the abundant mercy of Saint Macarius.

5-9.name: St. Abraam, Bishop of El-Fayoum
5-9.summary: St. Abraam departed in 1914 A.D., after serving as Bishop of El-Fayoum and Giza. Coptic Reader presents him as a holy father noted for his pastoral care and generosity to the poor. He departed, rather than being martyred, and the entry closes with a blessing asking for his prayers.

5-9.name: St. Phees
5-9.summary: St. Phees is commemorated on this day as a saint who departed in peace after a life of devotion and ascetic discipline. Coptic Reader describes his steadfast spiritual life and his separation from worldly concerns. It records his peaceful departure, not a martyrdom, and closes with a blessing asking for his prayers.

5-10.name: The Paramouni of the Honorable Theophany Feast
5-10.summary: This is not the commemoration of a person, but the preparatory eve before the Feast of the Theophany, or Epiphany. Coptic Reader explains that the Church observes this Paramouni in preparation for celebrating Christ's baptism and manifestation the following day. It therefore marks the transition into the feast, rather than recording a birth, death, or martyrdom.
hymnIds: Fraction to the Father for the Theophany: As You have bestowed...

5-10.name: St. Justus, Disciple of Anba Samuel the Confessor
5-10.summary: St. Justus was a disciple of Anba Samuel the Confessor and lived a monastic life under his guidance. Coptic Reader describes his obedience, ascetic struggle, and faithful service in the monastery. He remained with his spiritual father through hardship and persecution, and he departed in peace after a life of monastic devotion.

5-11.name: The Honorable Theophany Feast
5-11.summary: This feast commemorates the baptism of Jesus Christ by St. John the Baptist in the River Jordan. At the baptism, the heavens were opened, the Holy Spirit descended in the form of a dove, and the voice of the Father testified to the Son. Coptic Reader presents this event as the revelation of the Holy Trinity and the beginning of Christ's public ministry.

5-11.name: Pope Youannes VI, 74th Patriarch of Alexandria
5-11.summary: Pope Youannes VI departed after serving as the 74th Patriarch of Alexandria. Coptic Reader describes his leadership of the Church, his care for his flock, and his work in guiding the faithful. He departed in peace after completing his patriarchal service, and the entry closes with a blessing asking for his prayers.

5-11.name: Pope Benjamin II, 82nd Patriarch of Alexandria
5-11.summary: Pope Benjamin II departed after serving as the 82nd Patriarch of Alexandria. Coptic Reader describes his patriarchate, his shepherding of the Church, and his endurance through the difficulties of his time. He departed in peace, and the entry closes with a blessing asking for his prayers.

5-12.name: The Second Day of the Feast of the Holy Theophany
5-12.summary: This entry continues the celebration of the Theophany, the baptism of Christ in the Jordan by St. John the Baptist. It recalls the manifestation of Christ, the descent of the Holy Spirit as a dove, and the voice of the Father. The feast is therefore celebrated over more than one day, with this entry marking its second day.

5-12.name: The Commemoration of the Honorable Archangel Michael
5-12.summary: This entry commemorates the Archangel Michael, the chief of the heavenly hosts and a powerful intercessor for the faithful. The Church celebrates his commemoration on this day, recalling his service to God and his protection of believers. The entry does not record a death or martyrdom, since Michael is an archangel, and it closes with a blessing asking for his intercession.

5-12.name: St. Theodore El-Mishreke (the Oriental)
5-12.summary: St. Theodore, called El-Mishreke or the Oriental, was a soldier and martyr who openly confessed his Christian faith. He was brought before the authorities, refused to sacrifice to idols, and endured torture for his steadfast confession. He was finally martyred by beheading, receiving the crown of martyrdom.

5-12.name: St. Anatolius
5-12.summary: St. Anatolius was a Persian martyr who confessed Christ during a time of persecution. He was arrested, interrogated, and tortured for refusing to renounce his faith. He remained steadfast under suffering and was martyred, receiving the crown of martyrdom.

5-13.name: The Feast of the Wedding at Cana of Galilee
5-13.summary: This feast commemorates the wedding at Cana of Galilee, where Jesus, His mother, and His disciples were present. When the wine ran out, Jesus turned water into wine at His mother's request, performing His first recorded miracle. Coptic Reader presents this miracle as a revelation of Christ's glory and power, and as a blessing of marriage.

5-13.name: St. Demiana
5-13.summary: St. Demiana was a young virgin martyr who, with her father, withdrew to a life of prayer and devotion. When persecutors demanded that she renounce Christ, she refused and encouraged the virgins with her to remain steadfast. She was tortured and finally beheaded, receiving the crown of martyrdom together with the other virgins.

5-13.name: St. Theophilus, the Monk
5-13.summary: St. Theophilus was a monk who lived a life of asceticism, prayer, and devotion in the monastery. Coptic Reader describes his spiritual discipline, his love of solitude, and his faithful monastic struggle. He departed in peace after completing his monastic life, and the entry closes with a blessing asking for his prayers.

5-14.name: St. Archelides, the Monk
5-14.summary: St. Archelides was born in Rome to righteous Christian parents, and his father died when he was six years old. After serving as an honorable army officer, he was moved by seeing a drowned man's body on the shore and went to Palestine, where he became a monk under Father Romanus and lived in solitude. He received the gift of healing the sick and vowed never to see a woman's face for the rest of his life. When his mother finally came to his cell, he had already departed, and she also delivered up her soul beside him, so the two bodies were buried together.

5-14.name: St. Mahrati (Mohrael)
5-14.summary: St. Mahrati was born in Tamouh to godly Christian parents, and her father was a priest. As a young girl, she went without telling her parents to declare her Christian faith before Arianus, the governor at Ansena, and she remained steadfast when he tried to persuade her to change her resolve. She was tortured with the Hinbazeen and placed on an iron chair over a hot fire, which she endured patiently despite her youth and thin body. When the governor failed, he shut her in a cave full of serpents and scorpions, where she delivered up her pure soul and received the crown of martyrdom, and her body was later moved to Tamouh, where a church was built for it.

5-14.name: St. Maximus, the Brother of St. Dometius
5-14.summary: Coptic Reader gives only a short entry for St. Maximus, the brother of St. Dometius, stating that he departed in 382 A.D., and giving no further details of his life or place of origin. The entry refers the reader to the biography of St. Dometius recorded under the 17th day of Tobe. It then closes with a blessing, and no cause of death beyond his departure is given.

Doxology for St. Maximus and St. Dometius
Melody for St. Maximus and St. Dometius

5-15.name: Obadiah, the Prophet
5-15.summary: Obadiah was the fourth of the twelve Minor Prophets, and his prophecy is dated to about 584 B.C., after the fall of Jerusalem because of Edom's alliance with the Babylonians. He warned Edom that it would be judged by God and threatened with destruction and ruin, while also prophesying the return of the Jews from exile. His book consists of only one chapter, and the entry applies his message to proud souls and to those who rejoice in others' misfortunes. The prophecy is also read as pointing to the salvation, sanctification, and inheritance of Jacob in the Lord's kingdom, and Obadiah is recorded as having departed, not as having been martyred.

5-16.name: St. Philotheus
5-16.summary: St. Philotheus was martyred in 304 A.D., after being born in Antioch to pagan parents. At ten years old he refused his father's request to worship the bull they worshipped, and after an angel taught him about creation and the incarnation of Christ, he fasted, prayed, gave alms, and his parents came to believe and be baptized through his prayers. God granted him the gift of healing the sick, and when Emperor Diocletian ordered him to offer incense to idols, he refused despite promises and threats. He was severely tortured and finally beheaded, receiving the crown of martyrdom, and churches were later built in his name.
hymnIds: Adam Psali for the Martyrdom of Saint Philotheus
Watos Psali for the Martyrdom of Saint Philotheus

5-16.name: Pope John IV, 48th Patriarch of Alexandria
5-16.summary: Pope John IV, also called Youannes, departed in 799 A.D., after serving as the 48th Patriarch of Alexandria. He was born in the village of Abu Sair and became a monk in the monastery of St. Macarius, where he spent many years in worship, asceticism, and study before being ordained a priest for the church of St. Mina. After Pope Mina departed, he was chosen by lot and consecrated patriarch on the 16th day of Tobe in 777 A.D. He taught and visited his flock, cared for the poor during a severe famine, and built and renovated many churches. He departed in peace after telling the priests that he had been born, consecrated, and would depart on the same 16th day of Tobe, and he commended his disciple Mark to succeed him.

5-17.name: St. Dometius, the Brother of St. Maximus
5-17.summary: St. Dometius, who departed in 382, was a son of Emperor Valentinian and was raised with his brother Maximus and their sister in a true Christian upbringing. Visits by monks to the imperial palace drew the two brothers to monastic life and solitude, and with their father's permission they went first to Nicaea, where they met the monk John, and then to Syria to be disciples of St. Aghabius. After six years with Aghabius, and after his death, they fled to Egypt when others wanted Maximus made patriarch, and St. Macarius gave them a cave, taught them to plait palm leaves, and gave them bread, salt, and the exercises of the solitary life. They spent three years in prayer, fasting, and asceticism, attending church in silence every Sunday, and Macarius saw them praying all night with a ray of light rising from their mouths to heaven while an angel guarded them with a sword of fire. Maximus died of a severe fever on Tobe 14, Dometius died three days after his brother, and Macarius buried them in their cave.
hymnIds: Adam Psali for the Departure of Saints Maximus and Dometius
Watos Psali for the Departure of Saints Maximus and Dometius
Doxology for St. Maximus and St. Dometius
Melody for St. Maximus and St. Dometius

5-17.name: Anba Yusab el-Abbah, Bishop of Girga
5-17.summary: Anba Yusab, born Joseph in 1735 in el-Nekhila in Assiut governorate in Upper Egypt to righteous Christian parents, was raised in piety and dedicated from youth to reading and studying the holy books. At 25 he entered the Monastery of Anba Antonios, where he became known for meekness, love of the ascetic life, and profound theological knowledge. Pope John (Youannes) XVIII, the 107th Patriarch, was impressed by him in discussion, brought him to the patriarchate, and ordained him bishop of Girga and Akhmeem in 1791. He visited his flock, taught and reformed morals, opposed foreign missions entering Upper Egypt, answered letters from the Pope of Rome with theological proofs, toured Egyptian cities teaching, and published books and articles confirming Orthodox faith. In old age he returned to the Monastery of Anba Antonios, where he departed in peace in 1826 at 91, and the entry says his pure body remained whole in a shrine in the monastery.

5-18.name: St. James, Bishop of Nisibis
5-18.summary: St. James, who departed in 338, was born in Nisibis in Mesopotamia, was brought up in godliness and love for the poor, and studied the Holy Bible and some other subjects. He cherished the monastic life of worship, prayer, fasting, and asceticism, and God granted him the gift of performing miracles, so the fame of his holiness and virtues became well known. When the bishop of Nisibis departed, the clergy and people chose James as bishop to shepherd them in 319, and he persevered in piety and asceticism, comforting mourners, visiting the sick, attending to the poor, widows, and orphans, and building churches. He was one of the bishops who attended the First Universal Council at Nicaea in 325 and agreed to its decisions and canons. When Shapur, the Persian king, besieged Nisibis and opened a crevice in its wall to enter the city, James prayed for God to protect his people, and in the morning Shapur found the walls standing as before while God sent swarms of mosquitoes and wasps over the army, which fled, after which James completed his good endeavor and departed in peace.

5-18.name: Mary and Martha, the Sisters of Lazarus
5-18.summary: The church arranged a commemoration for Mary (Mariam) and Martha, the sisters of the beloved Lazarus, whom the Lord raised from the dead, and the two saints were born in Bethany, where Jesus found rest in the house of Lazarus and his sisters. Each expressed love for Christ in her own way: Martha showed hospitality and did what would comfort him, while Mariam sat at his feet, heard his word, and anointed the Savior's feet with very costly oil of spikenard. The Lord praised her, saying that wherever the gospel is preached in the whole world, what this woman did would also be told as a memorial to her. When Lazarus died, a conversation between the Lord and the two sisters expressed their faith that Christ is the Son of God who is to come into the world.

5-18.name: Anba Andrew (Andras), known as Abou El-Leef
5-18.summary: Anba Andrew, known as Abou El-Leef, was a seventh-century father and a disciple of Anba Pisentius (Bisentious), bishop of Qift. He was born in Shanhor to Christian parents, his father was a simple farmer, and he was raised in a Christian upbringing, gave his food to the needy, fasted until evening, and used tending his father's sheep as an opportunity for seclusion, prayer, and conversing with God. The entry records his departure as the close of that ascetic and obedient life, and it gives no martyrdom account for him.

5-19.name: The Discovery of the Relics of Sts. Abahour, Bisoura, and Their Mother Ampera
5-19.summary: The entry commemorates the discovery, in 1238, of the relics of St. Abahour, his brother Bisoura, and their mother Ampera, who had been martyred in the pagan era and whose bodies were kept in a wooden reliquary in the church at Shabas el-Shouha'da in the Desouk district. During the Fifth Crusade, when the Crusaders invaded Egypt and occupied Damietta in the days of El-Kamil, soldiers ruined churches, including the church at Shabas, and a soldier took the reliquary, thinking it valuable, then threw the relics beside a wall and sold the box. A priest's wife found them, placed them in the church, and covered them with brick, and after 20 years she remembered them, the priests uncovered them, and they were placed in a new reliquary. The entry says many miracles and healings then took place through the relics.

5-20.name: St. Prochorus, One of the Seventy Apostles
5-20.summary: St. Prochorus was one of the Seventy and one of the seven deacons chosen in Acts 6, and he was related to St. Stephen, the archdeacon and protomartyr. He accompanied St. John the Theologian on most of his missionary journeys, and John later ordained him bishop of Nicomedia. There he preached, baptized believers, and endured hardships for the sake of evangelism. The entry says he departed in peace rather than by martyrdom.

5-20.name: Anba Kloag (Bagoug) the Priest
5-20.summary: Anba Kloag, also called Bagoug, was a priest from Elfant who was martyred in 304, and his parents were the Christians Dioscorus and Euphemia. He was educated in the church school, was known from youth for holiness and mercy to the poor, and was ordained priest of his village church, where he shepherded his flock sincerely. When Arianus the governor came to Elfant to force idol worship, Kloag gathered his flock for the liturgy, preached steadfastness until the last breath, and then went to Arianus and confessed Christ. Arianus tried to entice him with high positions, then tortured him severely, first in Elfant and again in Ahnasia, but an angel strengthened him and miracles occurred in prison. He was ordered back to his hometown and beheaded there, receiving the crown of martyrdom, and the entry says a church bearing his name in Elfant still holds his body in a reliquary.

5-20.name: St. Behna (Bahnu)
5-20.summary: Coptic Reader gives only the heading and the one-line statement that St. Behna (Bahnu) was martyred on this day, with no further life or martyrdom detail, so none is recorded here.

5-20.name: The Consecration of the Church of St. John, the Owner of the Golden Gospel
5-20.summary: This entry commemorates the consecration of the church of St. John, known as El-Kokhy and as the owner of the Golden Gospel, in Rome. It says his body was relocated from Constantinople to that church. It also cross-refers his departure to the 16th day of Epep and gives no separate life narrative in this entry.

5-21.name: The Departure of the Virgin St. Mary, the Mother of God
5-21.summary: The Virgin St. Mary, the Mother of God, is said to have departed in 48, after living for 15 years in the house of St. John the Beloved following the Ascension and often visiting the holy sepulcher to pray. When the Holy Spirit informed her that the time of her departure had come, she rejoiced, the apostles gathered, and she blessed them. The entry says the Lord Jesus came in person, surrounded by holy angels, and received her pure spirit, which ascended to heaven. The apostles carried her body to Gethsemane and entombed it with great veneration, after an incident on the way in which a Jew who tried to stop the procession had his arms separated and then restored when he repented and believed. The entry puts her whole earthly life at about 60 years.

Watos Psali for the Assumption of the Virgin St. Mary
