The Hymn of the Ten Strings of the Harp

5-21.name: St. Hilaria, the Daughter of Emperor Zeno
5-21.summary: St. Hilaria, daughter of Emperor Zeno, departed in 513, after being raised with her sister Thaopesta in a true Christian upbringing in the later fifth century. Longing for virginity and monastic life, and unable to enter a convent near Constantinople because she feared her father, she dressed as a man, sailed to Alexandria, and went to the wilderness of Shiheet, to the Monastery of St. Macarius the Great. Anba Pemwah received her as the monk Hilary, placed her in a cave far from the monastery, and for 15 years she lived in austere asceticism, coming to the monastery only to partake of the Holy Mysteries and being called Hilary the eunuch because she did not grow a beard. When her sister Thaopesta was possessed by an unclean spirit and sent to Shiheet, the monks prayed for many days without healing her, then entrusted her to Hilary, who recognized her sister, prayed fervently, and healed her. After her father, troubled by Hilary's embracing and kissing of Thaopesta, summoned Hilary to Constantinople, she obtained an oath on the Bible that she could return to the wilderness, revealed that she was his daughter Hilaria, and, after a month in the palace and her father's provision of annual wheat and oil for the monks and help in building a fortress at the Monastery of St. Macarius, returned to Scetis, where she lived another 12 years in asceticism before departing and being buried with great veneration.

5-22.name: St. Anthony the Great
5-22.summary: St. Anthony the Great was born in 251 at Qiman El-Arous to rich parents who loved the church and the poor, and after his father's death he was moved by Matthew 19:21 to sell all he owned, provide for his sister in a house of virgins, and give the rest to the poor and the churches. He first lived in a hut beside the Nile, learned from nearby hermits, and then lived in an ancient Pharaonic tomb beside a fig tree on the eastern bank, where he endured fierce attacks from the devil and was beaten until he lost consciousness and speech. He later went deep into the eastern desert, lived beside a spring and cave for 20 years in fasting and worship, and then emerged to guide the many disciples who gathered around him, founding what the entry calls the first monastic institution in the world and becoming the father of all monks. He went to Alexandria in 311 to encourage believers during the persecution under Maximinus and again in 355 to defend the Orthodox faith beside Pope Athanasius, and he corresponded with Emperor Constantine, urging him to seek his own salvation and the success of his kingdom. He visited St. Paul the first anchorite before his death, shrouded and buried him, later gave his staff to St. Macarius and his sheepskins to Athanasius and Serapion, and departed at 105, asking that his body be hidden.
hymnIds: Adam Psali for the Departure of Saint Antony the Great
Watos Psali for the Departure of Saint Antony the Great
Doxology for St. Anthony and St. Paul
The Great Saint Abba Antony Father of Monks (Tobe 22)

5-23.name: St. Timothy the Apostle
5-23.summary: St. Timothy the Apostle, martyred in 97, was born in Lystra in Asia Minor to a Greek father and a Jewish mother, and his mother raised him in godliness and the study of the Holy Scriptures, with the genuine faith that had dwelt in his grandmother Lois and his mother Eunice. He believed, was baptized by St. Paul, became his disciple, accompanied him on most of his missionary journeys, and was ordained by Paul as bishop of Ephesus. Paul wrote him two epistles, the first in 64 on pastoral duties and church ordinances and the second in 67 urging him to strive and keep the faith. His pastoral work attracted many pagans to Christianity, and wicked Jews and heathens rose against him, beat him severely with sticks and rods, and killed him in Ephesus, where the faithful buried his body with great veneration.

5-23.name: Pope Cyril (Kyrillos) IV, 110th Patriarch of Alexandria
5-23.summary: Pope Cyril IV, the 110th Patriarch of Alexandria, departed in 1861, after being born in 1816 in Sawamaa in the Sharq district of Akhmeem and being taught church subjects with great care by his father. He longed for monastic life, became the monk Daoud el-Antony at the Monastery of St. Anthony, and was later ordained priest and appointed abbot by Pope Peter el-Gawly, the 109th Patriarch, whom he also served by going to Ethiopia to settle a dispute. After Peter's death in 1852, he was consecrated general metropolitan in April 1853 as Anba Kyrillos and enthroned as patriarch in 1854. He devoted himself to education, founding schools for boys and girls, promoting the Coptic language and church hymns, buying a printing press to publish church books, renovating St. Mark's Church in Azbakyah in Cairo, consecrating bishops, and visiting the church in Ethiopia. He sat on the throne of St. Mark for about seven years, was buried in St. Mark's Church in Cairo amid national grief, and was called the father of reformation, Abi el-Eslah, for his many accomplishments.

5-24.name: St. Mary the Ascetic (The Shut-In)
5-24.summary: St. Mary the Ascetic, called the Shut-In, was born in Alexandria to wealthy Christian parents who raised her in a Christian upbringing, and she declined marriage proposals from many sons of the city's nobles. After her parents died, she distributed all they had left among the poor and needy, became a nun in a convent near Alexandria, and spent 15 years in much worship before putting on the holy Eskeem, with clothes made of hair. With the abbess's permission she shut herself in her cell, leaving only a small window for her spiritual and physical needs, fasting two days at a time on dried bread and every three days during Lent, and remaining in her cell for 22 years. On the feast of Theophany she asked for a little Lakkan water, washed her hands and feet, partook of the Holy Mysteries, then became ill, bade farewell to the abbess and nuns, and departed in peace, after which she was carried to the church, prayed over, and placed with the bodies of the holy virgins.

5-24.name: Anba Bisada the Priest
5-24.summary: Anba Bisada the Priest, also called Psate or Ibsadeh, was martyred in 304, and his mother, the daughter of a pagan priest from Eh-Reet, had believed in Christ, fled a proposed marriage to a pagan priest's son, and married a Christian farmer in El-Kais. He was raised in the fear of God and keeping of the commandments, inherited great wealth when his father died at Bisada's age of 20, gave alms to the poor, grew in worship and godliness, and was ordained a priest. When Diocletian renounced the faith, a voice from heaven asked why he was slackening when the crown was ready, so he confessed Christ before the governor, was scourged with whips and pins, had his nails pulled out, and had his fingers dipped in vinegar and lime, yet the Lord supported and healed him. He was sent in chains to El-Fayyoum, where he raised a child killed by a large falling stone, confessed his faith again before its governor, was tortured severely and strengthened by the Lord, and was then sent to Armanius, governor of Alexandria, where he confessed a third time and was beheaded, receiving the crown of martyrdom. St. Julius El-Akfehasi took his body to Ah-Reet, where it was buried with great veneration, and the entry says the Lord manifested many miracles from his body.

5-25.name: St. Peter of Scetis (the Ascetic)
5-25.summary: St. Peter was at first a hard-hearted, merciless tax collector who refused a poor man charity and instead hit him on the head with a loaf of bread so he would not return. That night he dreamed of the Last Day, with a scale of justice on which devils placed his sins and injustices, while luminous angels found no good deed for the other pan except that loaf of bread. Waking trembling and terrified, he rebuked himself for his cruelty, sold all his possessions and gave the money to the poor, and when nothing remained he sold himself as a slave and gave that price to the poor as well. When his fame became well known he fled to the wilderness of Shiheet and became a monk, living an ascetic life of great devotion and good repute. Knowing the day of his departure, he called the monks, bade them farewell, and departed in peace.

5-25.name: St. Askala (Asela)
5-25.summary: St. Askala was brought up in the region of Ansena, where Arianus, the governor of Ansena, summoned him during a visit to his hometown and commanded him to raise incense to the idols, but Askala held fast to his faith with courage and determination. The governor ordered him tied to a horse and dragged through the streets until his body was torn and his flesh scattered, and then ordered torches of fire applied to his sides and stomach, yet the Lord healed and comforted him. Arianus then took Askala aboard a ship to cross the Nile, and when Askala prayed for a sign to glorify God's name, the ship stopped in mid-river and could not be moved by the soldiers until Askala prayed again. The governor nevertheless hardened his heart, tied a huge rock to Askala's neck, and threw him into the Nile, where he delivered his pure spirit into the hand of the Lord and received the crown of martyrdom.

5-26.name: The Forty-Nine Saints, the Elders of Shiheet, and Martinos and His Son Zius
5-26.summary: The forty-nine elders of Shiheet were martyred in 444 A.D., when Berbers attacked the monastery of St. Macarius and slaughtered them with their companions, while the elders' bodies were gathered in a cave. A church was later built in their name, and their commemoration is tied to the consecration of the church of St. Macarius. The page also records that Pope Theodosius I, the 33rd Patriarch, consecrated that church in 528 A.D., and that after a long time the bodies were revealed and venerated. This entry is counted as one entry, as presented under one heading in Coptic Reader.
hymnIds: Watos Psali for the Martyrdom of the Forty-Nine Martyrs and Elders of Scetis

5-26.name: St. Bagoush
5-26.summary: St. Bagoush was a wealthy man from the village of Tima in the Souhag governorate who loved the poor, and when Diocletian's persecution began the Archangel Michael appeared to him and encouraged him to seek martyrdom. He distributed his possessions, went before the governor, who at first befriended him and then imprisoned him, and his mother came to him grieving that he had left her behind without a martyr's crown. After a night of prayer, his mother walked beside him the next morning openly declaring her faith, and the governor beheaded her before him. Bagoush himself endured many tortures and was finally beheaded, receiving the crown of martyrdom.

5-26.name: St. Anastasia
5-26.summary: This St. Anastasia was a noble, wealthy and beautiful woman of Constantinople in 576 A.D., whom the emperor wished to marry, but she refused and, with the empress's help, fled to Egypt aboard a private ship and built a convent near Alexandria. When the emperor continued to pursue her, she dressed in men's clothing, called herself Anastasy, and went to the wilderness of Shiheet, where she revealed her story to Anba Daniel, the hegumen, and was accepted into a cave in the inner wilderness. She lived there in seclusion for 28 years, unknown to others, receiving water and food weekly from Daniel's disciple, who left them at the door without seeing her, while she wrote her thoughts on pottery left there. When she fell ill, Daniel came to her, and she departed in peace after a life of hidden asceticism. She is a different Anastasia from the martyr of Rome commemorated on Koiahk 26.

5-27.name: The Honorable Archangel Suriel
5-27.summary: Suriel is presented as one of the seven archangels, the seven spirits before the throne of God, sent to minister to the sons of men, whose luminous and translucent nature can behold God as much as it can tolerate. His name is explained as meaning 'trumpet of God,' because he will sound the trumpet on the last day and gather the elect from the four winds. St. John Chrysostom built a splendid church in his name in Constantinople, which was consecrated on the 27th of Tobe, and many miracles are attributed to his intercession.
hymnIds: Fraction to the Father for the Feasts of the Virgin and Angels: Behold, Immanuel our God...

5-27.name: St. Abe-Fam the Soldier (Phoebammon)
5-27.summary: St. Abe-Fam was born in Oseem (Awsim) to wealthy Christian parents, was raised in the fear of the Lord, was merciful to the poor and diligent in prayer and fasting, and declined a proposed marriage. When Diocletian apostatized and declared persecution, Abe-Fam confessed Christ before the governor, who tortured him extensively, and Arianus, governor of Ansena, took him to Kaw, tied him to the tail of a horse and dragged him through the city, and ordered him squeezed in the Hinbazeen, yet the Lord healed and strengthened him. Arianus then tied a rock to his neck and threw him into the river, from which an angel saved him from drowning, and then placed him in a fiery furnace that did not harm him. Finally, after further tortures, Abe-Fam was beheaded, and believers took his body, shrouded it, buried it with great veneration in the city of Tima, and built a church in his name, from which many signs and miracles were manifested.
hymnIds: Adam Psali for the Martyrdom of Saint Abe-Fam the Soldier
Watos Psali for the Martyrdom of Saint Abe-Fam the Soldier

5-27.name: St. Serapion
5-27.summary: St. Serapion was martyred in 305 A.D. and was born in Binosa (Babousah) in Lower Egypt to wealthy Christian parents, growing up loving and charitable to the poor and needy. Hearing of the torture of Christians in Alexandria, he went there with his friend Theodore (Tadros) and a shepherd named Thomas, confessed the Lord Christ before Governor Armanius, and was imprisoned. He was tormented by squeezing in the Hinbazeen, casting into boiling tar, crucifixion and arrows, while an angel healed, strengthened and comforted him. When the governor grew weary, he ordered the commander Orion to behead Serapion, who received the crown of martyrdom.

5-27.name: The Translocation of the Relics of St. Timothy the Apostle
5-27.summary: This entry commemorates the transfer of the relics of St. Timothy, bishop of Ephesus and disciple of the Apostle Paul, from the city of Ephesus to Constantinople by order of the Emperor Constantine the Great. His relics were placed there with great veneration in the church of the holy fathers, the apostles. The entry itself notes that the account of his martyrdom is recorded under the 23rd of Tobe.

5-28.name: St. Anba Kaou
5-28.summary: St. Kaou was an ascetic born in Dimoshah (Bamway, Bimay), one of the cities of el-Fayyom, in the later part of the third century, who loved reading and contemplating the Holy Scriptures and dwelt in a cave in the desert of el-Fayyom. In 305 A.D., during a persecution, an angel appeared to him in a vision telling him that crowns were prepared for martyrs and that he should rise and go to el-Lahoon to confess the name of the Lord Christ. He immediately went there, where the governor's envoy marveled at his white hair and fair appearance and showed him a gold idol decorated with precious stones, a gift from the emperor to Governor Ansena, which Kaou admired for its workmanship and then cast to the ground and smashed. The envoy, angered, bound him and took him to Governor Ansena, who tormented him by scourging and squeezing in the Hinbazeen, and then sent him to the governor of Bahnasa, who struck him with iron hammers and flogged him until his flesh was torn and tied red-hot iron rods to his body, yet the Lord Jesus healed and saved him. When the governor was helpless, he ordered Kaou beheaded by the sword, and believers took his body, shrouded it with great veneration, and buried it in the place where he used to worship.

5-28.name: St. Clement, Bishop of Angora
5-28.summary: St. Clement was martyred in 309 A.D. and was born in Angora in 257 A.D. to a heathen father who died while Clement was still a suckling infant, while his Christian mother raised him, feeding him the milk of faith. He loved the poor and needy, caring for their spiritual and physical needs, grew in virtue, was ordained deacon and then priest, and later became bishop of Angora, struggling for his flock with love and rigorous zeal. His fame reached Emperor Diocletian, who ordered the governor of Galatia to seize him, and when Clement refused to worship idols he was tortured by tearing his flesh with iron hooks, stoning and imprisonment. The governor, helpless, sent him to the emperor, who befriended him and tried often to make him deny the faith, but could not change his conviction, and ordered his body torn in an iron closet with sharp teeth, yet the Lord saved him and many pagans believed. He was tortured before seven courts, the last in Angora, growing each time in conviction and courage, and was finally beheaded and received the crown, after which a believing woman named Sophia took his body and buried it with great veneration.

5-28.name: St. Babylas (Philyas), Bishop of Thmoui (Tamai) el-Amidid
5-28.summary: St. Babylas was martyred in 310 A.D., was born to a respectable family in Thmoui el-Amid, studied philosophy, sciences and literature and excelled, and was appointed by the emperor as governor for his region. Because of his piety and holiness, he forsook governmental duties and was consecrated bishop of the same region, where he devoted himself to exhorting and teaching his flock and visiting them, leading them in holiness and steadfastness in the faith during the persecution. He went to Alexandria to receive the blessing of Pope Peter, the Seal of Martyrs, saw the torment of the martyrs there, and encouraged and strengthened them, but the governor seized and imprisoned him, from prison he sent a pastoral epistle to his diocese urging them to stand firm in the faith under suffering. At the place of execution he stretched out his arms in the shape of a cross, prayed aloud, and was struck on the neck by a soldier's sword, receiving the crown of martyrdom.

5-29.name: St. Eksanie (St. Xene)
5-29.summary: St. Eksanie was the only daughter of one of the noble families of Rome, raised in loving worship, reading the biographies of saints and being compassionate to the poor, and she frequently visited the houses of virgins in Rome trying to follow their footsteps. When the son of one of Rome's government ministers asked to marry her and her father prepared all the needs of her wedding, she asked her mother to let her go visit some nuns to bid them farewell, and when allowed she took two maiden servants and her precious ornaments and sailed to Cyprus, where she met St. Epiphanius, bishop of Cyprus. She told him of her desire for the monastic life, and on his advice she obeyed and sailed to Alexandria, where she met Pope Theophilus, the 23rd Patriarch, told him of her desire and handed him all her jewels. He attached her to one of the houses of virgins, sold the jewels and built with their price a church after the name of St. Stephen in Alexandria. Eksanie persevered in asceticism and worship for more than twenty years, and when her departure drew near a cross of light appeared in heaven surrounded by an illuminated circle of stars in the middle of the day, remaining until her pure body was buried, which the people of Alexandria understood as a heavenly sign of the eminence of her spiritual life.

5-29.name: St. Seriakus (Syriacus) the Struggle-mantled
5-29.summary: Coptic Reader gives only the one-line statement that St. Syriacus the struggle-mantled departed on this day, with no further life, place, or manner of departure, so none is recorded here.

5-30.name: Sts. Pistis, Helpis, Agape and Their Mother Sophia
5-30.summary: Sophia was from a rich and noble family in Antioch, and God granted her three daughters whom she called Pistis, meaning faith, Helpis, meaning hope, and Agape, meaning love, while Sophia itself means wisdom. She took her three daughters to Rome to teach them church subjects and worship, and when their report reached Emperor Hadrian he summoned them and tried to force them to forsake the Christian faith, but their mother encouraged them to stand steadfast in the faith of the Lord Christ to receive the crowns of martyrdom. Pistis was 12 years old, Helpis 11 and Agape 9, and when the emperor saw their dedication he tore Pistis's body with whips, cast her in a fiery furnace and then beheaded her, combed Helpis's body with sharp iron combs and then struck her neck with the sword, and, finding the youngest, Agape, firm in faith and unterrified by the killing of her two sisters before her, ordered her cast in the fiery furnace, crushed in the Hinbazeen and finally beheaded. Their mother Sophia rejoiced exceedingly and thanked the Lord that her daughters had remained steadfast, received the crowns of martyrdom and become brides for the Lord Christ, then took their bodies, shrouded them with expensive shrouds, asked the Lord to receive her own spirit, and, when the Lord hearkened to her prayer, delivered her pure spirit into the hand of the Lord, after which believers buried their pure bodies with great honor.

5-30.name: Pope Mina I, 47th Patriarch of Alexandria
5-30.summary: Pope Mina I departed in 776 A.D., was born in the city of Samanoud and brought up with a Christian upbringing, and when he grew he became a monk in the monastery of St. Macarius under the name of the monk Mina. After the departure of Pope Khaeil (Michael) I, the bishops and the people convened and unanimously agreed to choose the monk Mina for his many virtues and knowledge. After his enthronement he paid great interest to shepherding his people and visiting them, built and renovated ruined churches, and faced a severe hardship incited by one of the monks who desired to receive the bishopric rank by any means, enduring many pressures over this issue with patience and courage. When he had finished his good endeavor he departed in peace and was buried in St. Mark's church in Alexandria, having sat on the apostolic throne for 8 years and 10 months.

5-30.name: St. Ibrahim el-Rahawy the Hermit
5-30.summary: St. Ibrahim was born in the city of el-Raha in Mesopotamia at the beginning of the fourth century to pious Christian parents, grew in a life of virtues loving worship, and longed for the monastic life, asking God often to direct his own salvation. He dwelt in a cave in the mountain near his city, and when his family searched for him and found him there he refused to go with them and asked them not to visit him again, then shut his cave, leaving only a small window to receive his rations, and remained in seclusion for about fifty years, becoming an example for hermits and very simple in his way of life. When St. Jacob of Serug, the bishop of the area, asked him to preach to a nearby village inhabited by heathen, wicked people whom no Christian could enter to preach, Ibrahim felt strong zeal for the mission, left his cave, entered the village and began calling in the name of the Lord Christ, but the heathen persecuted, beat him severely and expelled him. He remained outside the village entreating God to visit them with His mercy, God answered his prayers and moved their hearts, they came to him, listened to the words of life until they believed in the name of Christ and asked to be baptized, and the bishop came and baptized a large number of them, after which Ibrahim taught and confirmed them in the faith for a time and then returned to his cave to resume his solitary life. He also brought back to a life of repentance his brother's orphaned daughter Mariam, who had fallen into sin and then dwelt in a cave near his cave practicing a good monastic life, and when Ibrahim had finished his good endeavor he departed to the Lord in peace at 85 years old.

6-1.name: The Second Universal Council in Constantinople
6-1.summary: In 381 A.D., during the reign of Theodosius the Great, 150 fathers met in Constantinople to confront Macedonius, who denied the divinity of the Holy Spirit. The council affirmed that the Holy Spirit is God, consubstantial with the Father and the Son, and also addressed related heretical teachings. Its decisions strengthened the Nicene faith and the Church's teaching on the Trinity. This entry is a conciliar commemoration, not the death of an individual saint.

6-1.name: St. Abadion, Bishop of Ansena
6-1.summary: St. Abadion was bishop of Ansena in Egypt during the persecution under Diocletian. He was seized by the governor, confessed Christ, and was subjected to severe torture rather than renounce his faith. He remained steadfast through the torments imposed on him. He was finally beheaded in 304 A.D., receiving the crown of martyrdom.

6-1.name: The Consecration of the Church of St. Peter, the Seal of the Martyrs, in Alexandria
6-1.summary: This entry commemorates the consecration of a church dedicated to St. Peter, called the Seal of the Martyrs, in Alexandria. The church was built west of Alexandria during the reign of Constantine. It remained in existence until shortly after the Arab conquest of Egypt. The entry records a church consecration, not a martyrdom or departure.
hymnIds: Doxology for St. Peter the Seal of the Martyrs
St. Peter the Seal of the Martyrs (Hathor 29)

6-2.name: St. Paul, the First Hermit
6-2.summary: St. Paul was born in Thebes in Egypt and, after a dispute with his brother Peter over their inheritance, fled to the desert to preserve his faith and inheritance from being used against him. He lived in a cave in the eastern desert for about 70 years, sustained by a palm tree and spring, wearing palm leaves and devoting himself to prayer and asceticism. St. Anthony later found him, and the two hermits shared a loaf brought by a raven. Paul departed in peace in 341 A.D., and, according to the entry, lions helped dig his grave after Anthony buried him in his own cloak.
hymnIds: Adam Psali for the Departure of Abba Paul the First Hermit
Watos Psali for the Departure of Abba Paul the First Hermit
Doxology for St. Paul the Hermit
Doxology for St. Anthony and St. Paul
The Great Saint Abba Paul the First Anchorite (Meshir 2)

6-2.name: St. Longinus, the Abbot of El-Zugag, and His Father Lucianus
6-2.summary: St. Longinus was born in Cilicia in Asia Minor, lost his mother in childhood, and later became a monk with his father, who also embraced monastic life. After living in Syria and working many miracles, he came to Egypt and settled at El-Zugag, west of Alexandria, where he was made abbot against his will. His father later joined him there, and the two lived together in asceticism and service, including making boat sails for their livelihood. Longinus departed in peace, and his father also departed after him, both being remembered as righteous monastic fathers.

6-3.name: St. James the Monk
6-3.summary: St. James renounced the world while still young and lived in a cave for 15 years in fasting, prayer, and seclusion, never leaving it during that time. The devil tempted him through a wicked woman who came to his cave, but James preached to her and she repented, after which he was known for miracles and spiritual counsel. He continued his ascetic life and became a guide to many who sought him. After a short illness, he departed in peace.

6-3.name: St. Hedra of the Rock of Banhadab
6-3.summary: St. Hedra was the first monk to settle in solitude at the rock of Banhadab, where he lived a life of asceticism and worship. A man named Juda, who did not believe in the resurrection of the dead, came to dispute with him, and Hedra's teaching and example converted him to faith in the resurrection. Hedra continued to teach and guide the monks and people around him. He departed in peace, leaving a reputation for holiness and steadfast monastic witness. He is a different Hedra from Hedra, Bishop of Aswan, commemorated on Koiahk 12.

6-4.name: St. Agabus, One of the Seventy Disciples
6-4.summary: St. Agabus was one of the Seventy Disciples and is known from the Acts of the Apostles for prophesying a great famine that occurred in the days of Claudius. He preached in many countries, converting Jews and Greeks to Christianity. In Jerusalem, Jews seized him, scourged him, put a rope around his neck, and dragged him outside the city. He was then stoned to death, and a Jewish woman who confessed Christ at his martyrdom was also stoned and departed in peace, sharing in his crown.

6-5.name: The Relocation of the Relics of the Forty-Nine Elders of the Wilderness of Shiheet
6-5.summary: This entry commemorates the transfer of the relics of the Forty-Nine Elders of Scetis to the church of the Monastery of St. Macarius. Pope Benjamin I, the 38th Patriarch, re-shrouded and embalmed the bodies and re-buried them in the middle of the church, establishing a feast for them. The relics remained there until the church fell into ruin, after which the monks kept them in a cell. In 1732 A.D., El-Moalem Ibrahim El-Gohary built a church for them, where their bodies still lie in the Church of the Elders.
hymnIds: Watos Psali for the Martyrdom of the Forty-Nine Martyrs and Elders of Scetis

6-5.name: St. Agrippinus, 10th Pope of Alexandria
6-5.summary: St. Agrippinus was born in Alexandria, lived a pure and God-fearing life, and was ordained a priest there before succeeding Celadion as the 9th Patriarch's successor, becoming the 10th Pope. He preached diligently, owned no silver or gold beyond his needs, and supported the faithful during the persecution under Marcus Aurelius. He also preached to heathens and converted many to Christianity. He departed in peace after a life of pastoral care and steadfast witness.

6-5.name: St. Anba Bishay, Founder of the Red Monastery
6-5.summary: St. Bishay was born in the village of Absounah and, after a sickness and a vision of the places of torment, repented, was cured, and renounced the world, even leaving the sheep he tended. He went to the mountain, met Anba Pigol, the uncle of St. Shenoute, and lived with him on Mount Adribah in worship, fasting, vigils, and ascetic struggle against temptations. He became known throughout Egypt for his discourses and teachings to monks and laity, once fasting a whole month while people's deeds were revealed to him. When he finished his good endeavor, he departed in peace, and Shenoute shrouded and buried him in the monastery later named after him, the Red Monastery west of Souhag.

6-5.name: St. Apollo, the Companion of Anba Abib
6-5.summary: St. Apollo was a fourth-century saint born in Akhmeem who resembled his parents in piety from his youth and practiced asceticism and the solitary life. He spent his time studying the Holy Bible, contemplating, and praying, and he had a close friend, Abib, who shared his monastic aspiration. Apollo lived in seclusion in a cell in a monastery, practicing fellowship with God, and met Abib from time to time, being present at Abib's departure. Apollo himself departed in a good old age.

6-5.name: St. Hippolytus, Pope of Rome
6-5.summary: St. Hippolytus was a perfect and righteous man chosen for the Roman See after the departure of Father Augius (Hyginus Pius), in the first year of the enthronement of Abba Celadion, 9th Patriarch of Alexandria. As pope, he constantly taught his people and defended the Orthodox faith. When Claudius Caesar (Antonius), the Roman emperor, heard of him, he summoned him and demanded that he worship idols; Hippolytus refused and was severely tortured. A heavy stone was tied to his feet and he was thrown into the sea, where he departed in peace and received the crown of martyrdom; the next day a faithful man found his body floating with the stone still tied to his feet, took it home, shrouded it richly, and buried it. He left many teachings and 38 church canons that are still in use.

6-5.name: St. Aba-Noub, the Owner of the Golden Fan
6-5.summary: Coptic Reader gives only the heading and the one-line statement that St. Aba-Noub (Apanoub), known as the Owner of the Golden Fan, departed on this day, with no further life, place, or death details, so none is recorded here.

6-6.name: Sts. Cyrus, John, the Three Virgins and Their Mother
6-6.summary: St. Cyrus (Abakir) was born in Alexandria to godly parents, learned medicine, and became known for his knowledge, godliness, and love for the poor, but he was accused of healing by sorcery and magic and fled to the eastern desert, where he joined and served the hermits. St. John was a high-ranking officer in the army of Mesopotamia who left military service, visited the holy places in Jerusalem, and then joined Cyrus in the desert, becoming his spiritual brother and disciple. During Diocletian's persecution, soldiers seized the Christian woman Athanasia and her three virgin daughters, Theodora, Theopisti, and Theodosia, and led them bound to Kanoub, east of Alexandria, for trial and torture. Cyrus and John went down to Alexandria to stand beside and encourage them, but the governor ordered the mother and daughters beheaded before them to frighten them, and, after a long series of tortures, Cyrus and John were also beheaded at Kanoub, later called Abu-Kir after Abakir. St. Julius of Aqafhs carried their bodies and buried them in a tomb near the Church of St. Mark in Alexandria and wrote down their struggle and martyrdom.
hymnIds: Adam Psali for the Martyrdom of Saints Apakir and John
Watos Psali for the Martyrdom of Saints Apakir and John
Doxology for St. Apakir and St. John

6-6.name: Pope Mark (Marcus) IV, 84th Patriarch of Alexandria
6-6.summary: Pope Mark IV was a native of Qalyub who became a monk in the Shahran monastery under the name Ghabrial and was known as righteous, knowledgeable, and godly. After the departure of Pope Peter V, the bishops and lay leaders chose him, and he was consecrated Patriarch on the 8th of Thoout, year 1065 of the Martyrs (1348 A.D.), as Pope Mark IV. During his pontificate, a severe persecution befell the Copts, some churches were destroyed and monasteries ruined, the country faced many difficulties, and the pope himself was imprisoned until the Christian King of Ethiopia intervened to secure his release. After thankfully enduring these trials, he departed in 1079 of the Martyrs (1363 A.D.) and was buried in Shahran monastery.

6-6.name: St. Zanofios
6-6.summary: St. Zanofios was abbot of a large community of monks in the region of el-Mara'igh, in the district of Akhmeem, and was known for asceticism and worship. He taught his monastic children the virtues of monastic life, worship, and the fear of God, and he established a convent for virgins, placing a righteous mother in charge and sending them epistles explaining the commandments and monastic rules. He continued this pastoral and monastic leadership until he finished his good endeavor. He departed in peace and was buried in his monastery, where God worked many signs through his pure body.

6-7.name: St. Alexandros II, 43rd Pope of Alexandria
6-7.summary: St. Alexandros II was born in the village of Bana, El Mahalla el-Kobra, was raised in piety, godliness, and love of the solitary life, and became a monk in the monastery of Pateron, also known as El-Zugag monastery, under the name Alexandros. He lived in asceticism, fasting, and prayer until the fame of his virtues became well known, and the fathers ordained him a priest for the monastery church. After the departure of Pope Simeon I, the bishops and people unanimously chose him, and he was consecrated Patriarch on the 30th of Parmoute, year 420 of the Martyrs (704 A.D.). Although the early days of his pontificate were tranquil, rulers then mistreated the Christians and seized the patriarch, releasing him only after three thousand dinars were collected; conditions worsened under the next ruler and the following four rulers, with hardships from within the Church and from the Chalcedonians. He endured all these pains in prayer and supplication until he departed in peace in year 445 of the Martyrs (729 A.D.).

6-7.name: St. Theodorus (Theodore) I, 45th Pope of Alexandria
6-7.summary: St. Theodorus became a monk under the name Tadros in a monastery near Mariot and a disciple of the holy elder monk Yoannis (John), who was inspired by the Holy Spirit that Tadros would one day become Patriarch and told the people in church about this vision. Tadros struggled in worship and was perfect in humility and meekness. When the apostolic throne became vacant by the departure of Pope Cosma I, the bishops and lay leaders remembered Yoannis's prophecy, brought Tadros from the monastery against his will, and consecrated him Patriarch on the 1st day of Epep, year 446 of the Martyrs (730 A.D.). After his enthronement, he devoted himself to the pastoral care of his flock, and although he faced many hardships and witnessed calamities brought by the rulers, the Church continued to grow spiritually. He completed his good strive and departed in peace in year 458 of the Martyrs (742 A.D.).

6-8.name: The Feast of Presenting the Lord Christ to the Temple
6-8.summary: This is one of the minor feasts of the Lord, celebrated on the fortieth day after the birth of the Lord Christ, when His mother, the Virgin St. Mary, took Him with St. Joseph the carpenter to the temple to do for Him according to the custom of the law and offer the required sacrifice according to their ability. Because of the poverty of the Virgin and Joseph, they offered the sacrifice of the poor, two young pigeons. The Virgin, who conceived by the Holy Spirit and gave birth to the Savior in all purity, submitted to this law to exercise humility and obedience and to give an example for believers to follow, as did her Son, who obeyed the law of the Old Testament in humility before establishing the law of the New Testament. In the temple, the just and devout old priest Simeon took the Child in his arms, blessed God, and said that the Lord was now letting His servant depart in peace, and he blessed Mary and Joseph, prophesying that the Child was destined for the fall and rising of many in Israel and for a sign spoken against, and that a sword would pierce Mary's own soul. The prophetess Anna, daughter of Phanuel, also gave thanks and spoke of Him to those looking for redemption in Jerusalem, after which the family returned to Nazareth in Galilee and the Child grew strong in spirit, filled with wisdom, with the grace of God upon Him.
hymnIds: Doxology for the Presentation of the Lord Christ in the Temple
Watos Psali for the Feast of the Presentation of the Lord Christ in the Temple
Adam Psali for the Feast of the Presentation of the Lord Christ in the Temple
Fraction to the Son for the Feasts of Our Lord: We praise and glorify...

6-8.name: St. Simeon the Elder
6-8.summary: St. Simeon was one of the seventy elders who translated the Old Testament from Hebrew into Greek in Alexandria by order of Ptolemy Philadelphus, king of Egypt. While translating Isaiah 7:14, 'Behold, the virgin shall conceive and bear a Son, and shall call His name Immanuel,' he was afraid to translate that a virgin would conceive, lest the king mock him and accuse him of ignorance, and he wanted to render 'virgin' as 'young lady or damsel.' Doubting that a virgin could conceive, he received a vision from God that he would not die before seeing Immanuel born of a virgin, and he lived about 300 years until Christ was born of the Virgin Mary without human seed but by the Holy Spirit, by which time he was advanced in age and his sight had dimmed. When he came by the Spirit into the temple and carried the Divine Child in his hands, his sight returned, and the Holy Spirit told him that this was the child he had been waiting for. He blessed God, saying that the Lord was letting His servant depart in peace because his eyes had seen God's salvation prepared before all peoples, blessed Joseph and Mary, prophesied about the Child's future and the pains the Virgin would suffer, and departed in peace on the same day.

6-8.name: The Contemporary Martyrs of the Coptic Church
6-8.summary: The Church commemorates its contemporary martyrs, foremost among them the 21 Coptic martyrs in Libya, who were executed by beheading in the city of Sirte on the shores of the Mediterranean Sea, an execution depicted in a video released by a terrorist group in Libya in 2015 A.D. In recent years, many other children of the Coptic Church have also been martyred in various regions of Egypt and joined the chorus of martyrs in Heaven. In recognition of their sacrifice, the Holy Synod, under the leadership of His Holiness Pope Tawadros II, designated the 8th of Meshir as a feast and commemoration day for all the martyrs of the Coptic Church in its modern era. They are celebrated to honor them, keep their memory, and draw blessings from their lives as living examples of divine love and steadfast faith, in line with the saying that one may move a mountain from its place but cannot move Copts from their faith, and believers are called to consider the outcome of their way of life and imitate their faith, as St. Paul advises in Hebrews 13:7.
hymnIds: Melody for the 21 Coptic Martyrs in Libya

6-9.name: St. Barsauma, the Father of the Syrian Monks
6-9.summary: St. Barsauma departed in 458 A.D. He was born in Samosata, Syria, where a holy man had prophesied before his birth that a righteous fruit from his parents would spread fame everywhere. After leaving his parents, he lived by the Euphrates with a holy man named Abraham, then in solitude on a mountain in prayer, fasting, and austere asceticism, gathering many disciples. God worked many miracles through him, including making salty water sweet and lifting a famine through his prayers. He resisted the heresy of Nestorius, attended the Council of Ephesus in 431 A.D. at Emperor Theodosius the Less's invitation, and later resisted the Chalcedonian teaching on two natures, suffering hardships from the Chalcedonians. Knowing the day of his departure, he gathered his disciples, urged them to remain steadfast in the Orthodox faith, and departed in peace, with a pillar of light appearing at his cell door, after which he was shrouded and buried with great honor.

6-9.name: St. Paul the Syrian
6-9.summary: St. Paul was martyred in 305 A.D. His family had moved from Syria and settled in Ashmunain, where his father gained great wealth through trade, and Paul was raised in a true Christian upbringing, growing in godliness. After his parents died, he prayed for guidance, and the Lord sent an angel in a vision telling him he would receive the crown of martyrdom, so he rejoiced and distributed all his money to the poor and needy. He went to the governor of Ansena (Antinoe) and confessed Christ, and the governor had him stripped naked, beaten with whips, and burned with torches at his sides, then tried to entice him with money, which Paul refused, saying he had already rejected his parents' fortune of gold and silver for Christ. The governor tormented him in various ways, but the Lord healed and strengthened him, and venomous serpents placed on him did not harm him. Taken to Alexandria and imprisoned, he met his friends, the saints Esi and his sister Thecla, and when the governor decided to return to Ansena, he ordered Paul beheaded, receiving the crown of martyrdom, after which the faithful took his body, shrouded it, and buried it with great honor.

6-9.name: St. Simeon
6-9.summary: Coptic Reader gives only the heading and the single line that St. Simeon was martyred on this day, with no further life, place, or manner of martyrdom detail, so none is recorded here. This Simeon is not identified in the entry with any other Simeon.

6-9.name: St. Euphrosyne of Alexandria
6-9.summary: St. Euphrosyne departed in 470 A.D. She was born in Alexandria as the only child of a godly and wealthy family, raised in a true Christian upbringing, and learned from her parents the fear of God and charity toward the poor and needy. At eighteen, she left home wearing men's attire and went to a monastery, where the abbot accepted her and placed her in a solitary cell, and she devoted herself to fasting, prayer, and austere asceticism, which changed her appearance. Her father visited the monastery often, asking the monks to pray that the Lord grant him peace and comfort, and Euphrosyne recognized him although he did not know her, receiving and encouraging him, and he found consolation in her words of grace. When she became ill and knew the day of her departure, she revealed her identity to her father when he came to the monastery, told him she was about to depart, and departed in his arms after encouraging and consoling him. He was deeply moved and agreed with his wife to forsake worldly vanity, sold all his possessions and distributed the money to churches and the poor, while his wife joined a convent and he lived in his daughter's cell for ten years before departing in peace.

6-10.name: St. Philo, Bishop of the Persians
6-10.summary: St. Philo, bishop of the Persians, was martyred by the hand of the Persian Emperor. The emperor tried to force him to worship fire and kneel to the sun that the emperor worshiped, but Philo refused to obey the emperor's orders and stood fast in his faith in the Lord Christ. The emperor therefore tormented him with different kinds of tortures. Finally, the emperor ordered him beheaded with the sword, and so he received the crown of martyrdom.

6-10.name: St. Justus, the Son of Emperor Numerian
6-10.summary: St. Justus, son of Emperor Numerian, was a prince and high-ranking army commander who returned victorious from war against the Persians to find that his father had died and Diocletian, who had married his sister, had become emperor. When the empire's nobles met to enthrone Justus as emperor, he refused, preferring the heavenly kingdom over the earthly one. After a while, Diocletian abandoned faith in the Lord Christ and worshiped idols, and when Justus objected, Diocletian seized him, his wife Theoclea, and his son Abali and sent them to Alexandria to be tortured far from their country and people. In Alexandria, the governor tried to persuade them to worship idols, but they refused, declaring their steadfastness in faith in the Lord Christ, so he sent Justus to Antinoe (Ansena), Abali to Basta, and Theoclea to Sa el-Hagar. The rulers there tortured them and then beheaded all three saints, who received the crowns of martyrdom.

6-10.name: St. Isidore of Pelusium
6-10.summary: St. Isidore departed in 450 A.D., having been born in Alexandria in 370 A.D. He was a relative of Pope Theophilus, the 23rd patriarch, and Pope Cyril I, the 24th patriarch, and he excelled as a scholar in Greek philosophy, history, and logic. He became a monk, first at el-Farama and then in solitude at Pelusium, where he wrote commentaries on the Old and New Testaments and about two thousand epistles to emperors, patriarchs, bishops, and monks. He departed in peace at a good old age.

6-11.name: Pope Yoannis XIII, 94th Patriarch of Alexandria
6-11.summary: Pope Yoannis XIII departed in 1524 A.D. He was born in Sedfa, was godly and charitable, and became a monk at the Monastery of the Virgin Mary at el-Moharrag. He was consecrated patriarch in 1484 A.D., after Pope Yoannis XII, and shepherded the Church for about forty years, during which he returned the relics of St. Philopateer Mercurius (Abu-Seifein) to his church in Old Cairo, renovated churches, and supplied books. He departed in peace and was buried in the Church of the Virgin Mary in Haret Zuweila, which was then the papal residence.

6-11.name: Pope Fabianus, Pope of Rome
6-11.summary: Pope Fabianus was a righteous scholar who became bishop of Rome and taught Christian perfection. During the persecution of Emperor Decius, he was brought to Ephesus and refused to offer incense to the idols, enduring severe tortures for a long time. He was finally beheaded, after sitting on the throne of Rome for twelve years.

6-12.name: The Commemoration of the Honorable Archangel Michael
6-12.summary: This is a short monthly commemoration entry for the Archangel Michael, presented as the intercessor for mankind. The page gives no life, martyrdom, or departure details for this entry, and none are added here.
hymnIds: Doxology for Archangels Michael and Gabriel
Fraction to the Father for Archangel Michael
Archangel Michael (12th of Every Coptic Month)

6-12.name: St. Gelasius the Ascetic
6-12.summary: St. Gelasius was born to Christian parents who taught him in the church, and he was ordained a deacon before becoming a monk in the wilderness of Shiheet. An angel guided him to the inner wilderness, where he became a teacher and guide for monks desiring the solitary life, and he transcribed the Holy Scriptures. He was known for love and forgiveness, and he raised a dead man through prayer. After a long life of monastic asceticism, worship, and guiding his brethren, he departed in peace to eternal rest.

6-13.name: St. Sergius of Atripe, His Father, His Mother, His Sister, and Many Others
6-13.summary: St. Sergius was born in Atripe to pious parents, and at about twenty he left worldly vanity, went to the governor Cyprian, and professed his faith, for which he was tortured and imprisoned. In prison he had a vision of the habitations of the righteous, and his wounds were healed. The captain Ohios then tortured him further, including skinning him, applying salt and vinegar, using the pressing wheel (Hinbazeen), pulling his nails, and placing him on an iron bed over fire, but the Lord strengthened and healed him. When Ohios grew weary, he ordered Sergius beheaded, and Sergius's family came and, seeing him tied to a horse's bridle and dragged toward execution, protested the soldiers' cruelty. The captain then ordered the family beheaded as well, and they all received the crowns of martyrdom.

6-13.name: Pope Timothy III, 32nd Patriarch of Alexandria
6-13.summary: Pope Timothy III departed in 536 A.D. He was born in Alexandria, studied in the church and excelled, and was ordained a priest for the Church of St. Mark in Alexandria. After Pope Dioscorus II, the bishops, priests, and archons chose the priest Timothy, and he was consecrated on 1 Hathor in 518 A.D., sending a fellowship epistle to the Eastern bishops and bringing joy, peace, and love. He endured great hardships in preserving the Orthodox faith, refusing Emperor Justin I's call to a council to excommunicate Severus, Patriarch of Antioch, and the emperor ordered his exile, while soldiers killed many of the faithful who opposed carrying out the order. Timothy was exiled for three years, and after his return he was pursued from town to town and monastery to monastery together with Severus, writing epistles to comfort and strengthen his people in the Orthodox faith. He persevered in teaching his flock and directing church affairs amid these hardships until he departed in perpetual peace after about seventeen years on the apostolic throne.

6-14.name: St. Severus, Patriarch of Antioch
6-14.summary: St. Severus was born in 459 A.D. in Sozopolis in Asia Minor to Christian parents, and he studied religious and secular learning, philosophy in Alexandria, and law in Beirut, where he excelled. An ascetic prophesied that he would become Patriarch of Antioch and a teacher and defender of Orthodoxy, and he became a monk at the Monastery of St. Romanus, gaining fame for his virtues and knowledge. He was ordained Patriarch of Antioch by consensus of bishops and people in 512 A.D., and the universal Church was illuminated by his teachings. Emperor Justin I, a supporter of the Chalcedonian council, offered him honors to persuade him to adopt that faith, but Severus stood firm in Orthodoxy, so the emperor, angered, ordered him killed. The Orthodox Empress Theodora warned him, and he fled to Egypt during the papacy of Pope Timothy III, wandering among monasteries and Egyptian cities in simple monk's attire and confirming believers in Orthodoxy, while the emperor incited severe persecution against the Coptic Church for receiving him. He later lived in Sakha at the home of the righteous archon Doretheos, where God performed many miracles through his hands, and he departed in Sakha, after which his body was later relocated to the Monastery of El-Zugag near Alexandria.
hymnIds: Doxology for St. Severus, Patriarch of Antioch
Melody for St. Severus Patriarch of Antioch

6-14.name: Pope James (Jacob), 50th Patriarch of Alexandria
6-14.summary: Pope James departed in 830 A.D. He was born in Nabaroh to Christian parents who taught him in the church, and he became a monk at the Monastery of St. Macarius in the wilderness of Shiheet, living a godly monastic life. After Pope Mark II departed, James was chosen by consensus for the patriarchate and was consecrated in 819 A.D. He renovated churches, populated monasteries, and was granted miracles and signs from God, including raising a child from the dead in Nabaroh. He finished his good endeavor and departed in peace after sitting on the apostolic throne for ten years and nine months.

6-15.name: St. Paphnoute the Monk
6-15.summary: St. Paphnoute was a monk in a monastery in Upper Egypt whose holy life was described as more like an angel than a human, and he enjoyed the company of blessed spirits and saints and great favor in prayer, attracting many to the monastic life. By grace, he was moved to travel into the inner wilderness to meet anchorites and record their biographies, walking for many days and suffering hardships until an angel appeared to encourage and strengthen him. He reached anchorites there, including the well-known Anba Timothy and Anba Nofer (Onnuphrius), and he shrouded and buried Nofer. Although he longed to remain as an anchorite there, Nofer told him it was not God's will, and he was to return to his monastery and tell the brethren what he had seen and heard for the benefit of monks seeking righteousness. After Nofer's departure, the palm tree that had fed him fell, the spring dried up, and the cave collapsed, so Paphnoute returned sorrowfully, persevered in asceticism and worship, and was finally called by an angel to depart to the eternal habitations. The brethren gathered, listened to his useful sayings, and he delivered up his pure soul.

6-15.name: St. Zechariah the Prophet, Son of Berechiah, Son of Iddo
6-15.summary: St. Zechariah was of the tribe of Levi, born in the land of Gilead, and his father Berechiah died when he was young, so the prophet was named after his grandfather Iddo. He was one of the twelve Minor Prophets, was exiled to the land of the Chaldeans, and in exile he prophesied in the eighth month of the second year of King Darius, about 520 B.C., after the king allowed the men of Judah to return to Jerusalem. His message centered on strengthening the people's frail determination to live in godliness and rebuild the temple, and it uncovered a glorious future in Jesus Christ, giving hope after the destruction of Jerusalem and the cities of Judah during the seventy-year exile. He prophesied the incarnation of the Word in the midst of Zion, Christ's triumphant entrance into Jerusalem, His sale for thirty pieces of silver, the piercing of His hands and feet, the darkness at the crucifixion, the piercing spear, the scattering of the disciples, and the sending of the Holy Spirit. The Jews, angered by his admonitions, conspired and slew him between the temple and the altar, as the Savior told the scribes and Pharisees concerning the blood from Abel to Zechariah, son of Berechiah, whom they murdered between the temple and the altar.

6-15.name: St. Anba Begoul (Pigol) the Priest
6-15.summary: St. Begoul was martyred in 305 A.D. He was born in Upper Egypt, lived in piety and good conduct, and was ordained a presbyter, emphasizing exhorting the people, teaching them, and confirming them in faith. Hearing of the torment of Christians, he went to Alexandria and met his namesake, St. Anba Begoul the soldier, during his torture, and he was seized and handed to the prefect Closianus, who tortured and imprisoned him. When Armanius became governor of Alexandria, Begoul the priest was brought before him, was scourged severely and tortured, yet endured in peace and serenity, and the Lord performed miracles through his hands, which the governor attributed to witchcraft. Armanius told him that the One he relied on could not save him from his hands this time, then ordered him crushed in the Hinbazeen, placed on an iron bed under hot fire, and finally beheaded. Begoul said that his joy was now complete and his priesthood fulfilled, for he had served the Lord for forty years for the sake of that hour, and the swordsman beheaded him, granting him the crown of martyrdom. A church named after him still exists in the village of Talah, west of the city of el-Menia.

6-15.name: The Consecration of the First Church Dedicated to the Forty Martyrs of Sebaste
6-15.summary: This entry commemorates the consecration of the first church built in the name of the Forty Martyrs of Sebaste, where their bodies were located in Sebaste. The martyrs had been martyred in Sebaste by the hands of Emperor Licinius. St. Basil the Great consecrated the church, also wrote the martyrs' biographies, and established a great feast day for them on this day.

6-16.name: St. Elizabeth, Mother of St. John the Baptist
6-16.summary: St. Elizabeth, wife of Zacharias the priest and mother of John the Baptist, was born in Jerusalem to a righteous father named Matthan (Matthew), from the tribe of Levi and the house of Aaron the priest, and her mother was a pious woman named Sofia. There was a familial relation between her and the Holy Virgin St. Mary, since their mothers were related, and Scripture testified that she and her husband were both righteous before God, walking blamelessly in all the Lord's commandments and ordinances. Elizabeth was barren, and she and her husband constantly prayed and entreated God for offspring, persevering for many years until they were well advanced in age, because God delayed answering for a divine purpose, until the appointed time for the incarnation of the Lord Christ, the Son of God, the Logos, for whom John, son of Zacharias and Elizabeth, would prepare the way. In the fullness of time, God sent the angel Gabriel to Zacharias to announce Elizabeth's conception of John and what would become of the child, and Elizabeth rejoiced with her neighbors and relatives. The Virgin Mary visited her to congratulate and serve her during her pregnancy in old age, and when Mary greeted her, the babe leaped in Elizabeth's womb and Elizabeth, filled with the Holy Spirit, blessed Mary and the fruit of her womb, after which Mary remained with her about three months. When Elizabeth's full time came, she brought forth a son, and her neighbors and relatives rejoiced at the Lord's great mercy, and the child was called John, as the angel had named him. When Elizabeth completed her days, she departed in peace.

6-16.name: Pope Michael III, 92nd Patriarch of Alexandria
6-16.summary: Pope Michael III departed in 1478 A.D. He was born in Samalut, in the el-Minya governorate, to Christian parents who taught him the Christian subjects, and he longed for the monastic life, became a monk in one of the monasteries, and lived a godly life. After Pope Gabriel VI departed, the bishops and lay leaders (archons) unanimously agreed to choose this monk for the patriarchate, and he was consecrated on the 13th of Meshir in 1477 A.D. He did not last long on the apostolic throne, but only one year and three days, before departing in peace, and he was buried with great honor in the Church of the Virgin at Babylon el-Darag in Old Cairo.

6-16.name: St. Michael (Mikhael) el-Behairy, el-Muharraqy, the Hegumen
6-16.summary: St. Michael el-Behairy departed in 1923 A.D., and he was a disciple of the great St. Anba Abraam, bishop of el-Fayyum and el-Giza. He was born in 1847 A.D. in Eshneen el-Nasarah to pious Christian parents who raised him in a true Christian upbringing, and he was called el-Behairy after his family name (el-Beharrwah), because his family was originally from the el-Beheira governorate. When he was twelve, his father became seriously ill and died, and while he was on a roof at a relative's house, he saw his father's spirit ascending to heaven surrounded by luminous angels praising and singing hymns, and an angel told him to ask and pray that his end would be like his father's. During that period he met Hegumen Tawadros of el-Muharraq Monastery, who often spoke to him about the nobility of monasticism and the angelic life of monks, so he passionately loved virginity and the monastic life, practiced it at home, and later joined el-Muharraq Monastery during the time of Hegumen Bolos el-Dalagawy el-Muharraqy, who later became St. Anba Abraam. After a period as a novice, the abbot and monks, seeing his meekness and obedience, ordained him a monk named Michael, entrusted him to the holy old monk Hegumen Saleeb el-Owlwany to learn the monastic path, and he grew in piety and asceticism, was ordained a priest in 1874 A.D. and then hegumen, and later became father of confession and spiritual guide to all the monastery's monks. God granted him the gift of healing the infirm, many sought his prayers, and he became well known for giving and compassion to the needy, like his teacher Anba Abraam, offering from the little he had with love and contentment, and in the later part of his life he lost his vision but thanked God and persisted in prayer. After a life full of righteous deeds, holiness, asceticism, compassion, and purity, he reposed in the Lord at age seventy-six, after twenty years in the world and fifty-six years in the monastery in hard monastic struggle, and at his departure an older Ethiopian monk in the monastery saw his pure spirit ascending to heaven accompanied by angels singing and praising God. On the feast of his repose in 1991 A.D., during the papacy of Pope Shenouda III, the 117th Patriarch of Alexandria, his relics were uncovered with great veneration in the presence of fourteen bishops, and his body was placed in a special shrine in the monastery for the Christ-loving people to receive his blessings.

6-17.name: St. Mina the Monk
6-17.summary: St. Mina was born in Akhmim to Christian parents, and his father worked in farming. Raised in a Christian household and inclined from youth to renounce the world, he became a monk in a monastery in Akhmim and later lived in a monastery at el-Ashmunain, where he remained for 16 years. When Arab rulers denied the doctrine of the divine incarnation, he obtained his abbot's permission, went before the Arab captain of the soldiers, and defended the faith, explaining that the incarnation of the Word was necessary for salvation and that the Son's sonship is like light proceeding from the sun rather than parental procreation. The enraged captain ordered his soldiers to cut Mina into pieces and throw him into the river, so he received the crown of martyrdom, and believers gathered the pieces of his body, shrouded them, and buried them with great honor. He is a different Mina from St. Mina the Wonderworker and from Pope Mina I.

6-17.name: The Consecration of the Church of St. Castor of Bardanouha
6-17.summary: St. Castor was martyred in Alexandria, and when his body arrived in his hometown of Bardanouha, all the people went out to receive it and carried it with great veneration to his house. After the persecution ended, his home was changed into a church named for him and was consecrated on this day. The entry states that a church in Bardanouha bearing his name still existed at the time of writing.
hymnIds: Adam Psali for the Martyrdom of Abba Castor of Bardanuha
Watos Psali for the Martyrdom of Abba Castor of Bardanuha

6-18.name: St. Malatius the Confessor
6-18.summary: St. Malatius is presented as a confessor and bishop of Antioch who defended the orthodox faith in a time of controversy. The entry describes his suffering and exile for that confession rather than a peaceful, unopposed episcopate. He departed after a life marked by steadfast confession, and the day commemorates his departure as a confessor, not a martyrdom by execution.

6-18.name: The Consecration of the Church of St. Paul the Simple
6-18.summary: This entry commemorates the consecration of a church dedicated to St. Paul the Simple. It is presented as a church-consecration commemoration, rather than a detailed account of Paul's life or martyrdom, and no further narrative is given in the entry.

6-19.name: The Relocation of the Relics of St. Martianus (Martinianus) the Monk to Antioch
6-19.summary: St. Martianus was a monk associated with Antioch who later went to Athens. He departed in Athens, and the entry commemorates the transfer of his relics from Athens back to Antioch. Patriarch Demetrius is said to have sent priests to bring the body, which was placed in a sarcophagus in Antioch. The day is therefore a relic-relocation commemoration, not the day of Martianus's original departure.

6-20.name: St. Peter II, Patriarch of Alexandria
6-20.summary: St. Peter II is presented as a successor in the Alexandrian patriarchate after St. Athanasius, with whom he had been closely associated. His patriarchate is described in the context of persecution and opposition, including exile, followed by return to his see. He served the church in Alexandria through that turbulent period and departed in peace after completing his pastoral work. The entry commemorates his departure as patriarch, not a martyrdom.

6-20.name: Sts. Basil, Theodore, and Timothy
6-20.summary: Sts. Basil, Theodore, and Timothy are presented together as martyrs who suffered during the persecution under Septimius Severus. They had been imprisoned for a long time, and they then came forward and openly declared their Christian faith. The entry says they received the crown of martyrdom, but it does not give a separate, detailed method of execution for each man.

6-21.name: The Monthly Commemoration of the Holy Virgin St. Mary
6-21.summary: This is the regular monthly commemoration of the Virgin Mary observed on the 21st day of each Coptic month. It is a feast of commemoration rather than an account of a saint's death or martyrdom on this date. The entry therefore has no life, martyrdom, or departure narrative of the kind given for individual saints.

6-21.name: St. Onesimus the Disciple of St. Paul
6-21.summary: St. Onesimus was a servant of Philemon who fled to Rome, where he met St. Paul and became a Christian. Paul sent him back to Philemon, who forgave him and set him free, and Onesimus then devoted himself to preaching and church service. The entry presents him as a disciple of Paul who later received the crown of martyrdom.

6-21.name: St. Gabriel I, 57th Patriarch of Alexandria
6-21.summary: St. Gabriel I is presented as a monk who was chosen to lead the Alexandrian church as its 57th patriarch. He guided the church during his patriarchate and is commemorated for his pastoral leadership. He departed in peace after completing his service as patriarch.

6-21.name: St. Zacharias, Bishop of Sakha
6-21.summary: St. Zacharias served as bishop of Sakha and is commemorated for his episcopal ministry. The entry presents him as a shepherd of his diocese who lived a life of faithful service. He departed in peace, and the day commemorates his departure as bishop. He is a different Zacharias from Zacharias the Priest, father of John the Baptist, and from Zacharias the Child.

6-22.name: St. Maruta (Marouta) the Bishop
6-22.summary: St. Maruta was bishop of Mia-Farkain, in the land between the two rivers, Mesopotamia, and was described as knowledgeable and righteous. Emperor Theodosius the Great sent him to Shapur, king of Persia, to negotiate the conditions of a truce, and the king welcomed him and housed him in a royal palace. When Maruta learned that the king had an infirm daughter, he asked that she be brought to him, prayed over her, and she was healed, greatly rejoicing the king. Having found favor, he asked for the relics of the saints martyred in Persia, collected them, built a church for them with a great wall around it, and a city later built inside the wall was named Maruta. After finishing his good struggle, he departed in peace.

6-23.name: St. Eusebius, Son of Basilides the Vizier
6-23.summary: St. Eusebius was martyred in 303 A.D., and was one of the great generals of the Roman army who fought in the war against the Persians. During that war, Diocletian abandoned the Christian faith and worshiped idols, but when Eusebius returned after the war, he agreed with his relatives Abadir, Yustus, Ekladius, and Theodore (Tadros) to confess their faith in Christ before the emperor. When the emperor proposed idol worship, they all refused, and Eusebius was exiled to Egypt, where the governor of Qift (Coptos) tortured him, dismembered him with the Hinbazeen, and beat him severely, while an angel healed, strengthened, and comforted him. He saw in a night vision paradise, the mansions of the saints, and the place prepared personally for him, and his soul was consoled. Later the governor ordered him burned in a fiery furnace outside Ahnas (Hnes), but an angel put out the fire and brought him out safely, and finally the governor ordered him beheaded, so he received the crown of martyrdom.

6-24.name: St. Agapetus the Bishop
6-24.summary: St. Agapetus, bishop of Synnada in Phrygia, departed in 336 A.D., after being born in Cappadocia to Christian parents who raised him in godliness and piety. When he grew up, he served the hermits and learned worship and asceticism from them, and during the time of Diocletian he became a monk in a monastery. Licinius the governor heard of him, brought him by force, and enlisted him as a soldier in the army, but this did not prevent him from continuing his ascetic life and worship; instead he greatly increased in godliness. After Diocletian perished and Constantine the Great reigned, Constantine learned his story, released him, and Agapetus returned to his place of asceticism and worship. The bishop of Synnada then brought him, made him his assistant, and ordained him a priest, and when that bishop departed, the people chose Agapetus as his successor. He showed fiery zeal in shepherding and serving souls, persevered in exhorting and teaching his flock, cared greatly for the poor and needy, and many splendid signs were performed through his hands, and when he completed his good endeavor, he departed in peace.

6-24.name: St. Timothy and St. Matthias
6-24.summary: Coptic Reader gives only the heading and the one line that on this day also was the martyrdom of St. Timothy of Gaza and St. Matthias of the City of Qus, with no further life, place, or manner-of-death detail in the entry, so none is recorded here. These are not identified in the entry with Timothy the Apostle or Timothy the Anchorite.

6-25.name: Sts. Philemon, Apphia, and Their Son Archippus
6-25.summary: Sts. Philemon, Apphia, and their son Archippus were martyred in 65 A.D. and were natives of Colosse, capital of Phrygia in Asia Minor. They believed in Christ through the apostle St. Paul, shared in his missionary ministry, and Philemon received Paul's epistle urging him to receive the repentant runaway slave Onesimus as a brother rather than a slave. The apostles later consecrated Philemon bishop of Colosse, where he served his people in righteousness and purity. After Nero's persecution following the burning of Rome, heathens seized Philemon and his family while they were praying, scourged them severely, placed them in a pit, and stoned them until they delivered their spirits and received the crowns of martyrdom.

6-25.name: St. Quona, in the City of Rome
6-25.summary: Coptic Reader gives this entry as a heading only, with no body text, so no life, place, or manner of martyrdom detail is recorded here.

6-25.name: St. Mina, in the City of Quos
6-25.summary: Coptic Reader gives only the one-line statement that St. Mina, in the City of Quos, was martyred on this day, with no further detail, so none is recorded here. This Mina is not identified in the entry with any other Mina.

6-25.name: St. Abu-Fana in Mount Delga
6-25.summary: St. Abu-Fana departed in the reign of Emperor Theodosius the Great. Born to pious Christian parents, he loved solitude, contemplation, and mercy to the poor, became a monk in his youth at a monastery of el-Ashmunain, and supported himself by manual work, eating part of his earnings and giving the rest to the poor. With his abbot's permission he lived in a cave in the western desert west of the village of Abu-Sair, where God granted him a spring of water, and he fasted daily until evening in summer and for two days at a time in winter, with many prayers and prostrations. His dwelling became a spiritual center where monks sought his guidance and God granted him miracles and signs, and when an angel told him his departure was near, he received the Holy Mysteries standing, bade his brothers farewell, blessed them, and delivered his spirit; he was buried with great honor and a monastery named for him was built near Bani-Khaled, still in the wilderness west of Mallawy.

6-26.name: The Prophet Hosea
6-26.summary: The entry commemorates Hosea as a prophet of Israel, the son of Beeri, whose prophetic ministry is presented as calling Israel back to God during the period of the kings of Judah and Israel. His book is presented as a message of judgment for unfaithfulness and of God's enduring love and restoration for a repentant people. The entry records that he completed his prophetic service and departed in peace, and that he was buried in his own land.

6-26.name: St. Zadok the Priest and the 128 Who Were with Him
6-26.summary: The entry presents St. Zadok as a priest in Persia who, with 128 companions, refused to abandon the Christian faith during persecution. They were seized, tortured, and pressed to deny Christ, but remained steadfast in their confession. The entry records that they were then martyred together, receiving the crown of martyrdom for their faithfulness.

6-26.name: St. Tyrannius, Bishop of Tyre, St. Silvanus, Bishop of Emesa, and St. Zinopius the Priest
6-26.summary: Sts. Tyrannius, Silvanus, and Zinopius were martyred in 304 A.D., during the persecution under Diocletian, and Tyrannius is identified as bishop of Tyre, Silvanus as bishop of Emesa, and Zinopius as a priest from Antioch. They were arrested for their Christian faith and steadfast preaching, subjected to severe tortures, and exposed to wild beasts without denying Christ. The entry records that they were finally beheaded, completing their martyrdom and receiving the crown of life.

6-27.name: St. Eustathius, Patriarch of Antioch
6-27.summary: St. Eustathius departed in 337 A.D. and was born in Pamphylia in the middle of the third century. He became patriarch of Antioch in 324 A.D., attended the Council of Nicaea, and defended the Orthodox faith against Arian teaching. Arians plotted against him, falsely accusing him, and secured his exile to Thrace by the emperor. The entry records that he departed in peace in exile, steadfast in the Orthodox faith. He is a different Eustathius from the martyr Eustathius commemorated on Thoout 26 and 27.

6-27.name: St. Perpetua
6-27.summary: St. Perpetua was martyred in 203 A.D. and was born in 181 A.D. in Carthage, was 22 years old, and was a noblewoman and nursing mother. She was arrested with companions for refusing to sacrifice to idols, remained steadfast through imprisonment and trial, and was exposed to a wild cow in the arena. The entry records that she was finally beheaded by the sword, receiving the crown of martyrdom.

6-28.name: The Relocation of the Relics of St. Theodore (Tadros), the Oriental (el-Mishreke)
6-28.summary: The entry records that St. Theodore had been martyred by burning in Amasia, capital of Pontus in Asia Minor, in 306 A.D. After the empire settled and Emperor Constantine proclaimed the Edict of Milan establishing religious freedom for Christians, divine providence willed the relocation of his relics. His pure relics were moved to the city of Nyssa, where a church was built in his name. The entry records that many miracles and signs were manifested from his relics, which were honored in their new resting place.

Watos Psali for the Church Consecration for Saints Theodore the Eastern and Theodore of Shotep
Adam Psali for the Martyrdom of Saint Theodore Anatolius
Watos Psali for the Martyrdom of Saint Theodore Anatolius

6-29.name: St. Polycarp, Bishop of Smyrna
6-29.summary: St. Polycarp was martyred in 167 A.D. and was bishop of Smyrna, known as Izmir, a contemporary and disciple of St. John the Evangelist. He met St. Ignatius of Antioch on Ignatius's way to Rome for martyrdom, and in 157 A.D. he went to Rome to settle the dispute between Rome and the Eastern churches over the date of the feast of the Resurrection, reaching agreement with the pope of Rome before returning to his see. He carried out his pastoral work with zeal, wrote on the virginal birth, death, hell, eternal torment, St. Mary, and the economy of salvation, and drew many souls to faith. Under Emperor Marcus Aurelius he was arrested and urged to deny Christ, answering that he had served his Lord for 86 years without harm and could not blaspheme his King who saved him. The entry records that fire did not harm him, so the emperor ordered him stabbed with a spear; his blood flowed profusely and put out the fire, he delivered his pure spirit and received the crown of life, and believers shrouded and buried his body with great honor.

6-30.name: The Appearance of the Head of St. John the Baptist
6-30.summary: The entry celebrates the appearance of the head of St. John the Baptist in Homs, Syria, after St. John appeared in a vision to Abba Martianus, Bishop of Homs, and guided him to its whereabouts, where he found it and celebrated its appearance with great veneration. It recounts that Herod had cut off John's holy head because of his marriage to Herodias, then regretted the beheading and hid the head in his house, where its place remained unknown for a long time. Two Christian men from Homs, traveling to Jerusalem during Lent, spent the night near Herod's palace, where St. John appeared to one of them, told him his name and the place of his head, and ordered him to take it home; on waking they dug where the saint specified and found the head in a pottery vessel, from which a sweet aroma came when it was opened. The entry records that the man who saw the vision took the head home and lit a lamp before it, and that after his departure it passed from person to person in Homs until St. John appeared to Bishop Martianus in the later part of the fourth century, guided him to it, and he found it and celebrated a great feast for it.
