6-30.name: Pope Kyrollos VI, 116th Pope of Alexandria
6-30.summary: Pope Kyrollos VI departed on March 9, 1971 A.D. He was born in Damanhour to godly parents as Azer Yousef Atta. He practiced monastic life at home, went to the monastery of el-Baramous in July 1927 and became a monk named Mina el-Baramousy, was ordained a priest on July 18, 1931, fled to Upper Egypt and stayed at St. Shenouda monastery in Souhag when he heard Pope Youannis intended to ordain him bishop, and later lived in a cave an hour's walk from the monastery, coming only on Saturday nights for vespers and Sunday liturgy. In early 1936 he lived in a deserted mill on Mokattam mount in Old Cairo, in 1941 became abbot of Anba Samuel the Confessor monastery at Qalamoun mount, which he renovated, and in 1947 returned to Old Cairo and built a church named for St. Mina, where many pious monks became his disciples and many later became bishops, while he healed the sick, cast out evil spirits, and solved visitors' problems through prayer. After Pope Yousab II departed, the anchorite Hegumen Mina el-Baramousy was chosen by altar lot as the 116th Pope of Alexandria and consecrated on Sunday, May 10, 1959 as Pope Cyril VI; in June 1959 he consecrated a Patriarch Catholicos for the Ethiopian church, in November 1959 laid the foundation stone of the monastery of St. Mina in the Mariot wilderness and relocated his relics there, in 1967 compounded the holy Myron, in April 1968 witnessed the transfiguration of the Virgin Mary on the domes of her church in Zeitoun, and in June 1968 received the relics of St. Mark after nearly eleven centuries away and laid them under the altar of the great St. Mark cathedral he built at Anba Rowais, el-Abbasyah. The entry records that he remained a poor, simple monk in food and life, diligent in midnight praise and daily liturgy, that God granted him great miracles even after his departure, and that after a brief illness, on the day of his departure he received his children, raised the cross saying 'May the Lord arrange your affairs,' and delivered his pure soul to God; on November 25, 1972 his pure relics were relocated to the monastery of St. Mina at Mariot according to his handwritten will, and on that day heaven honored him with thunder and rain such as had never been seen before.
hymnIds: Adam Psali for Pope Kyrillos VI
Watos Psali for the Saint Pope Kyrillos VI

7-1.name: Sts. Makronius and Thecla
7-1.summary: Coptic Reader gives this entry as a heading only, with no further life or death detail, so none is recorded here.

7-1.name: St. Alexandrus, the Soldier
7-1.summary: St. Alexandrus was born in Rome and served as a soldier under Maximianus. When he refused to offer incense to idols and confessed Christ, he was hanged, had a stone tied to his feet, was beaten, and was cast into fire, from which he emerged unharmed. He was then beheaded with the sword in the year 297 A.D., in the thirteenth year of the martyrs.

7-1.name: St. Narcissus, Bishop of Jerusalem
7-1.summary: St. Narcissus was a bishop of Jerusalem who was accused during persecution and withdrew to the wilderness, where he lived in solitude. After the persecution ended, he returned to his see and shepherded his flock again. He departed in peace in 222 A.D., after about thirty-seven years in his office.

7-1.name: Anba Marcura, the Bishop
7-1.summary: Coptic Reader gives this entry as a heading only, with no further life detail, so none is recorded here.

7-1.name: Monk George (Guirguis) Ebn El-A'ameed, Known as Ebn el-Makeen
7-1.summary: George was a learned monk and priest from Egypt who spent many years in monastic life and in the study of the Scriptures. He lived to the age of 105, with the account dividing his life between his years in the world and his years as a monk and priest. He was known for prayer, fasting, and teaching, and he departed in peace after a long and disciplined life.

7-2.name: St. Macrobius, the Bishop
7-2.summary: St. Macrobius was born in Ashmun Grais in Menofia to wealthy Christian parents and was raised in fasting, prayer, and reading. He was ordained bishop of Nikiu, but when he refused to worship idols before the governor, he was beaten, insulted, and had melted lime mixed with vinegar poured down his throat, yet was healed. He was then sent to Alexandria, imprisoned, ordered to be crushed and dismembered, and cast to wild beasts, which did not harm him. He was finally beheaded with the sword, and Julius el-Akfehasi took his body, with a cross placed on his chest, and returned it by ship to his diocese, stopping at his hometown of Ashmun Grais, where he was buried with honor. The account says he lived 130 years, including 69 years in the episcopal rank.

7-3.name: Pope Cosmas III, 58th Patriarch of Alexandria
7-3.summary: Pope Cosmas III excelled in the Scriptures from his youth and succeeded Gabriel I, being consecrated in Alexandria on the fourth of Paremhotep in 920 A.D., or 636 of the martyrs. He was known for purity, chastity, care for the poor and needy, teaching, building churches, and consecrating bishops for vacant dioceses, including Anba Peter as metropolitan of Ethiopia. During the Fatimid conquest of Egypt, with its famine, looting, and killing, he supported his flock through prayer, fasting, and visitation. Weakened by asceticism and sorrow, he departed in peace in 932 A.D., or 648 of the martyrs, after about twelve years on the throne.

7-3.name: St. Porphyry, the Martyr
7-3.summary: St. Porphyry was a wealthy man from Banias who was generous to the poor and needy and visited prisoners. During the persecution under Diocletian, he stood in front of his house and openly declared himself a Christian when the prince passed by. When the prince tried to dissuade him and he refused, he was beheaded, and the people of his hometown took his body, shrouded it richly, and buried it with veneration. He is a different Porphyry from Porphyry, Bishop of Gaza, commemorated on the same day.

7-3.name: St. Porphyry, Bishop of Gaza
7-3.summary: St. Porphyry, Bishop of Gaza, was born in 353 A.D., or 69 of the martyrs, in Thessalonica to rich Christian parents, and was raised in both Christian and secular learning. At age twenty-five he became a monk in the wilderness of Shiheet for five years, then lived alone in a cave in severe asceticism until he was near death. He went to Jerusalem, where he was healed after prayer at the holy places, and he later became bishop of Gaza. As bishop he struggled against idolatry, built churches, and served his flock with teaching and charity, departing in peace in 420 A.D., or 136 of the martyrs. He is a different Porphyry from the martyr Porphyry commemorated on the same day.

7-3.name: St. Hadid, the Priest
7-3.summary: St. Hadid was born in 1387 A.D., or 1103 of the martyrs, in the village of Singar near el-Borollos Lake, to pious parents; his father was a fisherman, and his mother had been told in a vision that God would grant her a blessed son. He refused marriage, worked as a fisherman with his father and as a laborer, gave his earnings to the needy, and served faithfully in the church named for the Virgin Mary in the village of Matobas el-Romman, after a vision of the Virgin directed him there rather than to the monastery of St. Macarius. The villagers unanimously nominated him for the priesthood, and the bishop ordained him; he taught by word and example, was known for healings and signs, and endured tribulations from which the Lord delivered him. After completing his course, he became ill with a severe fever and delivered his pure soul, and the people mourned him, shrouded him, and buried him with great veneration.

7-4.name: The Assembly of the Holy Council on the Island of Bani-Omar
7-4.summary: This council met against the Quartodecimans, or Fourteenthans, who celebrated the Holy Resurrection with the Jews on the fourteenth of Nisan, in April, regardless of the weekday. The bishop of the island excommunicated them and informed Serapion, Patriarch of Antioch; Democratus, Archbishop of Rome; Demetrius, Patriarch of Alexandria; and Symmachus, Patriarch of Jerusalem. Each sent an epistle directing that the feast be kept only on the Sunday following the Jewish feast, and ordering the excommunication of anyone who disobeyed. Eighteen bishops then convened, read the epistles, and excommunicated those who persisted in the error, deciding that the Feast of the Resurrection should be celebrated as ordered by the Holy Apostles, on Sunday, and that anyone celebrating it on another day, together with the Jewish feasts, would be separated from the Christians.

7-4.name: St. Haboulyous (Hanulius), the Prince
7-4.summary: St. Haboulyous was born in the city of Perga in Pamphylia to Christian parents, was raised in true faith, and loved the Lord, worship, and piety, becoming prince, or governor, of Perga. When Emperor Diocletian heard that he was a Christian, he sent Barnabakhas the governor with orders to arrest him, and Haboulyous declared his Christian faith before the governor. The governor became angry and ordered him to be crucified, but the Lord comforted and strengthened him. He finally departed in peace and received the crown of martyrdom.

7-5.name: Anba Serapamon, Hegumen of the Monastery of Abba Yehnis (John)
7-5.summary: Anba Serapamon was raised from youth in piety and virtue and became a monk in the monastery of St. Abu-Yehnis the Short, or Colobos, where he persevered in worship, asceticism, fasting, and prayer. His virtues became known, he was ordained hegumen, and he added still more piety and asceticism, fasting all day from the time he joined the monastery until his departure. For many years he managed the monastery and served its fathers and monks, then shut himself in a cell in austere asceticism, reading and contemplation. Near his departure, an angel of the Lord appeared to him in a vision and gave him a cross of fire, telling him not to fear, since the Lord Christ had not given fire dominion over him, and that he should partake of the Holy Mysteries and that the angel would return after three days to take him. He told the elders the vision, wept, bid them farewell, asked to be remembered in their prayers, and departed in peace on the third day, surrounded by the elders, who shrouded and buried him with great honor.

7-5.name: St. Eudoxia (Eutychia)
7-5.summary: St. Eudoxia was of Samaritan origin, from the city of Ba'albek in Syria, and her beauty led many into sin while she acquired great wealth. A monk named Germanus, pretending to be a visitor, exhorted her with the fear of eternal torment and answered her questions about the resurrection and judgment, explaining from the Scriptures that God would accept sincere repentance through faith in the Lord Christ, who came into the world, took sins by the Crucifixion, and rose from the dead. Her heart was opened, she went to Anba Theodorus, bishop of Baalbek, confessed the Holy Trinity and the Incarnation of God the Word, repented, confessed her sins, and was baptized. She then distributed all she owned to the poor and needy, joined a house of virgins, and persevered in prayer, fasting, and asceticism. Accused before Emperor Trajan, she refused his attempts to make her deny her faith in the Lord Christ, and he ordered her beheaded, so she received the crown of martyrdom in the year 114 A.D.

7-6.name: St. Dioscorus
7-6.summary: St. Dioscorus was born in Alexandria to Christian parents but, during the time of the Arabs, for an unexplained reason left the Christian faith and adopted the faith of the Arabs. His sister, hearing this, sent him a letter from el-Fayyom saying that she would rather have heard that he had died a Christian than that he was alive and had abandoned the faith of the Lord Christ, and that the letter marked the end of relations between them. Reading the letter touched him, he wept bitterly, signed himself with the cross, prayed fervently, and went out into the streets of the city, declaring that he had been born a Christian, would die a Christian, and knew nothing else. The governor threatened him, scourged him severely, and imprisoned him, but could not change his conviction, and sent him to the Khalifa of Egypt, who ordered him to be burned. He was cast into fire and burned outside the city, thus receiving the crown of martyrdom. He is a different Dioscorus from Dioscorus of the Dioscorus and Esculapius pair commemorated on Tobi 1.

7-6.name: St. Theodotus, Bishop of Corinth, the Confessor
7-6.summary: St. Theodotus was bishop of the city of Corinth on the island of Cyprus and confessed the Lord Christ before Julius, the governor of that city, during the reign of Emperor Diocletian. When he refused to deny his faith or raise incense to idols, he was painfully scourged with whips of buffalo hide, his body was combed with iron combs that tore his flesh, and he was imprisoned. He remained in prison until the reign of Constantine, when he was released along with all those imprisoned for the faith, and he returned to his episcopal seat. He continued to tend the flock entrusted to him and, after finishing his good course, departed in peace.

7-7.name: Sts. Philemon and Apollonius
7-7.summary: Sts. Philemon and Apollonius were a singer and a flute-player in the service of Arianus, the persecuting governor of Ansena, or Antinoe, and they were very close friends who desired the crown of martyrdom. Philemon went to the governor, confessed the Lord Christ before him, and was ordered to be shot with arrows, thus receiving the crown of martyrdom in the year 21 of the martyrs, or 305 A.D. Apollonius then came before the governor, also confessed the Lord Christ, and Arianus angrily ordered him to be shot with arrows as well. While he was being shot, one arrow glanced back and struck the governor's eye, and on the advice of some Christians present, the governor smeared his eye with some of Apollonius's blood and immediately regained his sight. He regretted what he had done in tormenting the saints and believed in the Lord Christ, while Apollonius completed his struggle and received the crown of martyrdom. This Philemon is a different Philemon from Philemon of Colosse commemorated on Amshir 25.

7-7.name: St. Mary, the Israelite
7-7.summary: St. Mary, the Israelite, did not know anything about the Lord Christ and lived a sinful life, until the Lord sent her a holy man who preached to her, revealed the way of salvation and faith in the Lord Christ, and told her that the soul must answer for all its deeds on judgment day, according to the Old Testament. Hearing this, she was fearful and trembling, and grace moved her heart; when she asked whether God would accept her repentance and pardon her sins, he replied that if she believed that the Lord Christ had come into the world for the salvation of mankind, was crucified on our behalf, died, and rose from the dead on the third day, she would be accepted. She repented, believed, and was baptized with holy baptism. When the governor learned of her, he brought her before him, and she confessed her faith in the Lord Christ and remained steadfast, refusing his promises and threats. He ordered her tortured and finally beheaded with the sword, so she received the crown of martyrdom.

7-8.name: St. Matthias, the Apostle
7-8.summary: St. Matthias was born in the region of Galilee, followed the apostles, and was chosen in place of Judas Iscariot during the apostolic assembly in the upper room of Zion, after Peter recalled the Scriptures concerning Judas, who had become a guide to those who arrested Jesus, had bought a field with the wages of iniquity, and had fallen headlong so that his entrails gushed out, with the field becoming known as Akel Dama, the Field of Blood. The disciples proposed Joseph called Barsabas, surnamed Justus, and Matthias, prayed for the Lord to show which of the two He had chosen for the ministry and apostleship, cast lots, and the lot fell on Matthias, who was numbered with the eleven apostles, as recorded in Acts 1:15-26. After being filled with the Holy Spirit on the day of Pentecost, he preached the Gospel in Judea, Samaria, and Cappadocia, and, it is said, in the country of the cannibals, until he reached the city of Bartus, where the people did not accept the Word and imprisoned him. He prayed, interceding with the Virgin St. Mary, who came on a cloud, melted all the iron in the city as wax, released Matthias and all imprisoned with him for the faith, healed the governor's possessed son, and, after the governor and all the people believed, restored the iron and went up on a luminous cloud, while Matthias baptized the people, taught and confirmed them, and ordained priests for them. He then went to Damascus, preached in the Name of the Lord Christ, was seized and tormented, and was laid on an iron bed with fire lit beneath it, which did not harm him while his face shone like the sun, so that the people marveled, believed, were baptized, and received priests from him. After tarrying many days to confirm them in the faith, he returned to Jerusalem, where the Jews stoned him, so he was martyred in the year 68 A.D. and received the crown of martyrdom. He is a different Matthias from Matthias of Qus commemorated on Amshir 24.

7-8.name: St. Julian, 11th Pope of Alexandria
7-8.summary: St. Julian was a student in the theological school of Alexandria established by St. Mark and a disciple of St. Pantaenus, and he excelled and surpassed many in knowledge, righteousness, and purity. He was ordained a priest in Alexandria and then Patriarch on the ninth of Paremhotep in the year 178 A.D. Before his departure, the angel of the Lord announced to him that the one who would bring him a cluster of grapes would succeed him on the Patriarchal Throne, and while the bishops and lay leaders were gathered around him, he foretold that a person carrying a cluster of grapes would come to present it to him. Demetrius the vine dresser, a layman trimming his vine, found a cluster of grapes out of season, decided to present it to Patriarch Abba Julian as a gift, and arrived carrying it in his hand while the others were still perplexed, so Julian rejoiced at the fulfillment of his vision and commanded them to enthrone Demetrius as Patriarch after him. Julian occupied the apostolic throne for ten years, gave great attention to the spiritual growth of his flock, and, because the pagans would not allow him to leave Alexandria, used to leave the city in secret to ordain priests everywhere and visit his flock, until, after finishing his good course, he departed in peace in 188 A.D.

7-8.name: St. Arianus, the Governor of Ansena
7-8.summary: St. Arianus was a cruel and unjust governor of Ansena who persecuted Christianity and slew Christians, and his conversion is tied to the martyrdom of Apollonius on Baramhat 7. When he ordered Apollonius to be shot with arrows, one arrow glanced back, struck his eye, and destroyed it, and, after Christians told him that Apollonius's blood applied to his eye would restore his sight, he at first did not believe but, because of severe pain and loss of his eye, smeared some of Apollonius's blood on his eye and immediately regained his sight. He believed in the Lord Christ, regretted greatly all he had done in tormenting the saints, rose up, destroyed his idols, and refrained from torturing any believers. When Diocletian heard the report, he brought Arianus before him and asked why he had forsaken the worship of his idols, and Arianus told him of the signs and wonders God worked through the holy martyrs, who, despite torture and the cutting of their bodies, rose again whole. The emperor, furious, ordered him severely tormented and cast into a pit and covered until he died, but the Lord saved him, and Diocletian then ordered him placed in a hair sack and cast into the sea, so he delivered his soul and received the crown of martyrdom in the year 21 of the martyrs, or 305 A.D. Before bidding his kinsfolk farewell, he told them that the Lord had told him in a night vision that He would care for his body, return it to his hometown, and that they could find it on the shore of Alexandria, and the Lord ordered a dolphin to carry the body to the shore of Alexandria, where his men took it, brought it to Ansena, and placed it with the bodies of Saints Philemon and Apollonius.

7-8.name: Pope Shenouda III, 117th Pope of Alexandria
7-8.summary: Pope Shenouda III was born under the name Nazir Gayed Roufail on August 3, 1923 A.D., in the Asyut Governorate, began service in the Church's Sunday Schools in 1939 A.D., joined the Clerical College in 1946 A.D., dedicated himself to service and teaching there in 1949 A.D., took over the editorship of the Sunday Schools Magazine in October 1949 A.D., and began teaching at the Monastic School in Helwan in 1953 A.D. On July 18, 1954 A.D., he became a monk at the Monastery of the Virgin Mary, El-Sourian, in the Wadi El Natrun Desert, under the name Fr. Antonious El-Souriani, living a solitary life in a cave about seven miles from the monastery in meditation and prayer, and he was ordained a priest on Sunday, August 31, 1958 A.D., by Bishop Theophilus, bishop and head of the monastery, before being chosen by Pope Kyrillos VI in June 1959 A.D. as his personal secretary. On September 30, 1962 A.D., he was consecrated as Bishop for Education under the name Bishop Shenouda, established spiritual meetings for preaching and education around St. Ruweis Monastery in Abbassiya, and published the first issue of 'Al-Kiraza' magazine in January 1965 A.D. After the departure of Pope Kyrillos VI on March 9, 1971 A.D., elections were held under 'Regulation 57,' Bishop Shenouda was one of three candidates for the papacy, he was selected through the Altar Lot on Sunday, October 31, 1971 A.D., and he was crowned and enthroned on the Papal throne on Sunday, November 14, 1971 A.D. In January 1991 A.D. he was elected President of the World Council of Churches for Oriental Orthodox Christians for more than one term, and on November 8, 1994 A.D. he was selected Deputy President of the Middle East Council of Churches for more than one term, while undertaking 104 trips outside Egypt for pastoral and ecumenical purposes, establishing new dioceses in Egypt and in lands of emigration, and seeing churches in Europe, America, and Australia multiply from seven at his consecration to more than 450 at his departure, including consecrating the first Patriarch of Eritrea, Abuna Philipos I, in 1998 A.D., and Abuna Antonios I of Eritrea in 2004 A.D. He consecrated 117 metropolitans and bishops and ordained 1,001 priests for Cairo, Alexandria, and lands of emigration, performed the rites of Holy Chrismation, or Myron, seven times, including once for the Church in Asmara, Eritrea, brought the relics of St. Athanasius the Apostolic to Egypt in 1973 A.D., issued regulations for ecclesiastical work including those of the Holy Synod in 1985 A.D. and of consecrated sisters in 1991 A.D., and established the Bishopric for Youth Services in 1980 A.D., the General Bishopric for African Affairs in 1976 A.D., the Bishopric for Evangelism in 1995 A.D., the Institute of Pastoral Care and Education and the Institute of the Holy Bible in 1974 A.D., and the Papal Residence in St. Ruweis, Abbassia, inaugurated in January 1985 A.D., along with scientific and cultural centers including the Coptic Orthodox Cultural Center in 2008 A.D., the Pope Shenouda III Foundation for Organization and Information Technology in 2000 A.D., and the St. Mark Foundation for Coptic History Studies in 1998 A.D., while also receiving nine honorary doctoral degrees. Despite his many responsibilities, he spent three days a week in the monastery, and his love for monastic life and solitude helped revive it, with hundreds of monks and nuns consecrated and numerous monasteries established inside and outside Egypt, while he also took part in ecumenical agreements, conferences, and theological dialogues, and protected the church during President Muhammad Anwar Sadat's decisions of September 5, 1981 A.D., including stripping him of the title of Patriarch of Alexandria and Pope of the See of St. Mark, after which he was exiled and placed under house arrest at the papal residence in St. Bishoy Monastery in Wadi El Natrun for forty months, returning to his seat in January 1985 A.D. He authored about 150 books on spirituality, theology, and religious beliefs, composed about 20 spiritual poems, most transformed into spiritual songs in the Coptic Church, and confronted heresies and deviant teachings of his era, bearing responsibility for education in the church since his ordination as bishop for education in 1962 A.D. He departed on the evening of Saturday, the eighth of Paremhotep, 1727 of the Martyrs, corresponding to March 17, 2012 A.D., his funeral prayer took place on Tuesday, March 20, 2012 A.D., at the Coptic Cathedral in Abbassia, Cairo, in the presence of church representatives from around the world, political figures, and hundreds of thousands of people, both Christians and Muslims, and he was buried in a designated location in St. Bishoy Monastery in accordance with his will, after sitting on the patriarchal throne for 40 years, 4 months, and 4 days, making him the seventh longest-reigning pope on the See of St. Mark, having lived 88 years, 7 months, and 14 days.

7-9.name: St. Konan
7-9.summary: In the year 50 A.D., St. Konan departed after being baptized by the apostles, who also taught him the Christian faith. He was ordained a priest and, after seeing many people won to the faith, he built a church for them and performed miracles, including healing the sick. His ministry was marked by teaching, baptism, and good works among those people. The entry presents his departure as peaceful, following that life of priestly service, rather than as a martyrdom.

7-9.name: Sts. Andrianus, Martha His Wife, Eusebius, Armanius, and Forty Martyrs
7-9.summary: St. Andrianus was a prince, or governor, of Nicomedia who believed in Christ through the martyrs Maximus, Damianus, and others, and he was imprisoned for his faith. When Martha came to him, she urged him to hold fast to Christ and even to despise death, and he remained steadfast rather than renouncing his faith. His wife Martha, Eusebius, Armanius, and the forty martyrs were then martyred together with him. The entry closes by saying that he and his companions received the crown of martyrdom.

7-10.name: The Appearance of the Honorable Cross
7-10.summary: This entry commemorates the appearance of the Honorable Cross above Golgotha during the time of Constantine the Great and his mother Helena. Helena searched for the Cross and, after the three crosses were identified, the true Cross was recognized through the healing of a sick woman, a sign also confirmed by the patriarch Macarius. It was then raised and shown to the people, who cried out 'Lord have mercy' and prostrated before it. The account adds that in the seventh century, after the Persians carried the Cross away, Emperor Heraclius recovered it and returned it to Jerusalem with great honor.
hymnIds: Doxology for the Feast of the Cross
Watos Psali for the Feast of the Cross
Adam Psali for the Feast of the Cross
Syrian Fraction for the Feasts of the Cross and Standard Days: Thus truly the Logos…
Fraction to the Father on the Slaughter of Isaac: And it came to pass…

7-11.name: St. Basil (Basilius), the Bishop
7-11.summary: St. Basil was ordained a bishop in 298 A.D. by Abba Armoun, Patriarch of Jerusalem, among bishops without stated sees, and he was sent to preach and teach. He went to the city of Sharsunah in Syria, where he was driven out, and he retired to a cave to pray. When the governor's only son died, Basil was called to pray, and the son was raised, leading the governor and his companions to believe and be baptized. Jews and others who were envious then seized Basil, beat him, and dragged him through the streets until he delivered up his spirit and received the crown of martyrdom. He is a different Basil from Basil the Great.

7-12.name: The Monthly Commemoration of the Honorable Archangel Michael
7-12.summary: Coptic Reader presents this as the monthly commemoration of the Archangel Michael, who stands before the Lord and intercedes for mankind. No further biographical or death details are given for this commemoration, and it is not presented as a martyrdom or departure narrative.
hymnIds: Doxology for Archangels Michael and Gabriel
Fraction to the Father for Archangel Michael
Archangel Michael (12th of Every Coptic Month)

7-12.name: The Revealing of the Virginity of St. Demetrius, 12th Pope of Alexandria
7-12.summary: St. Demetrius had been a vine dresser who, though married, lived with his wife in complete purity, and an angel was said to shadow them during their sleep. After he was enthroned as Patriarch of Alexandria, an angel commanded him to reveal this so that no one would stumble because of him. Following the Divine Liturgy on a Sunday, he brought his wife forward, placed burning charcoal in his own shawl and in hers, and prayed until it was shown that neither shawl had burned. He then told the congregation that they had lived as brother and sister for forty-eight years since their marriage, which their fathers had arranged against their will.

7-12.name: St. Malachi (Malachious) of Palestine
7-12.summary: Coptic Reader gives only the one-line statement that the righteous St. Malachi was martyred in the land of Palestine, with no further life, date, or manner-of-death details, so none is recorded here.

7-12.name: St. Glathinos in Damascus
7-12.summary: St. Glathinos was a heathen actor from Marmin near Damascus who, with fellow actors, staged a mockery of Christian baptism, dipping him in water and clothing him in white apparel. During the performance he instead declared that he preferred to die as a Christian, having witnessed a wondrous miracle in the baptism itself. Those present were furious and seized him, stoning him until he delivered up his soul and received the crown of martyrdom. His family and many Christians then took his body, buried it with great honor, and built a church in his name in that place.

7-12.name: St. Hegumen Pishoy Kamel
7-12.summary: St. Pishoy Kamel was born on December 6, 1931, in Damanhur to a pious Christian family, later moved to Alexandria, and earned a Bachelor of Science in 1951, a Bachelor of Theology in 1955, and a diploma in psychology. He began Sunday School service at the Church of the Virgin St. Mary in Muharram Bek in Alexandria, became a leader of youth services in Alexandria, and was ordained a priest on December 2, 1959, for the newly founded Church of St. George the Martyr in Sporting, Alexandria. He built seven new churches in Alexandria, founded Coptic Orthodox churches in the western United States in 1970 and in New Jersey in 1974, established a church nursery in 1972 and St. George's House for children in difficult circumstances in 1976, and wrote many spiritual booklets. He bore illness with gratitude and praise until his soul departed on March 21, 1979, and his body was laid in a special shrine in the Church of St. George in Sporting, with his sanctity later recognized by the Holy Synod on June 9, 2022.

7-13.name: The Forty Martyrs of Sebaste
7-13.summary: In the year 36 of the martyrs, 320 A.D., these high-ranking officers of a Roman legion in Sebaste in Syria refused to sacrifice to idols and confessed Christ, saying they would rather lose their military positions than lose God. After imprisonment and prayer, they were stoned, but the stones rebounded on their attackers, and they were then thrown into an icy lake, where their limbs were severed by the cold. One martyr weakened and left the lake for a nearby hot bath, where he died quickly, while a guard, seeing angels placing crowns on the thirty-nine who remained, entered the lake declaring himself a Christian and completed the forty. Their bodies were ordered thrown into the sea, but on the third day they appeared to the Bishop of Sebaste in a vision, and he and his clergy and people recovered them from the sea and placed them with great honor. They are distinct from the Forty-Nine Elders of Shiheet and from the Forty Martyrs church consecration of Amshir 15.

7-13.name: Pope Dionysius, 14th Patriarch of Alexandria
7-13.summary: Pope Dionysius, who departed in 264 A.D., was born in Alexandria in the later part of the second century to parents who worshipped the stars. He was drawn to the Christian faith after buying pages containing an Epistle of St. Paul from an old Christian woman, then going to church, studying under a deacon named Augustine, and being baptized by Pope Demetrius, the twelfth pope. He excelled in the theological school, became a deacon and then a priest and dean of the school under Pope Heraclas, and was consecrated Patriarch on the first day of Tobe in 246 A.D. He shepherded his flock with care, escaped the persecution under Decius, wrote a compassionate letter to Emperor Gallus after which the persecution quieted, resisted the heresies of Sabellius and Paul of Samosata, and departed at a good old age after writing many spiritual and doctrinal epistles.

7-13.name: The Return of Sts. Macarius the Great and Macarius of Alexandria, from Exile
7-13.summary: In the year 92 of the martyrs, 376 A.D., Sts. Macarius the Great and Macarius of Alexandria returned from exile on the island of Philae, south of Aswan in Upper Egypt, where the Arian Emperor Valens had exiled them. The island's idol-worshipping natives tortured them severely for three years, but when St. Macarius the Great prayed over the demon-possessed daughter of a pagan priest, she was healed, and the priest and the people of the island believed and were baptized on the eve of the Feast of Epiphany. The saints taught them the Christian faith and turned the island temple into a church where they prayed and administered the Holy Mysteries. When they wished to return, an angel guided them to Alexandria, and from there they went to the wilderness of Shiheet (Scetis), where the monks came out to receive them with great joy.

7-14.name: Sts. Eugenius, Agathodorus, and Elpidius, the Bishops
7-14.summary: Sts. Eugenius, Agathodorus, and Elpidius were Christians by ancestry who walked faithfully in the way of God and had a great deal of knowledge of church subjects. St. Armoun, Patriarch of Jerusalem, ordained them bishops without stated sees so that they could go around preaching and teaching the word of God. They traveled to many cities, and in one city the people beat them severely and mercilessly. They were then stoned until they departed in peace and received the crowns of martyrdom.

7-14.name: St. Shenouda (Sinouti) El Bahnasawy
7-14.summary: In the year 20 of the martyrs, 304 A.D., St. Shenouda, a devout Christian born in the city of el-Bahnasa, was accused before Prince Maximianus, appointed by Diocletian, of being a Christian. He confessed his faith in the Lord Christ and did not deny it, so he was thrown to the ground, beaten with hammers until his flesh was torn and his blood flowed, and then cast into a foul-smelling prison. The Lord sent Michael the Archangel, who healed his wounds, strengthened him, and promised him the crown of glory, and the next morning he was found standing and praying, unharmed. The prince called him a sorcerer, ordered him crucified upside down and burned with fire that did not harm him, then had him crushed with the Hinbazeen and finally beheaded, after which believers took his pure body, anointed it with expensive perfumes, shrouded it in costly wrappings, and buried it with great honor. He is a different Shenouda from Shenouda the Archimandrite and from Pope Shenouda III.

7-14.name: Pope Kyrillos (Cyril) III, 75th Patriarch of Alexandria
7-14.summary: In the year 959 of the martyrs, 1243 A.D., Pope Kyrillos III, known as Ebn-Loqloq, departed after being born in El-Fayyom to Christian parents and becoming a monk in the monastery of Mar Victor near Cairo. After the departure of Pope Youannes (John) VI, the monk Daoud Ebn-Loqloq was chosen for the patriarchate in 1235 A.D. During his patriarchate a holy council attended by fourteen bishops issued many canons to reorganize the church, published in five books covering the legislation and management of the Patriarchate, baptism, matrimony and counsel to the newly wed, endowments and pledges, Coptic Church rituals, and the organization of the Patriarchal Court. He also ordained the scholar Paul El-Boushy as bishop for Cairo, who assisted him in managing church affairs, and after seven years and seven months on the Patriarchal Throne he departed and was buried in El-Shama'a (Wax) Monastery near Tamouh in Giza.

7-15.name: St. Sarah, the Nun
7-15.summary: St. Sarah was born in Upper Egypt to wealthy Christian parents who had no other children, and they raised her with a Christian upbringing, teaching her to read the Holy Bible and the biographies and sayings of the monastic fathers. Influenced by their lives, she desired the monastic life, went to a convent in Upper Egypt, dwelt there for many years as a novice, and then put on the monastic garb. She persevered in fighting the devils for thirteen years until Satan, wearied by her steadfastness and purity, tried to overcome her by pride, appearing as an angel and praising her for overcoming Satan, but she answered that she was a weak nun who could conquer him only by the power of her Lord Jesus Christ, and Satan immediately disappeared. She later dwelt in a cave on the banks of the river for a long time, unseen except when she came to partake of the Holy Mysteries, and when she completed her struggle she departed in peace at eighty years old.

7-15.name: St. Helias of Ahnas
7-15.summary: St. Helias grew up in a village near Ahnas (Ahnasia) and worked as a farmer in the orchards of Prince Klekianos, the heathen governor of Ahnas, while learning worship and asceticism from his uncle Abba Jacob, a hermit in the desert near Ahnas. The prince's daughter became attracted to him and pursued him to make him fall into sin, but he fled from her and, when she continued to pursue him intensely, he castrated himself in the naive hope of removing any hope of her falling into sin with him. The girl, furious, falsely complained to her father that Helias, a Christian, had tried to force himself on her, and though Helias proved his innocence, he strongly refused the prince's demand that he sacrifice to idols to be pardoned. After severe tortures from which the Lord saved him, he rejoiced at the order to behead him, prayed while an angel told him that Julius of Aqfa was nearby writing his biography and would shroud his body and take it to his uncle, and then extended his neck to the soldiers and received the crown of martyrdom, after which a church was built in Ahnasia, his body was relocated to it, and that church remained until the beginning of the thirteenth century before being destroyed.

7-16.name: The Apparition of the Virgin St. Mary in the Church of St. Demiana in Papadouplo, Shoubra, Cairo
7-16.summary: On Tuesday, March 25, 1986 A.D., in the year 1702 of the martyrs and the fifteenth year of the pontificate of Pope Shenouda III, the pure Virgin St. Mary appeared above the Church of St. Demiana in Papadouplo, Shoubra, Cairo. The apparitions were seen by thousands of people on the domes of the church and were marked by innumerable miracles performed by the Virgin without distinction, continuing over many months from 1986 to 1991. What happened in the church was described as tangible and gradual, beginning as wondrous light of unknown source that then took form and shape, while people felt miracles and signs around them that confirmed the faith in their hearts. The apparition was also accompanied by repeated appearances of the Virgin in different forms, pigeons flying at night, the smell of incense over the church, and luminous light inside the church towers shining outward, and it was covered by foreign and Arabic news media and confirmed by a special synodal committee entrusted by Pope Shenouda III to investigate and verify it.

7-16.name: Pope Khail I, 46th Patriarch of Alexandria
7-16.summary: In the year 483 of the martyrs, 767 A.D., Pope Khail I departed after a life that began as a pious monk in the monastery of St. Macarius the Great in the wilderness of Shiheet. After Pope Theodorus (Tawadros I) departed, bishops, priests, and lay leaders unanimously chose Khail el-Maquary for the patriarchate because of his godliness, piety, and knowledge, seized him against his will, brought him to Alexandria, and consecrated him Patriarch on the seventeenth day of Thout in 743 A.D. On the day of his enthronement it rained heavily for three days after two consecutive years of drought, which the people of Alexandria took as a good omen. He later endured beating, imprisonment, chains, and torture from the ruler Abdel-Malek Ebn Marawan, until King Kyriakos of Nubia marched about one hundred thousand soldiers toward Egypt and encamped around el-Fostat, prompting the terrified ruler to release Khail and ask him to mediate a truce, which the king accepted. The ruler then respected Khail, lifted his persecution of his people, and increased his respect further after Khail's prayers healed the ruler's daughter, who had been possessed by an unclean spirit, and Khail departed in peace after twenty-three years and six months on the apostolic throne.

7-17.name: The Departure of Lazarus, the Beloved of the Lord
7-17.summary: Lazarus was the brother of Martha and Mary, and the Lord found rest in their house. When Lazarus fell sick, Jesus stayed two more days where he was in order to magnify the miracle, then came to Bethany and had the stone removed from the tomb after Lazarus had been dead four days. At Jesus' call, 'Lazarus, come forth!', he came out bound in grave clothes, and many believed because the reality of his death made the miracle clear. The entry is titled for his departure and recounts this raising as its central event.
hymnIds: Fraction to the Son for the Feasts of Our Lord: We praise and glorify...

7-17.name: St. Sidhom Bishay in Domiat
7-17.summary: St. Sidhom Bishay was born and raised in Damietta, was devout and celibate, and was in charge of the deacons of his church; in 1820 he moved to Alexandria as a lumber merchant and took an interest in restoring the church of St. George the Zahimian in Bosat el-Nasarah. On his way to church in Damietta, a man blocked and insulted him, false accusations were made, and a court gave him the choice of forsaking his faith in Christ or being killed. He refused, was dragged through the streets, and his friend el-Moallem Apanoub Ibrahim, who tried to rescue him, was beaten on the head with palm branches and later died. A mob then tortured Sidhom for five consecutive days, which he endured thankfully invoking the Lord Jesus and the compassionate Lady St. Mary, until he delivered his pure spirit, with the Virgin present at his departure, and received the crown of martyrdom. An investigation ordered by the Khedive showed his innocence, crosses were permitted in his funeral, he was buried with great veneration in the ground of St. George's church in Damietta, a pillar of light was seen above his tomb on the night of burial, and his still-whole body is kept in a shrine in the Virgin St. Mary's church in Damietta.

7-17.name: St. Basilius, Bishop of Jerusalem
7-17.summary: St. Basilius was born in 1818 in the village of el-Dabah to godly parents who raised him in piety, faith, and church subjects, and at twenty-five he became a monk in the monastery of St. Antonios, persevering in worship and asceticism. For his godliness and knowledge he was ordained priest, then hegumen and abbot, and Pope Kyrollos IV ordained him Metropolitan of Jerusalem. He managed his diocese prudently, built churches, bought endowments to support them, and was loved by people of different religions and political affiliations for his meekness and wisdom. During a dispute with Ethiopian monks over ownership of El-Sultan monastery in Jerusalem, which belonged to the Coptic Church, his vigilance prevented the Ethiopians from taking it over. He spent his days in continuous effort for the good of the church and his people, and in 1899 (1615 of the martyrs) he finished his good endeavor and departed in peace. He is a different Basilius from Basil the Great and from Basil, Bishop of Sharsunah (7-11).

7-17.name: St. George the Ascetic, St. Belasius the Martyr, and Anba Joseph the Bishop
7-17.summary: Coptic Reader gives only the one-line commemoration of St. George the ascetic, St. Belasius the martyr, and Anba Joseph the bishop, with no further detail for these three, so none is recorded here.

7-18.name: St. Isidore, the Friend of St. Sina, the Soldier
7-18.summary: St. Isidore was born in Deknash (Dafnas), worked as a wool weaver, and was charitable, giving to the poor and fasting, and he had a vision of the Virgin with crowns for martyrs. He confessed Christ before the governor of Pelusium, was imprisoned, and was comforted by an angel, while his soldier friend Sina was sent to Alexandria and then returned. Isidore endured torture and was cast into a fiery furnace, prayed, and received the crown of martyrdom in 305. Sina's mother wept for him, saw angels, and took his body, shrouded it, and buried it. He is a different Isidore from Isidore of Pelusium and from Isidore the Priest.

7-19.name: St. Aristobulus, One of the Seventy Apostles
7-19.summary: St. Aristobulus was one of the Seventy Apostles, received the Holy Spirit at Pentecost, accompanied the disciples in preaching, turned many to the faith, baptized them, and taught them the commandments. He was consecrated a bishop, preached, worked miracles, and endured hardships from Jews and Greeks. He was stoned to death and received the crown of martyrdom, and St. Paul mentions him in Romans 16:10.

7-19.name: Sts. Alexander, Agabius, and Their Companions
7-19.summary: This entry commemorates seven martyrs from Alexandria, Gaza, Pontus, and Tripoli, who were united in love of God and went before the governor of Caesarea in Palestine to confess Christ. The governor tried to befriend them and persuade them to abandon the faith, but they would not. He then ordered severe tortures for them, and in the year 21 of the martyrs (305 A.D.) they all received the crown of martyrdom.

7-20.name: Pope Khail III, 56th Patriarch of Alexandria
7-20.summary: Pope Khail III was a virtuous monk of the monastery of St. Macarius in Shiheet, and after Pope Shenouda I he was unanimously chosen by bishops, priests, and archons and consecrated on 30 Parmoute, 596 of the martyrs (880 A.D.). He suffered hardship under the rulers, was accused before Ahmad Ibn Tulun, governor of Egypt, and was imprisoned for a year on the claim that he held a great sum of money. He was not released until he agreed to pay 20,000 dinars, for which he wrote a promissory note, and bishops and people paid half of it. After Ahmad died, his son Khumarawaih comforted the Patriarch, tore up the promissory note, and forgave the debt. Khail then rested from his toil and departed in peace in 907 (623 of the martyrs), after 27 years on the apostolic throne.

7-20.name: The Raising of Lazarus from the Dead
7-20.summary: This short entry records that the Lord raised his beloved Lazarus after four days in the tomb. It presents this as a great miracle through which many believed, and asks the risen Savior to raise us from the death of sin.
hymnIds: Fraction to the Son for the Feasts of Our Lord: We praise and glorify...

7-21.name: The Monthly Commemoration of the Theotokos, the Pure Virgin St. Mary
7-21.summary: Coptic Reader gives only the one-line monthly commemoration of the Virgin as intercessor of mankind, with no further detail, so none is recorded here.

7-21.name: The Visit of Our Savior to Bethany and the Consultation of the Chief Priests to Kill Lazarus
7-21.summary: Jesus came with his disciples to Bethany near Jerusalem, where a supper was made, Lazarus sat at table, Martha served, and Mary anointed the Savior's feet with spikenard and wiped them with her hair. The Lord praised her, pointing to his burial, saying she had kept this for the day of his burial. Many Jews came not only to see Jesus but also to see Lazarus, whom he had raised, and because many Jews were going away and believing in Jesus, the chief priests plotted to kill Lazarus also.

7-21.name: Sts. Theodore and Timothy
7-21.summary: Coptic Reader gives only the one-line commemoration of the martyrdom of Sts. Theodore and Timothy, with no further detail identifying which Theodore or Timothy, so none is recorded here.

7-22.name: St. Kyrollos (Cyril), Bishop of Jerusalem
7-22.summary: St. Cyril was born in Jerusalem in 315, was raised as a Christian, excelled in spiritual subjects and Greek literature, and was ordained deacon and then priest by St. Maximus, bishop of Jerusalem, who entrusted him with instructing catechumens, Jews, and pagans at the Church of the Resurrection. After the bishop's departure he was chosen as successor, and he strongly resisted the widely spread Arian heresy, for which he was persecuted and exiled three times from his diocese, enduring patiently and thankfully before returning to his parish. He was a prominent attendee at the Second Universal Council of Constantinople in 381, wrote many books on the Incarnation, the Creed, and the baptism of catechumens, and departed in peace in 386 (102 of the martyrs). He is a different Cyril from Pope Kyrillos III and Pope Kyrillos VI.

7-22.name: The Just Man Joseph of Arimathea
7-22.summary: Joseph was from Arimathea, a city of the Jews, was wealthy, just, and devout, waited for the kingdom of God, and did not consent to the council's counsel and deed. After the crucifixion he boldly asked Pilate for the body of Jesus, took it down, wrapped it in linen, and laid it in his own new tomb hewn from rock, in which no one had yet been laid, and rolled a stone against its entrance. The entry presents him as a righteous witness who honored the Lord in burial and concludes with his peaceful departure.

7-22.name: St. Michael, Bishop of Naqadah
7-22.summary: St. Michael was consecrated bishop of Naqadah on 12 Mesore, 1391 of the martyrs (1675 A.D.), by Pope Mettaos IV, the 102nd Patriarch, and he participated in the consecration of Pope Youannis XVI, the 103rd Patriarch. The entry records his episcopal service in Naqadah in this period and concludes with his peaceful departure. He is a different Michael from the Archangel Michael and from Michael el-Behairy.

7-23.name: Daniel, the Prophet
7-23.summary: Daniel was taken captive at sixteen during the time of Nebuchadnezzar, king of Babylon, together with the three holy young men Hananiah (Shadrach), Mishael (Meshach), and Azariah (Abed-Nego), and he purposed not to defile himself with the king's delicacies. In the fourth year of captivity he received from God and told Nebuchadnezzar both his forgotten dream and its interpretation, was given great gifts, and was appointed chief administrator over all the wise men of Babylon. He later interpreted another dream foretelling that Nebuchadnezzar's arrogance would drive him to dwell among beasts and eat grass like an ox for seven years before God restored him to his kingdom, and all of this was fulfilled. Under Belshazzar he interpreted the writing on the wall, 'Mene, Mene, Tekel, and Upharsin,' as God numbering and finishing Belshazzar's kingdom, weighing him and finding him wanting, and dividing his kingdom and giving it to the Medes and Persians. Under Darius he refused to pray to anyone but the God of heaven, was cast into the lions' den, was preserved when the Lord sent his angel to shut the lions' mouths, and was lifted out alive while his accusers were cast in and destroyed. He also prayed and confessed his people's sins, received the vision of the seventy weeks to anoint the Most Holy, prophesied the last day and final judgment, and, when he had completed his endeavor, departed in peace.

7-24.name: The Apparition of the Pure Virgin St. Mary on Her Church in Zeitoun
7-24.summary: On April 2, 1968 (1684 of the martyrs), during the papacy of Pope Kyrollos VI, the 116th Patriarch of Alexandria, the Theotokos began to appear in luminous spiritual forms in and around the domes of her church in Zeitoun, a suburb of Cairo. These apparitions continued on some nights for many hours before tens of thousands of people of every race and religion and lasted for a period of about two years. At times she appeared in full figure and at other times in half figure in a cloud of heavenly white light, adorned in an angelic white dress and holding an olive branch in her hand. Many spiritual signs accompanied the apparitions, including flying spiritual beings at night in the form of doves and the fragrance of incense seen and smelled by thousands, while crowds came nightly from inside and outside Egypt and kept vigil in praise and hymns awaiting her blessed apparition. The apparitions were accompanied by many healing miracles for people of different religions and races, the greatest miracle being the planting and establishment of faith in hearts, the news was covered by media inside and outside the country, and a great cathedral built on the site of the garage across from the original church was consecrated on April 2, 1989, by Pope Shenouda III.

7-24.name: Pope Macarius I, 59th Patriarch of Alexandria
7-24.summary: Pope Macarius I was born in Shoubra to godly Christian parents, his father died while he was young leaving him an only child to his mother, and he desired the monastic life and became a monk in the monastery of St. Macarius in the wilderness of Shiheet, where he lived a good and virtuous life. After the departure of Pope Kosma III, bishops, priests, and archons unanimously chose him for the patriarchate, he was consecrated in 932 A.D., and after his enthronement he went to the monastery of St. Macarius as was the custom of his predecessors. On his way back, the people of his hometown invited him to visit them, and he visited his righteous mother, whom he found sitting and weaving without greeting him; when he asked whether she knew him as her son Macarius who had received patriarchal rank, she wept and warned him that he was now responsible for the souls of his whole flock, not only his own soul, and must not let the glory of the presidency veil his eyes. Her words resounded in his ears all his life and moved him to care for his own salvation and faithfully attend to his duties, exhorting and guiding his people and carefully choosing bishops and priests according to 'Do not lay hands on anyone hastily' (1 Timothy 5:22). He finished his good endeavor and departed in peace in 952 A.D. (668 of the martyrs), after about 20 years on the apostolic throne.

7-25.name: St. Prisca, One of the Seventy Apostles
7-25.summary: St. Prisca was a Jew of the tribe of Benjamin whose parents kept the Law of Moses, and he followed the Savior, listened to His teachings, and witnessed His miracles. He was among the seventy apostles appointed by the Lord and was present with the disciples in the upper room of Zion when the Holy Spirit came upon them. He preached the Gospel in many countries and was then ordained bishop for Khorinyas, where he preached to the people and baptized them. Having finished his holy endeavor, he departed in peace and received the crown of heavenly glory.

7-25.name: St. Onesiphorous, One of the Seventy Apostles
7-25.summary: St. Onesiphorous was one of the seventy apostles and served in Ephesus, and when St. Paul was arrested and imprisoned in Rome, Onesiphorous visited him in prison and assisted and ministered to him. Later, Adrianus, the governor of Ephesus, seized him and tortured him severely. He was dragged amid rocks and thorns, whereupon he delivered his pure soul and received the crown of martyrdom. St. Paul praised him in his second epistle to Timothy for often refreshing him and for not being ashamed of his chains.

7-25.name: Pope Mattheos III, 100th Patriarch of Alexandria
7-25.summary: Pope Mattheos III was born in Toukh el-Nasarah to Christian parents, became a monk in the monastery of St. Macarius, and rose to become a priest, then a hegumen, and then an abbot. He was consecrated patriarch in 1631 and shepherded his flock, and he also ordained a metropolitan for the Ethiopian church. He departed in peace in 1646 A.D. (1362 of the martyrs) and was buried in the church in his hometown of Toukh.

7-26.name: St. Euphrasia, the Virgin
7-26.summary: St. Euphrasia was born in Rome to a noble family related to Emperor Honorius, and after her father died, her mother brought her to Egypt and, when she was nine, placed her in a convent where she embraced the monastic life. Her mother gave her money to the poor and lived with her daughter in the convent for many years before departing in peace. Euphrasia lived an ascetic life of fasting, wearing sackcloth, sleeping on the floor, and studying Scripture, and she was given the gift of healing and was beloved by the sisters. She died after a severe fever, while signing herself with the sign of the Cross.

7-26.name: Pope Peter VI, 104th Patriarch of Alexandria
7-26.summary: Pope Peter VI was born in Assiut and was called Mourgan, became a monk in the monastery of the great St. Antonios, and later became a priest and abbot at the monastery of St. Paula the first hermit. He was consecrated the 104th Patriarch on 17 Mesore 1434 of the martyrs (1718 A.D.), visited Lower and Upper Egypt, consecrated bishops, and built many churches, while permitting divorce only for adultery. He departed in peace in 1726 A.D. (1442 of the martyrs) and was buried in the tomb of the patriarchs in the church of the martyr Mercurius Abu-Saifain in Old Cairo.

7-27.name: The Crucifixion of Our Lord Jesus Christ
7-27.summary: In 34 A.D., Christ was crucified in the flesh for the salvation of the world, and darkness covered the land from the sixth hour to the ninth hour. He yielded up His spirit, the veil of the temple was torn, there was an earthquake, rocks were split, and saints were raised. The entry presents these events as the fulfillment of salvation and redemption.

7-27.name: St. Macarius the Great
7-27.summary: St. Macarius the Great was born in Shabsheer in the district of Menuf in 300 A.D. to the priest Abraham, who had been childless until an angel promised him a son whose name, Macarius, means 'Blessed,' and who would become the father of many spiritual children. Although his father pressed him to marry, he pretended illness, went into the wilderness, and received a vision of a Cherub granting him the desert as an inheritance for himself and his sons, and after his wife, still a virgin, and his parents had died, he gave his inheritance to the poor and went to a hut at Shanshour. The bishop of Ashmun ordained him a priest, and after a girl falsely accused him, he was beaten and forced to care for her and her child, but after four days of labor she confessed the accusation was false, he forgave her family, and at age thirty he fled to Shiheet. He lived at el-Baramus in fasting and prayer, visited St. Antonios, received the Eskeem, healed the possessed daughter of the king of Antioch, and founded the cell and church that became the monastery of St. Macarius, and although the Arian emperor Valens exiled him to the island of Philae south of Aswan for defending the Orthodox faith, he converted a pagan priest there by healing his possessed daughter. At the end of his life, St. Antonios and St. Pachomius came to him with angels and saints, he delivered his soul into the hand of the Lord, and he departed in 390 A.D. at the age of ninety, while his body remains in his monastery in the wilderness of Shiheet.
hymnIds: Adam Psali for the Church Consecration of Saint Macarius the Great in His Monastery
Watos Psali for the Church Consecration of Saint Macarius the Great in His Monastery
Doxology for St. Macarius the Great
Another Doxology for St. Macarius the Great
Glorification for St. Macarius the Great

7-27.name: St. Domicos
7-27.summary: In the year 78 of the martyrs (362 A.D.), St. Domicos, a native of Antioch, lived a pious and righteous life in seclusion in an isolated place, where he was given the gift of healing and of casting out demons, so that multitudes came to him. When the emperor Julian passed by, he was angered and questioned the saint, who answered that he had given his soul and body to God and could not dismiss those who came to him in strong faith. The emperor therefore ordered his men to seal the door of the cave, and the saint delivered his soul and received the crown of martyrdom.

7-28.name: Emperor Constantine the Great
7-28.summary: Emperor Constantine the Great was born in 272 A.D., the son of Constantius Chlorus and Helena, and Helena, a Christian, raised him well and sowed mercy and compassion toward Christians in him. After his father's death in 306 A.D., he was given the title of Caesar and reigned with justice and integrity, and when the nobles of Rome asked him to save them from the injustice of Maxentius, he marched against him after seeing a shining Cross at midday with the words 'With this you shall conquer.' He ordered a large flag bearing the Cross, defeated Maxentius, who drowned in the Tiber with most of his soldiers, entered Rome in joy, and became emperor of East and West. He freed Christians imprisoned for their faith, ordered that no work be done during Passion Week, sent his mother Helena to Jerusalem to search for the Holy Cross, and built the Church of the Resurrection where the Holy Cross was placed. In the seventeenth year of his reign, in 325 A.D., the First Ecumenical Council of 318 bishops assembled at Nicea, condemned the Arian heresy, set forth the Nicene Creed and other canons, and he rebuilt Byzantium and called it Constantinople, building many churches there and relocating to them many relics of the apostles and saints. He departed in peace in Nicomedia in 337 A.D. (53 of the martyrs), was laid in a gold sarcophagus, was carried to Constantinople, and was buried by the patriarch, bishops, priests, and people in the Church of the Apostles in the tomb he had prepared for himself.

7-28.name: Pope Peter (Petros) VII, 109th Patriarch of Alexandria
7-28.summary: Pope Peter VII was born in the village of Gawly and was called Petros el-Gawly, became a monk in the monastery of the great St. Antonios, and was ordained a priest and then a hegumen because of his good reputation and many virtues. Pope Marcus VIII summoned him to be ordained metropolitan for Ethiopia but instead ordained him a general bishop in 1808 A.D. under the name Theophilus, and after Marcus departed, everyone unanimously agreed to enthrone Theophilus as his successor, Pope Peter VII, in 1810 A.D. He was ascetic in food and clothing, adorned with meekness and humility, devoted to studying and learning the Holy Book, and greatly opposed simony, refusing to ordain anyone to a priestly rank unless he was sure of his suitability, while the church enjoyed peace and tranquility during his pontificate. When the water of the Nile had greatly decreased, the ruler of Egypt asked him to pray for its rising, and he celebrated the Divine Liturgy in a tent on the riverbank and, after washing the service utensils, threw the water and a blessed Kourban into the Nile, whereupon the waves rose up to the tent. During his papacy, Ibrahim Pasha, the son of Muhammad Ali Pasha, asked him to come to Jerusalem to verify the Holy Fire that proceeds from the Holy Sepulcher on Bright Saturday, and the Holy Light appeared and Ibrahim Pasha personally witnessed it, while the pope also refused a Russian Caesar's offer, conveyed by a prince, to place the Coptic Church under the Caesar's protection, answering that the church was under the protection of the King who does not die, the Lord Jesus Christ. He departed in peace in 1852 A.D. (1568 of the martyrs) and was buried in St. Mark's church in El-Azbakiah.

7-28.name: Anba Sarabamon, Known as 'Abu Tarha' (the Veiled), Bishop of El-Menufia
7-28.summary: Anba Sarabamon was born in one of the villages of el-Sharqia to pious Christian parents, who called him Saleeb and raised him with a true Christian upbringing, and when he grew up he worked in selling oil. One day an evil woman accused him in the market of killing her son, and in court before the judge he ordered the dead child to rise and tell the truth, whereupon the child rose and testified to the saint's innocence before everyone, and as a result of this miracle Saleeb fled vainglory and went immediately to the monastery of St. Antonius, where he became a monk. He grew in virtues until Pope Petros el-Gawly chose him, against his wish, as bishop for El-Monufia, and God granted him the gift of healing the sick and casting out evil spirits, including casting an unclean spirit from Princess Zahra, the daughter of Muhammad Ali Pasha, and casting out many evil spirits by the power of the Cross. He loved giving in secret, carrying a basket of gifts that he distributed himself to the needy without anyone knowing his identity, and he was known for simplicity and wisdom, while the Lord hearkened to his prayers, especially for those who asked him to pray that the Lord would grant them children, and he could foretell some future events. After he finished his good strife, he departed in peace in 1853 A.D. (1569 of the martyrs).
hymnIds: Doxology for St. Sarapamon the Veiled

7-29.name: The Feast of the Glorious Annunciation
7-29.summary: The church celebrates this feast because, when the time appointed by God since eternity for the salvation of mankind had come, God sent Gabriel the Archangel to Nazareth in Galilee, to a virgin betrothed to Joseph of the house of David, whose name was Mary. The angel greeted her as full of grace and blessed among women, and when she was troubled, he told her not to be afraid, for she had found favor with God, and that she would conceive and bring forth a Son named Jesus, who would be great and called the Son of the Highest, would receive the throne of His father David, and would reign over the house of Jacob forever with a kingdom that would have no end. When Mary asked how this could be, since she did not know a man, the angel answered that the Holy Spirit would come upon her and the power of the Highest would overshadow her, so that the Holy One to be born would be called the Son of God, and that with God nothing would be impossible, whereupon Mary said, 'Behold the maidservant of the Lord! Let it be to me according to your word,' and the angel departed from her (Luke 1:26-36). From that moment, the Only Begotten Son, the Word of God, came and dwelt in the womb of Our Lady the Virgin St. Mary, and the entry calls this day the first-born of all the major feasts of the Lord, because in it was the glad tidings of the salvation of the world.
hymnIds: Watos Psali for the Feast of the Annunciation
Adam Psali for the Feast of the Annunciation
Adam Aspasmos: Hail to the Mother of the True Light, the Virgin Mary, the Theotokos…
Watos Aspasmos: The Archangel Gabriel appeared to the Virgin Mary, the Mother of the True Light…
Fraction to the Son for the Feasts of Our Lord: We praise and glorify…

7-29.name: The Resurrection of the Lord Christ from the Dead
7-29.summary: In 34 A.D., the Lord fulfilled the economy of salvation and redemption by His holy Resurrection from the dead and became the first-fruits of those who have fallen asleep. The entry closes by asking the Good Savior to raise believers from the death of sin, forgive their trespasses, and grant them eternal life.

Adam Psali for the Feast of the Resurrection
The Conclusion of the Adam Theotokia
Doxology for Archangel Michael for the Resurrection
First Greek Hymn for the Procession
Second Greek Hymn for the Procession

Fraction to the Father for the Resurrection and the Pentecost Period: O Master, Lord God…
