7-30.name: The Commemoration of the Archangel Gabriel, the Announcer
7-30.summary: The church celebrates the honorable Archangel Gabriel, the announcer, because he was worthy to announce the birth of God's only begotten Son to the Virgin St. Mary. He also foretold Daniel the prophet about the return of the people of Israel from exile, about the advent of the Lord Christ for the salvation of the world, and about bringing an end to animal sacrifices. He prophesied about what would happen in the last days and announced to Zacharias the priest the birth of the forerunner, John the Baptizer. Because of what God had done through him, the entry says it is fitting to honor and venerate him and to ask for his intercession at all times.
hymnIds: Adam Psali for Archangel Gabriel the Announcer
Watos Psali for Archangel Gabriel the Announcer
Doxology for Archangels Michael and Gabriel

7-30.name: Samson, One of the Judges of Israel
7-30.summary: Samson was from the tribe of Dan and was born in Zorah by a divine revelation, for the angel of the Lord appeared to his barren mother and announced his birth, commanding her not to drink wine or eat unclean food during her pregnancy and that no razor should come upon his head, because the child was to be a Nazirite dedicated to God from the womb who would deliver Israel from the Philistines, and the angel also appeared to his father Manoah with the same words. The woman conceived and gave birth to Samson, God blessed him, and the Spirit of the Lord began to move upon him at Mahaneh Dan between Zorah and Eshtaol, and after marrying a gentile woman from Timnah, he tore apart a young lion that roared against him on the way, though he had nothing in his hand, and later found bees and honey in the lion's carcass. At a feast in Timnah, he told the Philistines the riddle, 'Out of the eater came something to eat, and out of the strong came something sweet,' and when they pressured his wife to learn the answer, he killed thirty men at Ashkelon in anger, his wife was given to his companion, and when her father instead offered her younger sister, Samson burned the shocks, standing grain, vineyards, and olive groves of the Philistines and dwelt in the cleft of a rock. When the Philistines rose against Judah and demanded Samson, three thousand men of Judah bound him with two new ropes, but when he was brought to the Philistines, the Spirit of the Lord came mightily upon him, his bonds broke loose, and he killed a thousand men with a fresh jawbone of a donkey, and he judged Israel for twenty years in the days of the Philistines. At Gaza he carried the doors of the city gate to the top of a hill at midnight, and later Delilah, after many attempts, learned the secret of his strength, that no razor had ever come upon his head because he had been a Nazirite to God from his mother's womb, lulled him to sleep on her knees, had his locks shaved so that his strength left him, and the Philistines put out his eyes, brought him down to Gaza, bound him with bronze fetters, and made him a grinder in prison. His hair began to grow again and his strength returned, and when the lords of the Philistines gathered to sacrifice to Dagon and called Samson from prison to perform for them between the pillars, he prayed that God would remember him just this once so that he might take vengeance for his two eyes, took hold of the two middle pillars, and said, 'Let me die with the Philistines,' whereupon the temple fell and three thousand Philistines died, so that those he killed at his death were more than those he killed in his life, and his brothers buried him in the tomb of his father Manoah (Judges 13-16).

7-30.name: The Relocation of the Relics of St. James the Persian, Known as Intercisus or Sawn-Asunder
7-30.summary: This is a short entry, not a full life account: it commemorates the relocation of the relics of St. James the Persian from the city of Gaza to the land of Egypt. A church was built in his name in Old Cairo, where his body was laid. The account of his martyrdom is said to be mentioned under the twenty-seventh day of the month of Hathor.

8-1.name: Abba Silvanus, the Monk
8-1.summary: Abba Silvanus departed in the year 121 of the Martyrs (405 A.D.). He became a monk in his youth under St. Macarius the Great in the wilderness of Shiheet and later spent time in the monastery of Abba Macarius in Palestine, where he taught the monks to work with their hands and wrote discourses. He returned to Shiheet after the first Berber raid in 407 A.D., was given a vision of paradise and Hades in answer to prayer, and lived an austere, ascetic life. When God revealed the time of his departure, he summoned the fathers, asked their forgiveness, commanded love, humility and obedience, and then gave up his soul peacefully in good old age.

8-1.name: Aaron, the Priest, of Qus
8-1.summary: Aaron was a priest from the city of Qus, in Upper Egypt, who was chosen as a priest in his old age and remained at the altar in righteousness for 52 years. He was a virgin and a model of purity, so that he was said to enjoy such grace that his hand was supported by an angel when he elevated the bread. On the first of Parmoute, when he elevated the bread for the third time, the Lord took his soul, and he departed in peace. His body was then taken to his brother St. Pishoy, who buried him.

8-1.name: The Raid of the Arabs of Upper Egypt on the Wilderness of Shiheet
8-1.summary: On this day the Church commemorates a raid by Arabs from Upper Egypt on the monasteries of Shiheet. The entry records that the monks fled from the violence, that many of them were killed or taken captive, and that the monasteries suffered great destruction. It presents the event as a time of suffering and loss for the desert fathers and their communities. No individual martyr is named in the entry.

8-2.name: St. Christopher
8-2.summary: St. Christopher, whose name before baptism was Reprobus, was a tall man from the land of the cannibals who became a Christian and was baptized. The emperor sent soldiers to bring him, but through a miracle in which his dry rod blossomed, many of the soldiers believed, and two women, Nicetius and Aquilina, also confessed Christ and were martyred. Christopher was then brought before the emperor, tortured in various ways, and remained steadfast in his faith. He was finally beheaded, receiving the crown of martyrdom.

8-2.name: Pope Yoannis (John) IX, 81st Patriarch of Alexandria
8-2.summary: Pope Yoannis IX was a monk from the Monastery of St. Macarius who was consecrated Patriarch on the first day of Paope in the year 1037 of the Martyrs (1320 A.D.). He shepherded the Church with care, was known for his humility and teaching, and ordained bishops and priests for the service of the Church. He departed in peace in the year 1043 of the Martyrs (1327 A.D.) after a patriarchate of about seven years. He was buried in the Monastery of St. Macarius, and his memory is honored for his faithful leadership.

8-3.name: Pope Michael II, 71st Patriarch of Alexandria
8-3.summary: Pope Michael II was a monk from the Monastery of St. Macarius in Shiheet who lived an austere life of prayer, fasting and manual work. After a dispute over the choice of patriarch, the lot fell upon him, and he was consecrated on the 5th of Mesore in the year 861 of the Martyrs (1145 A.D.). He reigned for eight months, during which he cared for the Church and its people with humility. He then fell ill, returned to Shiheet, and departed in peace, being buried in the monastery.

8-3.name: St. John, Bishop of Jerusalem
8-3.summary: St. John was born to Jewish parents in Jerusalem, was well versed in the Law of Moses, and after debating Christians came to believe that Christ is the true God. He was baptized by St. Justus, Bishop of Jerusalem, was ordained a deacon, and was chosen as bishop after Justus departed. He shepherded the Church in Jerusalem with wisdom and teaching, and he is remembered for guiding the faithful during the rebuilding of Jerusalem under the emperor Hadrian. He departed in peace after a life of service and confession of the faith. He is a different John from John the Evangelist, John the Baptist, John of the Golden Gospel, and John Colobos.

8-4.name: Sts. Victor, Decius, Acacius, and Eirene (Irene) the Virgin, and Those with Them
8-4.summary: Sts. Victor, Decius, Acacius, and Eirene lived in the time of the emperor Constantine and his son, when pagan temples were being destroyed and the Christian faith was spreading. Under the apostate emperor Julian, they confessed Christ openly and refused to worship idols. They were tortured by beating, hanging and iron combs, yet they remained steadfast and encouraged one another. They were finally beheaded, receiving the crowns of martyrdom together.

8-4.name: St. Okeen (Eugene)
8-4.summary: St. Okeen was born in Qulzum near the Red Sea, was a contemporary of St. Antony, and worked as a diver for pearls before becoming a monk under St. Pachomius in Upper Egypt. He later returned to his homeland, went to Mesopotamia with seventy monks, and settled in a cave near Nisibis, where about 250 monks gathered around him and a monastery was built. He established monastic life in that region, and St. James, Bishop of Nisibis, prophesied that he would be a bishop, though Okeen remained a monk. He departed in peace after a life of asceticism, prayer and the founding of monasteries.

8-5.name: The Prophet Ezekiel, Son of Buzi
8-5.summary: The Prophet Ezekiel was born in Palestine about 624 B.C. and was taken into exile in Babylon with King Jehoiachin in 598 B.C., where he lived by the River Chebar. He prophesied for twenty-two years, rebuking the priests and people of Israel for idolatry and foretelling the coming of Christ, His birth from the Virgin, baptism, resurrection and the perpetual virginity of Mary. He also wrote sayings and performed signs among the exiles in Babylon. Because he rebuked the leaders of Israel for their idol worship in Babylon, they rose against him and killed him, and he was buried in the tomb of Shem and Arphaxad.

8-5.name: St. Hypatius, Bishop of Gangra
8-5.summary: St. Hypatius was consecrated Bishop of Gangra early in the fourth century and was known as a wonder-worker who defended the divinity and equality of the Son with the Father against the Arians. He attended the First Universal Council at Nicea in 325 A.D., where he confessed the orthodox faith. On his way back from the council, heretics attacked him on the road, stoned him and struck him with clubs, and left him for dead. He was martyred in the year 41 of the Martyrs (325 A.D.) and received the crown of martyrdom.

8-6.name: St. Mary of Egypt, the Anchorite
8-6.summary: St. Mary of Egypt was born in Alexandria to Christian parents in the year 61 of the Martyrs (345 A.D.), but at the age of twelve she was deceived into a sinful life that lasted seventeen years. She traveled to Jerusalem, was prevented by an unseen power from entering the Church of the Resurrection, repented before an icon of the Virgin, and then entered and venerated the Cross. A voice told her to cross the Jordan to find rest, so she confessed, received Communion, took three silver coins and a loaf of bread, and crossed into the wilderness. She spent seventeen years fighting her former lusts and then lived on herbs for many years, until the elder Zosima found her in the forty-fifth year of her seclusion, gave her Communion, and later buried her after she departed in peace. She is a different Mary from the Virgin Mary, Mary the Israelite, and Mary the Ascetic the Shut-In.
hymnIds: Doxology for St. Mary of Egypt
The Great Saint Mary of Egypt (6 Parmoute)

8-7.name: St. Joachim, Father of the Virgin Mary
8-7.summary: St. Joachim was from Nazareth, a descendant of David of the tribe of Judah, and was married to Hannah. He and Hannah were childless and prayed earnestly, and God gave them Mary, whom they presented in the temple as they had vowed. Joachim lived a righteous life of prayer and giving, and he departed in peace at the age of eighty, when Mary was three years old. He is honored as the father of the Mother of God and grandfather of Christ according to the flesh.

8-7.name: St. Macrobius
8-7.summary: St. Macrobius was the son of the governor of the city of Kaw, and he served St. Severus, Patriarch of Antioch, accompanying him as he wandered in Upper Egypt and visiting the Monastery of Anba Moses. Desiring the monastic life, he resigned his position, gave up his money, appointed his brother in his place, and became a monk. His brothers Paul, Elias and Joseph also became monks, and he built many monasteries and guided about a thousand monks and a thousand nuns, while also caring for the poor and building churches. He was given the gift of healing, departed in peace, and his body was later found and buried in the church of his monastery, where miracles were reported. He is a different Macrobius from Macrobius, Bishop of Nikiu, commemorated on Baramhat 2.

8-7.name: Sts. Agapius and Theodora
8-7.summary: Coptic Reader gives only the commemoration heading for Sts. Agapius and Theodora, with no further life or martyrdom detail, so none is recorded here.

8-8.name: The Holy Virgins Agape, Eirene, and Shiona
8-8.summary: Sts. Agape, Eirene and Shiona were natives of Thessalonica who worshipped Christ as their parents had, chose a life of chastity, and persevered in fasting, prayer and asceticism with the nuns. During the persecution under Maximianus, who restored idol worship, they fled to a mountain and hid in a cave, where an old Christian woman brought them food and sold the work of their hands for the poor. A wicked man followed the old woman, discovered the cave, and informed the governor of Thessalonica. When they stood before the governor, they confessed Christ and refused to offer sacrifices to the gods, were severely tortured, and were then cast into the fire, receiving the crowns of martyrdom in the year 20 of the Martyrs (304 A.D.). This Agape is a different Agape from Agape of the Pistis, Helpis, Agape and Sophia group commemorated on Tobi 30.

8-8.name: The 150 Believers, Martyred by the Hand of the King of Persia
8-8.summary: On this day the Church commemorates one hundred and fifty believers who were martyred by the hand of the king of Persia. The king had besieged Christian cities near the borders of his country and captured many Christians. When these believers refused to worship the sun and the stars, he commanded that they be beheaded. They thus received the crowns of martyrdom for their steadfast confession of Christ.

8-9.name: St. Zosimus, the Hermit
8-9.summary: St. Zosimus was a priest and hermit in Palestine who lived for fifty-three years in a monastery. He was known for his struggle and asceticism and was visited by an angel who told him to go to a monastery near the Jordan River. There he met Mary the Egyptian, heard her story, gave her communion, and later found her dead and buried her with the help of a lion. He then returned to his monastery and told the monks about her, and he departed in peace at the age of ninety-nine.

8-9.name: Pope Shenouda I, 55th Patriarch of Alexandria
8-9.summary: Pope Shenouda I was from El-Bahnasa, was raised by pious parents, and became a monk in the monastery of St. Macarius, where he was known for his virtue, worship, asceticism, and knowledge. He was ordained a priest, then a bishop, and was chosen as patriarch on the 10th of Parmoute in 571 A.M. (855 A.D.). He built several churches, including a church dedicated to St. Sergius in El-Bahnasa, and he opposed those who said the Holy Spirit was created. He departed on the 9th of Parmoute in 580 A.M. (864 A.D.) after sitting on the throne for eight years and nine months. He is a different Shenouda from Shenouda the Archimandrite, Shenouda III, and Shenouda El Bahnasawy.

8-10.name: St. Isaac, Disciple of St. Apollo
8-10.summary: St. Isaac was a native of Akhmin and a disciple of St. Apollo in the mountain monastery, where he practiced fasting, asceticism, and worship, and worked hard to fight his desires. He was known for his good qualities, never ate a cooked meal, and for his love of silence and solitude, especially in a cave in the mountain. He often read the biography of St. Antony, and he died after a life of fasting and asceticism, with his departure described as a blessing.

8-10.name: Pope Gabriel II, 57th Patriarch of Alexandria
8-10.summary: Pope Gabriel II was from Cairo, became a monk in the monastery of St. Macarius, and was ordained a priest before becoming patriarch in 1146 A.M. (1430 A.D.). He was a virtuous, pious, and learned patriarch who cared for the needs of the poor, and he issued some canons forbidding the appointment of bishops who were not from the Coptic Orthodox faith. He sat on the throne for thirteen years, then departed in peace in 1159 A.M. (1443 A.D.), after which he was buried in the Church of St. Mercurius in Old Cairo.

8-11.name: St. Theodora, the Nun
8-11.summary: St. Theodora was an Alexandrian woman and the only daughter of wealthy Christian parents who refused marriage, sold her clothes and jewelry to give to the needy, and built a church west of Alexandria with a private room where she lived in prayer. She cared for the poor and sick, was tonsured as a nun by Pope Athanasius, and became a model of asceticism, fasting, and prayer, living in the church for many years. She was contemporary with five patriarchs — Athanasius, Peter, Timothy, Theophilus, and Cyril — and her sayings, which include that the soul is strengthened by prayer and that the monk should not be idle, were preserved and quoted in the entry. She departed in peace after a life of holiness and was buried in the church she built.

8-11.name: St. John, Bishop of Gaza
8-11.summary: Coptic Reader gives this entry as a heading-only/short entry, recording only the departure of St. John, Bishop of Gaza, with no life or departure details, so none is recorded here.

8-12.name: The Monthly Commemoration of the Honorable Archangel Michael
8-12.summary: Coptic Reader presents this as the monthly commemoration of the Archangel Michael on the 12th day of each Coptic month, not a life story. The entry records the commemoration of the Archangel Michael and gives no new biographical or martyrdom details for this date.
hymnIds: Doxology for Archangels Michael and Gabriel
Fraction to the Father for Archangel Michael
Archangel Michael (12th of Every Coptic Month)

8-12.name: St. Alexander, the Confessor, Bishop of Jerusalem
8-12.summary: St. Alexander was a fellow student of Origen who studied under Pantaenus and Clement in Alexandria and became bishop of a city in Cappadocia. In 202 A.D. he confessed his faith before Septimius Severus, was seized, tortured, and imprisoned for many years, and after his release he went to Jerusalem, where the aged Bishop Narcissus was assisted by him. He was made bishop of Jerusalem, where he remained for about three years, and he departed in peace in 250 A.D., having been a confessor of the faith.

8-12.name: St. Antonios, Bishop of Thmoui
8-12.summary: Coptic Reader gives this entry as a heading only, recording only the departure of St. Antonios, Bishop of Thmoui, with no life, place, or death details, so none is recorded here.

8-13.name: Sts. Joshua and Joseph, Disciples of St. Milius
8-13.summary: Sts. Joshua and Joseph were disciples of St. Milius on Mount Khorasan, where they lived in a cave in asceticism and prayer. They were caught by the king's sons while hunting, and when they refused to offer incense to the sun and fire, the king seized, tortured, and slew them. They received the crown of martyrdom, and the entry closes with the blessing of their prayers.

8-13.name: Pope Yoannis XVII, 105th Patriarch of Alexandria
8-13.summary: Pope Yoannis XVII was born in Mallawy in Upper Egypt as Abdel-Sayed, became a monk at the age of twenty-five in the monastery of St. Antonios, and was later ordained a priest. He was chosen as patriarch in 1443 A.M. (1727 A.D.), renovated the monastery of St. Paul and other churches, and was known for his care for the poor and for the church. He departed in peace in 1461 A.M. (1745 A.D.) after a patriarchate of about eighteen years.

8-13.name: St. Dionisa, the Deaconess
8-13.summary: St. Dionisa was a deaconess appointed by the apostles to serve women in the church, including by bringing water and helping with their needs. The entry records only this role and her departure, with no place of origin or further life details given.

8-13.name: St. Midius
8-13.summary: Coptic Reader gives this entry as a heading only, recording only that the church celebrates the martyrdom of St. Midius, with no life, place, or martyrdom details, so none is recorded here.

8-14.name: St. Maximus, 15th Patriarch of Alexandria
8-14.summary: St. Maximus was born in Alexandria to Christian parents, studied at the Theological School, and was known for his knowledge of Greek philosophy and the church. He was made a deacon by Heraclas and a priest by Dionysius of St. Mark, endured suffering under Decius, and became patriarch in 264 A.D. He opposed the heresy of Mani, which had come from Persia to Egypt and forbade marriage and meats, and he exhorted and confirmed the Orthodox in the faith. He departed in peace in 282 A.D. after sitting on the throne for seventeen years and five months. He is a different Maximus from Maximus, brother of Dometius, commemorated on Tobi 14.

8-14.name: St. Ehron, the Syrian of Serugh
8-14.summary: St. Ehron was born in Serugh in Mesopotamia to godly Christian parents, loved prayer and worship from his youth, and lived as a shepherd and then in a monastery and a cave for three years. He later lived with the Armenians on a mountain with his disciple Gregory the hermit, went to Jerusalem, and returned to found a monastery with many disciples, where he was known for his gifts and miracles. He gathered his disciples, blessed and instructed them, and departed in peace in 389 A.D. (105 A.M.).

8-15.name: The Consecration of the Church of St. Agabus, one of the Seventy Disciples
8-15.summary: This is a short consecration entry, not a full life or martyrdom account, and it gives no death details for Agabus. It commemorates the consecration of a church dedicated to St. Agabus, who was one of the Seventy Disciples. The entry recalls his prophecy about St. Paul, in which he took Paul's belt, bound his own hands and feet, and said that the Jews at Jerusalem would so bind the belt's owner and deliver him to the Gentiles (Acts 21:10-11). No further life, martyrdom, or departure details are given in this entry.

8-15.name: St. Alexandra, the Empress
8-15.summary: St. Alexandra was the wife of Emperor Diocletian and a contemporary of St. George of Cappadocia, whose sufferings she witnessed. Moved by what she saw, she secretly asked George to explain his faith, and he explained the divinity of the Lord Christ and the Holy Scriptures, after which she believed. When George prayed before the idols and they were destroyed, the humiliated and enraged emperor returned and told the Empress what had happened, and she replied that she had warned him not to oppose the Christians, for their God is powerful. Diocletian then realized she believed in Christ, tortured her severely, and threw her into prison, where she received the crown of martyrdom.

8-15.name: Pope Mark VI, 101st Patriarch of Alexandria
8-15.summary: Pope Mark VI was born in Bahgora and became a monk in the Monastery of St. Antonios, where he lived a life of asceticism, worship, and fasting. He was enthroned as patriarch on 15 Parmoute, 1362 of the Martyrs (1646 A.D.), during the reign of Sultan Mohammed IV, and he departed on 15 Parmoute, 1372 of the Martyrs (1656 A.D.), after a reign of ten years. During his papacy, he ordained a bishop for Cyprus and was involved in the building and renewal of churches, including a church in Haret El-Roum in Cairo, the Church of St. Mercurius in Old Cairo, and other churches, despite opposition from some adversaries. He also traveled through Upper Egypt to strengthen the faithful, and after a period of illness he departed in peace. He is a different Mark from St. Mark the Evangelist.

8-16.name: St. Antipas, Bishop of Pergamos
8-16.summary: St. Antipas was Bishop of Pergamos in the latter part of the first Christian century and was a disciple of St. John the Evangelist, who mentioned him in Revelation 2:12-16. During the severe persecution under Emperor Domitian, Satan spoke from an idol, saying he could not remain in the city while Antipas was present, so the pagans seized Antipas and brought him before the city's ruler. The ruler ordered him to sacrifice to the idols, but Antipas refused and instead explained the principles of the Christian faith, for which he was severely tortured and imprisoned. While imprisoned, St. John sent him a comforting message calling him the faithful priest and the good shepherd. Finally, when the ruler could not persuade him, Antipas was placed inside a brass statue of a bull, a fire was lit beneath it, and he praised God for making him worthy to be martyred for His name before delivering up his soul in peace and receiving the crown of martyrdom; the heathens threw his body away, and believers took it and placed it with great veneration in the church.

8-16.name: Enoch the Just, Taken Alive to Heaven
8-16.summary: Enoch was the son of Jared and, as St. Jude the Apostle called him, the seventh from Adam, and his son was Methuselah, the longest-living man, who lived 969 years. The Holy Bible testifies that Enoch walked with God, meaning he pleased God by good conduct and lived in obedience among a wicked generation full of corruption and profanity. The entry explains that 'God took him' meant God ascended him to heaven alive with his body, so he did not taste death, exactly as later happened with Elijah the prophet. It adds that these two saints will remain with their bodies in heaven until they come and the beast makes war against them and kills them, so they will taste death as all humans do. Enoch lived 365 years before he was taken alive to heaven.

8-17.name: St. James, the Son of Zebedee, the Apostle
8-17.summary: St. James, the brother of John, was from Bethsaida in Galilee and was called by Christ on the same day as Peter and Andrew, leaving his boat and father to follow him. He witnessed the raising of Jairus's daughter, the Transfiguration, and the agony in Gethsemane, and after receiving the Holy Spirit he preached in Judea and Samaria while urging almsgiving. Hostile Jews accused him before Herod Agrippa of diverting taxes to the poor and the churches, and Herod had him beheaded with the sword. He was the first apostle martyred, and the entry says his is the only apostle's martyrdom recorded in the Bible; his body was later placed in Compostela, Spain, where a splendid cathedral was built. He is a different James from James of Nisibis, James the Persian, and James the son of Alphaeus.

8-17.name: St. Nicodemus, the Pharisee
8-17.summary: St. Nicodemus was a Pharisee and member of the Sanhedrin who came to Christ by night and was taught about the second birth. He later defended Christ before the Sanhedrin and, at the Crucifixion, brought about a hundred pounds of myrrh and aloes. With Joseph of Arimathea, he wrapped Christ's body in linen with the spices and laid it in the tomb. He then believed and lived a distinguished Christian life before departing in peace.

8-18.name: St. Arsenius, Disciple of St. Sousnyous
8-18.summary: St. Arsenius was a disciple of Sousnyous who was martyred in 305 A.D. during the reign of Diocletian. The entry gives no place of origin beyond this discipleship and persecution context. He was beheaded before his teacher, and his body was carried by Sousnyous to a place called the mountain. The entry presents his death as a faithful martyrdom under Diocletian's persecution. He is a different Arsenius from Arsenius the Great.

8-18.name: St. Apollo, Disciple of St. Samuel the Confessor
8-18.summary: St. Apollo was a disciple of Samuel the Confessor at the Monastery of El-Qalamun on the mount, where he was noted for obedience, energy, and skill. He managed the monastery's affairs, brought building material by camels for the church of the Virgin Mary, helped the brethren with their problems, and exhorted three monks to remain. When Samuel went into seclusion, Apollo was appointed to oversee the brethren and sought God's help in their affairs, and he departed in peace after a life of service.

8-19.name: St. Simeon the Armenian, Bishop of Persia
8-19.summary: St. Simeon was an Armenian bishop in Persia who shepherded his people during the reign of Shapur, son of Hormiz. He refused the king's order to worship idols and was put in iron fetters and imprisoned, where he preached to sun-worshippers and converted 150 of them. When one convert weakened, Simeon encouraged him to close his eyes and receive the sword without fear, and that man was beheaded. The other 149 converts were then beheaded, and Simeon himself, aged 120, was beheaded after them.

8-19.name: The Blessed Youhanna (John) Abu Nagaah El-Kabeer, the Vizier Abu Elaala Fahd ibn Ibrahim, and Their Companions
8-19.summary: Youhanna (John) Abu Nagaah El-Kabeer was a devout Christian who secretly built churches, monasteries, and places for the poor while serving as a senior official in the Fatimid-era administration. When his Christian charity and church-building were exposed, the governor and the caliph's officials questioned and tortured him, and he was beheaded after steadfastly confessing his faith. His brother Abu Elaala, a vizier who had embraced Islam outwardly, and their companions were also examined and martyred after refusing to abandon Christianity. The entry says the remaining three were brought to the governor and likewise beheaded, and that their bodies were later recovered and buried with honor.

8-19.name: St. Daoud (David), the Prophet
8-19.summary: St. David was the prophet-king of Israel, the son of Jesse, who is remembered in the entry as the psalmist and the ancestor of Christ according to the flesh. The entry is short and does not recount his battles, reign, or sins in detail. It records his departure in peace after a life of repentance and praise, and presents his psalms as his enduring spiritual legacy.

8-20.name: St. Babnuda, of Dendereh
8-20.summary: St. Babnuda was from Dendereh in Upper Egypt and lived as a monk noted for asceticism and prayer. During persecution he was arrested and brought before the governor, where he steadfastly confessed Christ and refused to sacrifice to idols. He endured severe tortures, including beatings and imprisonment, without denying his faith. He was finally beheaded, and his body was taken by the faithful and buried with honor in his native region.

8-21.name: The Monthly Commemoration of the Virgin Mary, the Mother of God
8-21.summary: Coptic Reader presents this as a short, heading-only monthly commemoration entry, not a life narrative. It states only that on this day in every Coptic month the Church celebrates the commemoration of the Virgin Mary, the Mother of God, and asks her intercession. No additional biographical detail is given in this entry.

Watos Psali for the Assumption of the Virgin St. Mary

8-21.name: St. Hierotheos, Bishop of Athens
8-21.summary: St. Hierotheos was an Athenian philosopher of the Areopagus who met the Apostle Paul, believed, was baptized, and was ordained a priest in Athens. He preached the Gospel and, after the departure of Dionysius the Areopagite, was chosen as bishop of Athens despite initially preferring to remain a priest. He was a contemporary of the apostles and disciples, was present at the departure of the Lady Virgin Mary, and composed melodies and hymns that he sang with instruments. He wrote books and spiritual hymns, brought Jews and Gentiles to Christ, and departed in peace after a life of teaching and pastoral care.

8-22.name: Pope Alexander I, 19th Patriarch of Alexandria
8-22.summary: Pope Alexander I was born in Alexandria to Christian parents and was ordained reader by Maximus, deacon by Theonas, and priest by Peter the Seal of the Martyrs, before being chosen patriarch after Archillas and consecrated in 312 A.D. He refused to absolve Arius, citing the command of Peter, and when Arius denied the divinity of Christ and spread his teaching through hymns and songs, Alexander convened councils in Egypt and wrote epistles and a treatise defending the Orthodox faith. He urged bishops in Asia, Syria, and Libya to confirm their signatures against Arianism, and many agreed, though Eusebius of Nicomedia persuaded Emperor Constantine to ask for Arius's absolution. Alexander refused, and the controversy culminated in the Council of Nicaea in 325 A.D., attended by 318 bishops, which excommunicated Arius. He departed in peace after serving 15 years, 9 months, and 20 days on the apostolic throne.

8-23.name: St. George, the Prince of the Martyrs
8-23.summary: St. George was born in Cappadocia in Asia Minor in the first half of the third century to a wealthy, godly family; his father Anastasius was governor of Melitene, and his mother Kira Theognosta was the daughter of the governor of Lydda in Palestine. After his father died when George was young, his mother took him to Lydda, where he later enlisted in the army, became a commander noted for horsemanship, and served under Justus, governor of Palestine. When Dadianus, king of Tyre in Syria, issued an edict against Christians in 303 A.D., George openly confessed Christ and refused the king's promises and threats. He endured prolonged tortures, including the wheel, iron shoes, and imprisonment, and was repeatedly healed and strengthened, while his steadfastness converted the magician Athanasius and many others. He was finally beheaded, and his body was taken to Lydda, where a church was built in his honor.
hymnIds: Adam Psali for the Consecration of Saint George's Church in Lydd
Watos Psali for the Consecration of Saint George's Church in Lydd
Adam Psali for the Martyrdom of St. George
Watos Psali for the Martyrdom of St. George

8-24.name: St. Sina, the Soldier, Companion of St. Isidore
8-24.summary: St. Sina was a soldier and companion of Isidore who was arrested with him at Farma, where the governor tortured them both and martyred Isidore. Sina remained in prison until that governor was removed, and a new governor, learning that Sina was of high rank, ordered him tortured to make him abandon his confession. He refused to turn from Christ and was beheaded while his mother stood beside him, and she saw his soul ascending as she had seen Isidore's. Believers shrouded his body and laid it with Isidore's, and their bodies were later kept at Samannoud, where feasts and wonders are associated with them.

8-24.name: Pope Sinuthius (Shenouda I), 55th Patriarch of Alexandria
8-24.summary: Pope Sinuthius (Shenouda I) was born at el-Batanon in Monufia, became a monk at the Monastery of St. Macarius, and advanced in righteousness until he was ordained hegumen of the monastery church. He was chosen by clergy and people and consecrated patriarch on 13 Tobe, 575 of the Martyrs (859 A.D.), and was known for wisdom, godliness, and care for churches and monasteries. During his patriarchate he confronted a village dispute at Boukhnessa in Marriot, explained the hypostatic union of divinity and humanity to those who erred, renovated ruined churches under the just governor A'anbassa ibn Ishaq, and dug small streams in Alexandria to supply fresh water. He also endured heavy taxes and persecutions on monks and clergy, sent envoys twice to the caliph to lift unjust levies, and, after a three-year drought at Marriot, prayed after the Divine Liturgy until rain filled wells, vineyards, and farms. In 866 A.D. he faced Berber raiders at St. Macarius's monastery unarmed, holding his staff and cross high on Maundy Thursday, and they fled before his courage; he later fortified the monastery and built cells and grain silos. He departed in peace after 21 years, 3 months, and 11 days on the apostolic throne. Note: Coptic Reader also lists a Pope Shenouda I, 55th Patriarch, on Baramouda 9 with different birthplace, consecration date (855 A.D.) and reign length (eight years and nine months); both entries are recorded here as Coptic Reader gives them.

8-25.name: St. Sarah and Her Two Sons
8-25.summary: St. Sarah was from Antioch and the wife of Socrates, a commander in Diocletian's army. When she took her two sons to Alexandria to be baptized by Pope Peter, who was in prison, the baptismal water froze three times, and she cut her breast and baptized them with her blood, making them, in the entry's words, 'sealed martyrs.' After she was denounced before Diocletian and refused to worship idols, she endured severe tortures, and she and her two sons were burned with fire and received the crown of martyrdom.

8-25.name: St. Theodore the Hermit and 120 Martyrs
8-25.summary: This is a short entry: Theodore, a hermit, and 120 martyrs with him suffered in Persia because of their faith in Christ, endured many tortures, and received the crown of martyrdom. No further life or martyrdom details are given in the entry.

8-26.name: St. Sousnyos
8-26.summary: St. Sousnyos was from Nicomedia, the son of Sosipater, an officer in Diocletian's household, and he embraced Christianity despite his father's opposition. After his father tried to kill him and denounced him, Diocletian had him tortured, including being dragged and placed in a thresher, and the entry says the idols were swallowed by the earth when he prayed. He was finally beheaded in 305 A.D., and the entry says 1,100 people who witnessed his steadfastness believed in Christ and were also beheaded. He was the teacher of St. Arsenius, commemorated on Baramouda 18.

8-26.name: Pope Yoannis VII, 78th Patriarch of Alexandria
8-26.summary: Pope Yoannis VII served as Patriarch for six years, nine months and nineteen days and is presented as a faithful shepherd of the Church. The entry records that he departed in peace in 1293 A.D. and was buried in the church of St. Mercurius in Egypt.

8-27.name: St. Boctor (Victor), Ebn Romanus
8-27.summary: St. Boctor (Victor) was from Antioch, the son of Romanus, a minister under Diocletian, and his mother was Martha; he became a stratelates and a friend of Prince Claudius. He visited imprisoned Christians, buried the bodies of martyrs, and, after his father denounced him, was sent to Alexandria to be tortured away from Antioch. He endured many tortures, including having his tongue cut out and hot nails driven into his body, and he was kept in prison for a time and worked as a carpenter. He was finally beheaded in Alexandria in 306 A.D., and his body was taken to Antioch and buried there. He is the Victor Son of Romanus whose page was NOT counted for the Victor/Decius/Acacius/Eirene group on Baramouda 4, because that group is a different commemoration.
hymnIds: Adam Psali for the Martyrdom of Saint Victor Son of Romanus
Watos Psali for the Martyrdom of Saint Victor Son of Romanus

8-28.name: St. Milius, the Ascetic
8-28.summary: St. Milius lived as an ascetic in a cave on Mount Khurasan, with his disciples Anba Joshua and Anba Joseph, and the sons of the king of Khurasan, who were hunting, came upon him and were converted from sun and fire worship. The king's sons denounced the three monks, and the disciples were tortured and slain. Milius was tortured for two weeks, shot with arrows, and departed in peace while receiving the crown of martyrdom. The entry adds that the next day the princes were killed by their own arrows, which turned back against them. He was the teacher of Sts. Joshua and Joseph, commemorated on Baramouda 13.

8-29.name: The Commemoration of the Three Major Feasts
8-29.summary: This is a short commemorative entry, not a biography: the Church commemorates the Annunciation, the Nativity and the Resurrection together. These three feasts are celebrated on the 29th of each Coptic month with a joyful liturgy, and the entry says there is no strict abstinence or prostrations on that day.

8-29.name: St. Erastus, one of the Seventy Apostles
8-29.summary: St. Erastus was among the Seventy Apostles and was present in the upper room in Zion, and Paul sent him with Timothy to Macedonia, where he suffered with Paul. He later returned to Jerusalem and became bishop of Paneas, where he demolished temples, built churches, and performed miracles, including turning bitter, salty water sweet and making dry wood bear fruit. After healing many sick people, he grew old and departed in peace.

8-29.name: St. Acacius, Bishop of Jerusalem
8-29.summary: This is a short entry: Acacius was raised in purity and godliness and served as Bishop of Jerusalem. He endured persecution for a long time and performed signs and wonders, and he departed in peace. He is a different Acacius from Acacius of the Victor/Decius/Acacius/Eirene group commemorated on Baramouda 4.

8-30.name: St. Mark, the Evangelist
8-30.summary: St. Mark was born in Cyrene in Pentapolis, Libya, to the tribe of Levi, and his family emigrated to Palestine after barbarian attacks; his mother's house became a place of prayer and the first church, associated with the Last Supper and the descent of the Holy Spirit. He accompanied Paul and Barnabas on missionary journeys, later preached in Egypt and Pentapolis, and ordained Anianus as Bishop of Alexandria in about 62 A.D., also founding the theological school and building a church at Bokalia. On 29 Parmoute, 68 A.D., while Christians were celebrating the Resurrection feast, which coincided with the pagan feast of Serapis, pagans seized Mark, bound him with a thick rope, dragged him through Alexandria's streets, and threw him into a dark prison, where an angel healed him and Christ appeared to console him. On the morning of 30 Parmoute, the pagans dragged him again through the streets, and he delivered up his soul and received the crown of martyrdom. The pagans then tried to burn his body, but a severe storm and heavy rain extinguished the fire, and the believers took his body and buried it in the church with great veneration.

9-1.name: The Nativity of the Blessed Virgin Mary, the Mother of God
9-1.summary: In Judea, Joachim, of the tribe of Judah and the house of David, and his wife Anna were righteous but childless, Anna being barren, and they prayed constantly and vowed to offer any child to serve in the temple like Samuel the prophet. An angel announced to Joachim, while he prayed on the mountain for forty days, that the Lord would give him offspring through whom the salvation of the world would come, and Anna likewise received the announcement that she would conceive a blessed daughter. Joachim and Anna went to the temple, where Joachim saw a crown of light descend from heaven, and they returned home rejoicing. Anna spent her pregnancy in fasting and prayer until she gave birth to Mary, the Mother of God and Savior of the world.
hymnIds: Adam Psali for the Birth of the Virgin
Watos Psali for the Birth of the Virgin

9-2.name: The Righteous Job
9-2.summary: Job, a prophet from the land of Uz, is presented as a blameless, upright man who feared God and avoided evil, and who was tested by Satan with the loss of his wealth, children, and health, while remaining patient and blaming no one. He is said to have lived 120 years, and his patience through suffering is held up as an example of endurance, with his prayers said to have delivered his friends from God's wrath. He departed in peace, having been given double what he had lost, and his life is noted as an example of patience under trial.

9-2.name: St. Tadros (Theodore), Disciple of St. Pachomius
9-2.summary: Theodore, born in Upper Egypt in the year 280 A.D., was drawn to the monastic life at age fourteen, went to the monastery at Tabennisis, and was chosen by Pachomius as his successor. After Pachomius departed, Theodore, also called Tadros, governed the community and was noted for his humility, prayer, and teaching. He departed in peace on this day in the year 364 A.D., after leading the monastery in the tradition of Pachomius, and his commemoration is joined to that of his teacher. He is a different Theodore from Theodore of Shotep, Theodore the Oriental, and Theodore the Hermit of Baramouda 25.
hymnIds: Adam Psali for the Departure of Saint Pachom of Koinonia
Watos Psali for the Departure of Saint Pachom of Koinonia
Doxology for St. Pachom and St. Theodore

9-2.name: St. Philotheos, from Doronka, Assuit
9-2.summary: This is a brief entry: Philotheos, from Doronka in Assiut, was martyred in the year 1096 of the martyrs (1380 A.D.), together with 1,096 others, after being severely tormented for refusing to deny his faith. He endured the tortures without renouncing Christ, and received the crown of martyrdom. No further biographical detail is given in the entry.
hymnIds: Adam Psali for the Martyrdom of St. Philotheus
Watos Psali for the Martyrdom of St. Philotheus

9-3.name: St. Jason, one of the Seventy Disciples
9-3.summary: Jason was born in Tarsus, was related to St. Paul, and ministered before the Passion, receiving the Holy Spirit at Pentecost; he accompanied Paul to Tarsus and many countries, and worked as a tentmaker in Thessalonica. In Thessalonica, Jews stirred up trouble, dragged Jason and others before the rulers, and had them arrested, but they were released on a guarantee and Jason continued his ministry. He later went to Corfu, where he baptized many, built a church to St. Stephen, and converted the governor's daughter, seven thieves, and others, several of whom were martyred in boiling pitch. After further torture, imprisonment, and a shipwreck from which he was saved, Jason continued teaching, became bishop of Tarsus and then of Corfu, and departed in peace in good old age.

9-3.name: St. Otimus, the Priest
9-3.summary: Otimus was born in Fowwa, was ordained a priest in his hometown, and taught the people there. During the persecution under Diocletian, he was brought before the governor, refused to worship idols, and was tortured, but the Lord strengthened him. He was burned alive and received the crown of martyrdom; a God-fearing priest took his body, shrouded it, and hid it until the end of the persecution, after which a church was built in his name and miracles were worked there.

9-3.name: Pope Gabriel IV, 86th Patriarch of Alexandria
9-3.summary: Pope Gabriel IV was born in Cairo and became a monk at the monastery of St. Macarius; he was enthroned as the 86th Patriarch on the 5th of Misra, 1088 of the martyrs (1372 A.D.), after the departure of Pope Mark IV. He shepherded the church for about eight years, during which time the church in Egypt was in a state of peace and he was noted for his piety and care for the poor. He departed in peace on this day in the year 1096 of the martyrs (1380 A.D.), after a patriarchate of about eight years, and was buried in the church of the Virgin Mary at Haret el-Roum in Cairo. He is a different Gabriel from the Archangel Gabriel and Gabriel the Announcer.

9-4.name: Pope John I (Yoannis), 29th Patriarch of Alexandria
9-4.summary: Pope John I was born in Alexandria to Christian parents, inclined to the monastic life in his youth and became a monk at the monastery of St. Macarius, but was compelled to accept the patriarchate and was consecrated on the 1st of Paope, 213 of the martyrs (496 A.D.). He taught and guided the church, resisted the Chalcedonian canons, and maintained union with Antioch, while the church flourished in peace during his time. During a plague in Alexandria, many died, and after a short illness he departed in peace on this day in the year 221 of the martyrs (505 A.D.), after a patriarchate of eight years and seven months.

9-4.name: Pope Yoannis V, 72nd Patriarch of Alexandria
9-4.summary: Pope Yoannis V, whose name was John Ebn Abe El-Fatah, was enthroned on the 2nd of the Little Month, 863 of the martyrs (1147 A.D.), during a time when Copts were persecuted by Muslim governors and Khalifas, churches were destroyed and plundered, and the layman el-Asa'ad Salib rebuilt many churches. He was imprisoned under El-Aadel Ebn El-Selar for refusing to ordain a metropolitan for Ethiopia while Abba Michael El-Atfihi was still living, and the ruler ordered Christians to wear girdles and belts and not shawls, but he was released two weeks later after El-Aadel's death. He added the word 'Life-giving' to the confession of faith, and endured famine, inflation, plague, and intensified persecution. He departed on this day in the year 882 of the martyrs (1166 A.D.), after a patriarchate of eighteen years, eight months, and four days, and was buried in the church of Abu Safain in Old Cairo.

9-5.name: Jeremiah, the Prophet
9-5.summary: Jeremiah, son of Hilkiah the priest, was born in Anathoth in the land of Benjamin near Jerusalem, and was called in a vision in the time of Zephaniah, while still young, when the Lord touched his mouth. He began prophesying in the 13th year of King Josiah, in 629 B.C., and served for eighteen years under Josiah, three months under Jehoahaz, eleven years under Jehoiakim, and eleven years and five months under Zedekiah, a total of about forty-one years, ending with the destruction of Jerusalem in 588 B.C. and continuing for a time in Egypt. He met resistance in Anathoth, dictated his prophecy to Baruch in the fourth year of Jehoiakim, saw the king tear and burn the scroll, and wrote it again; he was imprisoned, put in a dungeon, and later lifted out by an Ethiopian eunuch, and after Jerusalem was taken he refused to go to Babylon and chose to remain in Judah. After Gedaliah was killed, he was forced to go to Egypt, where he gave his last prophecies at Tahpanhes, foretold the end of the exile after seventy years and the fall of Babylon, and was known as the weeping prophet. He was martyred in Egypt, where the Jews stoned him to death.

9-6.name: St. Isaac, of Tiphre (El-Defrawi)
9-6.summary: Isaac, born in Tiphre (Defra), was twenty-five years old when an angel appeared to him in a vision in a field while he was asleep, filling him with a desire for the martyr's crown, and he bid farewell to his parents and went to Towa. He confessed Christ before the governor, was guarded, healed a blind man, and a soldier who believed was beheaded; he was then sent to El-Bahnasa, where a blind sailor was healed by a drop of water, and after further torture and healing by the Lord he was taken to Ansena before Arianus. He was tortured there, and was finally beheaded in Towa; his body was taken to Defra, where a church was consecrated on the 6th of Tobe, and his body was later relocated to Sonbat. He is a different Isaac from Isaac, Disciple of St. Apollo (Baramouda 10).

9-6.name: Mother Dolagy and Her Four Children
9-6.summary: Dolagy, with her four children Soris, Horman, Abanoufa, and Shentas, was martyred in the year 19 of the martyrs (303 A.D.) before Arianus, the governor of Ansena. When the children confessed Christ and refused to worship idols, they were tortured, and their mother went to encourage them and was imprisoned with them. The Virgin Mary appeared to her at night and told her that crowns were prepared for them, and the next morning, after refusing to offer incense, the governor ordered the children to be slain on their mother's knees, one after another, and then beheaded Dolagy herself, and all received the crown of martyrdom.
hymnIds: Melody for St. Dolagy and Her Four Children

9-6.name: Anba Paphnute, of El-Bandarah
9-6.summary: Paphnute, of noble descent, was martyred in the year 20 of the martyrs (304 A.D.); he worked as a farmer, was visited by an angel, distributed his money to the poor, and went to Alexandria to confess Christ. He was tortured and healed by an angel, healed a jailer's blind son in prison, and the jailer believed and confessed and was beheaded with his household; when Paphnute was taken to offer incense to an idol, he prayed, the devil in the idol spoke, and the idols fell, and many present confessed and were martyred. He was imprisoned without food or drink for fifteen days, hung by his feet with a stone around his neck, and saved by the Archangel Michael; a woman whose child was blind and ill with smallpox was healed by his blood and she and her son were beheaded. After further tortures before Arianus, governor of Ansena, he was beheaded, his body was taken to his hometown where a church was built and signs and wonders were worked, and his body was later relocated to el-Kershyah and then to Sonbat.

9-6.name: St. Macarius, of Alexandria
9-6.summary: Macarius, one of the three Abba Macarii, was born in Alexandria in 296 A.D. to a poor family, worked as a baker of sweets and cakes, was baptized at age thirty, and after hearing of the ascetics visited St. Anthony in 335 A.D. On his way back, he went to the wilderness of Nitria at about age thirty-eight, where monastic cells had been established around 315 A.D. by St. Amoun, and he became a disciple of St. Anthony and later of St. Pachomius, who complained that Macarius' asceticism was too severe. He was ordained a priest in 355 A.D. and became abbot of Cellia, presided over Nitria after Pamo in 373 A.D., and was exiled with Macarius the Great to Philae by the Arian Emperor Valens. Known for his gentleness, simplicity, and joy, and for many miracles, he departed in peace in the year 109 of the martyrs (393 A.D.). He is a different Macarius from Macarius the Great and Macarius, Bishop of Edkow.
hymnIds: Doxology for St. Macarius of Alexandria

9-6.name: The Arrival of the Relics of the Coptic Martyrs of Libya
9-6.summary: On the 6th of Pashons, year 1734 of the martyrs (May 14, 2018 A.D.), a private plane brought twenty coffins to Cairo International Airport, carrying the relics of twenty Coptic martyrs martyred in Libya, and Pope Tawadros II received them. Twenty ambulances took the coffins to the Church of the Martyrs at Al-Awar in Samalut, Minya, and the next morning the coffins were placed in the bottom of the church with their belongings, and the bodies were buried together under the altar in the bottom of the church, under the supervision of Anba Paphnutius, Metropolitan of Samalut, the governor of Minya, and the security director. The martyrs were from Minya villages and had gone to Libya for work; ISIS arrested two batches, seven Egyptians in Sirte on December 30, 2014, and thirteen Egyptians and one Ghanaian on January 3, 2015, tortured them for more than a month to deny their faith, and they refused. On February 5, 2015, as given in the entry, ISIS took them to the Mediterranean coast outside Sirte and slaughtered them, and their relics were later returned to Egypt. These are the same martyrs whose page was counted for the Contemporary Martyrs entry on Amshir 8.

9-7.name: St. Athanasius, the Apostolic, 20th Pope of Alexandria
9-7.summary: Athanasius was born in Alexandria around 297 A.D., was baptized by Pope Alexandros, became his deacon and disciple, was a monk and disciple of St. Anthony, and wrote Against the Heathen and On the Incarnation of the Word; he attended the Council of Nicaea in 325 A.D. with Alexandros and vanquished Arius. He was consecrated patriarch on the 8th of Pashons, 44 of the martyrs (328 A.D.), at age thirty, guided the church for seven years in tranquility, and ordained Frumentius, Anba Salama, as bishop of Aksum in Ethiopia around 330 A.D. He was exiled five times: first by Constantine for refusing to accept Arius, then under Constantius after the Council of Sardica, then in 356 A.D. after soldiers attacked the church of St. Mary at Theonas, then under Julian after a council of saints and confessors, and finally in 365 A.D. under Valens, hiding for nine months in a rural house. He returned to Alexandria in 366 A.D. at age seventy, held a council of ninety bishops in 369 A.D. confirming the Orthodox faith, and departed in peace in the year 89 of the martyrs (373 A.D.), after forty-five years on the throne. He is a different Athanasius from Athanasius III, 76th Patriarch.
hymnIds: Doxology for St. Athanasius the Apostolic

9-8.name: The Commemoration of the Ascension of Our Lord Jesus Christ to Heaven
9-8.summary: This is a short entry, not a biography: it commemorates the Ascension of the Lord Jesus Christ to heaven, noting that His Resurrection was on the 29th of Paremhotep, and that He ascended to the right hand of the Father. No further detail is given in the entry beyond this commemoration and its blessing.
hymnIds: Adam Psali for the Feast of the Ascension

9-8.name: St. John, of Senhout
9-8.summary: John was born in Senhout to his father Macarius and mother Anna, and while tending his father's sheep an angel appeared to him in a crown of light and encouraged him to go to Atrib to strive for martyrdom. He bid farewell to his parents, went to Atrib, confessed Christ before the governor, and befriended a soldier who believed after seeing miracles and was crowned by the governor. John was tortured, strengthened by the Lord, sent to Ansena, tortured again, and beheaded by the sword in the year 21 of the martyrs (305 A.D.); Julius of Aqfahs shrouded his body and sent it to his hometown Senhout, where the people received it with hymns and built a church, and his body is now in Shoubra El-Khema, Egypt. He is a different John from John the Evangelist, John the Baptist, John of the Golden Gospel, John Colobos, John of Gaza, and John, Bishop of Jerusalem.

9-8.name: St. Daniel, Hegumen of the Wilderness of Shiheet (Scetis)
9-8.summary: Daniel was born around 485 A.D., went to Shiheet in his youth, ate once daily at sunset, and worked making baskets; during Berber raids, when monks abandoned the wilderness, Daniel was captured by Berbers three times. After a life of worship and asceticism, the Pope ordained him Hegumen, and he saw Olagi (Eulogius), a stone cutter who fed the poor and housed sojourners; Daniel asked God to give Olagi more money so he could abound in mercy, but Olagi, after receiving much money, went to Constantinople, sought high rank, and forsook mercy, and Daniel had a vision of the Lord judging him and demanding Olagi's lost soul, for which Daniel entreated and was rebuked by an angel for rejecting God's judgment. Eulogius later participated in an upheaval against Emperor Justinian, and Daniel refused to sign the Tome of Leo and the Chalcedonian faith, was beaten by soldiers, took refuge at Tambok in Shoubra-Kheet, and returned after Justinian's death in 565 A.D. After a fourth Berber raid in 577 A.D., he returned to Tambok and departed to the Lord in the year 296 of the martyrs (580 A.D.), at more than ninety-five years of age. He is a different Daniel from Daniel the Prophet, commemorated on Baramouda 5.

9-9.name: St. Helena, the Queen
9-9.summary: Helena was born in el-Raha (Urfa-Edessa) about 247 A.D. to Christian parents, married Emperor Constantius I, and raised Constantine, who became emperor of the East with Constantinople as his capital. At about seventy she had a vision telling her to go to Jerusalem and search for the Cross of the Savior, and Constantine sent her there with soldiers. With Bishop Macarius of Jerusalem she located the site under a pagan temple of Venus built by Hadrian in 135 A.D., demolished the temple, and found three crosses, identifying the Lord's cross when a dead person placed on it rose immediately. She funded the Church of the Resurrection over the Holy Sepulcher, a church over the manger in Bethlehem, and a church at the Ascension on the Mount of Olives, and departed in peace in 327 A.D. at about age eighty.

9-9.name: Pope Yoannis (John) XI, 89th Patriarch of Alexandria
9-9.summary: Yoannis was a priest at the Church of St. Mercurius (Abu Safain) in Old Cairo before being consecrated patriarch on 16 Pashons, 1143 of the Martyrs (1427 A.D.), residing at Haret Zowaila. His patriarchate was marked by an earthquake, a low Nile, two years of inflation, and a plague, as well as trouble with rulers. He faced pressure over communication with Ethiopia, was beaten, imprisoned, and had his property confiscated, and he also dealt with a difficult deacon, yet he endured patiently. He departed in peace in 1168 of the Martyrs (1452 A.D.), after praying for the Nile, which then rose.

9-9.name: Pope Gabriel VIII, 97th Patriarch of Alexandria
9-9.summary: Gabriel was born in Meer, became a monk at the Monastery of Anba Bishoy under the name Shenouda, and was consecrated patriarch on 16 Paone, 1302 of the Martyrs (1586 A.D.), residing at Haret Zowaila. His time was troubled by heavy taxes, Mamluk oppression, injustice, famine, inflation, plague, and an earthquake that destroyed many buildings. The Pope of Rome tried to force the Copts to accept his doctrine and sent a delegation, but Gabriel refused and remained steadfast in the Orthodox faith. He departed in peace in 1319 of the Martyrs (1603 A.D.). He is a different Gabriel from the Archangel Gabriel and Gabriel the Announcer.

9-10.name: The Three Holy Young Men, Hananiah, Azariah, and Mishael
9-10.summary: The three were from the tribe of Judah and were taken by Nebuchadnezzar to Babylon, where they served in the palace with Daniel and refused the king's delicacies and wine, eating only vegetables. When they refused to worship the king's golden image, they were thrown into a fiery furnace, but the fire became cool dew and did not harm them, and they praised God. After completing their struggle, they died while praying and kneeling in their home, and an earthquake shook the place. The king then made ebony beds covered with silk for them and a gold bed for himself to be placed among them, and the entry records their commemoration as a martyrdom.
hymnIds: Doxology for the Three Holy Youth

9-11.name: St. Paphnute, the Bishop
9-11.summary: Paphnute was born to Christian parents, became a monk at the Monastery of St. Macarius, spent thirty-five years in the wilderness, learned to read and write and studied the Scriptures, canons, and fathers, and was ordained a priest. Pope Philotheos I, the 63rd Patriarch, ordained him bishop, and he wore goat-hair clothing except during the liturgy, with his body wasted by illness and asceticism. After serving as bishop for thirty-two years, he called his priests and deacons, handed over the sacred properties, having never kept even one dinar for himself, and departed in peace in 570 of the Martyrs (1034 A.D.) after an angel had told him of his approaching departure. He is a different Paphnute from Paphnute of El-Bandarah (Bashans 6) and from Paphnoute the Monk (Amshir 15).

9-11.name: St. Theoclia
9-11.summary: Theoclia was the wife of St. Justus, son of Emperor Numerianus, and was martyred in 20 of the Martyrs (304 A.D.). Diocletian sent her husband and their son Abali to the governor of Alexandria, Armanius, and Theoclia followed them there. She remained steadfast in the faith before Armanius, was tortured, and was beheaded, receiving the crown of martyrdom. Her body was later taken to her husband's city, and the entry presents her martyrdom as following the martyrdom of her family.

9-12.name: The Monthly Commemoration of the Honorable Archangel Michael
9-12.summary: Coptic Reader presents this as the monthly commemoration of the Archangel Michael, described as the head of the heavenly hosts and the intercessor for the Church. The entry is short and gives no life, place, or death narrative for Michael; it is a commemoration, not a biographical martyrdom or departure account.
hymnIds: Doxology for Archangels Michael and Gabriel
Fraction to the Father for Archangel Michael
Archangel Michael (12th of Every Coptic Month)

9-12.name: The Relocation of the Relics of St. John Chrysostom
9-12.summary: John Chrysostom's relics were relocated in 153 of the Martyrs (437 A.D.), in the reign of Emperor Theodosius II, from Comana in Pontus, where he had departed in exile, to Constantinople, about thirty years after his departure. A great multitude received the relics, and they were placed in the Church of the Holy Apostles. The emperor knelt before the relics asking forgiveness for himself and for his parents, Arcadius and Eudoxia, for their treatment of the saint.

9-12.name: The Appearance of a Cross of Light above Golgotha
9-12.summary: In 67 of the Martyrs (351 A.D.), in the reign of Constantius, son of Constantine, and in the time of St. Kyrillos, bishop of Jerusalem, a cross of light appeared above Golgotha and extended to the Mount of Olives. The whole city saw it, and the people praised God, and Kyrillos wrote to the emperor about the appearance. The entry presents this as a miraculous public appearance, not a person's death.

9-12.name: Pope Mark VII, 106th Patriarch of Alexandria
9-12.summary: Mark was born in Klosna with the name Simeon, became a monk at the Monastery of Abba Paul, was ordained a priest by Pope Yoannis XVII, the 105th Patriarch, and was consecrated patriarch on 24 Pashons, 1461 of the Martyrs (1745 A.D.), on the feast of the Entry of Christ into Egypt. His patriarchate was troubled by a mutiny of soldiers and Mamluk princes, from whom he fled to Upper Egypt, and by suffering for the Church from inside and outside. He ordained Peter as metropolitan of Akhmim, Girga, and Upper Egypt, and Yousab as metropolitan of Ethiopia, and sat on the throne for 23 years, 11 months, and 8 days. He departed in peace in 1485 of the Martyrs (1769 A.D.) at the Monastery of the Virgin at Adawyya in El-Maadi, Cairo, and at his death he was said to have seen St. Anthony and St. Paul. He is a different Mark from St. Mark the Evangelist.

9-12.name: St. Malati Yousef, the Master
9-12.summary: Malati was a scribe to Ayyub Beck and, during the French occupation of Egypt, became president of the administrative office, after which the Turks opposed Christian notables including Girgis El-Gohari, Wasef, and Malati. In the resulting disorder, Taher Pasha, then ruler of Egypt, arrested Malati and had him beheaded at the gate of Haret Zowaila in Cairo. He received the crown of martyrdom in 1519 of the Martyrs (1803 A.D.).

9-12.name: The Consecration of the Church of St. Demiana
9-12.summary: This entry commemorates the consecration, in 43 of the Martyrs (327 A.D.), of the church of St. Demiana at Belqas. It is a church-consecration commemoration; the entry gives no new biographical martyrdom narrative for Demiana herself on this day beyond the consecration.

9-13.name: St. Arsenius, Teacher of the Emperors' Children
9-13.summary: Arsenius was born in Rome in 350 A.D. to wealthy, devout parents, became a deacon, learned Greek and Latin, and was appointed by Emperor Theodosius the Great as tutor to his sons Honorius and Arcadius. He fled the world after hearing a voice, went to Alexandria and then to Scetis, was a disciple of John Colobos and then of Isaiah the Elder, and lived in great asceticism with fasting, prayer, vigils, and seclusion in a cave, often weeping so much that his eyelashes fell out. He frequently reminded himself of the purpose for which he left the world, fled the praise of men, and endured Berber raids and other trials in the desert. He departed in peace in 447 A.D. He is Arsenius the Great, Teacher of the Kings — a different Arsenius from Arsenius, Disciple of Sousnyous (Baramouda 18).

9-13.name: Abba Pigol (Begoul), the Soldier
9-13.summary: Pigol was born in Tala, el-Minya, to godly parents, lived in chastity, and served as a soldier, giving his salary to the poor and spending his time in vigils, fasting, and service to the infirm and prisoners. He left the army, went to the wilderness west of Tala, and lived in prayer and asceticism, spending Saturday nights in church in praise and receiving the mysteries. He was martyred in 21 of the Martyrs (305 A.D.) after confessing Christ and enduring tortures. He is a different Begoul from Begoul the Priest, commemorated on Amshir 15.

9-14.name: St. Pachomius, Father of the Communal Monastic Life
9-14.summary: Pachomius was born in Thebes (Luxor) about 290 A.D. to pagan parents, rejected paganism, served in the army, and was moved by the kindness of Christians at Latopolis (Esna), after which he was baptized in 314 A.D. by Serapion, bishop of Dandara. He became a monk under Balamon for seven years, and an angel then commanded him to establish communal monastic life, which he did at Tabennesi, building ten monasteries with a system of prayer, work, and discipline, and his brother John also became a monk. He departed in peace in 348 A.D. (64 of the Martyrs), after establishing the communal system that shaped later monasticism.
hymnIds: Adam Psali for the Departure of Saint Pachom
Watos Psali for the Departure of Saint Pachom
Doxology for St. Pachom and St. Theodore

9-14.name: St. Epimachus, of Pelusium
9-14.summary: Epimachus was born in Farma (Pelusium), worked as a weaver, and lived gently and quietly, loving silence, solitude, church, prayer, fasting, and almsgiving. He went to Alexandria, confessed Christ before the governor, and endured tortures including being hung and beaten. He was beheaded and received the crown of martyrdom in 250 A.D.

9-15.name: St. Simon, the Zealot, the Apostle
9-15.summary: Simon was born in Cana of Galilee, was a member of the Zealotes movement about twenty years before the Lord called him, and was present at the wedding in Cana. After Pentecost he preached in North Africa (Carthage), Spain, and the British Isles with Joseph of Arimathea, and later in Syria, Mesopotamia, and Persia with Judas Thaddeus, and in India, where idols were silenced and many believed. In Shinar he and Judas prophesied a truce between warring armies, which came to pass, but the priests of the idols then stirred up the people against them. He was martyred in 68 A.D. He is a different Simon from Simon the Tanner.

9-15.name: The 400 Martyrs of Dandara
9-15.summary: In 304 A.D., four hundred people at Dandara witnessed the hermit Babnuda (Paphnute) being tortured by Arianus, governor of Ansena, and believed in Christ. They openly declared their faith before the governor, and he had them burned, and they received the crown of martyrdom together.

9-15.name: Deacon Mina, the Anchorite
9-15.summary: Coptic Reader gives this entry as a heading only, recording only that the Church celebrates on this day the commemoration of the martyrdom of Deacon Mina the anchorite, with no further life, place, or death detail, so none is recorded here.

9-15.name: Shams El-Ri'asah Abi El-Barakat, known as Ebn Kabr, the Priest
9-15.summary: Ebn Kabr was born to a wealthy father, received a good education, became a government scribe, and was promoted to secretary of the minister (wazir). He left government service, became a priest, and devoted himself to writing, scholarship, and service to the Church, composing works on theology, liturgy, and canon law. He was known for his learning and for his defense of the faith, and he departed in peace in 1040 of the Martyrs (1324 A.D.).

9-16.name: The Consecration of the Church of St. John the Evangelist, in Alexandria
9-16.summary: This entry commemorates the consecration of the Church of St. John the Evangelist in Alexandria. John was the brother of James the Elder and a son of Zebedee, preached in Asia Minor, established the seven churches mentioned in Revelation, and wrote his Gospel, three epistles, and Revelation, being called the apostle of love. In old age he was carried to church in Ephesus and his sole exhortation was, 'Little children, love one another.' The entry is a church-consecration commemoration and gives no departure date or death detail for John on this day.

9-17.name: St. Epiphanius, Bishop of Cyprus
9-17.summary: Epiphanius was born in Palestine in about 307 to Jewish parents, and his father died while he was young, leaving his mother to raise him and his sister. He became a Christian after meeting a monk whose charity impressed him, was baptized, and then lived as a monk in Egypt from about 335 and later in Palestine, where he founded a monastery and learned Hebrew, Coptic, Syriac, Greek and Latin, a knowledge for which St. Jerome called him 'he who has five tongues.' He was chosen against his will as bishop of Salamis in Cyprus in 367, wrote extensively against heresy, and was known for stern asceticism and zeal for the faith. He departed in peace at about 96 years of age.

9-18.name: The Feast of Pentecost
9-18.summary: This feast commemorates the descent of the Holy Spirit upon the disciples in the upper room in Zion in Jerusalem on the day of Pentecost. The entry describes a sound like a rushing wind, tongues as of fire resting on each disciple, and their being filled with the Holy Spirit. It is presented as the fulfillment of Christ's promise to send the Spirit, and as the beginning of the disciples' public preaching. The entry closes with a blessing for the holy feast.
hymnIds: Adam Psali for the Feast of Pentecost
Watos Psali for the Feast of Pentecost
The Hymn of the Holy Spirit
Fraction to the Father for the Resurrection and the Pentecost Period: O Master, Lord God, the Great and True, Who Sent the Holy Spirit

9-18.name: St. George (Ga'orgi), Friend of St. Abraam
9-18.summary: George was born to godly Christian parents, tended his father's sheep as a boy, and was drawn to seclusion, fasting and prayer, often giving his own food to other shepherds. At 14 he left for the wilderness of St. Macarius, guided by a pillar of light, resisted the devil's attempt to turn him back in the form of an old man, and was strengthened by the appearance of the Archangel Gabriel. He lived with St. Abraam, served him during a long illness of 18 years, and after Abraam departed in peace, George departed less than five months later and was buried beside him. His cell at Bigeeg, beside Anba Yoannis, remained a place of veneration until the 14th century, when Pope Benjamin II, the 82nd Patriarch (1327-1339), visited it. He is a different George from George the Prince of the Martyrs, George the Ascetic, and George the Zahimian.

9-19.name: Abba Isaac, Priest of El-Qalali (the Cells)
9-19.summary: Isaac was born in Upper Egypt in about 350, visited St. Antony as a child, and as a young man became a disciple of St. Macarius. He became a monk at Nitria in 370, succeeded his teacher Cronius as priest of Cellia in 395, and became abbot of 210 monks, building a hostel for visitors and living in strict asceticism for 30 years. He was one of eight elders presiding over Cellia and Nitria, was expelled to Palestine in about 400 during the controversy over the Tall Brothers, and returned in about 403. He later bore a grievous sickness patiently, refused cooked food brought by the brethren, conveyed the teachings of Abba Pemwah to the monks of Cellia, and was remembered for stern modesty, humility and prompt reconciliation with a brother after the devil appeared to him. He is a different Isaac from Isaac of Tiphre (Bashans 6), Isaac Disciple of St. Apollo (Baramouda 10), and the Patriarchs Abraham, Isaac and Jacob.

9-19.name: St. Isidorus (Isidore), of Antioch
9-19.summary: Isidorus was born in Antioch to a noble family; his father, Bandilaous, was governor of the city under Emperor Diocletian, his mother was Sophia, and his sister was Euphemia. He is commemorated as a martyr in the year 20 of the martyrs, 304 A.D., during Diocletian's persecution. The entry presents him as confessing Christ and enduring torment for his faith rather than denying it. He received the crown of martyrdom, and the entry closes with the usual blessing on his prayers. He is a different Isidore from Isidore of Pelusium, Isidore friend of Sina, and Isidore the Priest.

9-20.name: The Six Soldiers who Accompanied Claudius Stratelates
9-20.summary: These six soldiers — Dioscorus, Dionysius, Phoebammon, Karus, Paphadius and Ammonius — accompanied Claudius Stratelates from Antioch to Egypt in the year 20 of the martyrs, 304 A.D., after Diocletian sent Claudius to Egypt to be tortured. On the journey Claudius spoke to them about the Lord Christ and eternal life, and they believed. When they arrived, they declared their faith before the governor Arianus, who ordered them beheaded, and Claudius encouraged them until they received the crown of martyrdom. Their martyrdom is thus linked directly to Claudius's own confession and journey to Egypt.

9-20.name: St. Ammonius, Hermit of Mount Tounah
9-20.summary: Ammonius was born in Upper Egypt in 294 A.D. and, as a youth, had a vision of St. Antony calling him to monastic life, after which he was guided to the ascetic Anba Isidore and received the holy Eskeem. After his teacher departed, he went to St. Antony, became his disciple, and lived in a cave nearby in worship and ascetic struggle. The devil, envying him, came in the form of a woman asking for prayer, but at Ammonius's prayer the apparition turned to smoke and fled. He departed in peace in the year 73 of the martyrs, 357 A.D. He is a different Ammonius from Ammonius of Esna and Ammonius the Hermit.

9-21.name: The Monthly Commemoration of the Holy Pure Virgin St. Mary
9-21.summary: Coptic Reader presents this as a brief monthly commemoration entry, not a life narrative. It states that the Church celebrates the monthly commemoration of the Mother of God, the pure Virgin, from whom the salvation of the world came. It asks for her intercession and closes with a blessing, without giving further biographical detail on this date.

Watos Psali for the Assumption of the Virgin St. Mary

Watos Psali for the Birth of the Virgin St. Mary

Watos Psali for the Consecration of the First Church of the Virgin St. Mary in Philippi
