Adam Psali for the Fast of St. Mary
Watos Psali for the Fast of St. Mary
The Hymn of the Ten Strings of the Harp

9-21.name: St. Marcian (Martinianus)
9-21.summary: Marcian was born in Caesarea in Palestine and, in the later 4th century, became a monk under a holy man on Mount el-Safina (The Ship), living in strenuous asceticism. An evil woman who came to his cell in ragged clothes and, the next morning, adorned and perfumed, tried to entice him; he lit a fire and threw himself into it repeatedly, saying that if he could not bear a little fire, he could not bear the fire of hell. Terrified, the woman repented, put on ragged clothes, and at his advice joined a convent in Bethlehem to spend the rest of her life in repentance. Fearing further snares, Marcian went to an island in the middle of the sea, where a shipwrecked woman was washed ashore; he gave her all his bread, crossed the sea on foot with God's help, and departed in peace. He is a different Marcian from Martianus (Martinianus) the Monk, whose relics were relocated on Amshir 19.

9-22.name: St. Andronicus, one of the Seventy Disciples
9-22.summary: Andronicus was of Jewish origin, a relative of the Apostle Paul, and is greeted with Junia in Romans as a kinsman, fellow prisoner and one 'in Christ before me'; his Greek name means 'victorious man.' He received the Holy Spirit in the upper room at Pentecost, preached in many cities with St. Junia before Paul's conversion, accompanied Paul in many places, most importantly Rome, and endured sufferings which St. John Chrysostom interpreted as a kind of imprisonment — exile, hunger, loss of family and continuous threat of death. After completing his good endeavor, Andronicus fell ill for a short time and departed in peace, and Junia shrouded him, prayed and buried him in a cave. Junia then prayed that the Lord would take her also, and departed the next day.

9-22.name: The 142 Young Men and 28 Women
9-22.summary: This entry commemorates 142 young men and 28 women from Asyut, martyred in the year 20 of the martyrs, 304 A.D., in the context of the Diocletianic persecution and the martyrdoms associated with St. Claudius at Ansena (Assuit). The entry presents them as a group who confessed the faith and received the crown of martyrdom together with their mothers' generation of Asyut Christians. It closes with the blessing on their prayers, without naming the individuals.

9-22.name: St. Amoun, Founder of the Wilderness of Nitria
9-22.summary: Amoun was born in 275 A.D. to a wealthy, godly Christian family near Mariout, west of Alexandria, lost his parents while young, and was raised by his uncle. At 22 he was forced into marriage, but he and his wife lived in virginity for 18 years before he went to the wilderness and she became a nun. He founded the monastery of Nitria, lived about 50 years in asceticism, eating little bread, sometimes abstaining for a day or two and sometimes for a whole week and eating no vegetables, and was given the gifts of healing and seeing angels. He departed in peace in the year 64 of the martyrs, 348 A.D. He is a different Amoun from Ammonius, Hermit of Mount Tounah (Bashans 20).

9-23.name: St. Junia, one of the Seventy Apostles
9-23.summary: Junia was born in Beit Gibrael in the tribe of Judah, received the Holy Spirit at Pentecost, and preached the Gospel together with St. Andronicus. She is associated with Paul, who sent her a special salutation in his Epistle to the Romans. After Andronicus departed, Junia shrouded and buried him, prayed that the Lord would not separate her from him, and departed the following day.

9-23.name: St. Thecla, during the Passion of St. Claudius
9-23.summary: Thecla was the daughter of Karas, a noble man of the city of Assuit, and was martyred in the year 20 of the martyrs, 304 A.D., during the torture of Claudius Stratelates before Arianus, proconsul of Ansena, alongside the martyrdoms of Abamoun, the six soldiers and the 142 young men and 28 women. Dressed in splendid garments, she came to the place of torment and spoke to Claudius and Abamoun as brothers in the faith. The governor was infuriated and ordered her beheaded early the next morning on the eastern side of Assuit, and she thus received the crown of martyrdom. She is a different Thecla from Thecla of the Makronius/Thecla group (Baramhat 1) and from Esi and Thecla (Koiahk 8).

9-23.name: St. Botamoun, the Confessor
9-23.summary: Botamoun was bishop of Heraclia in Egypt and departed in the year 56 of the martyrs, 340 A.D. Pope Athanasius testified that he was twice a martyr — first for witnessing to the truth under pagan persecution, when under Maximianus in 310 A.D. he suffered many tortures and lost one eye, and again against Arianism. He attended the Council of Nicaea in 325 A.D. and played a vital role against the Arians who denied the divinity of the Lord Christ. At the Council of Tyre in 335 A.D. he defended Pope Athanasius, champion of the faith, and was blamed by Bishop Eusebius, a fellow prisoner, before being exiled and later departing in peace.

9-23.name: St. Julius (Yulius) and His Mother, in Alexandria
9-23.summary: Coptic Reader gives this entry as a one-line entry, exactly as shown: 'On this day also, St. Julian and his mother were martyred in the city of Alexandria.' No life, torture or burial detail is supplied for this entry in the app, so none is recorded here.

9-24.name: The Entrance of the Lord Christ into the Land of Egypt
9-24.summary: An angel told Joseph in a dream to flee to Egypt because Herod sought to destroy the Child, and the Holy Family left Israel via Al-Arish, el-Farma and Sinai. At Tel Basta near Zagazig the idols fell, angering the priests, who mistreated the Holy Family; at el-Mahamma the Child caused a spring to gush and bathed in it, curing sickness. They then went through Belbeis and Meniet Genah in Samannoud, crossed the Nile to the west at Sakha, where the Child's footprint remained in a rock called Pekha Issous, 'the heel of Jesus,' blessed Wadi El-Natroun and many monasteries, and came to Ain Shams, El-Matariya and Old Cairo (Babylon), where they dwelt in a cave and crypt. The entry traces this journey through Egypt and closes with a blessing for the glorious feast.
hymnIds: Doxology for the Entrance of the Lord Christ into the Land of Egypt
Watos Psali for the Feast of the Entrance into Egypt
Adam Psali for the Feast of the Entrance into Egypt
Fraction to the Son: Our Lord, God, and Savior Jesus Christ, Who Came to Egypt to Be an Example for Us

9-24.name: Habakkuk, the Prophet
9-24.summary: Habakkuk was one of the twelve Minor Prophets, from the tribe of Levi, a singer who used stringed instruments, and his Hebrew name means 'embracer.' His prophetic ministry began after King Josiah's reformation in 622 B.C. and continued in 621-600 B.C. during the reign of King Jehoiakim. God told him the Babylonians, the Chaldeans, would be a chastening rod for the nation, and Habakkuk acknowledged that 'the just in any generation shall live by faith' (2:4). He prophesied the Incarnation and birth of Christ, saying 'God came from Teman, the Holy One from Mount Paran,' carried food to Daniel in the lions' den by an angel, and departed in peace. A church was built in his name at Kartsa in El-Behira governorate during the reign of the Christian Emperor Anastasius and was consecrated on the 24th of Pashons in the early part of the 6th century.

9-24.name: St. Bashnouna El-Maqari, the Monk
9-24.summary: Bashnouna was a holy monk of St. Macarius Monastery, martyred in the year 880 of the martyrs, 1164 A.D. During fighting between the men of Prince Dergham and the men of El-Wazir Shawer under Fatimid rule, he was arrested and threatened with death if he did not convert to Islam, but he firmly refused. He was burned alive and thus received the crown of martyrdom. Christians took his bones and carried them to the church of Abu Serga in Old Cairo, where he was buried.

9-25.name: St. Colta (Koulta), the Physician
9-25.summary: Colta was from Alexandria, born to Christian parents in the year 285 A.D., and his father died while he was still young. After his mother's death he left his wealth to the poor, studied medicine, and healed the sick without payment, while also teaching faith and helping people reject idolatry. The Roman authorities arrested him, demanded that he sacrifice to idols, and after he refused, scourged him, hung him by his hands, and subjected him to fire and other torments. His mother encouraged him, his fellow Christians visited and comforted him, and he remained firm, even when the governor commanded that he be thrown to wild beasts. In 300 A.D., on 25 Pashons, he was taken to the place of execution, where he was beheaded and received the crown of martyrdom.

9-25.name: The Honored Archon El-Mo'alem Ibrahim El-Gohari
9-25.summary: Ibrahim El-Gohari was a prominent Coptic layman, known for his generosity and service to the Church, who lived in Egypt during the 18th century. He was a wealthy man who used his resources to support the poor and to build and restore churches, and he worked diligently to improve the condition of Coptic Christians under difficult circumstances. During his lifetime he faced many challenges, including opposition and persecution, yet he remained steadfast in his faith and charitable works. He departed this life in 1795 A.D., on 25 Pashons, leaving behind a legacy of devotion and service to his community.

9-26.name: St. Thomas, the Apostle
9-26.summary: Thomas, also called Didymus or the Twin, was born in Galilee and was one of the twelve apostles chosen by the Lord. He was known for his initial doubt about the resurrection, asking to see the wounds of Christ, and after his encounter with the risen Lord he confessed his faith. Following Pentecost he preached the Gospel in many lands, including India, where he converted many people to Christianity and performed miracles. He faced opposition from idol worshippers and was ultimately martyred in 72 A.D., on 26 Pashons, when he was pierced by a spear. He is a different Thomas from Thomas the Anchorite of Shinshif Mount (Bashans 27) and Thomas, Victor and Isaac of Ashmunein (Hathor 21).

9-27.name: St. Lazarus, the Beloved
9-27.summary: Lazarus was the brother of Mary and Martha, from Bethany, and was a close friend of the Lord Jesus. He died and was buried, but after four days Jesus raised him from the dead, a miracle that strengthened the faith of many and foreshadowed Christ's own resurrection. Following the resurrection of the Lord, Lazarus followed the disciples and was later ordained as bishop of Cyprus, where he shepherded his flock faithfully. He lived for forty years after being raised, then departed in peace on 27 Pashons. Note: Coptic Reader also commemorates the Departure of Lazarus on Baramhat 17; both entries are recorded here as Coptic Reader gives them.

9-27.name: St. Thomas, the Anchorite, of Shinshif Mount
9-27.summary: Thomas was born in the village of Shinshif, near Akhmim, to God-loving and pious Christian parents, and was raised in the manners of the Church. He withdrew to the mountain of Shinshif, where he lived in contemplation, prayer, and praise with a melodious voice, and practiced strict asceticism, eating only once a week and memorizing the Bible. He was known for his virtues and for blessing visitors, and he associated with others only for prayer, while brethren living nearby visited him. He was visited by Abba Shenouda, and on a later visit Shenouda prophesied that he would follow Thomas within a few days, while a rock split as a sign. The Lord appeared to Thomas and promised that a church would be built in his name and visited by people and nations, and after three days Thomas left his body and received his crown in 452 A.D. He is a different Thomas from Thomas the Apostle (Bashans 26).
hymnIds: Doxology for St. Thomas the Hermit

9-27.name: Pope Yoannis II, 30th Patriarch of Alexandria
9-27.summary: Yoannis became a monk in his youth and lived a solitary life, becoming famous for his godly life and knowledge before he was chosen for the Alexandrian See. He was consecrated on 3 Paone in the year 221 of the martyrs, 505 A.D., and wrote many exhortations and homilies, while the Church enjoyed peace supported by Emperor Anastasius. After his enthronement, Saint Sawirus of Antioch sent him a letter congratulating him and confirming that the Lord Christ, after the union, has one nature. He guided the Church with wisdom and care until he departed in peace in 516 A.D., on 27 Pashons.

9-28.name: The Relocation of the Body of St. Epiphanius, Bishop of Cyprus
9-28.summary: Epiphanius was the bishop of Cyprus, and after his death his body was brought by boat from Constantinople, arriving in Cyprus on 28 Pashons in the year 119 of the martyrs, 403 A.D. Priests and people received the body with crosses and processions, and placed it in the church, while two deacons opposed digging a tomb and were excommunicated. The body remained for four days without change or stench, appearing as if asleep, and when a deacon of the saint struck the ground with an axe, the two deacons fell unconscious, were carried home, and died on the third day. The priests then anointed the body with costly spices, shrouded it splendidly, and placed it in a marble sarcophagus, where many miracles and signs occurred. Epiphanius's departure is commemorated on Bashans 17.

9-29.name: The Commemoration of the Three Major Feasts of the Lord
9-29.summary: This is a commemoration, not the life of a single saint, and it honors three great feasts of the Lord: the Annunciation, the Nativity, and the Resurrection. On this day the liturgy is celebrated with a joyful tune, reflecting the gladness of these feasts. There is no strict abstinence or prostrations on this day, in keeping with its festive character.

9-29.name: St. Simon, the Stylite
9-29.summary: Simon was born in Antioch around 389 A.D. to Christian parents named John and Martha, and after his brothers died young, he was sent as a poor shepherd to tend sheep, often depriving himself of food for the hungry. At the age of thirteen he was moved by the Beatitudes, fasted and prayed through nights kneeling, and after his father's death he gave his inheritance to the poor. He spent two years visiting ascetics, then became a monk at the Taladah monastery between Antioch and Aleppo for ten years, surpassing others in austerity, before living in a deserted cell at Tel-Nasin near Antioch for three years. He then stood on a pillar, where he lived for many years, healed the sick, exhorted visitors to disdain the world and avoid money, lying, and swearing, and resolved disputes among people. He departed in peace at the age of seventy in 459 A.D., after thirty-seven years on the pillar, and his body was later relocated to Antioch and then to Constantinople in 471 A.D., under Emperor Zeno, to a cathedral on the mountain of Simon, Sheikh Barakat, in northern Syria. He is presumably the Simeon the Stylite whose page was NOT counted for Simeon the Armenian on Baramouda 19; the hymn check will confirm whether that page is for this Simon.

9-30.name: St. Fournos (Fores), one of the Seventy Disciples
9-30.summary: Fournos was one of the seventy disciples chosen by the Lord, and he ministered with them for three years during the Lord's earthly ministry. After the ascension he served with the pure disciples, and after Pentecost he worked with Saint Paul, carrying his epistles to many countries. He taught both Jews and Gentiles, baptized many, and suffered many hardships and sorrows in his ministry, before departing in peace on 30 Pashons.

9-30.name: Pope Michael I, 68th Patriarch of Alexandria
9-30.summary: Michael was born in Sakha and raised in godliness and purity from his youth, becoming knowledgeable in the church books and memorizing many of them. He longed for the monastic life, became a monk at Saint Macarius monastery, was later ordained a priest, and then withdrew to the area of Singar, shutting himself in a cave for about twenty years in austere spiritual struggle. His fame for knowledge and virtues became well known, and he was chosen for the patriarchate and consecrated on 12 Paope in the year 809 of the martyrs, 1092 A.D. He lived an upright, pure, and modest life, owning no money, spending what remained on feeding the poor and needy, paying taxes for those who could not afford them, and renewing church vessels and books, while exhorting and teaching the people. During the reign of Caliph Al-Musta'ali bi-Allah and his minister el-Afdal, when the Nile inundation was seriously short, the caliph sent him to Ethiopia to negotiate with its king about raising the Nile's water, and he was received with great honor, asked the king to clear the watercourse of vegetation, and established cordial relations between the king and the caliph, becoming the first Alexandrian Patriarch to visit Ethiopia. When a plague epidemic spread, he moved among the sick until he himself was stricken, and after only a few hours of illness he departed to paradise on the next day in 1102 A.D., after serving the apostolic throne for nine years, seven months, and seventeen days. He is a different Michael from Pope Michael II, 71st Patriarch (Baramouda 3), and Michael III, 92nd Patriarch (Amshir 16).

10-1.name: St. Carpus, one of the Seventy Apostles
10-1.summary: Carpus was a companion and disciple of St. Paul, who mentions him in the Second Epistle to Timothy in connection with the cloak and books left at Troas. He preached in many countries, taught the faith, healed the sick, and baptized many people. He departed in peace.

10-1.name: St. Abe-Fame
10-1.summary: Abe-Fame was from the village of Oseem and was a soldier who confessed Christ before the governor Arianus at Ansena. He was tortured, and, according to the entry, his martyrdom was accompanied by miracles and the conversion of many who witnessed it. He was beheaded and received the crown of martyrdom, after a life of faithful confession under persecution. Note: the hymn check must confirm whether this Abe-Fame is the same saint as Abe-Fam (martyrdom on Tobi 27, church consecration on Koiahk 1); the two are not assumed identical here.

10-1.name: The Consecration of the Church of St. Leontius of Tripoli
10-1.summary: This entry commemorates the consecration of the church built in the name of St. Leontius in Tripoli. It presents Leontius as a martyr honored at Tripoli, whose church was consecrated on this day. The entry is a consecration commemoration rather than a full life narrative.

10-1.name: St. Qozman El-Tahawy and His Companions
10-1.summary: Coptic Reader gives this entry as a heading-only entry, with no further detail beyond the heading and the statement that this was their martyrdom, so no life or torture detail is recorded here.

10-1.name: St. Zikam
10-1.summary: Coptic Reader gives this entry as a heading-only entry, with no further detail beyond the statement that this was the martyrdom of St. Zikam, so no life or torture detail is recorded here.

10-2.name: The Appearance of the Bodies of St. John the Baptist and Elisha the Prophet in Alexandria
10-2.summary: The entry relates that the bodies of John the Baptist and the prophet Elisha, which had been buried in Sebaste, were revealed in Alexandria. It says the bodies were found in a church and were transferred with honor. The commemoration honors both John the Baptist and Elisha, whose relics were thus made known in Alexandria.

10-2.name: Pope Yoannis XVIII, 107th Patriarch of Alexandria
10-2.summary: Yoannis XVIII, born Joseph in El-Fayyoum, became a monk at the Monastery of St. Antonius and was later consecrated patriarch. He guided the Church with care for its people and clergy during his patriarchate. He departed in peace in 1512 of the Martyrs (1796 A.D.), after a life of monastic discipline and pastoral service.

10-3.name: St. Alladius, Bishop of the East
10-3.summary: Alladius was a bishop who shepherded his flock in the East with teaching and pastoral care. He was known for his steadfast faith and for strengthening Christians under difficult circumstances. He departed in peace, and the Church commemorates him as a faithful bishop and confessor.

10-3.name: St. Abraam, Bishop of El Fayyom
10-3.summary: Abraam was born Paul Ghorbrial in Delga in 1829 and became a monk, later serving as bishop of El Fayyom and Giza. He was renowned for his generosity to the poor, his care for the needy, and his refusal to accumulate wealth for himself. He built churches and schools and was beloved for his humility and charity. He departed in peace in 1914, after a long episcopate marked by almsgiving and pastoral love.

10-3.name: St. Martha, the Ascetic, from Egypt
10-3.summary: Martha was born in Egypt to wealthy Christian parents and at first lived a dissolute life, but she was moved to repentance when she was denied entry to church on the feast of the Nativity. She gave away her silk garments and gold, put on monastic garb, and entered a convent. She lived there in ascetic discipline for 25 years without leaving it. She departed in peace, remembered as a model of repentance and perseverance.

10-4.name: St. Shinosy (Sanusi) from Balkim
10-4.summary: Shinosy was a young shepherd from Balkim who, after an angel appeared to him, was guided by a righteous woman to confess Christ. He was brought before the governor and, after torture, was sent to Ansena, where he was again tried for his faith. He remained steadfast and was beheaded, receiving the crown of martyrdom.

10-4.name: St. John of Heraclia
10-4.summary: John was born in Heraclia in Asia Minor in 304 A.D., the son of a proconsul in the time of Diocletian, and he became a soldier who openly confessed Christ. He was arrested and tortured for refusing to worship idols, and he endured scourging and other torments with steadfastness. He was beheaded, and his body was honored by the faithful after his martyrdom. His uncle Bifam is commemorated on Paone 5.
hymnIds: Adam Psali for the Martyrdom of Abba John of Heraclia
Watos Psali for the Martyrdom of Abba John of Heraclia

10-4.name: Sts. Amoun and Sophia
10-4.summary: Amoun and Sophia were husband and wife who lived in chastity and devotion, and who, after Amoun's monastic calling, both embraced the ascetic life. They were arrested for their Christian faith and subjected to torture for refusing to deny Christ. They were martyred together, steadfast in faith and united in their confession. This Amoun is distinct from Amoun, Founder of Nitria (Bashans 22), and from Ammonius, Hermit of Mount Tounah (Bashans 20).

10-4.name: Abba Or, the Hermit of the Mount of El-Amoud, east of the Nile
10-4.summary: Or was born in Bahgora and, after the death of his parents, distributed his inheritance and became a monk in the wilderness of Shibot under Abba Ghalinicos. He lived a life of prayer, fasting, and ascetic struggle in the desert, and many were edified by his holiness. He departed in peace in old age, after a long monastic life in the Egyptian desert.

10-4.name: Pope Yoannis VIII, 80th Patriarch of Alexandria
10-4.summary: Yoannis VIII was born in Meniet Bani-Khosab and became a monk at El-Shahran before being consecrated patriarch on 19 Amshir, 1016 of the Martyrs (1300 A.D.). He shepherded the Church for about twenty years with care for its clergy and people. He departed in peace in 1036 of the Martyrs (1320 A.D.), after a patriarchate marked by pastoral service.

10-5.name: St. James the Oriental, the Confessor
10-5.summary: James, called the Oriental, was a monk and confessor who endured persecution for the Orthodox faith rather than deny it. He lived a life of ascetic discipline and steadfast confession, and he was honored for his endurance under suffering. He departed in peace, remembered as a confessor who bore witness to Christ without shedding his blood in martyrdom. He is a different James from James son of Zebedee, James the Persian, and James, Bishop of Nisibis.

10-5.name: St. Bifam
10-5.summary: Bifam, the uncle of St. John of Heraclia, was a soldier who confessed Christ during the persecution of Diocletian in 304 A.D. He was arrested and tortured for refusing to worship idols, and he remained firm in his faith through scourging and other torments. He was beheaded and received the crown of martyrdom, following his nephew in faithful witness.

10-5.name: Sts. Bishay and Botros (Peter)
10-5.summary: Bishay and Botros were brothers who lived in the time of persecution and confessed Christ together. They were arrested, tortured, and, after refusing to deny their faith, were beheaded. They are commemorated together as martyrs who remained united in confession and in death. Note: a church of Bishay and Peter was consecrated on Koiahk 26; the hymn check must confirm whether that pair is this pair.

10-5.name: The Consecration of the Church of St. Boctor (Victor) in Sho, east of El-Khesous, in the diocese of Abnub
10-5.summary: This entry commemorates the consecration of the church built in the name of St. Boctor in Sho. It honors Boctor as a martyr whose church was consecrated on this day. The entry is a consecration commemoration rather than a full martyrdom narrative. Note: Boctor (Victor) Son of Romanus has a hymn page used for his martyrdom on Baramouda 27; the hymn check must report whether that page has consecration-specific titles for this church.

10-6.name: St. Theodore, the Monk of Alexandria
10-6.summary: Theodore was a monk in Alexandria in 339 A.D. who opposed the Arian teaching promoted under Constantius and the Arian bishop Gawargios. He was seized, dragged by an unbridled horse, and torn, and his head was smashed, dying as a martyr for the Orthodox faith. He is commemorated for his steadfast defense of the Nicene faith. He is a different Theodore from Theodore of Shotep, Theodore the Oriental, Theodore the Hermit, and Tadros disciple of Pachomius.

10-6.name: The Four Archons of Esna
10-6.summary: The four archons of Esna — Ausaphius, Samoun, Hourwag, and Bakhou — were leading men of Esna who confessed Christ during the persecution in 303 A.D. They were arrested and tortured for refusing to worship idols, and they remained steadfast in their faith. They were beheaded together and received the crown of martyrdom.

10-6.name: St. Didymus the Blind
10-6.summary: Didymus was born in Alexandria in 313 A.D. and lost his sight at the age of four, yet he learned the alphabet from letters carved in wood, a method the entry notes anticipated Braille by fifteen centuries. He became dean of the Theological School of Alexandria in 346 A.D. under St. Athanasius, teaching pupils including Palladius, Rufinus, and Jerome, and defending the Nicene faith against the Arians. He lived a pious, ascetic life, was visited by St. Antonius, and, according to the entry, foresaw the death of the emperor Julian. He departed in peace in 398 A.D.

10-7.name: St. Abaskhiroun El-Qalin
10-7.summary: Abaskhiroun was a soldier from Qalin in 304 A.D. who, while serving in the regiment at Attribes under Diocletian, confessed Christ and was imprisoned, where an angel appeared to him. He was sent to Arianus at Ansena and Assiut, where he was scourged and flayed, and where the sorcerer Alexander, whose poison failed to harm him, believed and was himself beheaded. Abaskhiroun remained steadfast and was beheaded, receiving the crown of martyrdom. Note: a church of Abiskhiron was consecrated on Koiahk 8; the hymn check must confirm whether Abaskhiroun and Abiskhiron are the same saint.

10-7.name: St. Moises of Akhmim and the Mount
10-7.summary: Moises was a monk of Akhmim and the Mount who lived a life of ascetic struggle and prayer, and who blessed and encouraged his spiritual children to remain steadfast. His disciples Dioscorus and his brother Esculapius were martyred in the Akhmim massacre on 1 Tobe, 304 A.D. Moises continued his monastic life in the desert and, after a long struggle, delivered up his spirit in peace and was buried with veneration. He is a different Moises from Moses the Black and Moses the Prophet.

10-7.name: The Consecration of the Church of St. Matthew (Mettaos) El-Fakhory in the Mount of Esna
10-7.summary: This entry commemorates the consecration of the church of St. Matthew the potter in the Mount of Esna. It relates that the wife of the king of Nubia, who was possessed by an unclean spirit, was healed through the saint's intercession, and that the king then built the church. The church was consecrated on this day in honor of St. Matthew.

10-8.name: The Consecration of the Church of the Virgin Lady known as El-Mahamma
10-8.summary: On this day in 617 of the Martyrs (901 A.D.), the church of the Virgin St. Mary, the Mother of God, known as El-Mahamma, was consecrated. The name comes from a spring the Lord Jesus caused to well up, in whose water the Child Jesus was bathed during the flight into Egypt, when He, the Virgin His mother, and Joseph drank from it. A church was built in that place in the name of the Virgin St. Mary and was consecrated on this day. Note: the St. Mary page's consecration psalis are for the Philippi and El-Muharaq churches; the hymn check must report whether any El-Mahamma-specific title exists.

10-8.name: St. George (Girgis), the New Martyr
10-8.summary: George was an Ishmaelite who believed in the Lord Christ and became a monk in 1103 of the Martyrs (1387 A.D.). He was seized and punished severely, then brought before King El-Zaher, where he confessed his faith in the Lord Christ. The king tried to persuade him to forsake his faith by offering expensive gifts, but the saint refused, and the king ordered him beheaded, so he received the crown of martyrdom. He is a different George from George the Prince of the Martyrs, George the Ascetic, George the Zahimian, and George friend of Abraam.

10-8.name: St. Tamada and Her Children, and Armenius and His Mother
10-8.summary: Coptic Reader gives this entry as a heading-only entry, with no further detail beyond the statement that this was their commemoration, so no life or martyrdom detail is recorded here.

10-9.name: St. Samuel, the Prophet
10-9.summary: Samuel was the son of Elkanah and Hannah, born after Hannah's long barrenness and dedicated to God's service at Shiloh under Eli the priest. He grew up serving in the tabernacle, was called by God as a boy, and later anointed Saul and then David as kings of Israel. He lived as prophet, judge and priest, rebuking disobedience and guiding Israel. The entry presents him departing in peace in old age after a life of faithful service.

10-9.name: St. Lucilianus and Four Others: Claudius, Hypatius, Paul, and Dionysius
10-9.summary: Lucilianus was an elderly priest in Nicomedia who had abandoned idolatry and preached Christ, and he was arrested with four young men during persecution. The governor Silvanus tried to force them to renounce their faith, and they were tortured for refusing. They remained steadfast, encouraged one another, and were beheaded on a hill, receiving the crown of martyrdom.

10-9.name: Sts. Abamoun and Serna
10-9.summary: In 304 A.D., Abamoun, born in Basta in the district of el-Ashmonain, desired to give his life for God and sought out Arianus, the proconsul of Ansena. On the way he met the young man Serna, who shared the same desire, and together with St. Claudius and six soldiers they went to Assiut, where they were imprisoned. Before Arianus, Abamoun refused to worship idols and was tortured on the Hinbazeen and on an iron bed over fire, yet the Lord supported him and many believed through his sufferings. Finally the governor ordered the beheading of Abamoun and Serna, and they received the crowns of martyrdom. This Abamoun is part of the Claudius of Ansena group, distinct from other Abamouns.

10-9.name: The Relocation of the Relics of St. Mercurius Abu Safain to Cairo
10-9.summary: In 1488 A.D., during the papacy of Pope John (Yoannis) VI, 74th Patriarch of Alexandria, a relic of St. Mercurius Abu Safain was brought to his church in Old Cairo. Anba Macaroni, metropolitan of the Armenian monastery of Mar Yakobos in Jerusalem, had come to Egypt with a man named Constantine for the feast of the Archangel Michael, and after the liturgy he discussed with the Pope the presence of the martyr's relics in Caesarea of Cappadocia. The Pope asked him to obtain a member of the relics for the church in Old Cairo as a blessing for the Coptic Orthodox believers. By divine providence the holy member arrived, carried by Constantine, and the Pope received it in great celebration and placed it in a reliquary in the church of St. Mercurius.

10-10.name: St. Maxy El-Shinrawy
10-10.summary: Maxy was a soldier from the city of el-Shinrawy who lived in the time of Diocletian and was martyred in the reign of Diocletian and Maximian. He confessed Christ before the governor, was sent to Alexandria, and was tortured and imprisoned for refusing to worship idols, remaining steadfast under beating and other torments. While in prison an angel spoke with him, and his soul was delivered as the angel was speaking with him, so he died in prison as a martyr.

10-10.name: St. Dabamon, His Mother Epistemon, and His Sister Sophia
10-10.summary: Dabamon was from the city of Tukh, and his mother was Epistemon and his sister was Sophia. He confessed Christ and was arrested and tortured, including being hung and beaten, for refusing to deny his faith. His mother and sister shared his confession and were also martyred. Finally they were beheaded, receiving the crowns of martyrdom.

10-10.name: The Commemoration of the Opening of the Churches
10-10.summary: This entry commemorates the opening of the churches after a time when they had been closed and the Christians had been persecuted and prevented from worshipping openly. When the churches were reopened, the faithful rejoiced and returned to public prayer, liturgy and the sacraments. The commemoration marks the restoration of free Christian worship and the end of the enforced closure.

10-10.name: Pope John XVI, the 107th Patriarch of Alexandria
10-10.summary: Pope John XVI, also called Yoannis, was from a village called Tuh al-Khail in the district of el-Minya, and he was a monk in the Monastery of St. Anthony before becoming patriarch. He was enthroned in 1676 A.D. and shepherded the Church for about 42 years, a period marked by the building and restoration of churches and by care for the Coptic community. He departed in 1718 A.D. at an advanced age, after a long and faithful patriarchate. Note: the check reported him as the 107th Patriarch, the same number reported for Pope Yoannis XVIII on Paone 2; both numbers are recorded as Coptic Reader gives them, and the apparent conflict is flagged.

10-11.name: St. Claudius
10-11.summary: Claudius was a Roman soldier and a relative of Emperor Diocletian, from the city of Antioch, who openly confessed Christ and refused to worship idols. He was arrested, tortured in many ways, and imprisoned, but he remained firm and encouraged other Christians, including soldiers, to hold fast to the faith. He was finally beheaded, receiving the crown of martyrdom, and his body was taken and buried with honour. He is the Claudius Stratelates of the Bashans 20 six soldiers and the Bashans 23 Thecla passion group.

10-11.name: The Consecration of the Altar of the Church of the Forty Martyrs of Sebaste in Alexandria
10-11.summary: This entry commemorates the consecration of an altar in Alexandria dedicated to the Forty Martyrs of Sebaste, the soldiers who died for Christ in the frozen lake. The altar was consecrated so that the liturgy could be celebrated there in their honour and the faithful could receive blessing through their intercession. The commemoration marks the dedication of that holy place to the memory of the Forty Martyrs.

10-12.name: The Commemoration of the Archangel Michael
10-12.summary: This entry commemorates the Archangel Michael and the church dedicated to him in Alexandria, on the site formerly occupied by the temple of Serapis. Pope Theophilus, 23rd Patriarch of Alexandria, converted the idol temple into a church for the Archangel Michael in 385 A.D., after the destruction of pagan worship there. The feast was established on this day, the same day the pagans had formerly celebrated Serapis, so that Christians would honour Michael instead. The entry also notes the custom of praying a litany for the rising of the Nile waters, asking God through Michael's intercession to bless the land. Note: this 12th-day entry carries the Alexandria church-dedication story, unlike the brief monthly Michael entries on other months' 12th days.
hymnIds: Doxology for Archangels Michael and Gabriel
Fraction to the Father for Archangel Michael
Archangel Michael (12th of Every Coptic Month)

10-12.name: St. Euphemia
10-12.summary: Euphemia was a virgin martyr from Chalcedon who lived in the time of Diocletian and was arrested for confessing Christ. She was tortured in many ways, including being thrown to wild beasts, for refusing to worship idols. She remained steadfast in her faith and was finally martyred, receiving the crown of virginity and martyrdom.

10-12.name: St. Justus, the 6th Patriarch of Alexandria
10-12.summary: Justus was the sixth Patriarch of Alexandria, succeeding St. Mark's successors in the early Church, and he shepherded the See of Alexandria in the second century. He was a man of learning and piety who cared for the flock and preserved the apostolic teaching. He departed in peace after a faithful patriarchate, and his memory is honoured on this day.

10-12.name: Pope Kyrillos II, the 67th Patriarch of Alexandria
10-12.summary: Pope Kyrillos II, also called Cyril, was from the city of el-Mahalla and was a monk before becoming patriarch in 1078 A.D. He shepherded the Church for about 14 years, a period marked by the building of churches and by care for the poor and for monastic life. He departed in 1092 A.D. after a faithful and fruitful patriarchate, and his memory is honoured on this day.

10-13.name: The Commemoration of the Archangel Gabriel the Announcer
10-13.summary: This entry commemorates the Archangel Gabriel, called the Announcer because he announced the good news of salvation, above all the Annunciation to the Virgin Mary. Gabriel is honoured as the messenger who proclaimed the birth of John the Baptist to Zechariah and the birth of Christ to Mary. The Church celebrates his commemoration on this day, asking his intercession and honouring his service in God's plan of salvation.
hymnIds: Adam Psali for Archangel Gabriel the Announcer
Watos Psali for Archangel Gabriel the Announcer
Doxology for Archangels Michael and Gabriel

10-13.name: St. John, Bishop of Jerusalem
10-13.summary: John was Bishop of Jerusalem, enthroned in 388 A.D., and he shepherded the Church of Jerusalem for about 29 years. He was known for his learning, his defence of the faith, and his care for the holy places and for the poor. He departed in 417 A.D. after a long and faithful episcopate, and his memory is honoured on this day. Note: a John, Bishop of Jerusalem is also commemorated on Baramouda 3 (baptized by Bishop Justus, whom he succeeded); the hymn check must report whether they are the same John.

10-14.name: Sts. Apakir, John, Ptolemy, and Philip
10-14.summary: Apakir, John, Ptolemy and Philip were martyrs who confessed Christ during persecution and were arrested for refusing to worship idols. They were tortured in many ways, including beating and imprisonment, but they remained steadfast and encouraged one another in the faith. They were finally beheaded, receiving the crowns of martyrdom together. Note: a joint Apakir and John page was used for the different Cyrus/John group on Amshir 6; the hymn check must report whether that page applies to this group.
hymnIds: Adam Psali for the Martyrdom of Saints Apakir, John, Ptolemy, Philip
Watos Psali for the Martyrdom of Saints Apakir, John, Ptolemy, Philip

10-14.name: Pope John XIX, the 113th Patriarch of Alexandria
10-14.summary: Pope John XIX, also called Yoannis, was born in the city of el-Minya and was a monk in the Monastery of St. Macarius before becoming patriarch in 1928 A.D. He shepherded the Church for about 14 years, a period marked by the building of churches, schools and hospitals, and by care for the Coptic community in Egypt and abroad. He departed in 1942 A.D. after a faithful patriarchate, and his memory is honoured on this day.

10-15.name: The Consecration of the Church of St. Mari Mina in Mariut
10-15.summary: This entry commemorates the consecration of the church of St. Mina at Mariut, near Alexandria, where the martyr Mina had been buried. Mina was a soldier-martyr who had died for Christ, and his body was brought to Mariut, where a church was built over his tomb and became a famous place of pilgrimage and healing. The consecration of the church is celebrated on this day, honouring Mina and the miracles God worked through his intercession.
hymnIds: Adam Psali for the Martyrdom of Saint Mina the Wonder Worker
Watos Psali for the Martyrdom of Saint Mina the Wonder Worker
Adam Psali for the Church Consecration for Saint Mina the Wonder Worker in Mariut
Watos Psali for the Church Consecration for Saint Mina the Wonder Worker in Mariut

10-15.name: The Receiving of the Relics of St. Mark the Apostle, the Evangelist
10-15.summary: This entry commemorates the return of relics of St. Mark the Apostle and Evangelist to Egypt in 1968, during the papacy of Pope Kyrillos VI. The relics had been in Venice, Italy, for eleven centuries, having been taken there in the 9th century, and they were returned by Pope Paul VI of Rome. A great celebration was held in Cairo, with the relics placed in the Cathedral of St. Mark, and the event marked the restoration of the apostle's relics to his own See of Alexandria. Note: this 1968 return is distinct from the return of St. Mark's head (Paope 30) and his martyrdom (Baramouda 30); the hymn check must report whether the Mark page has relic-return-specific titles for this occasion.

10-16.name: St. Abba Nofer, the Anchorite
10-16.summary: Nofer was an anchorite who lived in the desert of Egypt, having left the world to serve God in solitude and prayer. He had been a monk in the monastery of Hermopolis before withdrawing to the desert, where he lived alone for about 60 years, sustained by God and visited by angels. He was found by St. Paphnoute, to whom he told his life story and who buried him after his departure. He died in peace after a long life of asceticism, and his memory is honoured on this day. Note: a 'St. Nopher the Anchorite' page was counted for Abu-Nofer on Hathor 16; the hymn check must report whether that page is this Nofer.
hymnIds: The Great Saint Abba Nopher (Hathor 16, Paone 16)

10-17.name: St. Latsoun, El-Behnesawy
10-17.summary: Latsoun was a monk from Behnesa in Egypt who left home at the age of 30 to embrace monastic life. The entry presents him as living a life of prayer, fasting and ascetic discipline in the monastery. He persevered in that monastic life and in humble service until his later years. He departed in peace, and his commemoration is kept on this day.

10-17.name: The Return of the Relics of St. Mark the Apostle to the New St. Mark Cathedral, Abbassia, Cairo
10-17.summary: In 1968, the relics of St. Mark, which had been taken to Venice, Italy, were returned to Egypt. Pope Kyrillos VI received the relics with great celebration. The relics were placed in the newly built St. Mark Cathedral in Abbassia, Cairo. This return restored the apostle's relics to the Church of Alexandria, and the event is commemorated on this day. Note: this is the 17 Paone occasion named in the St. Mark page's Veneration title, distinct from the 1968 return commemorated on Paone 15, the head return on Paope 30, and the martyrdom on Baramouda 30.
hymnIds: Adam Psali for the Consecration of a Church for Saint Mark the Apostle
Watos Psali for the Consecration of a Church for Saint Mark the Apostle
Adam Psali for the Martyrdom of Saint Mark the Apostle
Watos Psali for the Martyrdom of Saint Mark the Apostle
Doxology for St. Mark the Evangelist
Another Doxology for St. Mark the Evangelist
Saint Mark the Evangelist (30 Parmoute, 30 Paope, 17 Paone)

10-18.name: Pope Demianos, the 35th Patriarch of Alexandria
10-18.summary: Demianos was born in Alexandria and became a monk in the Monastery of St. Macarius, where he lived a life of prayer, fasting and spiritual struggle. After the departure of Pope Peter IV, he was chosen as Patriarch of Alexandria. He shepherded the Church with wisdom, wrote many epistles and homilies, and defended the faith. He departed in peace after a long patriarchate, and his departure is commemorated on this day.

10-18.name: The Inauguration of the New St. Mark Cathedral in the Monastery of Anba Rowais in Cairo
10-18.summary: In 1968, the new St. Mark Cathedral in the Monastery of Anba Rowais in Cairo was inaugurated. The cathedral was built as a major centre for the Coptic Orthodox Church in Egypt. Its inauguration was celebrated with Pope Kyrillos VI and the bishops and clergy of the Church. The event is commemorated on this day.

10-19.name: St. George, El-Mozahim
10-19.summary: George el-Mozahim lived in the tenth century and was martyred in 959 AD. He was a steadfast Christian who refused to renounce his faith despite persecution and severe tortures. He endured his sufferings with patience and remained firm in his confession of Christ. He was put to death as a martyr, and his martyrdom is commemorated on this day. Note: the hymn check must report whether this George is the George the Zahimian whose name was previously not counted for other Georges; he is distinct from George the Prince, the Ascetic, and friend of Abraam unless the page proves otherwise.

10-19.name: St. Bishai Anoub
10-19.summary: Bishai was born in Babanous and served as a soldier under Cyprian, the governor of Atripe. When he confessed Christ, he was tortured for his faith and then sent to Arianus, the governor of Ansena. He remained steadfast under further torture and refused to worship idols. He was beheaded in 304 AD, receiving the crown of martyrdom. He is distinct from Bishay of the Bishay/Botros pair (Paone 5) and from Bishoy.

10-19.name: Pope Archillas, the 18th Patriarch of Alexandria
10-19.summary: Archillas was a presbyter of Alexandria and a disciple of Pope Peter, the Seal of the Martyrs. He was enthroned as Patriarch on Koiahk 19 in the year 28 of the martyrs (311 AD), as Pope Peter had commanded. He accepted Arius back into communion, contrary to Pope Peter's command, and this caused controversy in the Church. He departed in peace after a short patriarchate of about six months, in the year 28 of the martyrs (312 AD, as given in the entry).

10-19.name: The First Pontifical Liturgy in the New St. Mark Cathedral, Abbassia, Cairo
10-19.summary: In 1968, Pope Kyrillos VI prayed the first pontifical liturgy in the new St. Mark Cathedral in Abbassia, Cairo. This followed the return of the relics of St. Mark and the completion of the cathedral. The liturgy marked the beginning of regular pontifical worship in the new cathedral. The event is commemorated on this day.

10-20.name: Elisha, the Prophet
10-20.summary: Elisha was a prophet of Israel and the disciple and successor of Elijah the prophet. When Elijah was taken up, Elisha received a double portion of his spirit and continued his prophetic ministry. He performed many miracles, including healing the waters of Jericho, multiplying the widow's oil, and raising the Shunammite woman's son. He served God faithfully throughout his ministry and departed in 847 BC, as given in the entry.

10-20.name: The Consecration of the Church of the Martyr Abba Klog, the Priest
10-20.summary: This is a short entry: after the building of the church of the martyr Abba Klog the priest was completed, Anba Kyrillos the bishop came and consecrated it. No further life, martyrdom or consecration detail is given in the entry.

10-21.name: The First Church Built for the Virgin Mary in Philippi
10-21.summary: While the apostles were preaching in the city of Philippi, they founded the first church named for the Holy Virgin St. Mary. The apostles prayed in this church, and the people of the city came to pray there. The entry presents this as the first church built in the name of the Virgin Mary. Its founding is commemorated on this day. Note: the St. Mary page contains Philippi consecration psalis; the hymn check must list them.
hymnIds: Adam Psali for the Consecration of the First Church for the Virgin in Philippi
Watos Psali for the Consecration of the First Church for the Virgin in Philippi

10-21.name: The Miracle of the Melting of the Iron in Bartus, by the Prayers of the Virgin Mary
10-21.summary: St. Matthias was sent to preach in Bartus, where the people worshipped idols. During his ministry there, iron melted through the prayers of the Holy Virgin Mary. When asked who had melted the iron, the Virgin replied that it was the true God, Jesus Christ. The people believed, and St. Matthias baptized them, and the miracle is commemorated on this day.

10-21.name: St. Timothy of Memphis (The Conscript)
10-21.summary: Timothy was a soldier from Memphis who served under Arianus, the governor of Ansena, during the persecution under Diocletian. When the imperial edict ordered the worship of idols, Timothy refused and confessed Christ. He was tortured severely for his faith but remained steadfast. He was finally beheaded, receiving the crown of martyrdom. He is a different Timothy from Timothy the Apostle and Timothy of Gaza.

10-21.name: St. Kedron, the 4th Patriarch of Alexandria
10-21.summary: Kedron was born in Alexandria and was baptized by St. Mark the Apostle, from whom he learned the doctrines of the faith. After the departure of Pope Milius, he was consecrated Patriarch of Alexandria in 95 AD. He shepherded the Church with wisdom and care for about eleven years. He departed in peace, and his departure is commemorated on this day.

10-22.name: Sts. Cosmas, Damian, Their Brothers and Their Mother
10-22.summary: Cosmas and Damian were brothers from Arabia who were physicians, treating the sick without charge and healing many by their prayers. Their mother was Theodota, and their brothers were Anthimus, Leontius and Euprepius. During the persecution under Diocletian, they were brought before Lysias the governor and confessed Christ. They endured severe tortures but remained steadfast in the faith. They were finally beheaded, together with their mother and brothers, receiving the crown of martyrdom. Note: a Cosmas/Demian page was used for their church consecration on Hathor 30; the hymn check must confirm whether that page is for this Arabia group.
hymnIds: Adam Psali for the Martyrdom of St. Cosmas and St. Demian, Their Brothers and Their Mother
Watos Psali for the Martyrdom of St. Cosmas and St. Demian, Their Brothers and Their Mother
Doxology for St. Cosmas and St. Demian, Their Brothers and Their Mother

10-23.name: St. Abba Noub, the Confessor
10-23.summary: Abba Noub was a devoted monk in one of the monasteries of Upper Egypt. In the year 20 of the martyrs (304 AD), Arianus the proconsul heard of him, brought him before him and commanded him to worship idols. The saint refused and confessed Christ, and Arianus tortured him severely. He was then exiled to the five western cities (Pentapolis), where he remained imprisoned for seven years. When Emperor Constantine ordered the release of those imprisoned for the faith, Abba Noub returned to his place of worship, completed his good endeavour and departed in peace. He is distinct from Aba-Noub, owner of the Golden Fan (Amshir 5), and from Abba Nofer/Nopher the Anchorite.

10-24.name: St. Moses the Ethiopian
10-24.summary: Moses was an Ethiopian who lived in Egypt in the fourth century; he was first a slave to a sun-worshipper, then, after escaping, became a notorious robber and leader of a band of robbers. Repenting, he sought the true God, was directed to the monks of Scetis (Shiheet), and was received by Abba Isidore the priest and taught by St. Macarius the Great. He was baptized, became a monk, and lived a life of severe asceticism, prayer and humble service to the elders, later being ordained a priest. St. Macarius foretold that he would die by the sword, and in 407 AD, during the first Berber raid on the monastery, Moses refused to flee and was killed with seven other brothers, receiving the crown of martyrdom. His pure body is present with that of his teacher Abba Isidore in a shrine in St. Mary El-Baramos Monastery in Wadi El-Natroun, Egypt.
hymnIds: Adam Psali for St. Moses The Strong
Watos Psali for St. Moses The Strong
Doxology for the Strong Abba Moses
The Great Saint Moses the Strong (Paone 24)

10-24.name: St. Isidore, the Priest of Scetis
10-24.summary: Isidore departed in the year 113 of the martyrs (397 AD); he first became a monk in the region of Nitria and was ordained a priest to serve the hermits of Celia. He then came to St. Macarius the Great in Scetis, became one of his early disciples and a fellow companion in establishing St. Macarius' monastic community, and was known as the priest of Scetis because he celebrated the divine liturgies for the monks. He was noted above all for gentleness and concern for the salvation of others, receiving and restoring monks who had been expelled after repeated attempts to reform them. He was a man of unceasing prayer, even while working with his hands, and God granted him the gift of casting out unclean spirits because of his longsuffering and victory over anger. When he completed his good endeavour, he departed in peace. Note: the hymn check must report whether the Male Saints 'Isidore the Priest' page is this Isidore of Scetis; he is distinct from Isidore of Pelusium, Isidore friend of Sina, and Isidore of Antioch.
hymnIds: Doxology for St. Isidore the Priest
Glorification Melody for St. Isidore the Priest

10-25.name: Pope Peter IV, the 34th Patriarch of the See of St. Mark
10-25.summary: He departed in 567 of the martyrs, 851 A.D., as the 34th Patriarch of the See of St. Mark. After his predecessor's death, the monks of the Monastery of St. Macarius chose and ordained him patriarch. He shepherded his flock well and was a man of piety and virtue. After completing his course, he departed in peace.

10-26.name: The Consecration of the Church of the Angel Michael in the City of Naklou
10-26.summary: This is a short entry: it records only the consecration of the church in Naklou, with a closing request for the angel's intercession, and gives no further narrative detail. Note: the body text names the Archangel Gabriel, although the heading names the Angel Michael; both are recorded here as Coptic Reader gives them, and the discrepancy is flagged for the hymn check.

10-26.name: The Sun Stood Still for Joshua, Son of Nun
10-26.summary: After the death of Moses, Joshua, son of Nun, led the Israelites and defeated the Amorite kings, whose five kings fled to a cave at Makkedah. Joshua commanded the sun to stand still over Gibeon and the moon over the valley of Ajalon, so that Israel could take vengeance on its enemies. The sun did not hasten to set, and the entry says there was no day like it before or after, for God hearkened to the voice of a man and fought for Israel.

10-27.name: St. Ananias, the Apostle
10-27.summary: Ananias, one of the Seventy Apostles and Bishop of Damascus, departed in 70 A.D. He preached in Damascus and its surroundings, baptized St. Paul after Paul's conversion, healed Paul's blindness, and converted many to the faith. The proconsul Lucianus seized him, tortured him by burning and scourging, and then stoned him outside the city of Damascus. He delivered up his soul and received the crown of martyrdom.

10-27.name: St. Thomas of Shentalet
10-27.summary: Thomas, from Shentalet (Shandalat), was martyred in 304 A.D. While he was sleeping in the field, an angel appeared to him and urged him to receive the crown of martyrdom, so he went to Alexandria and confessed Christ before the governor. He was tortured together with St. Babnuda of El-Bandara and St. Shinousy of Balkim, who encouraged one another, and was then sent to Arianus, governor of Ansena. Arianus beheaded him, and seven hundred men and nine women were martyred with him. He is a different Thomas from Thomas the Apostle, Thomas the Anchorite, and Thomas the Hermit.

10-27.name: St. John Ebn el-Abah
10-27.summary: John, a minister for the Fatimid caliph al-Mustansir Bi-Allah, departed in 1045 A.D. He was honored and loved for his honesty and knowledge, was appointed minister over all of Egypt, and was humble and compassionate to all people. After a wicked conspiracy led the caliph to order his beheading, John and his wife sought the intercession of St. Barbara, God revealed the truth, the caliph punished the conspirator and released John with greater appreciation. The caliph then allowed John to build a church near his house, but John instead rebuilt two ruined churches in Old Cairo, Abu Serga and St. Barbara, which were adjacent; when the caliph ordered one demolished, John, fasting and distressed, moved between the two churches and died leaning against the wall between them. The caliph wept, kept both churches, and John was buried in the church of St. Barbara, where a bright light shone over his tomb; he is called 'the martyr of the two churches.'

10-28.name: Pope Theodosius, the 33rd Patriarch of the See of St. Mark
10-28.summary: Theodosius departed in 283 of the martyrs, 567 A.D., as the 33rd Patriarch of the See of St. Mark. He was born in Alexandria, was a man of piety, and was ordained a priest; after the departure of Patriarch Timothy, he was ordained patriarch. He shepherded his flock and, after completing his course, departed in peace.

10-28.name: The Consecration of the Church of Anba Sarabamon, Bishop of Nikios
10-28.summary: This is a short entry: it records only that the church of Anba Sarabamon, Bishop of Nikios, was consecrated and that his body was laid in it, with a closing request for his intercession, and gives no further narrative detail. Note: this Sarabamon of Nikios is distinct from Sarabamon the Veiled (Baramhat 28, Clergy page) and from Serapamon (Baramhat 5); the hymn check must report whether the Sarapamon page used for Tobi 25 and Hathor 28 is this Bishop of Nikios and whether it has consecration-specific titles.

10-29.name: The Feast of the Annunciation, the Nativity, and the Resurrection
10-29.summary: This is a short entry: it records only that on this day the church celebrates the Feast of the Annunciation, the Feast of the Nativity, and the Feast of the Resurrection, and gives no further narrative detail. It follows the 29th-day Three Major Feasts pattern.

10-29.name: The Seven Ascetics in Tounah Mount: Basidi, Cotolus, Ardama, Moses, Aisi, Barkalos, and the Other Cotolus
10-29.summary: The seven ascetics lived in the mountain of Tounah, and an angel appeared to them and told them they would receive the crown of martyrdom. They went to the governor, confessed Christ, and were tortured with stones hung around their necks, imprisoned, and then sent to the governor of Alexandria, who put them in cauldrons of sulfur and pitch from which they were delivered unharmed. One hundred and thirty people who witnessed this believed, confessed Christ, and were martyred, and the governor then ordered the seven ascetics beheaded. The Moses among them is not Moses the Strong or Moses the Prophet.

10-29.name: St. Abba Hour and His Mother Theodora
10-29.summary: Abba Hour was a soldier from Antioch who went to Alexandria and confessed Christ before the governor. He endured successive tortures, including having his hands cut off, being dragged by an ox's tail, and being thrown into a pit of snakes that did not harm him, while his mother Theodora shared in his confession and suffering. He was then put into a cauldron of boiling oil and tar, where he praised God and died. He and his mother Theodora are commemorated together as martyrs. This Theodora is distinct from Theodora the Nun (Baramouda 11) and the other Theodoras.

10-30.name: The Nativity of St. John the Baptist
10-30.summary: The church celebrates the birth of St. John the Baptist, the son of the priest Zacharias and Elizabeth. The angel Gabriel announced his birth to Zacharias in the temple, after Elizabeth's long barrenness, and John was born as the forerunner who would prepare the way for Christ. He grew in the desert and later baptized Christ in the Jordan, fulfilling the prophecy that he would go before the Lord. His nativity is therefore celebrated as the birth of the greatest born of women and the forerunner of the Savior. Note: the St. John the Baptist page's Veneration title names Paone 30 among its dates; the hymn check must report whether the page has Nativity-specific titles.
