The Great Martyr and Saint John the Baptist (Thoout 2, Thoout 26, Meshir 30, Paone 2, Paone 30)

10-30.name: Pope Cosmas I, the 44th Patriarch of the See of St. Mark
10-30.summary: Cosmas departed in 446 of the martyrs, 730 A.D., as the 44th Patriarch of the See of St. Mark. He shepherded the flock of Christ and, after completing his course in piety, departed in peace. The entry closes with the usual request for his prayers and intercession.

11-1.name: St. Ephronia, the Virgin
11-1.summary: Ephronia was a virgin from a noble family in Alexandria who was betrothed to a man named Theodosius, but she fled her arranged marriage and entered a convent, where she lived in ascetic discipline. Her father later found her in the convent and, after she refused to leave, had her tortured for her Christian faith. She remained steadfast under torture and was finally beheaded, receiving the crown of martyrdom, and her body was buried with honor.

11-1.name: St. Athanasius, Bishop of the City of Clysma (Suez)
11-1.summary: Athanasius was bishop of Clysma in Egypt during the persecution under Diocletian, and he openly confessed Christ before the governor, refusing to sacrifice to idols. He was subjected to severe tortures, including beating and imprisonment, yet remained firm and encouraged other Christians. He was finally beheaded for his faith, and his body was taken by believers and buried with honor. He is a different Athanasius from Athanasius the Apostolic (20th Pope) and Athanasius III.

11-1.name: The Consecration of the Church of the Great Mari Mina at Mount Abnoub
11-1.summary: This entry commemorates the consecration of a church dedicated to St. Mina (Mari Mina) on Mount Abnoub in Egypt, rather than a martyrdom. The church was built in honor of the saint, whose relics and miracles had made him widely venerated in Egypt. Its consecration is remembered as a feast of thanksgiving for the saint's intercession and for the completion of the church, and the entry closes with a blessing rather than a life narrative. Note: the Mina page's consecration psalis are for Mariut; the hymn check must report whether any Abnoub-specific title exists.

11-2.name: St. Jude, the Apostle
11-2.summary: Jude, also called Thaddeus, was one of the twelve apostles of Christ and the brother of James, and he preached the Gospel after the Ascension, traveling through Mesopotamia, Syria and Persia. He performed miracles and converted many to Christianity, despite opposition from idol worshippers and rulers. He was finally martyred for his preaching, being beaten and then beheaded, and his body was buried with honor by believers.

11-3.name: St. Biakhi (Bioukha) and His Companions
11-3.summary: Biakhi and his companions lived during the persecution of Diocletian and openly confessed Christ, refusing to worship idols. They were arrested and subjected to cruel tortures, but an angel healed their wounds and strengthened them, and some of their persecutors were converted by what they saw. They remained steadfast, were finally beheaded, and their bodies were taken by their families and buried with honor.

11-3.name: St. Cyril I (Cyril of Alexandria), the 24th Pope of Alexandria
11-3.summary: Cyril was born in Alexandria and was the nephew of Pope Theophilus, who raised and educated him; he became pope in 412 AD and served for 32 years. He defended the Orthodox faith against Nestorius, who denied that the Virgin Mary was the Mother of God, and he presided over the Council of Ephesus in 431 AD, which condemned Nestorius. He also wrote extensively against heresies, cared for the poor, and departed in peace in 444 AD, after a long and fruitful patriarchate. He is a different Cyril from Cyril of Jerusalem and from Popes Kyrillos II and VI.
hymnIds: Doxology for St. Cyril of Alexandria

11-3.name: St. Celestine, Pope of Rome
11-3.summary: Celestine was born in Rome and was ordained pope in 422 AD, after the death of Pope Boniface, during a period of difficulty for the Roman Church. He lived a life of prayer and charity, supported monastic communities, and worked to uphold Orthodox doctrine, including sending missionaries to Britain and Ireland. When Nestorius' teaching spread, Celestine condemned it and supported Cyril of Alexandria, and he departed in peace in 432 AD after about ten years as pope.

11-4.name: The Relocation of the Relics of Sts. Cyrus and John (Abuqir and John)
11-4.summary: Cyrus and John were physicians and martyrs whose relics were originally buried in the city of Menouthis (Abuqir) in Egypt, where miracles were worked through them. On this day their relics were solemnly transferred to a church built in their honor, in the presence of bishops, clergy and a large crowd of believers. The relocation was celebrated with hymns and prayers, and the entry records the honor given to the martyrs' relics rather than a new martyrdom narrative. Note: Abuqir is Apakir; the hymn check must report whether the Apakir and John page used for the Amshir 6 group has relocation-specific titles.

11-5.name: Sts. Peter and Paul, the Apostles
11-5.summary: Peter, a fisherman from Bethsaida, became the chief apostle, denied Christ three times, repented, and preached in Jerusalem, Antioch and Rome, where he was crucified upside down under Nero because he counted himself unworthy to die as Christ had. Paul, born in Tarsus as Saul, persecuted Christians until Christ appeared to him on the road to Damascus, after which he was baptized, preached through three missionary journeys, was imprisoned in Caesarea and Rome, and wrote fourteen epistles. Both apostles were martyred in Rome under Nero, Peter by crucifixion and Paul by beheading, and the entry presents their martyrdoms together as a single feast.
hymnIds: Doxology for St. Peter and St. Paul

11-5.name: St. Marcus, Governor of el-Borolus and Father of St. Demiana
11-5.summary: Marcus was the governor of el-Borolus and the father of St. Demiana, but he weakened and denied the Christian faith out of fear of losing his earthly position. His daughter Demiana sent him a letter admonishing him, saying she wished she had heard of his departure from this world rather than his abandonment of Christ. Touched by her words, he repented, went to the rulers confessing Christ, remained steadfast despite attempts to appease him, and after much torture was beheaded, receiving the crown of martyrdom. He is distinct from Marcus el-Antony (Epep 8) and from St. Mark the Evangelist.

11-6.name: St. Aoulimpas (Olympus)
11-6.summary: Aoulimpas was a monk and priest who lived an ascetic life of prayer and fasting, and he was known for his humility, charity and care for the poor. During a period of persecution he openly confessed Christ and refused to deny his faith or sacrifice to idols. He was tortured for his confession, remained steadfast, and was finally beheaded, receiving the crown of martyrdom.

11-6.name: St. Theodosia, the Virgin
11-6.summary: Theodosia was a young virgin from a Christian family who dedicated herself to a life of purity and prayer. She was arrested during a persecution, confessed Christ before the governor, and refused to renounce her faith or worship idols. She endured severe tortures with patience, was finally beheaded, and her body was buried with honor by believers.

11-7.name: St. Shenouda, the Archimandrite
11-7.summary: Shenouda was born in Shandaweil near Akhmim in Upper Egypt to parents named Abigos and Deroba, and as a child he was entrusted to his uncle, St. Pigol, at the White Monastery, where he grew in ascetic discipline. He became abbot (archimandrite) of the White Monastery, led a large monastic community with strict rules, preached against paganism and heresy, and was known for visions, miracles and his care for the poor. He attended the Council of Ephesus with Cyril of Alexandria, lived to a great age, and departed in peace in 452 AD (year 168 of the Martyrs), after a long life of monastic leadership. He is the Archimandrite whose page was NOT counted for Shenouda I, 55th Pope (Baramouda 9/24).
hymnIds: Adam Psali for the Church Consecration for Abba Shenute the Archimandrite
Watos Psali for the Church Consecration for Abba Shenute the Archimandrite
Adam Psali for the Departure of Abba Shenute the Archimandrite
Watos Psali for the Departure of Abba Shenute the Archimandrite
Doxology for St. Shenute the Archimandrite

11-8.name: St. Pishoy (Bishoy), the Beloved of Christ
11-8.summary: Pishoy was born in Shansha in Monufia in 320 AD and entered monastic life in the wilderness of Scetis (Wadi El-Natrun), where he became a disciple of St. Macarius and lived in great asceticism, prayer and humility. He was known for washing the feet of strangers, carrying Christ in the form of a poor traveler, and for miracles, including raising the dead and healing the sick. He gathered many disciples, founded a monastery, and departed in peace in 417 AD (year 133 of the Martyrs) at the age of 97, and his body was later returned to his monastery in Scetis.
hymnIds: Doxology for St. Pishoy and St. Paul of Tammah

11-8.name: Sts. Piroou and Athom
11-8.summary: Piroou and Athom were from Sonbat in Gharbia, sons of wealthy Christian parents, and after their parents' death Piroou went to El-Farma (Pelusium) for trade, where he met soldiers carrying the body of St. Noua to cast into the sea and bribed them to give him the body for honorable burial. Both brothers then confessed Christ before governors, were tortured in many ways, including beating, imprisonment and having their teeth pulled, yet were healed and strengthened by God. They were sent from one governor to another, remained steadfast, and were finally beheaded, receiving the crown of martyrdom.

11-8.name: St. Balanah, the Priest
11-8.summary: Balanah was a priest from Bara in the diocese of Sakha who lived a life of prayer, charity and service to his flock. In 304 AD (year 20 of the Martyrs), during the persecution of Diocletian, he distributed his money to the poor, went to Antinoe (Ansena), and confessed Christ before the governor Arianus, refusing to sacrifice to idols. He was tortured, remained steadfast, and was finally beheaded, receiving the crown of martyrdom.

11-8.name: St. Epime (Pimanon)
11-8.summary: Epime was the chief of Panokleus in el-Behnesa, a wealthy and merciful man who distributed his money to the poor and needy. In 305 AD (year 21 of the Martyrs) he went to the governor of el-Behnesa, confessed Christ, and refused to offer incense to idols; he was tortured, had his tongue cut out and was burned, yet was healed by God and worked miracles. He was sent to Alexandria, where he also worked miracles in prison, was released, returned to his town, was arrested again, and was finally beheaded, receiving the crown of martyrdom.

11-8.name: St. Cyrus (Karas), the Anchorite
11-8.summary: Cyrus was the brother of the Emperor Theodosius the Great, but he left his wealth and imperial position to become a hermit in the inner Western Wilderness, where he lived for 57 years without seeing the face of another man. He lived in complete solitude, prayer and fasting, and was visited only at the end of his life by the monk Pemwah, to whom he revealed his story. He fell ill with a fever, prayed kneeling, delivered up his soul in peace, and was shrouded and buried by Pemwah in his cave. He is distinct from Cyrus the physician (of Cyrus and John) and from Cyrus of the Amshir 6 group.
hymnIds: Doxology for St. Karas the Anchorite

11-8.name: St. Marcus (Mark) el-Antony
11-8.summary: Marcus was born in a town in Upper Egypt, became a monk at the Monastery of St. Anthony, and lived a life of asceticism, prayer and obedience, later becoming known for his spiritual counsel and miracles. He was ordained a priest, served his brethren with humility, and was visited by many seeking his prayers and guidance. He departed in peace in 1386 AD (year 1102 of the Martyrs), after a long monastic life, and was buried with honor by his fellow monks. He is distinct from St. Mark the Evangelist and from Marcus, father of Demiana (Epep 5).
hymnIds: Adam Psali for the Departure of St. Mark Abba Antony
Watos Psali for the Departure of St. Mark Abba Antony

11-9.name: St. Simon, the Apostle, the Son of Clopas
11-9.summary: Simon was an apostle and the second bishop of Jerusalem after St. James. He led the church for a long period before being persecuted in the time of Emperor Trajan. He was scourged and then crucified at the age of 120, receiving the crown of martyrdom. He is distinct from Simon the Zealot, Simon the Tanner, and Simon the Stylite.

11-9.name: Pope Cladianus, the Ninth Patriarch of Alexandria
11-9.summary: Cladianus was born in Alexandria and rose through the clerical ranks to become the ninth Patriarch of Alexandria. He was ordained patriarch in 152 A.D. and served about fourteen years. He departed in peace in 166 A.D., and the entry closes with the usual blessing for his prayers.

11-10.name: St. Theodore, the Bishop of Pentapolis
11-10.summary: Theodore was a native of Pentapolis in Libya, where he was ordained priest and then bishop. He defended the faith during the persecution of Diocletian, was arrested, and refused to sacrifice to idols. After being tortured, he was beheaded and received the crown of martyrdom in 304 A.D. He is distinct from Theodore, Bishop of Corinth, commemorated the same day, and from the other Theodores.

11-10.name: St. Theodore, the Bishop of Corinth
11-10.summary: Theodore was from Corinth, where he also served as bishop. During Diocletian's persecution he was arrested for confessing Christ and refusing idol worship. He endured torture and was then beheaded, and his body was taken and buried with honour. He is distinct from Theodore, Bishop of Pentapolis, commemorated the same day, and from Theodotus, Bishop of Corinth (Baramhat 6).

11-11.name: Sts. John and Simon, the Martyrs
11-11.summary: John and Simon were from Shoubra-Malas and confessed Christ before the governor during the persecution of Diocletian. They endured torture rather than deny their faith. They were beheaded and received the crown of martyrdom in 304 A.D.

11-11.name: St. Isaiah, the Solitary of Scetis
11-11.summary: Isaiah was born in 337 A.D. and became a monk in Scetis (Wadi El-Natrun), where he lived a life of asceticism and prayer. He was known as a great solitary and spiritual father. He departed in 447 A.D. at about the age of 110. He is distinct from Isaiah the Prophet (Thoout 6).

11-12.name: The Commemoration of the Archangel Michael
11-12.summary: This is a monthly commemoration, not a martyrdom or departure. The Church commemorates the Archangel Michael, chief of the angels, on the twelfth day of each Coptic month. The entry honours his intercession and service before God, and closes with a blessing.
hymnIds: Doxology for Archangels Michael and Gabriel
Fraction to the Father for Archangel Michael
Archangel Michael (12th of Every Coptic Month)

11-12.name: St. Abba Hour El-Siriakousy
11-12.summary: Hour was a monk from El-Siriakousy who confessed Christ during Diocletian's persecution. He was arrested and tortured for refusing to sacrifice to idols. He was beheaded and received the crown of martyrdom in 304 A.D. He is distinct from Abba Hour of Paone 29 (with his mother Theodora).

11-12.name: St. Sisoes the Great
11-12.summary: Sisoes was born in 320 A.D. and became a monk in 340 A.D., living first in Shiheet and then, from 356 A.D., on the mountain of St. Antonius, whose life he closely followed. He ate only once every two days for seventy years and returned to Shiheet in 426 A.D. because of old age. He was known for sayings on humility, love, spiritual struggle, serenity and silence. He departed at the age of 110, his face shining with heavenly radiance, delivering his spirit into the hand of the Lord.

11-13.name: St. Pisentius, the Bishop of Qift
11-13.summary: Pisentius was born in Shamir, near Armant, in about 284 A.D. (the Coptic Reader gives his era as the Martyrs' era, corresponding to 568 A.D. for his departure). He became a monk and was later ordained Bishop of Qift, where he shepherded his flock in asceticism and teaching. He departed in peace in 568 A.D. after a long life of service. Note: a Pisentius, Bishop of Qift, is also commemorated on Mesore 7; the hymn check must report whether they are the same saint and whether any Pisentius page names either date.

11-13.name: St. Apamon (Ammon) of Toukh
11-13.summary: Apamon was born in Toukh, near Banha, and was commanded by the Archangel Michael to go to Ansena and confess Christ. Before the governor Eukhius he refused to sacrifice, and was tortured with red-hot iron rods, scourging and boiling water, from which the Lord healed him. His steadfastness and miracles led many to faith, and he was finally beheaded. Julius of Aqfas took his body, shrouded it, and sent it to his hometown. He is distinct from Ammonius of Mount Tounah, Ammonius of Esna, and Amoun of Nitria.

11-13.name: St. Shenoute, during the Early Arab Rule
11-13.summary: Shenoute was a righteous man living in the early period of Arab rule in Egypt. His enemies accused him before the Moslem ruler and he was offered release if he would forsake his faith. He refused, openly declaring his Christian faith, and was severely tortured. He was finally ordered to be beheaded and received the crown of martyrdom. The entry gives no place or exact year beyond the early Arab period. He is distinct from Shenouda the Archimandrite (Epep 7).

11-14.name: St. Proconius (Procopius) of Jerusalem
11-14.summary: Proconius was from Jerusalem and confessed Christ during the persecution of Diocletian. He was arrested, tortured for refusing to deny his faith, and was beheaded. He received the crown of martyrdom in 303 A.D.

11-14.name: Pope Peter V, the 83rd Patriarch of Alexandria
11-14.summary: Peter was a monk in the Monastery of St. Macarius before being chosen as the 83rd Patriarch of Alexandria. He was ordained patriarch in 1340 A.D. and cared for the churches and his flock. He departed in peace in 1348 A.D. after about eight years on the apostolic throne.

11-15.name: St. Ephrem the Syrian
11-15.summary: Ephrem was born in Nisibis in 306 A.D. and became a deacon, living much of his life in Edessa. He was a great teacher and author of many hymns and writings defending the faith. He departed in peace in 379 A.D.

11-15.name: Sts. Cyriacus and Julitta, His Mother
11-15.summary: Cyriacus was born in Iconium in 302 A.D.; his father died early and his mother Julitta raised him in the faith. Fleeing Diocletian's persecution, they went to Seleucia and then to Tarsus when Cyriacus was three years old, with two handmaidens. Seized by the governor Iskandrus, Julitta was tortured while the child openly declared, 'I am Christian.' The governor threw the child from his chair, smashing his head, and the child died at no more than three years old; Julitta was then beheaded. Their bodies were taken by the handmaidens and buried near Tarsus in 305 A.D., and parts of their relics are noted as being in a Syrian monastery.
hymnIds: Doxology for St. Cyriacus and St. Julitta
St. Cyriacus and his Mother Julitta (15 Epep)

11-16.name: St. John, the Owner of the Golden Gospel
11-16.summary: John was born in Constantinople to Atrofius, a commander, and his wife Theodora. At the age of twelve he left home and joined a monastery, where he lived for seven years before a vision directed him to return to his parents. Unrecognised, he lived in a hut in their courtyard, sustained by food from their table, until he gave them the golden Gospel they had given him as a child. Recognised only then, he delivered his soul after three days and was buried in his hut, departing in 448 A.D.

11-16.name: The Relocation of the Relics of St. George, the Great Martyr, to His Church in Old Cairo
11-16.summary: St. George was buried in Palestine, where a church was built over his relics. The governor of the Oasis, who loved Christ, obtained part of the relics in a box from Palestine, built a church in the Oasis, and placed them there, with victories over the Berbers attributed to George's prayers. When Christians in the Oasis decreased, God preserved the relics: the monk Marcus, hegumen of El-Qalamun, was told in a vision to ask a Bedouin widow for the box her husband had brought from the Oasis church. He told Pope Gabriel V, the 88th Patriarch (1409–1427), who with the clergy carried the relics with honour and placed them in St. George's church in Old Cairo, where miracles followed. Note: the George Prince of Martyrs page's Veneration names Parmoute 23 and Hathor 7, not Epep 16; the hymn check must report whether it has relocation or Old Cairo-specific titles.

11-17.name: St. Euphemia
11-17.summary: Euphemia was from Chalcedon and was martyred in the year 22 of the martyrs (306 A.D.), in the reign of Diocletian. She refused to sacrifice to Apollo when her family was ordered to take part in a pagan festival, and she was accused before the governor Priscus after her mother reported her. She was tortured in many ways, including the wheel, fire and being thrown to wild beasts, but remained unharmed. At last she was beheaded, and a church was built over her body. She appears to be the same Euphemia commemorated on Paone 12.

11-17.name: Sts. Thecla and Martha, from Esna
11-17.summary: Thecla and Martha were from Esna and were martyred in the year 19 of the martyrs (303 A.D.), during the persecution of Diocletian. They were arrested when soldiers seized them while they were going to the church, and they refused to worship idols. They were subjected to many tortures, including being hung upside down and having their bodies lacerated, and they did not deny Christ. They were beheaded, and the text says that God glorified their bodies after their martyrdom. This Thecla is distinct from Thecla of the Claudius passion (Bashans 23), Makronius/Thecla (Baramhat 1), and Esi/Thecla (Koiahk 8).

11-18.name: St. James the Apostle, the Brother of the Lord
11-18.summary: James was a relative of Christ and became the first bishop of Jerusalem, called the brother of the Lord because he was the son of Joseph from his first wife. He was known for his holiness, prayer and ascetic life, and he wrote the Epistle of James. The Jews, angered by his preaching, seized him and took him to the pinnacle of the temple, where they asked him to deny Christ. When he confessed Christ openly, they threw him down, stoned him and struck him on the head with a club, and he was martyred in the year 63 A.D. He is distinct from James son of Zebedee, James the Persian, James of Nisibis, and James the Oriental.

11-19.name: Sts. Bidaba, Bishop of Qift, Andrew and Christodolos
11-19.summary: Bidaba was born in Armant to Christian parents and became bishop of Qift, while Andrew and Christodolos were his disciples. During the persecution of Diocletian they were arrested and brought before the governor Arianus, and they refused to sacrifice to idols. They were tortured severely, including being beaten and having their bodies torn, but remained steadfast. They were beheaded in the year 19 of the martyrs (303 A.D.), and their bodies were buried with honour. Bidaba is distinct from Pisentius, Bishop of Qift (Epep 13).

11-19.name: The Martyrs of the Massacre of Esna
11-19.summary: This entry commemorates the Christians of Esna who were killed during the persecution of Diocletian, when soldiers were sent to force the people to worship idols. The people of Esna, including men, women and children, refused to deny Christ and confessed their faith openly. Many were killed in the massacre, and their bodies were gathered and buried by the surviving Christians. The entry presents them as a large group of martyrs whose blood was shed for Christ in Esna.

11-19.name: St. Pantaleemon the Physician
11-19.summary: Pantaleemon was born in Ta'madan to a pagan father, Astochius, and a Christian mother, Aunala, and he learned the art of medicine. A priest guided him to the Christian faith, and after his conversion he healed a man bitten by a serpent and a blind man, and his father also believed and was baptized. When the emperor Maximian learned that he was a Christian, he was arrested and subjected to many tortures, including being beaten and hung, but he remained firm. He was beheaded, and the text says his blood flowed like milk and a dry tree beside him became green, and many who saw this believed. Coptic Reader spells his name Pantaleemon.

11-19.name: Pope Yoannis X, the 85th Patriarch of Alexandria
11-19.summary: Yoannis was a Syrian from Damascus, a godly and knowledgeable monk, who was chosen after Pope Mark IV and ordained on 12 Bashans 1079 of the martyrs (1363 A.D.). During his papacy he consecrated the holy Myron with twenty bishops in 1369 A.D. in the monastery of St. Macarius, and a severe famine lasting three years occurred in Egypt. He interceded for the poor and needy during the famine and cared for the flock, and he remained on the throne for six years, two months and eight days. He departed in peace in the year 1085 of the martyrs (1369 A.D.) and was buried in Dair el-Habash in Old Cairo, beside St. Simon the Tanner.

11-20.name: St. Theodore of Shotep
11-20.summary: Theodore was from Shotep, the son of John of Shotb, and his mother was a pagan who later believed, while his father was a Christian soldier. He became a general in the Roman army and was known for his courage, and he killed a dragon at Heraclia that had terrorized the people. When the governor Eukhitos ordered him to sacrifice to idols, he refused and confessed Christ, and he was tortured, including being hung and having his body lacerated. He was martyred in the year 320 A.D., and his father died five days after him, and a church was built in his name. He is distinct from Theodore the Oriental, Theodore the Hermit, Theodore the Monk of Alexandria, and the two Theodores of Epep 10.

11-21.name: The Commemoration of the Lady Virgin St. Mary
11-21.summary: Coptic Reader gives this as a brief, heading-type entry rather than a full life story: the text on this day simply commemorates the Holy Lady, the Virgin Mary, and asks for her intercession, without giving additional biographical or martyrdom detail in this entry.

11-21.name: St. Sisinnios (Sosenius) the Eunuch
11-21.summary: Sisinnios was a man of the royal palace of the Emperor Theodosius the Great and was known for his charity and godliness. He ministered to St. Cyril of Alexandria at the Council of Ephesus against Nestorius, and when he fell ill Cyril prayed for him and he was healed. He gave his money to the poor and lived a life of prayer and service, and he departed in peace in the year 147 of the martyrs (431 A.D.). Cyril prayed over his body, and he was buried with veneration, and his commemoration is kept annually. Coptic Reader spells his name Sisinnios (Sosenius).

11-22.name: St. Macarius, Son of Basilides the Minister
11-22.summary: Macarius was from Antioch in Syria, the son of Basilides the minister of Diocletian, and he refused the emperor's orders to force Christians to sacrifice to idols. He was exiled to Alexandria, where Christ appeared to him and strengthened him, and he was tortured by the governor Armanius, including having his tongue and arms cut and hot nails driven into him. He performed miracles in prison, including raising a dead man, and was then taken to Antinoe, where the ship stopped at Shatanof. He was beheaded there in the year 304 A.D., and in the time of Constantine his body was found by Eulogius, who built a church for him. He is distinct from Macarius the Great, Macarius of Alexandria, and Macarius, Bishop of Edkow.

11-22.name: St. Leontius (Lawendius) of Tripoli
11-22.summary: Leontius was born in Tripoli in Syria to Christian parents and became a soldier who preached Christ openly. His commander imprisoned him and tortured him until his blood poured out, while he continued to praise God. He delivered up his spirit in prison in the year 303 A.D., and a wealthy Christian woman, the wife of Diocletian's commander, took his body, shrouded it and placed it in a coffin in her home with a lamp burning before it. After the persecution ended, a church was built for him and his body was relocated on the first day of Paone. Note: a Leontius of Tripoli church consecration is commemorated on Paone 1; the hymn check must report whether a Leontius page exists and whether its titles are martyrdom titles or consecration titles.

11-23.name: St. Longinus the Soldier
11-23.summary: Longinus was from Cappadocia and was a Roman captain whom Pilate appointed to guard the crucifixion of Christ. He witnessed the darkness, the earthquake, the splitting of the rocks and the opening of the graves at Christ's death, and he confessed, 'Truly this was the Son of God.' He also guarded the tomb and refused a bribe to deny the Resurrection, and after St. Peter explained the faith to him he believed and was baptized. He resigned his military service and preached in Cappadocia, performing miracles, until Pilate wrote to Tiberius and soldiers seized him. He was beheaded in the year 45 A.D.

11-23.name: St. Marina of Antioch
11-23.summary: Marina was from Antioch in Pisidia in Asia Minor, of noble parents who worshipped idols, and after her mother died her father entrusted her to a Christian nanny. She longed for martyrdom and refused the governor's proposal of marriage when he demanded that she worship idols, and she was tortured by being combed with iron and washed with vinegar and lime. An angel healed her, and she was again tortured in a squeezing device and in a cauldron of boiling lead, but an angel saved her each time and many who saw this believed and were martyred. The governor, weary of her steadfastness, ordered her beheaded, and she extended her hands in prayer, bent her head courageously and received the crown, and her body is in the church of the Virgin Mary in Haret El-Rum in Cairo.

Watos Psali for the Church Consecration of Saint Marina the Martyr's Church in Antioch
Adam Psali for the Martyrdom of Saint Marina of Antioch
Watos Psali for the Martyrdom of Saint Marina of Antioch

11-24.name: St. Apa-Noub of Nahisah
11-24.summary: Apa-Noub was born in Nahisah to Christian parents and was meek and godly from childhood, and at the age of twelve, during the persecution of Diocletian, he distributed his inheritance to the poor. He confessed Christ before Lucianus, governor of Samannoud, and was beaten until his belly was broken and his entrails came out, but an angel healed him. He was taken by ship to Atripe, hung head downwards from the mast, and when the governor's glass turned to stone and his legs were unable to move and the soldiers were blinded, an angel released and healed him. The soldiers confessed Christ and were martyred, and Apa-Noub was also martyred in the year 303 A.D. He is distinct from Aba-Noub of the Golden Fan (Amshir 5), Abba Noub the Confessor (Paone 23), and Nofer/Nopher.

Watos Psali for the Martyrdom of Saint Apanoub of Nehis
Doxology for St. Apa-Noub of Nehis
Saint Apanoub the Martyr of Nehissa (Epep 24)

11-24.name: Pope Simeon I, the 42nd Patriarch of Alexandria
11-24.summary: Simeon was Syrian by nationality, and his parents came to Alexandria while he was still a child, where he often attended the church of St. Mark and visited Pope Agathon. He became a monk at El-Zugag Monastery west of Alexandria, was ordained a priest by Pope Agathon, and after the departure of Pope Isaac he was unanimously chosen and consecrated on 23 Koiahk 409 of the martyrs (692 A.D.). He was inclined to the ascetic life, rebuked luxurious living, and when wicked men gave him poison as medicine he drank it after receiving the Holy Mysteries and was unharmed, and a deadlier poison in figs made him ill for forty days. The Caliph ordered the wicked men burned, but the Pope interceded and saved them, except the magician who prepared the poison, who was burned alive, fulfilling the Gospel saying in Mark 16:18. He consecrated many godly bishops on Pentecost, visited the monasteries of Shiheet, returned to Alexandria, felt weak and departed in peace in the year 416 of the martyrs (700 A.D.), after seven years and seven months on the apostolic throne.

11-25.name: The Consecration of the Church of St. Mercurius Abu-Seifein
11-25.summary: This entry commemorates the consecration of the first church built in the martyr's name at Caesarea in Cappadocia, where he was martyred and buried. After his death, St. Mercurius appeared to a man in Caesarea and told him to build a church and monastery in his name. The man began the work, and the saint helped him with many miracles until the building was completed in splendid form. The church was consecrated on this day, while the saint's martyrdom itself is commemorated on 25 Hathor. Note: the hymn check must report whether the Mercurius page has Caesarea consecration titles; the Mercurius relic relocation to Cairo (Paone 9) was previously counted false for lack of relocation titles.
hymnIds: Adam Psali for the Martyrdom of Saint Philopater Mercurius
Watos Psali for the Martyrdom of Saint Philopater Mercurius
Adam Psali for the Consecration of a Church for Saint Philopater Mercurius
Watos Psali for the Consecration of a Church for Saint Philopater Mercurius
The Great Martyr Philopateer Mercurius of the Two Swords (Hathor 25)
Another Melody for St. Philopateer Mercurius

11-25.name: St. Isaac
11-25.summary: Isaac was from Shamah, in the district of Minya, and worked as a gardener and overseer of an orchard. He was pious, gentle and devout, abstained from meat and wine, fasted for two days at a time, and gave his earnings to the poor. An angel appeared to him in a vision and encouraged him, after which he went to the governor at el-Qus and confessed his Christian faith. He was tortured by burning and by squeezing with Hinbazeen, but the Lord healed him, and he was finally beheaded. His body was taken to his hometown and buried with honor, and many signs and wonders were reported there. He is distinct from Isaac of Tiphre, Isaac disciple of Apollo, and the Patriarch Isaac.

11-25.name: St. Hilaria (Liyarya)
11-25.summary: Hilaria was born to pious parents in a village near Damirah, and from childhood she loved chastity, fasting and prayer. At the age of 12, an angel told her to go and confess Christ before the governor, so she gave all her possessions to the poor and went to Sersana. There she confessed her faith, was comforted by St. Shenousy, and was tortured by the governor. She was then taken to Toah and thrown into a fire, from which she emerged unharmed, and she was finally beheaded. The hymn check must report whether any Hilaria page is for this Hilaria rather than another of the name.

11-25.name: Sts. Thecla and Mouji (Mugi)
11-25.summary: Thecla and Mouji were born in Kerakus and brought up as Christians. When they saw the governor torturing Christians, they were troubled, and an angel showed them the glory prepared for martyrs. They went to Alexandria and confessed Christ before the governor, who tortured them severely. Mouji was beheaded, Thecla was sent to Damtou, and she was also beheaded. This Thecla is distinct from Thecla of the Claudius passion, Makronius/Thecla, Esi/Thecla, and Thecla of Esna (Epep 17).

11-25.name: St. Antonius of Beba
11-25.summary: Antonius was born in Beba to pious and merciful parents, and he was martyred in the year 20 of the martyrs, 304 A.D. Hearing of the torment of Christians, he went to Arianus, the governor of Ansena, and confessed Christ, and was ordered to be shot with arrows, which did not harm him. He was sent bound, with Epimachus and two other martyrs, to Alexandria, where he endured consecutive tortures. He was then sent to the governor of Farma, who had his body combed with iron combs and cast him into a cauldron of boiling oil, but the Lord healed and strengthened him, and he was finally beheaded. He is distinct from Anthony the Great and Antonios of Thmoui.

11-25.name: St. Abakragoun
11-25.summary: Abakragoun was from El-Batanon and had formerly been a thief. He and two young men plotted to rob a monk's cell, but found the monk keeping vigil in prayer, waited until dawn, and then bowed before him, cast away their swords, and became monks at his exhortation. After a great spiritual struggle, the monk prophesied that Abakragoun would receive the crown of martyrdom. In the persecution, Abakragoun bid his spiritual father farewell, went to Nakyos, and confessed Christ before the governor. He was tortured, sent to Alexandria, thrown into the sea in a hide sack, and brought out by an angel, then commanded to go to Samannoud, where his miracles led many to believe and receive martyrdom. The governor of Samannoud beheaded him, an angel told a priest in Menuf where the body was, the priest kept it in his house, and after the persecution a church was built for him in El-Batanon and his body was placed in it.

11-25.name: St. Dometius El-Souriany (The Syrian)
11-25.summary: Dometius was brought up in Persia and learned astrology, but longed to become a Christian. He met a monk who taught him the way of God, believed, was baptized, and became a monk who performed many honorable deeds. He then dwelt with a hermit for ten years, during which he ate no cooked food, and was ordained a deacon. While serving in the sanctuary, he saw the Holy Spirit descending upon the sacrament as a white dove, and he was then ordained a priest, and the fame of his holiness became well known. When persecution was incited against Christians, he was seized and stoned until he delivered his pure spirit and received the crown of martyrdom. He is distinct from Dometius of the joint Maximus/Dometius page (Tobi 14 and 17).

11-25.name: St. Palamon
11-25.summary: Palamon, the great anchorite, departed in the year 32 of the martyrs, 316 A.D. He dwelt in the Eastern Mount near the city of El-Kasre and El-Sayyad, practicing austere asceticism and worship day and night, and fasting long fasts. After St. Pachomius believed and was baptized, he came and became Palamon's disciple for about seven years. Later, an angel commanded Pachomius to establish cenobitic monasticism, Palamon rejoiced and went with him to Tabennesi to help fulfill God's command, then left him there, blessed him, and returned to his dwelling. When Palamon had completed his good endeavor, he departed in peace.

11-26.name: The Departure of the Upright St. Joseph, the Carpenter
11-26.summary: Joseph, who departed in the year 16 A.D., was descended from David of the tribe of Judah, was born in Bethlehem, worked as a carpenter, and lived in Nazareth until honorable old age. He was chosen by lot, when a dove came out of his staff, to be betrothed to the Virgin Mary, and the priest Zacharias entrusted her to him. After the Annunciation, Joseph, being a just man, intended to put Mary away secretly, but an angel appeared to him in a dream, and he obeyed. He went with Mary from Nazareth to Bethlehem for the registration ordered by Caesar Augustus, where she delivered Jesus, and after the Magi he fled with them to Egypt at an angel's command in a dream. He endured the hardships of the journey, was comforted by beholding Jesus and blessing Mary, went yearly with them to Jerusalem for Passover, found the twelve-year-old Jesus in the temple, and continued working as a carpenter and caring for the Holy Family until he completed his good endeavor and rested in the Lord before the crucifixion, which is why the Lord entrusted Mary to John.
hymnIds: Doxology for St. Joseph the Carpenter

11-26.name: St. Timothy, the 22nd Pope of Alexandria
11-26.summary: Timothy, a disciple of St. Athanasius the Apostolic, departed in the year 101 of the martyrs, 385 A.D. He sold his possessions, became a priest and teacher in the School of Alexandria, and accompanied Athanasius to the Council of Tyre, where he helped expose a conspiracy when a woman who had accused Athanasius mistakenly addressed Timothy as Athanasius and revealed his innocence. After Pope Peter II, the bishops chose Timothy, and he was consecrated on 17 Paremhotep in the year 95 of the martyrs, 379 A.D. He cared for his flock, exhorted and taught them, warned against the Arian heresy, wrote pastoral epistles, renovated churches, and went to the Second Ecumenical Council at Constantinople in 381 A.D., where he judged Macedonius, enemy of the Holy Spirit, as well as Sebelius and Apollinaris. He was called 'the saint' by Emperor Theodosius the Great, sat on the throne for six years, four months and six days, and departed in peace, mourned by his flock and buried with veneration. He is distinct from Timothy the Apostle, Timothy of Gaza, and Timothy of Memphis.

11-27.name: St. Apamon (Abba Amoun)
11-27.summary: Apamon was from Turnout and was martyred in the year 19 of the martyrs, 303 A.D. He went to Ansena, Antinoe, and confessed Christ before Arianus the proconsul, who tortured him severely by beating and combing his body with long sharp nails, but the Lord healed and strengthened him. When the governor grew weary, he sent Apamon to Armanius, the proconsul of Alexandria, where an angel encouraged and strengthened him, and the governor tortured him with many tortures, but the angel healed him. Many believed through him and were martyred, including the virgin Theophila, who stood and confessed, was tortured, was ordered to be burned in fire from which the Lord saved her, and was then beheaded and received the crown. Apamon was finally beheaded. He is distinct from Apamon of Toukh (Epep 13), Ammonius of Mount Tounah, Ammonius of Esna, and Amoun of Nitria.

11-27.name: The Consecration of the Church of St. Abba Fam (Bifam)
11-27.summary: Coptic Reader gives this as a short entry, not a full life account. It states only that this day marks the consecration of the church of St. Abba Fam, a soldier of Oseem, in the city of Tima, and that the account of his martyrdom is mentioned under the 27th day of Tobe. No further detail is given on this page. Note: the Abe-Fam hymn page is already used for his church consecration on Koiahk 1 and his martyrdom on Tobi 27; the hymn check must report the page's titles for comparison.
hymnIds: Adam Psali for the Martyrdom of Saint Abe-Fam the Soldier
Watos Psali for the Martyrdom of Saint Abe-Fam the Soldier

11-28.name: The Departure of St. Mary Magdalene
11-28.summary: Mary Magdalene was born in the village of Magdala near Capernaum, was wealthy and of good reputation, and the Lord cast seven demons out of her. She followed and served the Lord, even at his passion and crucifixion, stood at the cross, was present at his burial, and came to the tomb with spices. She was the first to come to the tomb, the risen Lord appeared first to her, and after the resurrection he honored her by speaking with her and sending her to tell the disciples that she had seen the Lord. After the ascension, she ministered to the apostles, received the Holy Spirit at Pentecost, preached the good news of salvation, brought many women to faith, and was ordained a deaconess by the apostles to serve women. She received many insults and humiliation from the Jews, and then departed in peace.

11-29.name: The Commemoration of the Three Major Feasts of the Lord
11-29.summary: This is a short feast entry, not a saint's life. It commemorates together the Annunciation, the Nativity and the Resurrection, and states that the rite is kept with the joyful tune, without strict abstinence and without prostrations. No further biographical detail is given on this page.

11-29.name: The Relocation of the Relics of St. Andrew the Apostle
11-29.summary: In the year 357 A.D., by order of Emperor Constantine, the relics of St. Andrew the Apostle were relocated to Constantinople. A beautiful church was built after his name, was consecrated on this day, and his pure body was placed in it. This entry records the relocation and consecration, rather than a martyrdom or departure account. Note: the hymn check must report whether any Andrew page has relocation or Constantinople-specific titles.

11-29.name: St. Ouarshenoufa (Warshenofius)
11-29.summary: Ouarshenoufa was a learned, righteous and pious man who was chosen to be a bishop, but fled. He spent a night at the home of two sisters and their mother, an angel commanded him to go to the governor and confess the Lord Christ, and the next morning he told them, and they all agreed to go together. Before the governor, the emperor's edict commanding the worship of idols was read, and Ouarshenoufa jumped up, took the edict, and tore it to pieces. The enraged governor ordered him to be thrown into a fiery furnace, where he delivered his pure soul and received the crown of martyrdom.

11-30.name: Sts. Mercurius and Ephraem (Ephraim)
11-30.summary: Mercurius and Ephraem were born in Akhmim and brought up in the true Christian faith, and went to a nearby monastery. There they dwelt for twenty years in spiritual fellowship and love, persevering in fasting, prayer, asceticism and reading the Scriptures. When followers of Arius, incited during a persecution, entered churches to offer offerings upon the altars of the Orthodox, the two saints rose, cast aside the bread and wine the Arians had laid on the altar, and said that he who has not been baptized in the name of the Holy Trinity is only fit to offer an offering on the altar of idols. The Arians seized them and beat them severely until they delivered their souls and received the crowns of martyrdom. This Mercurius is distinct from Philopater Mercurius (Abu-Seifein); the hymn check must NOT count the Philopater page for this pair.
